title: The Ze blog
text: The Ze blog Design notes, deep dives, and engineering essays on how Ze is built. For week-by-week shipping notes, read the changelog. One configuration engine, many protocols (2026-11-22): How Ze uses YANG to validate changes across plugins, orders their application and lets operators roll back an unconfirmed remote change. Keeping documentation in step with the code (2026-08-22): Ze generates public reference from its code and records, with links to the decisions behind them. Operators and future AI sessions can use the same maintained account of the system. AI coding has not had its Rails moment (2026-08-10): AI coding needs shared conventions for connecting requirements and design decisions to their implementation, and for keeping those relationships current. The repository is half the AI harness (2026-08-09): Ze's development rules define what an AI agent must achieve and how to check the result, including the qualities a working demonstration can leave untested. The proof is the expensive part (2026-08-06): Ze aims to meet every applicable mandatory RFC requirement. Interoperability labs and tests tied to the RFC text help establish what the running router does and which claims remain unverified. How Ze reuses memory for BGP UPDATEs (2026-08-04): From the Amiga demo scene to BGP UPDATEs, earlier experience informs how Ze reuses memory and avoids unnecessary allocation in Go. AI slop is human slop (2026-08-03): AI often writes better code than I would, and far more tests per feature. I judge that code by what it does and the evidence behind it, and remain responsible for what Ze releases.

title: AI coding has not had its Rails moment
displayTitle: AI coding has not had its Rails moment
text: AI coding has not had its Rails moment 2026-08-10 by Thomas Mangin Shared conventions could give an agent a reliable route from a code change to the design it must follow, including how to keep both consistent. Comparison of a repository with predictable locations for designs, rules and tests, and one without a common organisation. Claude knew Go when I began building Ze, a network operating system, but I still had to teach it how to find the project's design decisions. I would like the next project to inherit a familiar way of connecting those decisions to the code. This article was co-authored with Claude and revised with OpenAI Codex. The argument and the conclusions are mine. Claude helped organise the material and draft the original text. Why I think of Rails At Exa in the early 2000s, we used the same layout across projects: configuration in etc/, working data in data/, reusable code in lib/ and the rest in src/. During development, the repository acted as the installed root. Changing $ETC and $DATA pointed the program at the installed locations, so we could use the same layout during development and after installation. Because the configuration was already beside the code, another developer could try the program without first recreating its environment. The first ExaBGP commit, from September 2009, contains daemon, etc, lib and test directories, and its commit message records a test announcing a route to a Cisco 7204. A familiar layout removed some of the work of getting started. Rails brought this benefit to a much larger community through Convention over Configuration. A project created with rails new has recognised places for application code, configuration, database migrations, libraries and tests. Rails uses those conventions to connect the parts of an application, so they tell a developer more than where to put a file. Understanding one Rails application helps when entering the next. Readers who have never used Rails may recognise the benefit in the component conventions shared by their team's React projects. React leaves more of the surrounding project structure to frameworks and developers, but those local conventions still give a newcomer somewhere familiar to start. Adding AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md gives a project a place for instructions, but leaves its author to invent how designs relate to source files and how an agent should use that relationship. What I am waiting for is an arrangement recognisable from one project to the next, so that understanding carries across too. A source file would lead an agent to its governing design, and the design would identify the code which implements it. Instructions for making a change would include checking the result against that decision and updating the explanation when the decision changes. Each author would still choose the architecture, within a familiar structure for recording and applying those choices. Useful pieces of this already exist; the missing step is making the whole arrangement familiar across projects. Connect the decision to the implementation In Ze, Claude could produce code that worked on its own but contradicted decisions I had already made. Knowing Go could not tell it why I had chosen one design over another. A feature request needed a route to those reasons before the agent chose an implementation. Requirements and designs are metadata about the software: they describe what we intend to build and the constraints on how we build it. Writing those reasons down gives us an explanation to consult, but the agent also has to find it and establish which code the decision governs. Otherwise it can read a perfectly good document and still miss its relevance to the change it is making. For example, the registration pattern explains why plugins must remain independent of the core and shows the code we expect. Ze's task index, ai/INDEX.md, gives an agent adding a plugin a route to that explanation. The index connects the requested task to the design that governs its implementation. A bug investigation can begin at the other end, with a function rather than a request for a new feature. The relevant design still applies, but the agent first has to discover which document describes it. Source files therefore identify their design documents, and documents cite the code they describe. Generated code-to-documents and design-to-code indexes make those connections available from either starting point. With these links, an agent investigating a function can find the constraints its fix must preserve. If I decide to change a design, the lookup in the other direction identifies source files which refer to it. That gives us a place to begin checking the effect of the decision, though the links cannot tell us whether every affected file has been identified. Keep the explanation and the code together Finding the registration document does not establish that a new plugin follows it. The agent has to use the design when choosing its implementation, and the reviewer has to compare the result with the stated constraints. The connections become useful because the development process requires the author and reviewer to follow them. In Ze, the root agent instructions direct a session to the relevant rules and design documents. ai/INSTRUCTIONS.md is the source for the copies supplied to different AI tools, so changing tools does not require maintaining another account of the project. The rules require documentation to change alongside code when a change would make its explanation wrong. That requirement matters when I revise a design. Leaving its old explanation in place would tell the next agent to follow a decision we had abandoned, while adding another account without resolving the old one would leave conflicting instructions. Links make the relationship discoverable; keeping the explanation current makes it useful to the next session. As the documentation became more useful, the generated code followed the intended design more closely. A correction that once had to be repeated in conversation could improve the explanation the next session was directed to read. I still have to judge whether the design is right and whether an implementation follows it, but each session can build on the reasoning already recorded. Shared conventions could give other projects a starting point for establishing the same relationship. The repository is half the AI harness examines how rules and validation help an agent recognise work below the required standard. The organisational problem here comes before that check: the agent and reviewer must be able to find the decision that sets the standard. Better tools still need a prepared repository The tools around a model affect the result even before we consider project knowledge. Stencil's February 2026 editing benchmark compared different edit formats across sixteen models and reported an average improvement of fifteen percentage points over its patch format, without changing the models. Stencil promotes its own format, so the figures deserve the usual caution, but the result illustrates how much can depend on the tools used to apply an edit. Perfect editing would still leave the problem of choosing the right change. A general coding tool can search a repository and run its tests, but neither operation supplies an unrecorded reason for using registration. Model and harness developers can improve how an agent uses its tools. Project authors still have to provide their decisions, although a shared structure could save each of us from inventing how to make them available. Other projects are connecting the same pieces Parts of this structure are already being explored elsewhere. Cloudflare's August 2026 account of its engineering standards system describes guidance spread across documents, repositories and conversations. Giving standards stable identifiers lets reviews refer back to the same requirement even when the discussion and the implementation are in different places. Clou

title: AI slop is human slop
text: AI slop is human slop 2026-08-03 by Thomas Mangin AI writes most of Ze's code. I remain responsible for what I release. Generated code is checked against protocol requirements, fuzz tests, integration tests and benchmarks. Ze is an AI-written network operating system, and I remain responsible for what I release. I judge its code by the behaviour we can establish, including what our tests still leave unchecked. This article was drafted and revised with OpenAI Codex. The ideas, experience and conclusions are mine. Why I keep using AI I decide Ze's architecture and the trade-offs I am prepared to accept, and coding agents write most of the code. Quite often Claude writes better code than I could have written myself, and far more tests per feature than I ever did. That lets me attempt more than I could write alone, although its mistakes can take much longer to find and correct than I had hoped. I use AI to help write these articles for much the same reason. Having help putting my thoughts into words leaves more time for developing Ze, but that saving is of little use to a reader who cannot follow the result. I am responsible for what goes out under my name, whether it is an explanation someone struggles to read or code that fails in their router. Slop is code accepted without enough scrutiny: merged because it compiled, or trusted because the demo worked once. Human-written code can be slop too, and AI makes it much cheaper to produce. Calling all AI-written software "slop" before examining it substitutes a judgement about its origin for an investigation of the result. We have changed how we write software before Judging programmers by their tools has a long history. In July 1983, Ed Post's Real Programmers Don't Use Pascal made fun of programmers who regarded FORTRAN and assembly as signs of competence. It is still amusing, although the preference for assembly sometimes had a practical basis: someone who knew the processor could choose instructions that made an inner loop faster than the compiler's version. Michael Abrash's Graphics Programming Black Book explains how much could be gained from that knowledge, and the released Quake source includes hand-written x86 assembly alongside its C rendering code. The extra effort could produce a result the compiler could not deliver. Improved compilers have made assembly a more specialised tool. When a video decoder has to keep up with playback on less powerful CPUs, spending time writing and optimising assembly for its most demanding routines can be worthwhile. I admire projects such as the dav1d AV1 decoder, which combines C with hand-written assembly tuned for particular processors. AI requires a different kind of checking because a model can misunderstand a request or invent an API, while a compiler translates code according to the rules of a language. The comparison is about choosing a tool for the job and judging whether its benefits justify the work needed to use it safely. That judgement has to be revisited as the tools change. Human authorship never guaranteed quality More capable tools give us choices, including the choice to produce wasteful software faster. We have spent decades writing programs which are slow and difficult to understand, with a human responsible for every line. I have little patience for applying "Clean Code" rules without considering whether they improve the program, or for using a high-level language as permission to ignore how much memory and processor time the result consumes. A project which generates code faster while keeping weak checks can produce more bad software before anyone notices. A person typing the code would not fix the weakness in those checks. Clear requirements and a way to establish whether the program meets them give us a more useful basis for judging either author's output. The failures deserve scrutiny Security testing shows how much can be missed when generated code is accepted on appearance. Veracode's 2025 GenAI Code Security Report found that 45 per cent of generated samples failed its security tests across Java, Python, C# and JavaScript. The figure describes those samples, so it cannot establish the vulnerability rate of every AI-written project. It does show why a plausible implementation needs testing before we trust it. Even a claim about time saved needs more than the developer's impression. In METR's early-2025 study, 16 experienced open-source developers took 19 per cent longer on tasks in repositories they knew when AI tools were allowed, although they believed they had been faster. Feeling productive while using a tool was a poor guide to how long the job took. Repeating that measurement as the tools improve is harder than it might seem. METR's February 2026 update says developers are likely to benefit more from newer tools, but its follow-up data gives only very weak evidence for the size of that improvement. Developers were reluctant to work without AI, which affected who took part, and concurrent agents made time spent harder to measure. Those results do not give me a productivity figure for Ze, and my impression of getting more done cannot supply one either. I am interested in the next measurements because a comparison must account for changes in how we use the tools as well as changes to the tools themselves. What makes a change acceptable Neither a broad study nor my experience of using Claude establishes that a particular change to Ze is correct. For a BGP encoder, we have to check the bytes it produces against what the protocol requires and check how it handles invalid input. An optimisation needs measurement too, or we could add complexity without reducing the cost of processing routes. The saving has to preserve correct behaviour. Reusing a buffer can reduce allocations, but overwriting it while another reader still needs its contents can corrupt a route. In How Ze reuses memory, I explain how we decide when data can be shared and when it must be copied. Checking the bytes returned by an encoder does not show that the running daemon sends them to another router. For that, we have to start the programs and observe their exchange. Ze's quality model describes the checks different changes require. Some parts of Ze do not yet meet those requirements, and a passing run says nothing about a case the tests never exercise. This is also why the number of tests Claude writes is a poor measure on its own. When a test fails, the model can change the expected result to match the bug or remove the assertion which caught it. The next run passes without restoring the required behaviour, so the tests need review against the requirements as well. Ze's development framework makes that review part of a change. An agreed specification states the required behaviour and how it will be checked, then an agent implements it and another independently reviews the code and tests against that specification. For RFC requirements, deliberately breaking the implementation and observing the test fail gives us evidence that it detects that particular fault. Changes which could weaken a test also require independent judgement under the testing rules. I review the structure and overall implementation, and rely on this process to establish that the tests check the details correctly. The proof is the expensive part explains the further work involved in connecting a protocol requirement to behaviour the running application actually demonstrates. A mistake shared by the author and reviewer can still survive, which is one reason my overview of the system remains necessary. Experience still matters I know BGP from operating it and implementing it, including being called late at night to fix my own code. That experience helps me judge a proposed shortcut in route selection or a change to how a peer's connection is managed. I have something to compare with the agent's explanation, and a way to recognise when the investigation is overlooking part of the problem. Before Ze, I ha

title: How Ze reuses memory for BGP UPDATEs
displayTitle: How Ze reuses memory for BGP UPDATEs
text: How Ze reuses memory for BGP UPDATEs 2026-08-04 by Thomas Mangin Memory efficiency starts with how you design the code. Readers share a received BGP UPDATE while it remains in the cache. Changed messages and routes kept in the RIB use separate storage. Rust, Zig or C may come to mind first when you think about control over memory. In Ze, I use Go, but bring the same attention to where memory is allocated and how it is reused. An unnecessary allocation looks harmless until a router repeats it for every route. When designing Ze, I brought some older programming habits to a language with a garbage collector. This article was co-authored with Claude and revised with OpenAI Codex. The architecture and design decisions are mine. Claude helped with implementation, tests and measurements, and with organising and drafting the original text. From the Amiga to Ze As a young and very inexperienced programmer, I learned assembly and low-level programming on the Amiga. I followed the demo scene, where programmers produced remarkable results within very limited memory and processing power. Those experiences still shape how I look at software. When I wrote ExaBGP, I wanted an ordinary program to be able to announce routes without implementing BGP itself. I also wanted the code to be easy to read and understand, so that other people could contribute and add support for more RFCs. I valued that accessibility more than performance. ExaBGP was never designed to be a particularly memory-efficient or CPU-efficient implementation. Ze, however, is. To my mind, too many newer RFCs give too little attention to efficient processing or compact protocol layouts. Modern machines make the constraints I grew up with much less pressing for everyday software development, but the knowledge still informs my design decisions. Knowing assembly is useful even when I am writing Go. With Ze, I wanted efficiency to be part of the design from the start. Go has a garbage collector, but we can write the repeated processing much as we would in C, allocating working storage ahead of time and managing its reuse ourselves. Pools let us keep buffers available and decide when they can hold new data, instead of creating and discarding an object for every operation. Avoiding those allocations can substantially reduce the work left to the garbage collector, although the runtime still manages the underlying memory. Before adding an object or copying a message, we should be able to explain why that storage is necessary. Following a BGP UPDATE through Ze makes those decisions concrete, because an unnecessary operation here can be repeated for every route. Use the data we already have A BGP UPDATE arrives as a sequence of bytes containing route announcements or withdrawals, together with attributes such as the next hop and AS path. Ze receives those bytes in a buffer, an area of memory used to hold them. One way to process the UPDATE would be to decode every attribute into a Go object, work with those objects, then encode them again when sending the route onwards. If the code only needs the next hop, decoding every attribute wastes CPU cycles and may also allocate memory for data it never uses. Ze's WireUpdate keeps the received bytes and provides access to the attributes within them. Its attribute index records where values occur, and a caller can read the next hop without constructing decoded objects for every other attribute. Several readers can also share the same stored message while it remains available. The input still has to be validated, so the saving comes from avoiding representations and copies which that processing does not require. Sharing stops being suitable when one reader needs different bytes. If policy changes an attribute before an UPDATE is sent, the other readers must still see the original message. Ze's buffer-first approach lets the encoder write the changed message directly into output storage supplied by its caller. The necessary new representation then goes into its destination without an intermediate message that would immediately be copied again. A fixed size makes reuse straightforward The traditional maximum BGP message size is 4,096 bytes, which is also a common memory-page size. A page is a unit in which the operating system maps memory. An implementation handling messages within that limit can allocate a pool of fixed-size buffers, then cycle through them as messages arrive and processing finishes. Once enough buffers are available, receiving the next message need not require another buffer allocation. The size limit has since been extended: RFC 8654 allows messages up to 65,535 bytes when the receiver has advertised support, with exceptions for OPEN and KEEPALIVE. A pool must accommodate the messages a session can receive. The useful principle survives the change in limit: reserve suitable storage and reuse it once its readers have finished. Ze's mixed-size overflow pool, MixedBufMux, uses 64 KiB blocks that can serve one extended message or sixteen 4 KiB messages. Once all the borrowed slices are returned, the block can be used in either form again. The memory can therefore follow the mix of small and large messages without being tied to separate pools for each size. Reuse needs a clear stopping point After the readers have finished with an UPDATE, its storage can hold another message. Keeping available buffers in a pool avoids allocating fresh storage for each arrival, but introduces a release decision: the code returning a buffer has to respect every reader's permitted lifetime. Garbage collection does not make this reuse safe. Returning a buffer to a pool leaves its underlying memory allocated, and a slice, a view of the bytes in that memory, can still refer to it. If the next message overwrites the buffer before that reader has finished, code expecting the old route will read a different message. The memory remains accessible throughout; its contents have changed too soon. Ze therefore has explicit rules for how long readers can use shared bytes. An event handler can inspect a received UPDATE during delivery, but keeping it afterwards requires a snapshot in independent storage. Taking that copy before returning lets later processing continue after the original buffer has been reused. Avoiding every copy would defeat the point if a retained route could change underneath its reader. A pool occupies memory even while its buffers sit unused, so fewer allocations can come at the cost of keeping more memory between bursts. Ze's shared buffer pools support a budget for growth and release surplus blocks when they have been returned and the remaining blocks have room. Those limits apply to the pools concerned, without bounding the daemon's total memory use, and growing storage still requires allocations. Store repeated route attributes once The routing information base, or RIB, keeps routes long after their receive buffers have been reused, so it needs independent storage. Keeping a copy of the whole packet would also keep bytes the RIB no longer uses. Giving every route its own attribute values avoids that waste but introduces another: many of those values are identical across the routing table. Routes often share an AS path or the same communities, the values operators attach to routes for policy. Ze's RIB storage stores common attributes individually, using an attribute pool to keep equal values together. The first occurrence is copied into independent storage, and later routes hold references to the existing value for as long as they use it. This technique is called interning. Sharing individual attributes lets two routes with different preferences still share the same AS path. Changing one value does not require another copy of all the others. Here, the saving concerns memory retained for the life of a route, as well as the temporary allocations avoided during message processing. title: One configuration engine, many protocols
text: One configuration engine, many protocols 2026-11-22 by Thomas Mangin A remote configuration change needs a way back even after the SSH session drops. When you change a router over SSH, the network carrying the session may be the one you’re changing. The proposed configuration can pass validation and still cut off the connection you need to undo it. This article was drafted with Gemini and revised with Sol. The architecture and design decisions are mine. Confirm the change from the network Junos has a command I like for this. commit confirmed applies the change and gives you time to check the result. If the change cuts off your access, the router can restore its previous configuration when the timer expires. Junos confirmed commits The same workflow is available in Ze. Use commit confirmed 120 to apply the change with a two-minute window, then open a fresh SSH connection from your usual management network. For a routing change, check that the affected peers have returned and that they see the routes you expect before issuing commit accept. The Ze daemon owns the timer and starts restoring the previous configuration when the timer expires, even if the SSH client that issued the commit has disconnected. Ze confirmed commits · SSH disconnect test What YANG checks before a commit Each plugin that supplies a YANG module contributes settings and constraints to Ze’s configuration schema. For example, the BGP listener uses a shared port type whose YANG range is 1 through 65535, so Ze can refuse a port of 0 before opening a socket. The editor and the configuration loader get that range from the same declaration. Ze’s configuration model Ze extends YANG so a schema can name checks registered in the daemon. A setting marked with ze:validate calls a validator by name. BGP uses it to refuse 0.0.0.0 as a router ID even though it has the form of an IPv4 address. Ze’s validation extensions ze:reference lets a setting name a source of values in the proposed configuration. BGP peers and static next hops both use ze:reference "bfd-profile" to refer to a named Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) profile. The editor offers the profiles you’ve defined, and Ze refuses a commit that names a missing profile. The two components get the same behaviour from the same lookup. BFD profile lookup Built-in and external plugins can import the same extension module and reuse the validators and reference sources registered in the running Ze build. Ze refuses a module that names one it cannot find. The engine checks ze:reference across the proposed configuration. The shared ze:validate pass currently covers selected sections, and BGP runs its own validation. An external plugin can enforce additional rules in its verify step before Ze applies its changes. Plugin schema guide · ze:validate coverage What the engine does when the change goes live Suppose you move an IP address from one interface to another and a BGP peer uses it as its local address. The BGP configuration can stay exactly as it was, yet the live session depends on an address that disappears during the move. The configuration engine orders the work across the two components. Ze stops the session before removing the address and starts it again after assigning the address to the other interface. The test watches the kernel’s address notifications and checks that the peer reconnects and sends its route again. Address-move test If a component fails during apply, Ze starts undoing the changes it has already made. In one test a later plugin fails after Ze has removed a BGP peer. The rollback puts the peer back, and the peer has to reconnect and announce its route again. A confirmed commit covers the case where apply succeeds and you still have to see what happened on the network before keeping the change. Rollback test

title: Keeping documentation in step with the code
displayTitle: Keeping documentation in step with the code
text: Keeping documentation in step with the code 2026-08-22 by Thomas Mangin Generated reference data and maintained design explanations give operators and future AI sessions a common account of Ze. Command definitions supply the reference pages, with links from the documentation back to the source. An outdated command reference can mislead an operator and give the next AI session the wrong account of the system. In Ze, the network operating system I am developing, I want both readers to work from the facts and explanations we maintain alongside the code. This article was drafted and revised with OpenAI Codex. The design, decisions and conclusions are mine. From a command definition to its reference page When a command reference is written separately from the code, keeping it accurate depends on someone remembering to update it each time the command changes. The code can be changed and tested while the website still describes the old syntax, leaving a reader to follow instructions that no longer work. The documentation was correct when written; it became misleading because maintaining it required a separate edit that was missed. In Ze, we address this by using shared command metadata to generate the reference pages. That metadata describes the arguments and their help text for use in the program, so it also provides the information needed to document them. An argument change is then recorded in one place and appears in the reference on the next documentation build. Keeping the two consistent becomes part of how we build the software and its documentation, instead of something a developer has to remember afterwards. Those same definitions supply Ze's built-in help. As well as displaying them in a terminal, we can request them as structured data with ze help command --json. The website build obtains this catalogue from Ze compiled from the checkout, so the command list comes from the code being documented. The reference generator uses this list to produce the syntax and descriptions for both the website and a Markdown reference. Because both versions use the same input, correcting a help description once updates the terminal help and, on the next build, both documents. We can change how the reference is presented without having to maintain its command list separately. The build also saves the catalogue as data/cli-commands.json. Someone writing another tool can use that data directly, without extracting it from the HTML page. Include the configuration supplied by plugins Configuration presents the same maintenance problem, with the added complication that plugins can contribute their own settings. A reference maintained separately would have to track those contributions as well as changes to the core. If a plugin adds a setting and its author forgets the website, the new option can remain undocumented even though it is available in the program. Ze's configuration tree already combines those definitions for the running program. The configuration reference generator obtains that tree with show yang tree --config | json, including the settings supplied by plugins in the build. Generating the reference from this tree includes their contributions without a second description of the available configuration. The plugin inventory reads the registrations from a committed source snapshot. Its entries identify plugins and their configuration roots, and the website links each entry to its implementation package. This gives a reader investigating a plugin's settings a route from the public reference into the source, without maintaining another list of packages for the website. Publish the support records we use during development Command names and configuration options can be taken directly from definitions in the program. Protocol support requires more judgement: the presence of BGP code does not establish that every requirement of a particular RFC has been implemented. A manually written list of supported RFCs would also need revisiting whenever we implemented a missing requirement or discovered a gap. For Ze, we record individual RFC requirements and connect them to tests and records of missing behaviour. These are the records we use to assess implementation progress, so we use them to generate the public compliance pages as well. The RFC ledger generator combines the requirement rows with our recorded descriptions of support. Updating a gap or a description changes the generated reference on the next full website build. The public account changes when that build is published. This also lets a reader examine what a support claim means. A partial-support entry links to the requirements Ze has not yet implemented and the tests cited for implemented behaviour. The page also shows where we have evidence that a test detects a particular mistake. The proof is the expensive part explains why a test can pass while leaving the required application behaviour unchecked. An agent changing that behaviour can use the same records as an operator to find the tests and source, then update them for the next public build. Neither reader has to depend on a separate account maintained by hand. Generating the page keeps it consistent with our records, but those records are only as accurate as the evidence behind them. Publishing the gaps alongside the claims gives someone considering Ze a way to inspect that evidence, including reasons to be less confident in the implementation. Keep the explanations alongside the generated facts The reason for a design choice cannot usually be recovered from the code that implements it. A dependency list makes this limit easy to see: go.mod records which modules we use and their versions, but it does not record why I chose them. The dependency page generator therefore combines those versions with explanations we maintain separately. Those explanations can become outdated too, so checkDependencyDrift compares the entries with the direct dependencies and refuses to publish a mismatched list. A new dependency needs an explanation, and an entry for a module no longer used directly needs removing. The check identifies the missing edit, while reviewing whether the explanation is accurate and useful remains a writing task. Give the next session the same context The reasons behind a design choice also matter when an agent comes to change it. Reading the implementation can show how a command works while leaving unexplained why I chose that interface or imposed a particular constraint. If the reason remains only in an earlier conversation, the new session can propose a design I already rejected, and I have to explain the decision again. We therefore keep those explanations in the repository and connect them to the code. The generated design-to-code and code-to-documentation indexes let a session reach the reasoning from an implementation, or find the implementation from its explanation. An operator following a source link from the public reference can reach the same account. Ze's documentation rules require the agent to read that account before investigating the code. When its change affects a command definition or a support record, it updates the source from which the reference is generated. When I change a design, the explanation has to change with the implementation too. The next agent and the operator can then recover the revised decision, without a separate account being written for each of them. Here, using the same records means that the agent maintaining Ze also maintains the information from which we publish its reference. Leaving an old explanation in place would pass the wrong decision to both readers. title: The proof is the expensive part
displayTitle: The proof is the expensive part
text: The proof is the expensive part 2026-08-06 by Thomas Mangin Tests can pass while the router still does the wrong thing. AI can write a feature and get its first tests passing quickly. If the code and its tests have both been written and reviewed by agents, someone considering the software still needs a reason to trust it. Establishing that the running router does what the protocol requires takes much longer. This article was drafted and revised with OpenAI Codex. The ideas, experience and conclusions are mine. The objective is RFC compliance Ze is the network operating system I am building. I review its structure and overall implementation, while relying on agents for much of the detailed code and test review. The basis for trusting their output has to be something an operator can examine independently. Our goal is to satisfy every applicable mandatory requirement in the protocol specifications Ze implements. These are published as Requests for Comments, or RFCs, and include MUST and MUST NOT obligations which define how the router must behave. Establishing that behaviour is part of deciding whether Ze is ready to depend on in a network. We are building an RFC testing framework to connect each obligation to tests which observe the required behaviour. That is ongoing work, and a claim of support needs to show which requirements have been checked and where evidence is still missing. Work with other implementations Ze has to exchange routes correctly with software people already use. Our interoperability labs run Ze alongside implementations such as FRR, BIRD and GoBGP, with checks on what those peers receive. This exercises both ends of a protocol exchange with independently developed software. A session reaching the established state is only the beginning. The tests must check the routes exchanged and the effects of the particular feature being exercised. A peer can accept an UPDATE while discarding an attribute Ze should never have sent, so even successful route delivery can leave a protocol defect hidden. Observe the exchange in the lab The lab gives us a controlled setup in which to arrange those exchanges and inspect their results. For example, LOCAL_PREF expresses a route's preference within an autonomous system, and normally has to be removed when a route is sent to an external peer. In a recorded lab run on 10 November 2026, Ze received three routes carrying LOCAL_PREF 200 from an internal peer. All three reached the external FRR and GoBGP destinations, and the test observed that both sessions remained established. It also inspected Ze's outgoing messages towards GoBGP through the scenario's declared observation interval and checked that LOCAL_PREF was absent. The wire observation matters because an external receiver is required to ignore LOCAL_PREF. Looking only at a receiver's stored routes could therefore hide a sender's mistake. The lab checker checks successful delivery as well as the transmitted bytes, so dropping every route cannot satisfy the test either. Establishing that result required a setup which exercised forwarding after the destination sessions were established, together with observations of both delivered routes and transmitted bytes. If the setup never reaches that forwarding path, or the test looks only at the receiver's stored routes, a passing result leaves the sender's behaviour unchecked. Finding such an omission sends us back to the setup or assertions before the test can tell us whether the implementation is correct. Derive the checks from the RFC Choosing those observations requires reading the protocol's exact requirements. RFC 4271 section 5.1.5 states: A BGP speaker MUST NOT include this attribute in UPDATE messages it sends to external peers, except in the case of BGP Confederations [RFC3065]. That sentence gives the LOCAL_PREF wire check its purpose, including an exception which matters when deciding where it applies. Adding tests only for the examples we happen to think of can leave another required case undiscovered. Ze's requirement checklists therefore start from the RFC's obligations and give each one an identifier. A test cites that identifier and states the particular behaviour it checks, so another reviewer can compare its assertions with the requirement. A test can agree perfectly with our checklist while both omit something required by the RFC. An obligation can appear in a table, a state machine or ordinary prose without using the word MUST. Some passages concern roles Ze does not perform, and others depend on another RFC, so the checklist itself needs review against the source text. We record which passages justify each requirement and why we exclude others. An automated check flags passages left unaccounted for and checklist requirements with no recorded basis. A reviewer still has to read the RFC and decide whether the interpretations and exclusions are justified. Recommendations remain distinct from mandatory obligations, because recording a recommendation as mandatory would misrepresent the RFC too. The records make those decisions available for someone else to challenge, but cannot reveal an obligation missed by both the tool and the reviewer. Cover the whole required response The required observations can extend beyond whether a session survives. RFC 7606 section 7.1 says a BGP UPDATE with a malformed ORIGIN attribute must receive treat-as-withdraw handling. Under section 2, the routes in that UPDATE are treated as withdrawn, removing them from the routes received from that peer. One of Ze's functional scenarios starts the daemon and a peer, sends an UPDATE with a two-octet ORIGIN where one octet is required, then expects a later valid announcement over the same connection. That announcement checks that the session survives. Ignoring the malformed UPDATE would also keep the session alive, so the later announcement alone cannot distinguish that mistake from correct treat-as-withdraw handling. The scenario does not inspect the receiver's stored routes before or after the malformed UPDATE. Its comments acknowledge that limit, and it does not claim to establish that a previously installed route was removed. Separate component tests install a route and assert that the malformed re-announcement removes it, but they drive component handlers directly. Establishing the same effect through the complete daemon requires observing route removal there too. Check whether the test would notice a bug A test can observe the expected result for the wrong reason. As I describe in The repository is half the AI harness, a route can arrive through an unintended path and keep a test passing after the feature under test has been disabled. Ze's fault-detection checks test this by first requiring the test to pass, then deliberately breaking the producing code and requiring that same test to fail. A build failure or an unrelated failing test cannot supply the required observation. If the selected test still passes, either the break did not affect the claimed behaviour or the test failed to notice it, and no successful fault-detection record is written. The LOCAL_PREF experiment included that second step. The 10 November record reports a successful lab run, followed by a failure after the code suppressing LOCAL_PREF towards external peers was deliberately disabled. The wire check reported that the attribute had appeared on the actual external destination connection. The record supports the observation for the versions tested and shows one specific fault the test could detect. The public report keeps that record separate from the requirement citation. The citation says what the test claims to check; the recorded failure shows that it detected a particular deliberately introduced mistake. Other mistakes can still pass unnoticed. This is the practical meaning of proof here, with its scope limited to the observation the record contains. Preserve what the evidence established An old observation can become misleading when the c

title: The repository is half the AI harness
displayTitle: The repository is half the AI harness
text: The repository is half the AI harness 2026-08-09 by Thomas Mangin The repository's instructions influence how agents implement a feature and decide whether it is finished. Diagram showing an agent using coding tools and project instructions, then using check results to correct its change. In Ze, the network operating system I am building with AI, a feature can work and pass its tests while violating the project's design. The instructions in the repository influence which result the agent will accept, so I have to develop and debug those instructions too. This article was co-authored with Claude and revised with OpenAI Codex. The architecture, design decisions and conclusions come from my work on Ze. The models helped organise the material and draft the text. Define the whole objective Suppose I ask an agent to add a plugin to Ze. It could add a branch to a central switch in the core, calling the new plugin directly. The feature could produce the expected result and pass a test of that result. Each later plugin would then require another core change. That defeats the independence I want for plugin authors, who should be able to extend Ze without editing the code which finds and runs their plugins. In Ze's registration pattern, each plugin adds its own definition to a shared registry, a table of available plugins and the functions needed to run them. The core looks up that definition by name, so the lookup code stays the same when a plugin is added. Giving the agent this explanation and an approved example makes the architectural constraint part of the task before it chooses an implementation. Independence is part of the objective, alongside handling invalid input and avoiding unnecessary resource use. Those expectations are familiar to me from developing a routing daemon, but leaving them out gives the agent an incomplete account of what it has to achieve. The test in this example would leave those other requirements unexamined. The repository supplies the objectives From the start, I wanted to design a system for developing Ze alongside the software itself. The repository would hold the requirements and explain how to check them, so an agent could recognise incomplete or incorrect work before presenting it as finished. The detailed procedures have evolved as we observed where agents went wrong, including where they followed my instructions and still produced the wrong result. Writing these instructions is a form of metaprogramming: I am writing rules for how another program develops and evaluates Ze. The application around the model, usually called its harness, supplies the tools to edit files and run commands. The repository supplies the objectives and the means of judging the result for this particular project. Getting that judgement wrong can teach an agent to satisfy a check while leaving the feature broken. Ze has many such constraints, so putting every rule into every prompt would surround the relevant guidance with pages unrelated to the task. The root instructions, maintained in ai/INSTRUCTIONS.md, explain how to find the applicable rules and design documents. The task index then gives the session a starting point for the part of Ze it is changing. The links between code and design are the subject of AI coding has not had its Rails moment. Once the agent has found the applicable requirements, it still needs to establish whether its implementation meets them. Choose evidence for the requested behaviour Suppose I ask for a setting to take effect when Ze reloads its configuration. A unit test can confirm that a helper parses the new value correctly while leaving unchecked whether the running daemon ever applies it. If the agent treats that result as completion, it can stop before the requested feature works. The instructions therefore have to say how far through the system the test must reach and under which conditions the result must hold. A parser needs checks of malformed input as well as valid packets. A subsystem that works in one operation may fail when several run concurrently, and Ze can agree with its own test peer while another implementation rejects its messages. Fuzzing, race detection and interoperability tests address different parts of those risks. Ze's testing rules and functional-test guide connect the kind of change to the evidence required. A change to BGP encoding calls for an observation of the transmitted bytes. A command must be exercised through the CLI, and a reload must be checked through the daemon using the new configuration. Stating those requirements before implementation gives the agent a way to recognise that a convenient passing unit test has left the requested behaviour unchecked. A routing daemon that produces correct results can still become unusable if it consumes excessive CPU time or memory. Too much processing per route can prevent it from keeping up with incoming updates, while excessive memory use can exhaust the host. A small test returning the right answer can leave both operational risks unchecked. Those operational constraints belong in the instructions too. The allocation checks described in How Ze reuses memory for BGP UPDATEs help detect unnecessary allocations in operations we have chosen to optimise. Benchmarks can show whether an operation has become more expensive, while tests of the running application are needed to establish how it behaves under load. The agent needs criteria for judging resource use alongside correct routing behaviour before it can decide that the change is complete. I rely on tests to check much of the implementation detail, which means I also need a process for judging the tests. Ze requires another agent to review the code and tests against the agreed specification, and defects found during review must be corrected and reviewed again. That gives my trust in the result a basis beyond the author's assessment of its own work. Both agents can still share a misunderstanding, so I retain responsibility for the architecture and for deciding what the work must achieve, as I discussed in AI slop is human slop. Give the agent useful feedback A rule can be clear in a document and become misleading when a check reports it. Plugin registration provided an example. Ze's import generator discovers plugin packages by their register.go files, so moving the registration to another filename can leave a plugin out of the generated imports. A check after an edit can catch that mistake before later code depends on the missing plugin. The Go edit check flags registration calls inside Go's init() function when they appear outside a registration file. Its message says BLOCKED: Implicit behavior in init(), although the approved pattern uses the same function inside register.go. An earlier version explained where the registration belonged and linked to the pattern, but that explanation was lost. The current message still omits it, so an agent could remove the registration mechanism while trying to resolve a problem with its location. The intended correction is to move the registration into register.go, where the generator can discover the plugin. The refusal needs to say that and link to an example, because its wording becomes an instruction for the agent's next edit. This remains a weakness in the check: it can undo the guidance we supplied before implementation began. Establish that the test detects the failure Even a test of the running daemon can pass for the wrong reason. In August 2026, three route redistribution scenarios continued to pass after late-join replay had been disabled. Replay is supposed to send existing routes to a peer which joins later, but the route reached the peer through another path in these scenarios. The expected route was present even though the feature under test was broken. Deliberately disabling replay exposed a weakness that another run of the unchanged test would not have found. A Claude session began doing this without being asked, which was a welcome use of i

title: Code of Conduct
text: Code of Conduct Ze is a technical project with a small community, and the rules for taking part are short. Speak respectfully. Disagree politely. Do not make it personal. Treat people the way you want to be treated. Be kind, and assume good faith. English is not everyone's first language, and words are just words: rough, blunt, or simple phrasing is fine as long as it is not aimed at someone. Take what people write in the best light it can carry, and do not read malice into a clumsy phrase. Malice shows as a pattern over time, not in one sentence, and it is worth treating as one only after it has been raised and has carried on anyway. People come from different places, and different cultures draw the line of acceptable behaviour in different spots. This project takes no side on whose version is correct. It uses an older and simpler line instead: your freedom stops where another person's begins. Stay on your side of that, and most of the rest takes care of itself. It is no one's place to tell other people how they should be. This is a space for technical work, and opinions on non-technical matters, whatever they are, are best kept for outside the project. That covers almost everything. Argue about the code, the design, and the trade-offs as hard as you like, and leave the person out of it. Strong technical disagreement is welcome, and it is how the project gets better. Personal attacks, insults, and harassment have no place here, whether open or implied, and they will be removed. Contributions are judged on their merit. Who you are does not earn you a pass and does not count against you: the work is what matters. Ze is built with AI assistance, and code written with AI help is as welcome here as any other. That is part of how the project works. The bar does not move for it: the code still has to be good, and it still has to pass the project's technical gates. How a contribution was written counts for far less than whether it holds up. This is not a corporate project. There is no HR department and no appeals process, and people here are expected to behave like adults. I am the maintainer, and my decision is final: on what belongs in the project, on how things are done, and on who is welcome to keep taking part. I will act on behaviour that breaks these rules, across the repositories, the issue tracker, and the project's Discord. If you run into a problem, or you are on the receiving end of one, contact me on Discord. This project will not try to be all things to all people. If the way things are done here does not suit you, that is fair enough and no hard feelings. There are many other projects, and you are free to find or start one that fits you better. None of this is hard. Everyone is more than welcome here, as long as they can follow the rules of decency.
