title: Open Source Network OS comparison
text: Open Source Network OS comparison A source-backed comparison of Ze, VyOS, and freeRtr as router operating systems rather than only BGP implementations. Scope and evidence: this page summarizes the local research artifact produced from the checked-out Ze, VyOS vyos-1x, and freeRtr sources. Runtime protocol daemons external to vyos-1x are intentionally labeled that way, and VyOS rows may cite FRR or other integrated projects when those projects own the runtime behavior. Not found means not found in the inspected source roots after targeted searches, not a universal upstream absence claim. The inline code paths link to upstream source where the site can map them. Find in this page Section Status legend Mark Meaning Yes or Present Direct source evidence found in inspected checkout. Partial Source evidence exists, but scope is narrower than the comparable feature in at least one other product. Unclear Related source evidence exists, but the exact feature or behavior was not traced to a producer. No or Not found Targeted and alternate searches did not find the feature in inspected sources. This is not a global claim about every version or external package. Executive conclusion VyOS has the widest range of integrated Linux router features in the inspected source. Its own code covers CLI schema, config and operational scripts, firewall, NAT, VPNs, services, commit-confirm, rollback, archive, REST/OpenAPI, GraphQL, and platform integration. Runtime protocol implementation mostly comes from FRR and the Linux/VPP/system service stack. freeRtr has the widest range of built-in routing protocols and services in the inspected source: many routing protocols, LSP/tunnel families, crypto/VPNs, NETCONF, Java CLI/config, internal services, and dataplane export paths. Most of that breadth sits in large Java registries and runtime classes. Ze has the most integrated management plane among the three in the inspected source. Its BGP/control-plane architecture, YANG-modelled config and commands, generated plugin registration, CLI, web, REST/gRPC, and MCP interfaces, built-in SSH management, HTMX web UI, minimal kernel/init, appliance runtime, diagnostics, and performance/testing tools are designed together. It is narrower than VyOS and freeRtr in legacy protocols and services today. Feature matrices by category These are the operator-facing feature matrices. Cells intentionally start with Yes, No, Partial, or Unclear so the table reads like the BGP comparison. The detailed source evidence remains in the appendices below. Routing and control plane matrix Feature Ze VyOS freeRtr Notes IPv4/IPv6 static routing Yes Yes Yes Ze and VyOS include static route configuration with ECMP; freeRtr has static route objects. BGP core Yes Yes Yes Ze and freeRtr implement BGP in source; VyOS exposes BGP through FRR config. BGP extended AFI/SAFI Yes Yes Yes Ze and freeRtr have broad in-tree AFI/SAFI support; VyOS exposes FRR AFI/SAFI config. BGP capabilities Yes Yes Yes ADD-PATH, route refresh, extended messages, extended nexthop and related capabilities are supported by the cited evidence. BGP Graceful Restart / LLGR Yes Yes Yes VyOS evidence comes from configuration options for FRR. Route server and route reflector Yes Yes Yes All three expose route-reflector-client and route-server-client modes; freeRtr has both as per-neighbor knobs. RPKI / ASPA Yes Yes Yes Ze and freeRtr include RPKI source; VyOS exposes RPKI config. Route maps, route policy, import/export chains Yes Yes Yes Ze uses plugin chains; VyOS uses policy and FRR templates; freeRtr has route-map and route-policy classes. Route redistribution / protocol import-export Yes Yes Yes Separate from IS-IS route leaking: all three expose redistribution, with Ze and freeRtr source-backed and VyOS documented for protocol route import/export. Prefix filters Yes Yes Yes All three have prefix-list style evidence. AS-path filters Yes Yes Yes All three have AS-path filter or manipulation evidence. Community filters Yes Yes Yes Standard, large, and extended community evidence exists for all three. OSPFv2 Yes Yes Yes Ze and freeRtr implement; VyOS exposes OSPF config. OSPFv3 Yes Yes Yes Evidence exists for all three. OSPF extensions: SR, TE, BFD, LDP sync Yes Yes Yes Scope differs by implementation and available configuration options. IS-IS L1/L2 Yes Yes Yes Evidence exists for all three. IS-IS route leaking Yes Unclear Yes Ze implements RFC 2966 L1/L2 leaking; VyOS documents IS-IS redistribution and attached-bit but no leak-specific command was found; freeRtr has source-visible IS-IS inter-level route handling tests. RIP / RIPng No Yes Yes Not found in Ze inspected source. EIGRP No Partial Yes VyOS schema exists, but generated templates are removed by Makefile in inspected source. Babel / OpenFabric / OLSR style IGPs No Partial Yes VyOS has Babel/OpenFabric files; freeRtr has broader IGP classes. BFD Yes Yes Yes Ze BFD attaches to BGP/OSPF/static; all three have evidence. RIB / FIB programming Yes Yes Yes Ze targets kernel and VPP, VyOS delegates through FRR/Linux/VPP, freeRtr has own forwarding core and dataplane exports. VRF / routing instances No Yes Yes Ze has named routing tables and some per-feature VRF fields, but no full product VRF/interface binding yet. Cross-VRF route leaking No Yes Yes Ze does not have VRF yet, so cross-VRF route leaking is not present. MPLS labels/dataplane Yes Yes Yes Evidence exists for all three. LDP Yes Yes Yes Evidence exists for all three. RSVP-TE Yes No Yes VyOS RSVP-TE was not found in inspected vyos-1x. Segment Routing / SRv6 Yes Yes Yes Evidence exists for all three. EVPN control plane Yes Yes Yes VXLAN dataplane integration differs and is covered under interfaces. Multicast routing: PIM, PIM6, IGMP, MSDP No Yes Yes Ze BGP multicast tooling is not a multicast routing daemon. Policy-based routing Yes Yes Yes Ze is experimental; VyOS has policy route/route6 interface-applied PBR with set table/VRF; freeRtr has interface and VRF PBR. BMP Yes Yes Yes VyOS evidence is BGP monitoring configuration. MRT dump/import/export Yes No Yes VyOS MRT was not found in inspected source. Routing telemetry exports Yes Partial Yes All have some export hooks, with different scope. Interfaces, L2, L3, and dataplane matrix Feature Ze VyOS freeRtr Notes Interface management model Yes Yes Yes Ze uses typed Go config and backend selection; VyOS uses XML plus Python owners; freeRtr uses central Java interface config. Linux netdev backend Yes Yes Partial Ze has a netlink backend; VyOS manages Linux interfaces; freeRtr abstracts interfaces through Java and helpers rather than a Ze-like netlink backend. VPP interface backend or configuration Yes Yes No Ze registers a VPP iface backend; VyOS has VPP root config plus selected VPP interface definitions; freeRtr VPP interface support was not found. Ethernet adoption/config Yes Yes Yes All three have ethernet interface evidence. Loopback Yes Yes Yes Evidence exists for all three. Dummy interfaces Yes Yes No freeRtr normal interface type list did not show dummy. Bridge Yes Yes Yes Evidence exists for all three. Bonding / LAG No Yes Yes freeRtr calls this bundle. VLAN 802.1Q Yes Yes Yes Evidence exists for all three. QinQ / stacked VLAN No Yes Yes Ze QinQ was not found. Interface VRF binding No Yes Yes Ze has routing tables elsewhere, but no iface VRF binding was found. VXLAN No Yes Yes Ze EVPN NLRI exists, but VXLAN interface/dataplane integration was not found. GRE / GRETAP Yes Yes Yes Evidence exists for all three. IPIP / SIT / IPv6 tunnel Yes Yes Partial freeRtr evidence is protocol imports and tunnel configuration, not exact CLI lines for every name. WireGuard interface/tunnel Yes Yes Yes Evidence exists for all three. OpenVPN No Yes Yes Ze OpenVPN was not found. PPP / PPPoE Yes Yes Yes Evidence exists for all three. L2TP Yes Yes Yes Ze focuses on L2TPv2/PPP BNG; VyOS evidence is L2TPv3 interface plus VPN L2TP; freeRtr has v2 and v3. Generic TUN/TAP No Yes Partial VyOS exposes TUN/TAP th

title: Contributing to Ze
text: Contributing to Ze Contributions to Ze can be code, documentation, bug reports, or results from trying it with other routers. Development happens in the public repository and issue tracker. AI-assisted contributions are welcome. We prefer recent, capable models, and this is a recommendation. The contribution policy lists example models and explains the requirements that apply to every contribution. Code Contribute a fix Small, tested changes are welcome: parser fixes, command output fixes, protocol edge cases, docs corrections, and tests that detect incorrect behavior. Evidence Bring a trace, lab, or transcript Reports of tests with other routers, QEMU test results, failing .ci test logs, and browser captures are useful because they show exactly what broke and what should be checked next. Care Handle security privately If an unauthenticated peer can trigger it, or if it can escalate access, use the security policy instead of a public issue. The contribution contract Hard requirement Every contribution requires a sign-off. Each contribution commit requires a Signed-off-by line, which signifies agreement to Ze's Contributor License Agreement. The commit preparation guide explains how to add it through the repository's commit-script process. You keep your copyright. What you grant is a broad, non-exclusive license for the Maintainer to use your contribution, including the right to relicense it, alone or combined with the rest of the project, under different license terms. Why this exists The CLA lets the maintainer offer a commercial license without seeking fresh permission from every past contributor. Ze remains available to everyone under AGPLv3. How Ze is funded Stewardship Supported by Exa Networks Ze is currently developed by Thomas Mangin, with his time on the project supported by Exa Networks. There is no subscription tier, no paid support contract, and no separate commercial entity behind it today. Exa Networks has been backing this work since 2009, when it started with ExaBGP, Ze's predecessor. Where to start Issues Browse or file a bug Use this for reproducible problems, missing docs, and clear feature gaps. Repository GitHub is the source repository Development moved off Codeberg in July 2026. Clone, issues and pull requests all live on GitHub. Discussion Discuss a contribution There is no formal good-first-issue program yet. Ask where help is most useful right now.

title: Developer Setup
text: Developer Setup Set up a Ze development environment with all build, lint, and test dependencies. Quick Start ./le is built from this repository with Go, so Go comes first. Install the release go.mod names on its go line from https://go.dev/dl/, or any Go 1.21 or newer, which downloads that release on first use. Then put two directories on PATH: the Go toolchain's, and the one go install writes to, where setup builds golangci-lint, staticcheck, goimports, gopls and govulncheck: export PATH="$PATH:/usr/local/go/bin" # the go.dev tarball's location export PATH="$PATH:$(go env GOPATH)/bin" # or $(go env GOBIN) when GOBIN is set Add both lines to ~/.profile (~/.zshenv for zsh) so every new shell has them. A non-interactive shell such as ssh host command reads no ~/.bashrc. Then: git clone <repo-url> && cd ze ./le setup install ./le setup check When the install directory is not on PATH, setup still builds the tools there, reports each as [pending ] <tool> (in /root/go/bin, which is not on PATH), and prints once the exact export PATH=... line for that directory and the profile to keep it in. check reports the same rows the same way: a tool no shell can run is never counted present. This detects your OS (macOS with Homebrew or Debian/Ubuntu with apt), installs missing tools, vendors Go dependencies, and reports what it did. le is the native development-tool personality built from cmd/ze. The root ./le is a dispatcher, and bin/le is an identical copy of it that ./le installs whenever the two differ. Both run the newest build in bin/builds/<UTC commit time>-<short sha>/le. Setup behavior lives in internal/le/setup.Answer. Builds follow HEAD, never your working tree, because a peer session's half-written source would otherwise break every call in every session. Each build records the git tree hash of le's inputs (internal cmd pkg api vendor go.mod go.sum feature-gates.txt feature-tags) at the commit it came from. When a commit changes them, the next ./le call starts one build of HEAD in the background and keeps running the newest build; the new one is smoke-tested and renamed into place only when it passes, so after a git pull the new commands arrive a couple of minutes later with no command of yours waiting. A commit that changes no input reuses the newest build. On a fresh checkout with no build at all, the first call builds HEAD in the foreground. A HEAD that fails to build is reported once on stderr, with its log at bin/builds/.failed-<commit>.log, and the newest good build keeps running. A build that does not start is moved aside to bin/builds/.failed-<name> and the call runs the next newest, saying so in one line. When the newest build starts but misbehaves, take it out by hand: ./le rollback It moves the newest build aside the same way, so the next call runs the one before it, and HEAD is not built again until a commit changes the inputs. Nothing is deleted: a peer executing that build keeps its file. ./le help lists rollback and Tab completes it; run it as ./le rollback, because only the launcher moves a build. ./le --update is gone and says so with exit 2. Do not delete bin/le or anything in bin/builds/. Several sessions share one checkout and one of them can be executing that file right now. When you need le to carry your own uncommitted edits, ask for a build of your own instead: ./le --name session verify current --name comes first, before the command, and the launcher consumes it. Every argument after it reaches the binary unchanged. --name session names the build after CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID (s-<its first eight characters>) and refuses with exit 2 when that variable is unset; --name mywork picks the name yourself. The build lands in bin/le-<name>/le, which bin/ already keeps out of git, and it is rebuilt from the working tree on every call, so the toolchain decides what to recompile and the binary carries your edits. The shared builds are never written and never wait for a peer. A name accepts letters, digits, dot, underscore and hyphen. A name carrying / or .. is refused with a message and exit 2, never repaired into something safe. The launcher exports the name to the process it runs and to that process's children, so a script that calls ./le inside a named session reaches the same build without repeating the option. A binary that is not the one you named refuses to answer and reports both names: le: --name asked for 'mywork' and this process is 'le' (/home/you/ze/bin/builds/20261025T114143Z-00b9273a2a/le). Reach the named build through ./le --name mywork, never through a hardcoded binary path. Check Mode Probe the current host without installing anything: ./le setup check The check action probes only and changes nothing: it installs no package, edits no sysctl, and adds no loopback address. It exits 0 if all required tools are present, nonzero if any are missing. Use it as a CI preflight check. Run ./le setup install to install what the probe found missing. One row is behaviour rather than a binary: gopls-answers runs the language server and checks that it replies. A server on PATH that does not answer fails this check, because every LSP call against it fails the same way. Editor plugin A language server on PATH is not the whole capability. Claude Code reaches it through a plugin, and without that plugin the LSP tool refuses every Go file. When Claude Code is installed (claude on PATH, or a ~/.claude directory) and the plugin is not, ./le setup check reports the plugin as a pending step and names the command that installs it. On a host without Claude Code the row is skipped with the reason "Claude Code is not installed", because there is no LSP tool to refuse anything and no session to run the slash command in. Plugin Serves Install gopls-lsp .go /plugin install gopls-lsp@claude-plugins-official Run the slash command inside a Claude Code session. The plugin and the binary it names fail the same way and have different fixes, so the report says which of the two is absent. Tool caches: le exec ./le exec <path> [args...] runs a program with its caches in the one per-user cache, $XDG_CACHE_HOME/ze, else ~/.cache/ze, instead of each tool's default folder (~/Library/Caches on macOS). It sets four variables, creates their directories, and then replaces itself with the program, so the program's exit status is the caller's and every argument after the path reaches it untouched. A heavy tool that needs a job slot is the exception: go test, golangci-lint run, staticcheck and the formatters, judged as the Bash hook judges a raw command. In a checkout, le exec waits for a slot, then runs the tool as its child on the same terminal, forwards every SIGINT, SIGTERM, SIGHUP and SIGQUIT to it until it exits, releases the slot and exits with the tool's code. Inside a live parent's slot (./le go lint run starting the linter) or outside a checkout it holds nothing and replaces itself, as for any other program. The main thread's post-edit lint goes past the shim on purpose and takes no slot (docs/contributing/running-commands.md, "Waiting for another session's job"). Variable Directory under the per-user cache GOCACHE go-cache GOPLSCACHE gopls GOLANGCI_LINT_CACHE golangci-lint-cache STATICCHECK_CACHE staticcheck-matrix When the working directory is inside a Ze checkout, the program also gets Ze's patched GOROOT, with GOTOOLCHAIN=local and the tree's bin first on PATH, so gopls analyzes the standard library Ze compiles. Anywhere else it gets the GOROOT, GOTOOLCHAIN and PATH its caller had, and never a patched tree, so a tool on another repository sees that repository's Go. A bare name is looked up on PATH, skipping any file that carries the shim marker. le exec refuses, with exit 1, a path that does not exist, is not an executable file, or is a shim ./le setup wrote, because a shim handed back to le exec would start it again in a loop; each refusal names the path and ./le setup. Warm, ./le exec /usr/bin/true takes about 50 ms on an Apple silicon Mac. Tool shims, PATH

title: Documentation Testing
text: Documentation Testing Ze ships native Go tools that compare documentation with the live registries and source tree. Pre-commit verification selects the checks affected by a change. Quick start ./le doc check all # Run all documentation tests ./le doc wiring # Run changed-file-aware wiring/doc/inventory gate ./le doc check all runs every documentation checker and returns non-zero if any of them report drift. Run it after editing documentation files, after adding or removing plugins, or as part of review. ./le doc wiring selects the checks needed for the current diff and is a stage of Thomas's release check, ./le verify current. What gets checked Native action What it validates ./le doc yang-contract doc-drift Published counts and lists agree with live registries and the tree ./le doc yang-contract command-contract Every YANG ze:command and every published -api rpc has a registered handler, every handler has a node, and every handler's method carries the prefix its registering package owns, as does every node no builtin handler serves, judged by the package that registered its module ./le doc yang-contract usage-contract The model states every command's argument grammar, and no description spells one in prose ./le doc yang-contract help-shape Every command node, every RPC, every offline local command and every config node declares a one-line summary a row renders whole, with a long text beside it, and the report states how much of each corpus is written ./le doc index check Documentation source paths and claimed symbols resolve ./le doc check links Tracked path citations resolve ./le ai digest Every file:line anchor in ai/digests/*.md resolves ./le doc consistency Design references, cross-references, JSON tags, and package citations agree; every .md page a // Design: header names exists, and its ## Design decisions section keeps the page format (docs/architecture/README.md, "Page format") ./le doc wiring Changed files trigger their documentation and inventory checks ./le doc ste check No ASD-STE100 habit grew against HEAD ./le doc check all combines documentation drift, command validation, the two command help gates, and source-anchor validation. ./le doc wiring is the changed-file-aware pre-commit gate. Among its checks, the added-symbol wiring check judges exported symbols the change adds under internal/ or cmd/. It refuses a symbol when no non-test Go file under internal/, cmd/ or pkg/ names it on a line other than its declaration, after stripping // comments. A public SDK alias is a consumer; exports added under pkg/ remain outside the candidate population. Three kinds of symbol are exempt: an entry in the reviewed allowlist, a name ending in ForTest, and an export of a test-only helper package. The test-only packages are the list the test-only-imports tier check reads (docs/architecture/module-tiers.md, "Test-only helpers"). The tier check restricts these helpers to tests and tooling under internal/le, so the wiring check exempts their exports without requiring a non-test reference. Native catalog lifetime The doc-drift action builds a native daemon before reading its command catalog. SIGINT or SIGTERM cancels that invocation's build or catalog command. The caller's context bounds both phases: the five-minute build bound and two-minute catalog bound never detach them from a caller that stopped. Each process group is stopped and joined before its temporary daemon directory is removed. A canceled build starts no catalog command, and a canceled invocation returns a failure verdict. The Go callers of Drift, BuildDaemon and CommandCatalog pass their context explicitly. The drift stage of doc check all has the same invocation-level cancellation. The aggregate documentation checker still runs its independent later stages after a failed stage; this is not a claim that one interrupt cancels that whole sequence. When to run Situation Recommended target After you write any prose, in any file ./le doc ste review-changed After editing any file under docs/ ./le doc check all After adding or removing a plugin ./le doc check all After writing a path reference in ANY tracked file ./le doc check links (./le doc check all does not cover it) After adding or renaming a YANG ze:command ./le doc yang-contract command-contract After writing the description or the ze:help of a command node, an RPC or a config node ./le doc yang-contract help-shape After writing the ShortHelp or the Description of a registry.Meta ./le doc yang-contract help-shape While an agent writes a ze:help in any .yang file ./le ai hooks pretool-writeedit answers on the proposed text, before the file lands After adding a doc validator, inventory source, command source, or exported Go API ./le doc wiring Before opening a documentation PR ./le doc check all The full ./le doc check all remains the explicit documentation review target. Thomas's release check, ./le verify current, runs ./le doc wiring, which invokes the relevant doc, command, inventory, and wiring checks for changed files. The change is the unpushed range. The base is the merge base of HEAD and the branch upstream, or of HEAD and refs/remotes/origin/HEAD when the branch tracks none (ResolveAnchor, internal/le/repo/changed/anchor.go), and the range runs from that base to the working tree. The gate is owed before a push, so a change committed without a run is still judged by the next run. The file set, the changed lines and every read of a file's earlier content come from that one base, so a change in the range is never missing from the file set. A file the change deleted is in the file set. A pure rename and a mode-only change are in the file set with no changed line, because the file set lists a rename as two paths and the line diff detects it. Neither hides a claim: a mode-only change touches no symbol, and a claim on a renamed file names the old path, which the change deleted, so that claim is unanswerable and counted. A failed read of a file's earlier content fails the run: it is never read as an empty file. A file named with changed-file <path> that holds no hunk in the range answers every line. The base reads refs only, so the detached worktree that Thomas's release check, ./le verify worktree, makes judges the same range. When no base resolves, the gate exits 2 and names why, and no check runs. How to interpret output ./le doc yang-contract doc-drift Documentation drift detected (N issues) x docs/DESIGN.md:708: claims 19 interop scenarios, actual is 32 x docs/DESIGN.md:0: plugin "bgp-nlri-vpn" registered but missing from Shipped Plugins table ... Each issue points at a file, a line number (0 = file-level), and a description. Most fixes are mechanical: update a count, add a missing table row, remove a stale entry. The fuzz count reads first-party _test.go files from the working tree, including files not yet committed. It uses the documentation index's source population by asking the index's own SkipsDir for every directory, so the two walks cannot drift apart. That walk does not enter dot-prefixed directories, vendor, tmp, testdata or node_modules at any depth, nor the top-level gokrazy/modcache and cache (the build cache, whose stdpatch trees link into whichever machine's GOROOT built them). Runtime evidence, module cache copies and build cache links therefore contribute neither targets nor read failures, while a package merely named cache is still counted. The Go unit-test count applies the same exclusions within internal, pkg, and cmd. A source file or directory that cannot be read still produces a finding, including a failed scan root. Absent optional roots contribute no files and no finding. A partial count is not evidence that a published claim is correct. ./le doc yang-contract command-contract # Command Validation YANG commands: 97 Registered handlers: 69 ## YANG commands with no handler (30) ze-bgp:show-decode (show > bgp > decode in ze-bgp-tools-cmd) ... ## Handlers with no YANG command (0) ... FAILED: 30 problem(s) Each s

title: Contributor guide
text: Contributor guide This guide explains how to propose a change to Ze, set up a build, and prepare the change for review. The contribute page explains how the project is funded and what its Contributor License Agreement grants. Everyone taking part is expected to follow the Code of Conduct. AI-assisted contributions AI-assisted contributions are welcome. We recommend recent, capable models. The contribution policy gives the current model examples and the same requirements for specifications, tests, documentation, and independent review that apply to every contribution. How work gets in An agreed spec records the expected behavior and tests before implementation, so the author and reviewer can check the change against the same requirements. Open an issue describing what you want to change or fix, on the tracker. Start here even for a fix, so the work is visible and nobody doubles up. Agree on a spec. The maintainer turns the issue into a spec that says what the change should do and how it will be tested. Implement the spec, starting with tests for the behavior it requires. Arrange independent deep review. The reviewer uses a context that did not produce the change. The repository guide links the review workflow. Prepare signed-off commits through the commit-script process. Each contribution commit requires a Signed-off-by line accepting the CLA. Open a pull request linking the agreed spec and giving the resulting behavior, scoped test results, documentation changes, and independent review. Setting up a build git clone https://github.com/ze-software/ze.git cd ze ./ze --help On a fresh checkout, the launcher builds Ze with the checkout's feature selection before running the command. Later invocations reuse the existing binary. The quickstart covers credentials and gets two BGP peers talking. For the full developer setup, including test dependencies, see developer-setup.md in the repository. What a good change looks like Tests come with it. Ze is test-driven; a change without tests is not finished. The relevant tests have run. Run the tests for the packages and behavior the change reaches, and include their results with the submission. GitHub CI runs the full verification on pushed commits. It arrives in one piece. Include the code, tests, and documentation in the same change so the instructions describe the behavior under review. It respects the project's standards. The coding, testing, and workflow rules the project follows live in the repository and apply to every contribution, whether written by hand or with AI help. Good first paths There is no formal good-first-issue program yet. The most useful things an outside contributor can do right now are the ones that need real routing experience: run a lab peer, migrate an ExaBGP config, stand up a looking glass, or run the interop labs and report what does not match. Come and ask on Discord where help is most valuable at the moment.

title: RFC Implementation Guide for Ze
text: RFC Implementation Guide for Ze This guide provides a step-by-step checklist for implementing an RFC in Ze. Use it alongside planning.md to ensure complete implementations. The implementation boundary is the owner's agreed capability scope. Completing started code includes its callers, error paths and documentation; it does not commission every absent feature in the RFC. Keep unimplemented requirements visible as gaps and leave unstarted specs in the backlog. Source inspection, executed tests and remaining verification must be reported separately. See ai/rules/rfc-compliance.md and docs/contributing/spec-workflow.md. Overview An RFC implementation typically touches these areas (not all apply to every RFC): Component Package When Needed Capability internal/core/bgp/capability/ RFC introduces a capability Attribute internal/core/bgp/attribute/ RFC introduces path attributes NLRI internal/core/bgp/nlri/ RFC introduces new AFI/SAFI Message internal/component/bgp/message/ RFC modifies message format FSM internal/component/bgp/fsm/ RFC affects state machine Config internal/component/config/ RFC needs configuration Plugin internal/component/plugin/ RFC needs plugin commands Context internal/core/bgp/context/ RFC affects encoding context Phase 0: Preparation 0.1 RFC Analysis [ ] Download RFC: curl -o rfc/rfcNNNN.txt https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfcNNNN.txt [ ] Create summary: rfc/short/rfcNNNN.md (use /rfc-summarisation) [ ] Identify RFC dependencies (other RFCs this one references) [ ] Check dependency RFCs are implemented or summarized [ ] Identify which components this RFC affects (table above) 0.2 Codebase Analysis [ ] Search for existing partial implementation: grep -r "RFC NNNN" internal/ [ ] Check if related capabilities exist: internal/core/bgp/capability/ [ ] Check if related attributes exist: internal/core/bgp/attribute/ [ ] Check if related NLRI types exist: internal/core/bgp/nlri/ [ ] Read architecture docs for affected areas (see planning.md keyword table) 0.3 ExaBGP Migration Consideration If this RFC adds features that ExaBGP users might rely on, check if migration support is needed: RFC Affects Migration Impact Action API commands/events ExaBGP plugins expect different JSON format Update internal/exabgp/bridge/ Config syntax ExaBGP configs have different syntax Update internal/exabgp/migration/ Capabilities ExaBGP may configure differently Check migration handles it [ ] Does ExaBGP support this RFC feature? [ ] If yes: is config migration needed? (internal/exabgp/migration/) [ ] If yes: is API bridge update needed? (internal/exabgp/bridge/) See ai/rules/go-standards.md for architecture details. 0.4 Spec Creation [ ] Create spec: plan/spec-rfcNNNN-<feature>.md [ ] Fill Required Reading section with identified docs [ ] git add the spec immediately Phase 1: Capability (if applicable) When: RFC introduces a BGP capability (advertised in OPEN message) 1.1 Define Capability [ ] Add capability code constant to internal/core/bgp/capability/capability.go - Code<Name> Code = NN // RFC NNNN [ ] Create capability struct in appropriate file (or new file) - encoding.go for wire-format affecting caps - session.go for session behavior caps - new file for complex capabilities [ ] Implement Capability interface: - Code() Code - Len() int - WriteTo(buf []byte, off int) int 1.2 Wire Format [ ] Document wire format with ASCII diagram in code comment [ ] Implement constructor: New<Name>(...) *<Name> [ ] Implement parser: parse<Name>(data []byte) (*<Name>, error) [ ] Add case to parseCapability() switch in capability.go [ ] Handle malformed data gracefully (return error, don't panic) 1.3 Negotiation [ ] If cap affects encoding: add field to EncodingCaps (encoding.go) [ ] If cap affects session: add field to SessionCaps (session.go) [ ] Update Negotiate() to handle intersection logic [ ] Update Negotiated accessors if needed [ ] Document negotiation rules in code comments with RFC section refs 1.4 Tests [ ] Unit test: WriteTo round-trips correctly [ ] Unit test: Parse valid wire bytes [ ] Unit test: Parse rejects malformed bytes [ ] Unit test: Negotiation logic (both have, one has, neither has) [ ] Boundary test: min/max values for any numeric fields Phase 2: Attribute (if applicable) When: RFC introduces new BGP path attribute(s) 2.1 Define Attribute [ ] Add attribute code constant to internal/core/bgp/attribute/attribute.go - Attr<Name> AttributeCode = NN // RFC NNNN [ ] Create attribute struct (new file if complex, or add to existing) [ ] Implement Attribute interface: - Code() AttributeCode - Flags() AttributeFlags - Len() int - title: Testing Guide
text: Testing Guide This guide covers how to run tests, what the different test types are, and how to interpret their output. For the full technical reference (.ci format spec, .et directives, fuzz target list), see docs/functional-tests.md. First-time setup ./le setup install ./le setup check ./le test unit pkg path ./internal/core/textbuf/ ./le setup check reports every tool setup installs, and the scoped package test proves the checkout builds and its tests run under the feature tags (../guide/developer-setup.md, "After Setup"). ./le verify current is the full verification, Thomas's release check, which GitHub CI also runs on a pushed commit. It runs only when stdin and stdout are both terminals, so Thomas starts it by hand at one. No agent runs any ./le verify command, ./le verify changed included: the evidence for a change is the scoped test runs of what it reaches. The main thread runs them in the main checkout, from the owed commands a subagent lists in its report (ai/rules/commands.md). ./le is the compiled repository development entry point. Each area exposes its own verbs, for example ./le test functional plugin, ./le test qemu installer-iso, and ./le test unit bgp. Legacy command names have no compatibility aliases. Action words describe the contract: check is a read-only verdict, verify is a composite policy gate, report is advisory output, and write or update changes tracked state. The escalation ladder Use the narrowest test that covers your change. Escalate only when needed. Step What you run When Time 1 ./le test unit pkg path ./internal/core/textbuf/ run TestName Iterating on one test seconds 2 ./le test unit bgp Checking one component group 10s to 1:30 3 ./le test functional plugin Checking the user-visible path varies 4 GitHub CI on the pushed commit Judging the pushed change set: no agent runs it locally minutes 5 ./le verify current The release check, which only Thomas starts, at a terminal the longest Steps 1 to 3 are development: run the ones that cover what you changed, and ./le repo changed scope print both names them (running-commands.md, "The changed-set selector"). Run them in the main checkout, never in a worktree or a copy of the tree. Step 4 is CI's: it runs once the work is pushed, and ./le commit push asks for no local verify record. A red it finds gets a fix commit; it does not hold the commit it judged. ./le verify changed still exists for Thomas, and no agent runs it. Step 5 is the full verification, and it is not an agent's to run. The dispatcher refuses ./le verify current, ./le verify current fast and every form of ./le verify worktree unless stdin and stdout are both terminals, because a full run loads the whole shared machine and only Thomas knows when that is safe. The refusal prints the exact command line for Thomas, and the scoped tests that are the change's evidence, which the main thread runs. No keyword or environment variable skips it. When Thomas starts ./le verify current, it runs every stage in a fresh detached worktree at HEAD, through the same lifecycle as ./le verify worktree, so an edit made while it runs cannot move the tree it judges; ./le verify current fast runs the changed-files stages in place, over the working tree. The narrower commands are development tools. ./le test unit pkg admits its run through internal/le/job, and ./le job run admits any other heavy command the same way, so concurrent sessions do not oversubscribe the machine. One package: ./le test unit pkg ./le test unit pkg path <dir>/ [run <regex>] [vet] tests the packages it names under the feature tags from feature-gates.txt, with the race detector and the toolchain's timeout, admitted under the job label unit-pkg. Repeat path for each package. run hands its regex to go test -run. vet runs go vet on the same packages and their test files instead, under vet-pkg. changed in place of path takes the packages the change reaches. The output goes to this session's scratch log. A green run answers one line, test unit pkg: exit 0, <n> packages ok, ..., log <path>, which counts only the packages that ran a test. With changed, a left out <package> line comes before it for each reached package that changed set aside behind a group's own tags, naming the group's command. A red run prints each failed test's --- FAIL: line with the lines beneath it, then that summary. A run in which no package ran a test, a run that matched nothing included, answers exit 1. It refuses with exit 2, before it takes a slot, a line that would test more than the packages meant: path ./... (the whole tree, ./le test unit all, is the owner's run), a group's whole pattern (run that group), a value that spans two or more groups, and a package under the installer group, whose ze_installer tag the feature set lacks (run ./le test unit installer). A changed answer the selector widened to every package is refused the same way. The race detector is always on, and the action takes no other go test flag: a run that needs -v, -count, -bench or a cover profile stays on ./le job run label unit-pkg quiet command go test -race -tags "$tags" ... with the tags written out (running-commands.md, "Testing one package while you develop it"). Component groups for step 3 Command Scope Time ./le test unit bgp BGP engine, wire, reactor about 1:30 ./le test unit core Core libraries about 30 seconds ./le test unit plugins All plugins about 40 seconds ./le test unit config Config parsing and YANG about 20 seconds ./le test unit cli CLI component about 10 seconds ./le test unit installer Installer initrd logic behind the ze_installer tag about 10 seconds ./le test unit all The whole checkout, then the groups their build tags hide from it minutes: it is every package under -race Pick the group matching your change. Each group is a subset of all, so a green group says nothing about the rest of the tree. The installer group runs the tests on Linux. On another host go test cross-compiles a Linux binary it cannot start, so the group runs go vet and type-checks the same files instead. ./le test qemu all runs them for real inside the Alpine virtual machine. Test types Ze has four levels of testing, each covering a different concern. Unit tests (*_test.go) Standard Go tests. They validate logic in isolation: does the parser produce the right output, does the state machine transition correctly, does the encoder round-trip. ./le test unit pkg path ./internal/component/bgp/message/... ./le test unit pkg path ./internal/component/bgp/route/ run TestParseOrigin Dynamic-group coverage exercises each plugin's real configuration boundary: capability declarations, policy lookups, validation, and command output. Opposite group and peer values expose lost inheritance; same-name peers and groups expose namespace collisions. A list of caller filenames or helper names proves neither. For example, the redirect tests pass plugin JSON through the RIB parser before querying the session's effective setting. Plugin transport fixtures Plugin transport fixtures use internal/test/pluginengine to run a plugin's actual entry point and SDK callbacks over the framed connection and bridge. Start returns only after the SDK's ordinary runtime-ready callback answers. That receipt joins OnStarted and entry into the callback loop on both transports. Stage 5 acknowledgement and bridge activation happen earlier and do not by themselves prove initialization finished. A fixture can run its first command immediately after Start returns. The wire fixture keeps serving ordinary engine requests while it waits, so an initializer can emit its startup events without waiting on the caller of Start. Ordinary command dispatch answers use the daemon's record-answer writer, including its warnings and completed record metadata. Physical and destination bound dispatch keeps the joined JSON receipt expected by the SDK's constrained command reader. A fake evaluator supplies the real answer value; the fixture selects the encoding from the request's bound i

title: Demonstrations
text: Demonstrations These recordings show how Ze behaves, and the labs let you try the same operations before deploying it. Terminal demonstrations: reproducible recordings of installation, configuration, and operator workflows. Labs: run protocol, forwarding, appliance, and interoperability tests. netlab topology: start a reusable three-node Ze topology under containerlab. Use cases: deployment examples with configuration for Ze and its neighboring routers, plus the checks for each setup.

title: Terminal Demonstrations
text: Terminal Demonstrations These recordings run real Ze commands against isolated local fixtures. Each checked-in tape file defines every keystroke, pause, and terminal size. A release can therefore regenerate the recordings when Ze changes. A terminal demo is an asciicast. The page replays terminal events as selectable text, so you can copy a command. The browser demonstration uses a WebP screenshot and a transcript, not encoded video. The recordings use no public service, and the terminal player is served from this site. Each demo also appears beside the documentation for the feature it exercises. The transcript below each player provides the same command sequence without replaying the recording. Continuous live configuration showcase One independently recorded session starts with ExaBGP migration and the live BGP dashboard. The migration preserves the neighbor's identity, local and remote AS numbers, and configured hold time. The session then loads, proves, diagnoses and repairs eight features on the same running Ze daemon. Each topic below uses the same configuration and demonstration fragments as this continuous recording. Demo: One running router, eight live configuration topics Migrate ExaBGP, operate the BGP dashboard, then configure, prove, diagnose and repair eight features in one continuous session without restarting Ze. Download the asciicast recording · Plain-text transcript Recorded with Ze 26.11.20 in a Linux namespace lab using Ze recorder. Duration: 21 minutes 57 seconds. One running router, eight live configuration topics 0. Migrate an actual ExaBGP neighbor configuration: ze exabgp migrate /src/demos/terminal/showcase/exabgp.conf Read the resulting bgp group and peer, remote address and AS numbers. This previews migration; it does not replace the lab's active configuration. 1. Connect to the base lab over SSH. Exit configuration mode, open monitor bgp, press s to sort by ASN, then q to return to the operational prompt. The transit and FRR peers are established before any feature is committed. 2. RPKI: add cache and validation binding live. Compare Valid, NotFound and Invalid routes; explain the ROA, stop the cache, diagnose and restore it. 3. IRR: query a local test server, bind AS-TEST and import filtering live. Prove accepted and refused routes; diagnose a wrong AS-SET and restore it. 4. BFD: add a profile and opt-in to the established FRR BGP peer. Cut its link, show BFD diagnostics and BGP history, restore the link and the sessions. 5. OSPF: add the area and interface. Follow Full adjacency through the router database to the loopback route. Diagnose a Hello mismatch and restore it. 6. IPsec: load IKE, ESP, authenticated peer/selectors and XFRM route in one candidate. Prove negotiated and kernel SPIs with protected-host traffic. Mismatch ESP alone, diagnose NO_PROPOSAL_CHOSEN without calling IKE down, restore the matching ESP group, clear the peer SAs and prove traffic again. 7. VRRP: add the gateway and uplink tracking. Observe master, tracked-link demotion and reduced priority; stop the companion master to show failover while the shown Ze stays running. Restore the companion and tracked link. 8. Traffic usage: attach accounting live, identify the heavy source and port, stop the burst, and observe recovery without changing forwarding. 9. Commit confirmed: leave a risky hostname change unconfirmed, observe its automatic rollback, then explicitly accept the next change and prove it stays. 10. Recap: the same daemon received each live commit, diagnostic and recovery. Every topic uses its standalone recording's configure.tape and show.tape. title: Developers
text: Developers The public plugin SDK lets you extend Ze. These pages explain how plugins communicate with the daemon and how to contribute a change to the project. Build extensions Plugin development: start with the SDK and plugin startup sequence. Protocol: connect a plugin to the daemon and manage its startup and shutdown. Configuration schemas: define plugin configuration with YANG. Handlers: receive events and implement plugin behavior. Commands: add commands to CLI, web, API, gRPC, and MCP. Metrics: publish operational measurements. Plugin testing: test plugin registration and behavior while Ze runs. Contribute to Ze Developer setup: build, test, and debug the source tree. Contributor guide: prepare and submit a change. Contributor testing: choose tests that exercise the behavior you changed. RFC implementation guide: implement and verify a standard. Documentation testing: keep examples tied to executable evidence. Style guide: follow the website's visual and content conventions.

title: Plugin Development
text: Plugin Development Ze plugins receive events, add configuration and commands, validate or apply configuration changes, implement address families and capabilities, and call the shared command dispatcher. External and in-process plugins use the same five-stage registration model. Start here The public Go SDK is pkg/plugin/sdk. An external plugin normally: Creates an SDK client from the environment supplied by Ze. Registers callbacks. Declares subscriptions, commands, schemas, families, or capabilities. Runs the five-stage startup protocol. Processes runtime events and commands until shutdown. package main import ( "context" "log" "github.com/ze-software/ze/pkg/plugin/sdk" ) func main() { plugin, err := sdk.NewFromEnv("example") if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } defer plugin.Close() plugin.OnEvent(func(event string) error { log.Print(event) return nil }) plugin.SetStartupSubscriptions([]string{"update", "state"}, nil, "") if err := plugin.Run(context.Background(), &sdk.Registration{}); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } } Ze starts an external plugin with a per-plugin token in ZE_PLUGIN_HUB_TOKEN and the certificate authority root that issued the engine certificate in ZE_PLUGIN_CA_PEM. sdk.NewFromEnv consumes these values and connects to the engine. Guide set Guide Purpose Protocol Five-stage registration, runtime framing, requests, responses, and shutdown Schemas Register YANG configuration and constraints Handlers Configure, verify, apply, event, and codec callbacks Commands Declare commands and return structured results Testing SDK harness, functional scenarios, and failure cases Metrics Register and expose plugin metrics without a second telemetry path The plugin operator guide covers loading, dependencies, process bindings, subscriptions, filters, and the built-in catalogue. Security model Each external process receives a token bound to its configured plugin name. The SDK validates the engine certificate chain against the supplied authority root, and refuses to dial without one. Configuration verification must fail closed on invalid candidate state. Commands remain subject to the shared dispatcher and authorisation path. Plugin output must be structured and bounded because it crosses process and operator boundaries. Development workflow Implement one registration or callback surface. Test the callback with the SDK harness. Add a functional scenario through the normal plugin process manager. Verify malformed requests and unavailable dependencies. Run the plugin against a minimal Ze configuration. Check command discovery, YANG registration, events, shutdown, and reload. Do not invent a private configuration parser, command transport, or metrics server. Register with the shared engine so the same surface remains available through CLI, web, REST, gRPC, and MCP.

title: Adding Commands
text: Adding Commands A plugin's commands are defined in YANG, the way the commands compiled into ze are. Ze builds the command and the check of its arguments from the module, and asks your plugin only with values that check accepts. An external plugin and a compiled-in plugin define a command the same way; they differ only in how they reach Ze (docs/architecture/plugin/plugin-system.md, "One plugin, two ways to reach the bus"). A command takes three things: What Where What it gives The command path, its help and its arguments A -cmd module The command in the tree, its help text, and the check of each argument The parameters the API surfaces publish The selected -cmd path's typed leaves; the named -api rpc input when that path has no typed CLI leaves The exact parameter names, types and placement MCP, REST and gRPC use for that command The route to your plugin An entry in the Stage 1 commands list, and a handler Ze asks your plugin when an operator runs the command Each command alias publishes its own typed CLI leaves. A command whose CLI leaf is named id publishes id, even when its named RPC uses session-id. The RPC input remains the fallback for a path without typed CLI leaves. An empty leaf is a presence-only flag: structured false omits it. A boolean leaf carries its explicit true or false value instead. Defining a Command in YANG This is the command module of the example plugin (examples/plugin/python/acme_monitor.py, and its Go twin examples/plugin/go/main.go). It defines show acme-monitor status and show acme-monitor target <name>: module acme-monitor-cmd { namespace "urn:acme:monitor:cmd"; prefix acmecmd; import ze-extensions { prefix ze; } container show { config false; container acme-monitor { config false; ze:help "Inspect the acme monitor."; container status { config false; ze:command "acme-monitor:show-status"; ze:help "Show the target and the probe interval."; } container target { config false; ze:command "acme-monitor:show-target"; ze:rpc "acme-monitor-api:show-target"; ze:help "Show the configured target of the acme monitor."; leaf name { type string { length "1..16"; } mandatory true; ze:help "Name of the target."; } } } } } And the rpc that describes the argument of target: module acme-monitor-api { namespace "urn:acme:monitor:api"; prefix acmeapi; import ze-extensions { prefix ze; } rpc show-target { ze:help "Show the configured target of the acme monitor."; input { leaf name { type string { length "1..16"; } mandatory true; ze:help "Name of the target."; } } } } How Ze reads the module: The name ends in -cmd. Ze takes commands only from a module with that suffix. A command is a config false container that holds ze:command. Every container on the way to it is config false too, and the first one is a verb (show, request, clear, ...). The path of the container is the command: show acme-monitor target. The containers on the way are shared. show is the verb container every module uses, and acme-monitor can hold commands from other modules too. A command path is yours alone: a path another module declares refuses the start. ze:command names the command's wire method, <word>:<word>, which no other module may declare. Each leaf is an argument. Its type, length, range, pattern or enumeration is what Ze checks the value against, and mandatory true makes it required. ze:help is the one-line summary shown in listings and completion, and description is the longer text, as for a config leaf (schema.md, "Best Practices"). ze:rpc "<module>:<rpc>" names the rpc whose input describes the command's parameters, in a module your plugin brings. Ze publishes the command with the parameters of that rpc. Give the input the same leaves as the command container, with the same types. Your plugin sends every module in its Stage 1 schemas list, one entry for each, beside its config module (schema.md, "Registering a Schema"). In Python, call plugin.schema() once for each module. Declaring and Handling Commands Ze asks your plugin only for a command its Stage 1 commands list names. List each command your -cmd module defines, by its path, and register a handler. The entry needs no help text when the module carries it. Every ze:command node your modules bring must be reached by a command your Stage 1 commands list declares: the declared command is the node's path, or a prefix of it that ends at a word boundary (show acme-monitor reaches show acme-monitor status). Ze sends a typed command to the longest registered command it starts with, whichever plugin registered it, so a node no declared command reaches could never be answered, and the start is refused: plugin "acme-monitor" brings command "show acme-monitor target" in module "acme-monitor-cmd", and declares no command at Stage 1 that reaches it Only a name Ze registers counts: a name with leading or trailing spaces, in upper case, or that breaks the command grammar, and a name a command of ze already holds, reach nothing. In the daemon, a longer command another plugin registered before yours takes the node from your shorter one. ze show plugin conformance run "<run string>" reports a node no declared command reaches in its command-nodes-served row, before the plugin is ever started (testing.md). A declared command with no ze:command node of its own is accepted, as it is for a plugin compiled into ze. In Go: p.OnExecuteCommand(func(serial, command string, args []string, peer string, pipe []sdk.PipeOperation) (string, any, error) { switch command { case "show acme-monitor status": return "done", map[string]string{"target": cfg.Target, "interval": cfg.intervalText()}, nil case "show acme-monitor target": // Ze checked the value against the leaf `name`: args holds it. if args[0] != cfg.Target { return "", nil, fmt.Errorf("acme-monitor has no target %s\nfix: show acme-monitor status", args[0]) } return "done", map[string]string{"target": args[0], "interval": cfg.intervalText()}, nil } return "", nil, fmt.Errorf("acme-monitor does not serve %q", command) }) err := p.Run(ctx, &sdk.Registration{ Schemas: []sdk.SchemaDecl{ {Module: "acme-monitor-conf", Namespace: "urn:acme:monitor:conf", YANGText: confYANG}, {Module: "acme-monitor-cmd", Namespace: "urn:acme:monitor:cmd", YANGText: cmdYANG}, {Module: "acme-monitor-api", Namespace: "urn:acme:monitor:api", YANGText: apiYANG}, }, WantsConfig: []string{"acme-monitor"}, Commands: []sdk.CommandDecl{ {Name: "show acme-monitor status"}, {Name: "show acme-monitor target"}, }, }) In Python, one decorator both lists the command at Stage 1 and serves it: @plugin.command("show acme-monitor target") def target(args): name = args[0] if name != state["target"]: raise CommandError("acme-monitor has no target %s" % name, fix="show acme-monitor status") return {"target": name, "interval": _interval_text()} The handler gets the values in args, as the operator typed them, and only after Ze accepted them. It does not check the type again, and it writes no usage message: Ze refuses a bad line before the handler runs. It still answers for what only it knows, such as a name the config does not hold, with an error whose last line is fix: and the command that clears it. What the Operator Gets Typed in a ze cli session, sent over SSH or with ze cli -c, the command runs in the running Ze, which asks your plugin: $ ze cli -c "show acme-monitor target web.example.net" A value the leaf's type refuses is refused by Ze, your plugin is not asked, and the command exits 1: $ ze cli -c "show acme-monitor target this-name-is-far-too-long" error: show acme-monitor target name: "this-name-is-far-too-long" is outside the accepted length (25 characters) name accepts 1..16 characters fix: show acme-monitor target <1..16 characters> A line with the mandatory leaf missing is refused before the plugin is asked, with the whole command as its correction: error: required argument missing: name This command needs name: The target name, from 1 to 16 characters. fix: show acme-monitor target name <name> MCP, REST and gRPC list

title: Plugin Handlers
text: Plugin Handlers Handlers process engine-initiated callbacks during startup and at runtime. They are registered on the sdk.Plugin before calling Run(). Registration Register handlers before calling Run(): p := sdk.NewWithConn("my-plugin", conn) // Startup handlers (named handler types defined in sdk package) p.OnConfigure(func(sections []sdk.ConfigSection) error { ... }) p.OnShareRegistry(func(commands []sdk.RegistryCommand) { ... }) // Runtime handlers p.OnEvent(func(event string) error { ... }) p.OnExecuteCommand(func(serial, command string, args []string, peer string, pipe []sdk.PipeOperation) (string, any, error) { ... }) p.OnConfigVerify(func(sections []sdk.ConfigSection) error { ... }) p.OnConfigApply(func(diffs []sdk.ConfigDiffSection) error { ... }) p.DeclareAppliesNothing("why a reload has nothing for this plugin to apply") p.OnValidateOpen(func(input *sdk.ValidateOpenInput) *sdk.ValidateOpenOutput { ... }) p.OnBye(func(reason string) error { ... }) // Post-startup callback (safe to make engine calls here) p.OnStarted(func(ctx context.Context) error { ... }) // NLRI handlers p.OnEncodeNLRI(func(family string, args []string) (string, error) { ... }) p.OnDecodeNLRI(func(family string, hex string) (any, error) { ... }) p.OnDecodeCapability(func(code uint8, hex string) (any, error) { ... }) p.Run(ctx, &sdk.Registration{...}) Handler Reference OnCurrentSelection Register this handler when a selecting plugin can answer its current desired selection for a destination session and native keys. The SDK declares support from the handler registration. This does not grant permission to send routes. Return the exact requested scope and ordered key/revision echoes, the current selection cut, and each key's explicit presence and current revision. Return no candidate routes. An absent key has revision zero; a present key's revision cannot exceed the cut. The handler runs on a separate bounded worker and may overlap ordinary events, execute-command and source-policy handlers. Read only a published snapshot; never call engine RPC, perform I/O or take election or peer locks. Honor the context. Run cancels and joins this worker before returning, so state remains owned until that return. OnConfigure Called during Stage 2 when the engine delivers config sections. p.OnConfigure(func(sections []sdk.ConfigSection) error { for _, s := range sections { // s.Root: config root name (e.g., "bgp") // s.Data: JSON-encoded config data var cfg MyConfig if err := json.Unmarshal([]byte(s.Data), &cfg); err != nil { return fmt.Errorf("parse config: %w", err) } // Store config for later use } return nil }) ConfigSection fields: Field Type Description Root string Config root name (e.g., "bgp") Data string JSON-encoded config data Return nil to accept the config, or an error to reject (aborts startup). OnShareRegistry Called during Stage 4 when the engine shares the command registry. p.OnShareRegistry(func(commands []sdk.RegistryCommand) { for _, cmd := range commands { // cmd.Name: command name (e.g., "peer") // cmd.Plugin: plugin that registered it // cmd.Encoding: encoding format } }) RegistryCommand fields: Field Type Description Name string Command name Plugin string Plugin that registered it Encoding string Encoding format This handler does not return a value. The registry is informational. OnEvent Called at runtime when the engine delivers a BGP event. p.OnEvent(func(event string) error { // event is a JSON string containing the BGP event var evt map[string]any if err := json.Unmarshal([]byte(event), &evt); err != nil { return fmt.Errorf("parse event: %w", err) } eventType, _ := evt["type"].(string) switch eventType { case "state": // Peer state change (up/down) case "update": // BGP UPDATE received case "sent": // Route sent to peer } return nil }) Return nil to acknowledge, or an error to signal failure. OnEventSettlement Register this handler before Run when an event starts deferred work. The global quiesce barrier calls it after earlier events were applied. Return only after their downstream effects complete, and honor the supplied context. The handler runs on an independent bounded worker, so events and nested engine calls can continue while it waits. A synchronous observer needs no settlement handler. OnExecuteCommand Called at runtime when the engine routes a command to the plugin. p.OnExecuteCommand(func(serial, command string, args []string, peer string, pipe []sdk.PipeOperation) (status string, data any, err error) { // serial: request correlation ID // command: the command name (e.g., "rib adjacent status") // args: additional arguments // peer: peer address (if command is peer-scoped) // pipe: the pipe operations the command declares, in the order typed switch command { case "rib adjacent status": result, _ := json.Marshal(map[string]any{ "running": true, "peers": 2, }) return "done", string(result), nil default: return "", "", fmt.Errorf("unknown command: %s", command) } }) Parameters: Parameter Type Description serial string Request correlation ID command string Full command name args []string Additional arguments peer string Peer address (may be empty) pipe []sdk.PipeOperation The operations the command declares in its Pipes entries with an argument, in the order typed, each a Name and its decoded Args; never inside args. The engine applies the rest of the chain to the answer (commands.md, "Declaring a Pipe Operation for Your Command") Return values: Return Type Description status string "done" or "error" data any The value the command produced, marshaled once by the SDK, or an sdk.Records walk err error Non-nil triggers error response A command that walks a large collection returns an sdk.Records for data. The SDK then writes one line for each row rather than one document, so neither the plugin nor the engine holds the whole answer. See commands.md, "Success with Rows". OnConfigVerify Called during config reload to validate a candidate config. The plugin receives the full candidate config sections and returns nil to accept or an error to reject. If no handler is registered, config-verify accepts. Either way, a plugin that registered neither OnConfigApply nor DeclareAppliesNothing is refused before the handler runs: see "A plugin with no apply handler" below. p.OnConfigVerify(func(sections []sdk.ConfigSection) error { for _, s := range sections { var cfg MyConfig if err := json.Unmarshal([]byte(s.Data), &cfg); err != nil { return fmt.Errorf("invalid config: %w", err) } // Validate semantic constraints if cfg.HoldTime > 0 && cfg.HoldTime < 3 { return fmt.Errorf("hold-time must be 0 or >= 3, got %d", cfg.HoldTime) } } return nil // Accept }) Return nil to accept the candidate config, or an error to reject the reload. OnConfigApply Called during config reload to apply config changes. The plugin receives diff sections describing what changed (added, removed, changed) and returns nil to accept or an error to reject. A plugin that declares WantsConfig must register it or call DeclareAppliesNothing; the handler must not be nil, and the call panics on a nil one. p.OnConfigApply(func(diffs []sdk.ConfigDiffSection) error { for _, d := range diffs { // d.Root: config root name // d.Added: JSON-encoded added config (may be empty) // d.Removed: JSON-encoded removed config (may be empty) // d.Changed: JSON-encoded changed config (may be empty) if d.Added != "" { // Apply additions } if d.Removed != "" { // Apply removals } if d.Changed != "" { // Apply modifications } } return nil }) ConfigDiffSection fields: Field Type Description Root string Config root name (e.g., "bgp") Added string JSON-encoded added config Removed string JSON-encoded removed config Changed string JSON-encoded changed config DeclareAppliesNothing A plugin that declares WantsConfig but holds nothing a reload can apply says so in place of an apply handler. Use it when the plugin reads no leaf of its roots, or reads only capability leaves. DeclareCapabilitiesFrom carries the candidate declaration at confi

title: Plugin Metrics
text: Plugin Metrics Register metrics in the process that performs the work. Plugins whose engines produce the observations use the existing ConfigureMetrics callback in the Registration struct. Code that runs in the daemon independently of its plugin process uses the deferred daemon hook described below. Implementation Pattern Each plugin follows the same three-step pattern used by bgp-rib and bgp-gr: Registration: Set ConfigureMetrics in the Registration struct inside init(). The callback receives a typed metrics.Registry; no assertion is needed. Storage: Declare a package-level atomic.Pointer holding a metrics struct. The struct contains the counters and gauges created from the registry. Usage: At metric update points, load the pointer. If nil (metrics disabled), skip. Otherwise update the metric. Naming Policy Every metric name is built from four parts in fixed order: ze_{scope}_{subject}_{detail} Part Rule Examples ze Always. Global prefix for all ze metrics. scope Plugin name, hyphens stripped, lowercase. Reactor uses functional area. rib, gr, fibkernel, systemrib, rpki, persist, watchdog subject Singular noun: the type of thing being measured. route, peer, timer, session, vrp detail What aspect. Depends on metric type (see below). inserts, active, expired Type-Specific Rules Type Pattern Suffix Examples Counter ze_{scope}_{subject}_{event}_total Always _total ze_rib_route_inserts_total, ze_gr_timer_expired_total Gauge ze_{scope}_{subject}_{qualifier} Never _total ze_gr_active_peers, ze_fibkernel_routes_installed Histogram ze_{scope}_{subject}_{action}_seconds Always unit suffix ze_peer_dial_seconds CounterVec Same as Counter, labels for dimensions _total ze_rpki_validation_outcomes_total with {result} label GaugeVec Same as Gauge, labels for dimensions No _total ze_rib_routes_in with {peer} label Subject Rules The subject is always a singular noun describing the category of thing measured. When the metric counts a quantity of that noun, the grammatical plural appears naturally in the detail. Subject (singular) Gauge (current count) Counter (cumulative events) route routes_installed route_installs_total peer peers_up peer_flaps_total vrp vrps_cached session sessions_active session_teardowns_total Detail Rules For counters, the detail is the event that happened, as a noun or past participle: inserts, withdrawals, expired, installs, removals, errors. For gauges, the detail is a qualifier distinguishing this gauge from others in the same scope: installed, active, up, cached, in, out. Label Rules Use labels for runtime dimensions. Never encode variable data in metric names. Label When to use Example peer Per-peer breakdown ze_rib_routes_in{peer="10.0.0.1"} family Per-address-family breakdown ze_rib_route_inserts_total{family="ipv4/unicast"} operation Error categorization ze_fibkernel_errors_total{operation="add"} result Outcome categorization ze_rpki_validation_outcomes_total{result="valid"} Scope-to-Prefix Mapping Plugin (Registration Name) Metric scope Rationale bgp-rib rib Established; bgp prefix would be redundant bgp-adj-rib-in adjribin bgp prefix redundant; hyphens stripped bgp-gr gr Established fib-kernel fibkernel Hyphen stripped rib (sysrib) systemrib Registration name is rib but ze_rib_ is taken by bgp-rib; systemrib reads naturally bgp-watchdog watchdog bgp prefix redundant bgp-rpki rpki bgp prefix redundant bgp-role role bgp prefix redundant bgp-filter-path-asn filter_path_asn The package name. The bgp prefix is redundant on a BGP filter, and the hyphen-stripped bgpfilterpathasn cannot be read bgp-filter-community filter_community The package name, for the same reason Full Inventory Metric
