title: Plugin Protocol
text:
Plugin Protocol Ze plugins communicate with the engine via newline-framed YANG RPCs over a single bidirectional connection. Internal plugins use net.Pipe() for startup; external plugins connect back via TLS. All messages use newline-delimited framing with the wire format #<id> <verb> [<json>]
. Wire Format Every message is a single newline-terminated line: Message type Format Request #<id> <method> [<json-params>]
 Success response #<id> ok [<json-result>]
 Error response #<id> error [<json-error>]
 Record answer #<id> <kind> <positional fields>
: a head, one line for each record, and a terminator The record answer applies to three methods. It replaces the single success line with a head, zero or more records, and a terminator. Every other method keeps the three forms above. An answer line carries no verb and no key name. The field after the id is a three-byte word saying what the line IS: Word The line is top the head, which opens the answer row one record the command produced bad one record it rejected. The walk goes on end the terminator, which ends the answer wrn the terminator of a command that completed and states a warning nay the whole answer to a command text naming no command The head carries a second three-byte word saying how the records read: Word The records are doc one document. The whole answer is that one value map one map of names to values for each record tab one positional row for each record, read against the column names Every field after those is positional and takes one of two shapes. A NUMBER is decimal digits closed by a space or by the end of the line. A TEXT is decimal digits, a colon, then that many BYTES. The count is a BYTE count, never a count of characters. A text of zero bytes is written 0:, so a line's field count never varies: #43 top doc 0: 0: | | | | | | | | | +----- column names, 0 BYTES, so the records are not positional | | | +-------- envelope name, 0 BYTES, so the document carries its own | | +------------ item type doc: the whole answer is one document | +---------------- kind top: the head, always the first line +-------------------- correlation id 43, echoed from the request #43 row 26:{"running":true,"peers":1} | | | | | | | +----- those 26 bytes, the handler's value byte for byte | | +-------- 26, the payload's BYTE count, then its colon | +------------ kind row: one record the command produced +---------------- correlation id 43 #43 end 1 0 0: | | | | | | | | | +----- message, 0 BYTES, so the command stated none | | | +------- 0 rows rejected | | +--------- 1 record produced | +------------- kind end: the terminator, always the last line +----------------- correlation id 43 Neither the head nor the terminator states an outcome. The verdict is DERIVED from what the terminator carries: The terminator Verdict no rejected row and no message done wrn, no rejected row and no message warning records and rejected rows, no message partial a message over no record error a message over records aborted no terminator at all truncated When the engine cannot build the answer to a dispatch-command, for example because the command's payload is not a JSON object or array, it still writes a head and a terminator whose message names the reason. Your plugin reads error with that message rather than waiting for its timeout. ipc_protocol.md, "Answer Protocol", carries the same grammar with the buffering threshold and the failure cases beside it. Method The plugin The engine dispatch-command reads the answer writes it dispatch-command-args reads the answer writes it execute-command writes the answer reads it One encoding covers both columns, on every connection. Nothing is declared and nothing is negotiated, so a plugin author sets no field and reaches no option. A plugin READS an engine answer in one of two ways, and both read the same frame. Plugin.DispatchCommandAnswer yields each row as it arrives, which is what bounds the memory of a walk over a large table. Plugin.DispatchCommand and Plugin.DispatchCommandArgs collapse the same answer into the one document a caller that wants the whole payload reads. A plugin WRITES its own answer to execute-command, and the frame is the same whatever the payload is. A handler that returns a plugin.Records writes one line for each row of the walk. A handler that returns a built value writes that value as the one record of a doc answer, byte for byte. <id> is a monotonically increasing uint64 correlation ID <method> uses YANG-style <module>:<rpc-name> naming (e.g., ze-plugin-engine:declare-registration) JSON payloads are optional (omitted when empty or null) Responses use ok or error as the verb; requests use the method name Routing: MuxConn multiplexes a single connection for concurrent RPCs. A background reader goroutine routes incoming lines by verb: ok/error responses go to the waiting CallRPC caller by #<id>, while method-name requests go to the Requests() channel. Examples: # Plugin sends declare-registration (Stage 1) #1 ze-plugin-engine:declare-registration {"protocol-version":1,"families":[{"name":"ipv4/flow","mode":"both","afi":1,"safi":133}]} # Engine answers the protocol version both sides speak #1 ok {"protocol-version":1,"plugin-name":"flow-export"} # Engine sends configure to plugin (Stage 2) #1 ze-plugin-callback:configure {"sections":[{"root":"bgp","data":"{...}"}]} # Plugin responds OK #1 ok # Engine sends event at runtime #42 ze-plugin-callback:deliver-event {"event":"{"type":"state",...}"} # Plugin responds OK #42 ok # Error response with payload #5 error {"code":"error","message":"unknown family: ipv4/unknown"} Protocol Stages The SDK handles the 5-stage startup protocol automatically via Plugin.Run(). Stage 1: Registration (Plugin to Engine) Plugin sends ze-plugin-engine:declare-registration with a DeclareRegistrationInput: Field Type Description protocol-version int REQUIRED. The highest plugin protocol version the plugin speaks (this engine speaks 1) exit-confirms-cleanup bool Declare only when exit zero confirms release of this original engine's native resources. The daemon reserves protected warning capacity at accepted Stage 1, before OnStarted. families []FamilyDecl Address families the plugin handles (name, mode, AFI, and SAFI) commands []CommandDecl Commands the plugin provides dependencies []string Plugin names that must also be loaded optional-dependencies []string Plugins this one starts after when both run. It loads nothing start-after []string Plugins this one starts after when both run, as an ordering edge alone. It loads nothing wants-config []string Config roots the plugin wants to receive config-operations []ConfigOperationDecl Config operation callbacks the plugin supports, and the operation labels it emits for each root. The labels are the plugin's own: the engine keeps no list of them config-completion bool Whether the plugin answers config-complete, the acknowledged cleanup after a whole reload was published or restored. The Go SDK sets it from OnConfigComplete source-policy-owner bool Whether the plugin retains source state, declared apart from source-policy source-policy bool Whether the plugin answers the acknowledged source-policy lifecycle callbacks origin-intake bool Declares the scoped-origin mutation callback and joined cancellation. The SDK derives this flag from OnOriginIntake. current-selection bool Whether the plugin answers the desired-selection snapshot callback origin-admission-lookup bool Whether the plugin answers read-only original accepted-record lookup event-settlement bool Whether the plugin acknowledges when its asynchronous work on an event is complete verify-budget int Estimated verify time in seconds (0 means trivial) apply-budget int Estimated apply time in seconds (0 means trivial) schemas []SchemaDecl The YANG modules the plugin brings, one entry for each module: a config module, a -cmd command module, an -api rpc module. Ze joins an external plugin's modules when it starts (schema.md) wants-validate-open b

title: YANG Schema Authoring
text: YANG Schema Authoring Plugins declare their configuration schema using YANG (RFC 7950). This guide covers the basics for plugin authors. What works today Plugin kind Its own YANG module Config it receives Internal plugin, compiled into ze (package added to internal/component/plugin/all) Registered at build, parsed and validated; the operator writes config under its roots Its WantsConfig roots External plugin (a separate process, SDK or any language) Joined to the schema at ze start, from the modules its Stage 1 declaration lists under schemas (config, command and rpc modules); the operator writes config under its roots. With no daemon running Ze starts no plugin, so ze config validate and the other commands that parse a config then cannot check a section under those roots The roots it declares, its own included At ze start the daemon reads the plugin declarations first (the plugin block and the plugins named on the command line), runs each declared external plugin, reads its Stage 1 declaration, joins every module it lists and only then parses the full config. The plugin waits for its Stage 1 answer in the meantime, so a plugin MUST NOT time out between sending its declaration and receiving the answer. A module that does not compile, or that clashes with a module Ze holds, refuses the start and names the plugin. A plugin and its modules change only when ze restarts. Ze enforces that rule while it runs: A reload whose config adds or removes an external plugin, or changes the run, encoder, respawn or timeout of one, is refused whole. The message names each plugin and what changed, and its fix is restart ze. The rest of the config reloads without a restart, your own section included. When Ze starts your plugin again (it ended and declared failure-policy restart, or the operator ran request plugin restart <name>), the plugin MUST declare the same modules: each with the same name, namespace and text, none missing and none added, or none if it declared none. This holds for a command or rpc module as for a config module. Another schema refuses the plugin at Stage 1. Ze does not run it, keeps the config under its root, and raises the warning doctor-plugin-schema-changed, which ze show doctor reports with the first module that differs. To ship a new schema, install the new program and restart ze. A plugin that cannot be run, or that sends no declaration within its stage timeout, declares nothing: a config section only its module defines is then refused as unknown top-level keyword: <root>, and the refusal names the plugin, why it did not declare and the command that checks it (ze show plugin conformance run "<command>"). The same holds for a plugin that sends its declaration with no YANG module: it defines no config section, and a section written for it is refused with a message that says so. Each of these outcomes has a doctor code: Code When Where you read it doctor-plugin-schema-undeclared Ze holds no config schema of your plugin: it could not be run, it sent no declaration in time, or it declared no module and the config holds a section no schema defines On the refusal and in the log when the start is refused, and then in ze doctor, from the record Ze wrote before it exited, until Ze next starts cleanly. In ze show doctor when the config holds no section of your plugin, so Ze starts doctor-plugin-schema-refused Ze refused your module at start: it does not compile, it clashes with a module Ze holds, it redefines a top-level node, it names a ze:validate validator or a ze:reference source Ze does not hold, it declares a command or a wire method another module declares, a ze:rpc names an rpc no module defines, or it adds nothing On the refusal and in the log. Ze does not start, and ze doctor reports the refusal from the record Ze wrote before it exited, until Ze next starts cleanly doctor-plugin-schema-changed Your plugin was started again with other YANG modules (a config, command or rpc module) In ze show doctor In a running Ze your config module is part of the schema every surface reads: the session editor parses and completes under your root, show config running answers your section, show yang tree config shows your nodes with their types and descriptions, and show schema list lists your module with the roots your plugin wants. Type them in a ze cli session or send them over SSH: both reach the running Ze, while ze cli -c answers these two in its own process, from the modules compiled into ze. A running Ze has no command that prints the YANG text of one module; ze schema show <module> prints it for a module compiled into ze only. The doctor check for config that reaches no plugin counts the roots your running plugin declared, so your section is not reported as having no effect. A change to your section that an operator commits in the session editor reaches your plugin as verify then apply, and Ze saves it: the next ze start on the same config directory runs your plugin, reads your modules again and configures your plugin with the committed value. Your plugin's process reads the settings of the config's environment block in its own environment, although Ze starts it before it has parsed the whole config and applied that block to itself. A variable set in the environment Ze was started from wins over the block, as it does for Ze. A plugin Ze starts again later inherits Ze's environment, which holds the block by then. With no daemon, ze schema shows the modules compiled into ze only. A --plugin that names your program does not start it: the answer is followed by a warning that your module is not available with no running Ze, whose fix is ze cli: typed in that session, show schema list lists your module and show yang tree config shows its nodes. With no daemon running, Ze never starts an external plugin's program. Your module reaches Ze only when ze start runs your plugin, so a command that parses a config with no daemon holds the schemas compiled into the ze binary and nothing else. It accepts a config that declares your plugin and holds no section under your roots. It refuses a section under your roots as unknown top-level keyword: <root>, and the message says why and how to check the section. ze config validate <file> asks the running Ze first when the config declares an external plugin: it sends the file's content, so the file may be anywhere, and the running Ze, which read your module when it started your plugin, judges the section in full. The output and the exit codes are those of a local verdict. With no Ze running it answers: config ze.conf does not parse: it holds a name that no config schema compiled into ze defines the config declares external plugin "acme-monitor"; the config schema of an external plugin is not compiled into ze: ze reads it from the plugin when `ze start` runs it. This command starts no plugin, so only a running ze that started with these plugins checks a section that such a plugin defines, and none answered: no ze listens at 127.0.0.1:2222 (...). Run the command below, then `ze config validate ze.conf` again. What the parser refused: line 8: unknown top-level keyword: acme-monitor fix: ze start ze config fmt, dump, diff and graph, and their ze show config spellings, ask the running Ze the same way: the answer is printed as a local answer is, fmt -w rewrites your file with the text the running Ze formatted, and with no Ze running the message above names the command you ran in place of ze config validate. ze config diff compares the resolved bgp block and the order of ordered lists, so a leaf that differs in your plugin's own section is not reported as a difference. The other commands ask no running Ze. Their message says so, and its fix is ze config validate <file>. title: Testing Your Plugin
text: Testing Your Plugin This guide covers testing strategies for ze plugins using the SDK (pkg/plugin/sdk). Checking That a Program Is a Valid Plugin The conformance checker judges a plugin program in any language. It starts the program in declare mode (ZE_PLUGIN_MODE=declare, described in protocol.md, "Query Mode: Answering Without Starting") and judges what the program wrote. It needs no daemon and no config file. With no daemon running, the checker is the only command that starts your program. ze show plugin declarations config <file> starts no external plugin then: it lists your plugin with the state not-available, and its reason names this checker and the form a running Ze answers. A running Ze starts your program in declare mode when you type show plugin declarations config <file> in the session ze cli opens, and the row then carries what your plugin declares. Two commands run the same checker and write the same rows: # The shipped binary, for a plugin author or an operator. ze show plugin conformance run "./my-plugin --flag" ze show plugin conformance run "./my-plugin --flag" name acme-monitor # The development launcher, inside the Ze repository. ./le plugin conformance check run "./my-plugin --flag" ./le plugin conformance check run "./my-plugin --flag" name acme-monitor The value after run is the run string you would configure under plugin { external <name> { run ...; } }, as one quoted token. A shell starts it, and a relative path is read from the directory you typed the command in. name is the plugin name the checks use in their refusals. Without it, the name is the file name of the program the run string starts. The program has the budget ze.plugin.query.timeout sets, 5 seconds by default. A caller cancellation or deadline stops the query's isolated process group and joins it before the checker answers. That interruption produces an error and no completed conformance report; it does not claim that the plugin failed. If the caller remains active and the query's own budget expires, the exits-clean row still fails. The report The report holds one row for each check, in the order the protocol reaches them. Each row carries these fields: Field Value check The name of the check stage The part of the protocol the check belongs to: declare for query mode, a stage number, or transport, runtime, shutdown, schema verdict pass, fail or not-judged reason What the check found. A passed row carries none fix The change that clears the row. A passed row carries none A not-judged row is a check that nobody ran, and its reason says why. A report with no failed row is therefore not full conformance: read the not-judged rows to learn what is still unproven. The first four rows judge the declare-mode run itself: Check It passes when program-starts The run string starts a program. A shell exit of 126 or 127 means that no program started exits-clean The program exits 0 inside the budget and leaves no process holding its standard output declaration-line Standard output holds exactly one line: #1 ze-plugin-engine:declare-registration and the declaration as compact JSON, ended by one line feed declaration-decodes The JSON of that line decodes as a Stage 1 declaration, read as the daemon reads it: a key ze does not know, the retired schema key among them, fails the row with the daemon's own refusal, and the Stage 1 rows after it are not judged The next rows are the daemon's own Stage 1 checks, run over the declaration the program wrote. The checker and the daemon read one table, so a row that fails here is a declaration the daemon refuses, with the daemon's own reason. These rows carry stage 1: protocol-version, dissemination, filter-declarations, filter-insertions, filter-insertion-paths, drain, resolver-caches, doctor-checks, enrichers, pipe-aliases, answer-shapes, help-texts and command-nodes-served. The row command-names carries stage 5. The daemon applies that rule at Stage 5, where a bad name refuses the command and keeps the plugin. command-nodes-served joins the YANG modules of the declaration to ze's own, as the daemon does at ze start, and fails when a ze:command node of those modules is not routed to a command the plugin declares: no declared command reaches it on a word boundary, or the only one that does is a name the daemon refuses at Stage 5. A module the join refuses fails the row with the join's own refusal. The daemon also counts the commands other plugins registered before this one, because the longest command that reaches a node takes it; the checker runs one program, so it judges the declaration alone. When the program did not start, every later row is not-judged. When no declaration was read, every Stage 1 row is not-judged. A row is never passed for a declaration that nobody read. What this version does not judge These rows are not-judged in every report. Test each behavior under a daemon: configure the plugin with plugin { external <name> { run ...; } } and start ze. Check Stage Why the checker does not judge it ambiguous-registration 1 The check compares the declaration with the other plugins the daemon runs doctor-check-declared-twice 1 The check compares the declared doctor checks with the registry row of the operator's block respawn-agreement 1 The check compares the declared failure policy with the respawn leaf of the operator's config schema-unchanged 1 The check compares the declared YANG modules with the ones the daemon read from the plugin when it started dependencies 1 The check looks for each declared dependency among the plugins the daemon configured or loaded registration-conflicts 1 The check writes the plugin's names into the daemon's registries, where another plugin can hold the same name tls-connect-back transport The checker starts no hub, so the TLS connect-back and the #0 auth exchange do not run stage-2-config 2 The checker sends no configure message stage-3-capabilities 3 The checker reads no declare-capabilities message stage-4-registry 4 The checker sends no share-registry message stage-5-ready 5 The checker reads no ready message, so the subscriptions are not judged config-callbacks runtime The checker opens no config transaction, so it calls no verify, apply, rollback or committed callback execute-command-framing runtime The checker sends no execute-command, so it reads no answer line bye-and-exit shutdown The checker sends no bye schema schema The checker joins the YANG modules in the schemas list of the declaration only for command-nodes-served, which fails with the join's refusal; it parses no config against them Exit codes Code Meaning 0 No row failed. Some rows are not-judged 1 One row or more failed 2 No completed report: no run string, no shell on this host, an invalid budget, a caller that is not local, or caller cancellation or deadline during the query A sample report This is the report of a conforming program. The reason and fix columns are left out here to keep the lines short. check stage verdict program-starts declare pass exits-clean declare pass declaration-line declare pass declaration-decodes declare pass protocol-version 1 pass dissemination 1 pass filter-declarations 1 pass filter-insertions 1 pass filter-insertion-paths 1 pass drain 1 pass resolver-caches 1 pass doctor-checks 1 pass enrichers 1 pass pipe-aliases 1 pass answer-shapes 1 pass help-texts 1 pass command-nodes-served 1 pass command-names 5 pass ambiguous-registration 1 not-judged doctor-check-declared-twice 1 not-judged respawn-agreement 1 not-judged schema-unchanged 1 not-judged dependencies 1 not-judged registration-conflicts 1 not-judged tls-connect-back transport not-judged stage-2-config 2 not-judged stage-3-capabilities 3 not-judged stage-4-registry 4 not-judged stage-5-ready 5 not-judged config-callbacks runtime not-judged execute-command-framing runtime not-judged bye-and-exit shutdown not-judged schema schema not-judged | json gives the same rows under the key checks. The le command answers one document that holds plugin, run, v

title: Frequently asked questions
text: Frequently asked questions These answers cover what Ze does, its release status, and what adopting it involves. If your question is missing, you can ask on Discord or open an issue. Product and readiness Start here if you are deciding whether Ze belongs in your network. What is Ze? Ze is an open-source configuration and protocol engine, also available as a Linux network operating system. It speaks BGP, manages network interfaces, updates the forwarding table, and lets you manage the same configuration through SSH, a web interface, APIs, and AI tools using MCP (Model Context Protocol). The core manages configuration, plugins, and communication between components, while individual subsystems implement the network protocols. Each subsystem defines its configuration in a YANG schema. Ze uses those definitions for its command syntax, completion, validation, web editor, reference pages, and MCP tools. Is Ze ready for production? No. Ze is pre-release software. The BGP engine has automated tests, but production exposure remains limited, and both APIs and configuration syntax can still change. A lab is a useful place to try Ze today, whether you want to build a route server, migrate an ExaBGP configuration, or test it against FRR or BIRD. Reports of failures help us find what those tests miss. The roadmap lists the release work, while the quality pages describe the available tests and their limits. What can Ze actually do today? Ze implements BGP and manages Linux interfaces and forwarding tables. You can change configuration through SSH, a web interface, or APIs, review and commit those changes, and roll them back. It also provides monitoring and a plugin system. OSPF, IS-IS, MPLS, firewall, VPN, PPPoE, and L2TP code also exists, but those areas remain experimental. Use the feature catalog for current status instead of treating this answer as a compatibility matrix. Why would I use Ze instead of BIRD, FRR, or GoBGP? A mature daemon is the better choice when you need an established production platform today. Ze may be worth evaluating if you want a shared configuration model across its CLI, web interface, and APIs, or if its plugins and ExaBGP migration tools fit your deployment. Its quality pages also make the test methods and evidence available for review. Each subsystem supplies a YANG model that defines its configuration and supplies the CLI, validation, web editor, reference pages, and MCP tools. The comparison pages describe the differences between Ze and other projects, including features Ze still lacks. Running and adopting Ze Practical questions about trying Ze before you commit a network to it. Where does Ze run? The daemon runs on Linux under systemd or another process supervisor. Development builds work on macOS and Linux with the supported Go toolchain. Windows is not a supported development or runtime platform. Start with the quickstart. Use the appliance lab when you want an immutable boot image for a VM or dedicated hardware. I run ExaBGP. Can I move to Ze? Yes. Ze includes ze exabgp migrate for configuration conversion and a compatibility bridge that lets existing ExaBGP process scripts run while you port them. The ExaBGP migration guide covers conversion, known differences, and the point where a native Ze plugin becomes the better choice. The daemon or the appliance: which should I run? Start with the daemon. It fits into Linux infrastructure you already supervise and is easier to inspect while Ze is still pre-release. The appliance packages the same binary and configuration into a read-only system with automatic supervision, no package manager, and no interactive shell. Use it when you want a purpose-built router image rather than another managed Linux host. Will my configuration keep working as Ze changes? Configuration syntax can change before the first release, and changes are described in the change log. An existing configuration may need editing when you update Ze. Silent reinterpretation is a bug. Configuration stability is an explicit milestone on the roadmap. Does Ze need an LLM to run? No. Ze runs without an AI service. MCP is an optional operator interface generated from the same schemas and command catalog as the CLI and web interface. It lets an authorized assistant discover and operate the capabilities compiled into a running daemon. Project and support How the project is licensed, maintained, and supported. What does the AGPLv3 license mean for me? You can run, inspect, modify, and redistribute Ze under the GNU Affero General Public License v3. Running an unmodified Ze for your own network does not require publishing your configuration. If you modify Ze and let users interact with that modified version over a network, the AGPL requires you to offer those users the corresponding source. Read the license itself when the distinction matters to a deployment. What does the contributor agreement grant? A signed-off commit (git commit -s) confirms agreement to the Contributor License Agreement. You keep your copyright. The agreement lets the maintainer offer Ze under additional license terms, including a commercial license. Every contribution remains available to the public under AGPLv3. The contributor guide covers the submission process. Who builds Ze, and how is it funded? Thomas Mangin develops Ze, with engineering time supported by Exa Networks. The ISP has backed the work since it began with ExaBGP in 2009. Ze currently has no subscription, paid support tier, or separate commercial entity. The contribute page explains how the project is maintained and how to help. How is AI used to develop Ze? AI coding agents write Ze's code under a process we developed to guide their work and check the result. We agree on a specification before implementation, write tests first, and ask a separate agent to review the change. Automated checks enforce the repository's rules before a change is committed. Keeping the instructions beside the code gives each new session the same requirements. How Ze is developed with AI explains how this process developed. As with human development, the first version is often not fully correct, and we improve it through repeated testing and review. Checking a feature thoroughly takes time and computing resources. For an RFC, every requirement has to be identified and tested, and each test has to detect a deliberate fault in the behavior it checks. That coverage keeps growing after the first implementation is published. The RFC compliance pages show what the tests establish and what is still missing. The website is harder to check automatically. An RFC can define behavior precisely enough for a test, while free text leaves more room for unclear explanations and mistakes. Most of the site's figures, feature lists, and references are generated from the code, but the prose still needs review and is likely to contain more mistakes than the code. We revise it as we find them. If you spot a mistake on the site or in Ze, we would appreciate a report on Discord or the issue tracker. How do I get help or report a security problem? Use Discord for discussion and the issue tracker for reproducible bugs and feature requests. Follow the security policy for anything security-sensitive. Report vulnerabilities privately instead of opening a public issue.

title: AI-First Design
text: AI-First Design Ze uses shared registrations to describe commands and configuration. The CLI, MCP and other operator interfaces read this metadata for the surfaces they support. AI tools can discover the command catalog, call daemon commands and read structured output while helping an operator use or debug the system. Shared Registrations The core design point is broader than AI. A feature added to Ze should avoid separate hand-written glue for every surface. The same registration path can feed the CLI, SSH sessions, the web workbench, REST/gRPC, MCP, generated references, completion, authorization, audit, and diagnostics. CLI commands as the API surface The CLI and MCP use the same command catalog and daemon dispatcher, with availability determined by each command's registration. Offline commands may have a different daemon path, interactive views require a terminal, and streaming-only commands are excluded from one-shot surfaces. A shared catalog therefore describes which commands each interface offers; it does not promise that every CLI interaction has an equivalent MCP call. Self-Describing Command Reference ze help command # full command catalog, filterable ze help command bgp # filter to BGP-related commands ze help command --json # machine-readable JSON (for tooling, wiki generation) ze help ai # AI-oriented summary with recipes and context ze help ai --json # machine-readable JSON reference ze help ai api # daemon API endpoints (ze-bgp:*, ze-iface:*, ...) The command and RPC listings are assembled from the binary's plugin registry, YANG schemas and command registrations. Generation removes a separately maintained list of those definitions. Descriptions can still be wrong, and the hand-written recipes need updating when command behavior changes. ze help command is the human-facing catalog. The native ./le cli catalog update file <destination> action renders the corresponding Markdown from the live registries. Both commands are served by the daemon too, so ze cli -c, SSH, REST, gRPC, MCP and the web reach them, under show command catalog (help command) and show command reference (help ai): help is an offline root, not a verb, so no daemon command path starts with it. --json, --verbose and -v are flags of the local ze help command only. On every other surface show command catalog answers its catalog rows as data: it prints the table, and show command catalog bgp | json gives the same rows as JSON. show command reference answers its Markdown page as text, and the structured reference is the MCP ze_reference tool. A bare word means the same on every surface: help command json filters on the word json, and help ai json prints the summary. Structured Diagnostics ze cli -c "show config validation <file> | json" ze show diagnostic [--json] <diagnostic-code> ze config fix --plan <file> The validation verdict is a record the pipe layer renders, so | json, | yaml and | table are three views of one payload and no command carries a rendering flag of its own. The fix plan prints for a reader. Config validation emits diagnostic records with a code, severity and message. Source spans, expected/actual facts, help and repair metadata are included when the producing check supplies them. Agents must handle their absence. Codes such as config-parse, config-yang-type and config-listener-conflict identify the kind of failure. ze show diagnostic <code> explains a registered code. The readiness checks ze doctor runs report codes from the same table, which the package owning each dependency declares: the DNS resolver's doctor-dns-resolver-port-unavailable (a listener port the system will not let ze bind) and doctor-dns-resolver-upstream-unreachable (no forward server answers a probe), for example. ze config fix --plan <file> reports candidate repairs without editing files. The same plan is available through show config supplied fix-plan content <base64> [name <filename>] on the daemon's command surfaces, including the browser's registered file/paste inspection controls. Both forms use the same validation and repair-plan producer; an invalid source still returns its plan. Where a repair is available, its diagnostic can carry a stable repair ID and a safety label such as format-only, section-local, behavior-preserving or requires-human-review. A diagnostic does not always have an automatic repair. A doctor diagnostic can also carry fix: the command or config statement the operator runs to clear the problem, held alone with no label of its own. It is not a repair ID and carries no safety label. The ze doctor text report draws it on a line of its own under the finding, opened by fix:, and JSON carries it under fix when the check names one. An entry of show errors and show warnings carries the same fix key when its producer named the command, and show doctor's row for that event shows it as the fix line. A transient code a component raises on the report bus (a plugin process that ended unasked, a refused plugin request) is registered by its owner as an event code, so ze show diagnostic <code> describes it and show doctor reports the event under it. Bundled Skills ze show skills ze show skill ze-diagnostics ze show skill ze --full The installed binary serves the workflow guides embedded when it was built. They cover diagnostics, config, commands and agent edit loops, so an agent can load the guide relevant to its task without fetching a separate version. Embedding fixes which text the binary serves. It does not check that every example describes the implemented behavior. Over the daemon (MCP, REST, gRPC, SSH, web) the expanded form is the model's flag leaf full, as in show skill ze full; the local --full means the same. Setting an agent up These commands set an AI coding agent up to use Ze. For the step-by-step how-to, with the command's output and the Codex trust step, see Use Ze with an AI agent; this section is the reference. ze create agent skill ze show agent skill ze delete agent skill At a shell, ze create agent skill writes a stub skill named ze for each agent harness it finds under the home directory: Claude Code's own ~/.claude/skills/ze/SKILL.md (under CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR when that is set), and the shared ~/.agents/skills/ze/SKILL.md that Codex, OpenCode and Pi read. A harness is found when its configuration directory exists (~/.claude, ~/.codex or CODEX_HOME, ~/.config/opencode, ~/.pi). agent <name> sets up that harness even where its directory does not exist yet; with no harness found and none named, the shared stub is written. The stub's frontmatter is the ze guide's name and description, its first line after that is Ze's marker, and its body tells the agent to run ze show skill ze, so the guide always matches the installed binary. Ze owns a stub only by that marker line. A second run leaves a current stub untouched (unchanged) and rewrites one an older ze wrote (updated); a SKILL.md without the marker is left as it is (foreign), with the command that replaces it. A link at the ze directory or at its SKILL.md is replaced by Ze's own file and its target is left. Anything else Ze did not write at that place, such as a file where the ze directory belongs, is left as it is (foreign) by every command; a linked skills directory (a dotfiles setup) is followed, and the stub is written in the directory it points at. ze show agent skill reports, for every harness the plugin knows, whether it was found and the stub's state (current, outdated, missing, foreign), and changes nothing. ze delete agent skill removes a stub Ze wrote and its emptied directory. Without agent it acts on every harness found, as agent all does, and agent <name> limits it to one harness. With one harness named, the shared stub stays while another harness found on the machine still reads it, and the answer names that harness. Each command answers one row per harness and item; the hook rows of OpenCode and Pi answer unsupported, because Ze knows no session-start hook format for them. For Claude Code an
