Build and install on Ubuntu: compile, install, initialize the store, and start SSH. Docker: build the image, keep state across recreation, and manage it with Compose. VM and gokrazy appliance: build and boot a disk image or installer ISO. containerlab and netlab: run the supplied topology with the lab image. CLI tour: use interactive, one-shot, pipe, and runtime commands. Configuration: understand the hierarchical configuration format. Lifecycle and rollback: reload, restart, archive, update, and recover. Also in this section: Command reference, Configuration editor, Config archive, Operations, Self-update, and Environment variables. Routing BGP peering: configure peers, groups, families, and capabilities. BGP policy: build import, export, validation, and redistribution policy. BGP resilience: configure refresh, graceful restart, persistence, reflection, and multipath. OSPF, IS-IS, and static routes: bring routing protocols online. BFD: configure fast failure detection. MPLS and RSVP-TE: configure label switching and traffic engineering. Also in this section: Route filters and redistribution, Route injection, RPKI origin validation, IRR prefix filtering, Graceful restart, ADD-PATH, BGP role (RFC 9234), BGP healthcheck, Policy routing, and VRRP. Services and security Firewall and policy routing: protect and steer traffic. FlowSpec protected router: translate FlowSpec into local protection. DDoS mitigation: detect floods and respond locally or upstream. PPPoE, L2TP, and IPsec: configure access and tunnel services. Authentication, authorization, RADIUS, and TACACS+: secure operator access. Also in this section: Traffic control, VPP data plane, FlowSpec route reflector, Behavioral anomaly detection, AS112, and Operator access with SSH and RBAC. Interfaces and automation Use Ze with an AI agent: set up Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode or Pi with ze create agent skill. REST and gRPC: use authenticated management APIs. gNMI: use Capabilities, Get, Set, and Subscribe. Web interface: edit configuration and run commands in the browser. MCP: connect tools, resources, and remote clients. Fleet configuration: distribute configuration to managed nodes. Also in this section: Plugins, Looking Glass, and Public Looking Glass. Diagnose, observe, and test System readiness: run offline doctor checks and inspect runtime health. Production diagnostics: start from symptoms and debug safely. Monitoring: configure flow export, MRT, and operational checks. Debugging tools: trace netlink, capture packets, and inspect state. Logging and audit: inspect operational and security history. Also in this section: BMP, Flow export, MRT analysis, Traffic usage, Benchmarking, and Chaos testing. Use site search for a specific protocol, command, or configuration leaf.

title: ADD-PATH and PATHS-LIMIT
text: ADD-PATH and PATHS-LIMIT ADD-PATH (RFC 7911) allows multiple paths per prefix by including a Path Identifier with each NLRI. Route servers use it to forward all available paths rather than one best path. PATHS-LIMIT (draft-abraitis-idr-addpath-paths-limit-04) lets a receiver request a maximum number of paths per prefix per family. Ze enforces the peer's negotiated limit on outbound routes, sending the paths bgp-rib ranks best, and enforces its own advertised limit on the routes it receives. Configuration All ADD-PATH and PATHS-LIMIT config lives under session > capability > add-path. Default Direction and Limit Enable ADD-PATH for all negotiated families, with an optional default path count limit: capability { add-path { direction send/receive; limit { receive 10; } } } The limit container holds one path count per direction. Only receive exists: the number of paths per prefix Ze asks the peer to send. The container's receive is inherited by all families, and a per-family entry can override it. Per-Family Override Override direction, set path count limits, or set negotiation mode per family: capability { add-path { direction send; family { ipv4/unicast { direction send/receive; limit { receive 10; } } ipv6/unicast { direction receive; mode require; } } } } A family entry can carry no block at all. family { ipv4/unicast; } takes the container direction and the container receive limit. A bare entry adds no family when the container states no direction. Full Example bgp { router-id 192.0.2.1; peer transit-a { connection { remote { ip 10.0.0.1; } local { ip 10.0.0.2; } } session { asn { local 65000; remote 65001; } capability { add-path { direction send/receive; family { ipv4/unicast { limit { receive 10; } } } } } family { ipv4/unicast { prefix { maximum 1000; } } ipv6/unicast { prefix { maximum 1000; } } } } } } Direction and Mode Direction Meaning send Advertise multiple paths to peer receive Accept multiple paths from peer send/receive Both directions Mode Meaning enable (default) Negotiate ADD-PATH if peer supports it require Reject peer if it does not support ADD-PATH refuse Reject peer if it advertises ADD-PATH disable Do not negotiate ADD-PATH for this family PATHS-LIMIT The limit { receive N; } setting advertises a PATHS-LIMIT capability (code 76) for the family. The value (1-65535) requests the maximum number of paths per prefix Ze wants to receive. The scalar spelling limit 10; was removed. Ze refuses a config that still carries it, and the error names the line to write instead: limit { receive VALUE; }. The peer is asked to honor this limit, and Ze also enforces it on what arrives: see Inbound Enforcement. It does not set Ze's outbound limit. Setting Effect No effective receive Ze requests no path count limit for that family limit { receive 10; } Request at most 10 paths per prefix from the peer limit { receive 1; } Request one path per prefix, still with ADD-PATH identifiers receive under mode disable Ze advertises no limit for the family. A limit reaches the wire only for a family Ze advertises in ADD-PATH receive on a family whose direction is send Ze advertises no limit for the family. A limit reaches the wire only for a family whose ADD-PATH direction includes receive The peer's nonzero limit applies only when Ze negotiates ADD-PATH send for that family. Ze's local limit applies only to negotiated ADD-PATH receive. An absent limit or an unnegotiated ADD-PATH direction imposes no PATHS-LIMIT restriction. Inbound Enforcement The receive limit Ze advertises is also the ceiling it applies to the paths it accepts. A peer that ignores capability 76 (BIRD has no support for it) cannot grow Ze's Adj-RIB-In past the number Ze asked for. Ze counts distinct path IDs for each AFI/SAFI and prefix on the session, with the same route identity as outbound enforcement. Event Effect New path below the limit Admit the path and count its ID New path at the limit Drop that path only. Every other route in the same UPDATE installs normally Replacement with an admitted path ID Accept the replacement without consuming another slot Withdrawal of an admitted path ID Remove the ID and free its slot Withdrawal of a refused path ID Accept it. It frees no slot, because it never held one UPDATE whose only paths were all refused Consume it without delivering anything; the session stays up Session reconnect Start with an empty count The check runs after RFC 7606 error handling and before the prefix limits (prefix { maximum N; }), so a prefix limit counts the UPDATE without its refused paths. When a prefix limit then drops the UPDATE, the path count is restored to what it was before it. The withdrawals RFC 7606 treat-as-withdraw produces free slots like any other withdrawal. Selection is by arrival order: the first paths admitted keep their slots, and a better path that arrives later is dropped until a withdrawal frees a slot. Ze does not hold a dropped path for later; the peer must announce it again. Each refused path increments ze_bgp_paths_limit_refused_total{peer,family}. The first refusal for a route logs one warning naming the peer, family, limit, route and path ID; further refusals for that route are counted but not logged until the peer withdraws a refused path. Ze tracks at most one refused path ID per route beyond the limit, so a peer cannot decide how much memory this costs. A limit configured on a family whose ADD-PATH direction does not include receive is neither advertised nor enforced. Outbound Enforcement Ze counts distinct advertised path IDs for each AFI/SAFI and prefix on the destination connection. The count persists across UPDATE messages and batches. All normal send and forwarding paths share this count, including route-server fast-path forwarding. The count uses each family's route identity, not its forwarding fields. Labels do not create a new labeled IP prefix; VPN route distinguishers do. EVPN, VPLS, and MUP omit their non-key forwarding fields. Insignificant prefix padding cannot create another slot. Event Effect New path below the limit Admit the path and count its ID New path at the limit Suppress the announcement and mark the prefix contested Replacement with an admitted path ID Send the replacement without consuming another slot Withdrawal of an admitted path ID Remove the ID and free its slot Destination reconnect Start with an empty count for the new connection Best paths under the peer's limit Arrival order fills the slots first, but it does not decide what the peer keeps. When a path is suppressed at the limit, or a slot of a contested prefix is released, Ze asks bgp-rib to rank the prefix's paths and sends the best ones in place of the first arrivals. The election runs on the destination's recovery worker, never on the write path, and repeated contests of one prefix merge into one election. Step What the peer sees A held path the RIB no longer ranks among the best A withdrawal of its path ID A better path that was suppressed An announcement under its own path ID, sent after the withdrawal that freed its slot A held path the RIB still ranks among the best Nothing: it keeps its slot and its path ID A path Ze originates itself Nothing: the RIB does not rank it, so it keeps its slot and the election fills only the remaining slots A path graceful restart retains for a source whose session ended Nothing: it keeps its slot. When the source is back and the RIB ranks the retained path among the best, it still counts as one slot, so the next best path fills the rest and the peer receives its full limit Withdrawals always go before the announcements that replace them, so the peer never holds more paths than its limit, not even for one UPDATE. The election needs bgp-rib loaded and attached to every source peer with receive [ update-received ], which a route server or route reflector configuration already has. Without a RIB that can rank the paths, the first paths to arrive keep their slots, each contested prefix increments ze_bgp_paths_limit_elect

title: Use Ze with an AI agent
displayTitle: Use Ze with an AI agent
text: Use Ze with an AI agent If you test Ze with Claude Code or Codex, one command sets the agent up. It installs a skill named ze that sends the agent to the guide your installed ze serves, so the agent works from the version you run. For Claude Code and Codex it also adds a hook, so every new session starts knowing the Ze version, whether the daemon answers, and where the configuration is. Ze is pre-release software. Give the agent a lab, not a live network. Before you start ze must be installed on the machine the agent runs on, and on the path the agent sees: the skill and the hook both run ze. To build and install it, see Quick Start. Check with ze version. Set the agent up Run the command as the user who runs the agent, on the machine the agent runs on: $ ze create agent skill Ze set the ze skill up for each harness below. A refused row names its fix. claude skill: created (harness found) /home/you/.claude/skills/ze/SKILL.md claude hook: created (harness found) /home/you/.claude/settings.json codex skill: created (harness found) /home/you/.agents/skills/ze/SKILL.md Codex, OpenCode and Pi all read this one file. codex hook: created (harness found) /home/you/.codex/hooks.json Codex skips a new or changed hook until you trust it. To trust it, open Codex, run /hooks, and trust the hook that runs ze show agent context. Ze sets up each harness whose configuration directory exists: ~/.claude for Claude Code, ~/.codex for Codex, ~/.config/opencode for OpenCode and ~/.pi for Pi. To set up one harness before its directory exists, name it: ze create agent skill agent codex. When Ze finds no harness, it writes only the shared skill and says so. The command exits 1 when a row is refused, and the row names the fix. Trust the hook in Codex Codex does not run a new or changed hook until you trust it. Open Codex, run /hooks, and trust the hook that runs ze show agent context. Do this again when a later ze create agent skill updates the hook. Ze never writes Codex's trust store, so ze show agent skill can say the hook is installed, but it can not say whether Codex trusts it. What to ask the agent first Ask it to use the ze skill, for example "use the ze skill and check my configuration". The agent reads the guide itself: the skill sends it to ze show skill ze, the guide built into your ze, which names the entry points (configuration validation, diagnostic codes, repair plans and the command reference from ze help ai --json). ze show skills lists the other guides the binary carries, and the agent loads the one its task needs with ze show skill <name>. The guides come from the binary, so they change when you upgrade it. What changed on your machine File What Ze put there ~/.claude/skills/ze/SKILL.md The ze skill, for Claude Code ~/.claude/settings.json A session-start hook that runs ze show agent context ~/.agents/skills/ze/SKILL.md The ze skill that Codex, OpenCode and Pi read ~/.codex/hooks.json The same session-start hook, for Codex When CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR is set, both Claude Code files are under that directory. When CODEX_HOME is set, only Codex's hooks.json moves there: the skill Codex reads stays at ~/.agents/skills/ze/SKILL.md. Ze adds its hook to the settings file and leaves the rest of the file as it was. OpenCode and Pi get the skill only, because Ze knows no session-start hook format for them. At each session start, the hook adds a few lines like these to the agent's context: ze dev (built unknown) daemon: not answering at 127.0.0.1:2222 (dial tcp 127.0.0.1:2222: connect: connection refused) config directory: /etc/ze guide: the ze skill, read it with ze show skill ze The hook waits at most one second for the daemon and always succeeds. When ze is not on the path the harness sees, the hook prints nothing and the session starts as usual. Check the setup ze show agent skill It reports, for each harness Ze knows, whether Ze found it and the state of its skill and hook. It changes nothing. Run ze create agent skill again after you upgrade Ze: it rewrites what an older version wrote and leaves a current setup as it is. Remove the setup ze delete agent skill It removes only what Ze wrote: a skill file Ze did not write and every hook Ze did not add stay as they are. Without agent it acts on every harness Ze finds, and agent <name> limits it to one. When you name one harness, the shared skill under ~/.agents stays while another harness on the machine still reads it. An agent that reaches a remote router When the agent runs on another machine and reaches Ze over MCP, REST, gRPC, SSH or the web, send the same commands over that connection, for example create agent skill through the ze_execute MCP tool. The router reads and writes nothing. It answers, for each harness, the path relative to your home directory and the skill to write there, on the agent's machine. That skill tells the agent to ask the Ze system it is connected to for show skill ze over the connection it already uses. There is no hook, because the hook needs a local ze. To connect an agent over MCP, see MCP Integration. Details The full behavior of each command (every state a row can answer, how Ze edits the settings files, what it refuses) is in Setting an agent up and Session context. The command reference has one entry per command: create agent skill, show agent skill, delete agent skill and show agent context.

title: Behavioural Anomaly Detection
text: Behavioural Anomaly Detection Pre-Alpha. This page describes behaviour that may change. Ze includes a report-only behavioural anomaly detector. It builds a per-source behavioural baseline, scores how far each source deviates from its own history and from its peers, and correlates weak signals into a single incident. It is separate from the volumetric DDoS subsystem, which reacts to raw packet and bandwidth rates. DDoS detects interface floods. Anomaly detection detects sources behaving unlike themselves and unlike their neighbours. For the volumetric subsystem, see DDoS detection and mitigation. Traffic-feature facts layer Both detectors read from a neutral facts layer. trafficfeature is a second, independent consumer of the observation feed that derives domain-neutral per-source feature signals. These are measurable facts rather than verdicts. Detection plugins apply judgement on top, and this layer never decides that traffic is an attack. Feature Meaning fan-out Count of distinct destinations a source talked to in the window, used as a scanning or spread signal out-in-ratio Outbound bytes divided by inbound bytes for the source, used as an exfiltration signal; a pure sender with no inbound bytes is surfaced as inf port-entropy Shannon entropy, in bits, of the source's destination-port byte distribution; near 0 for a single port, higher for a scan new-peer The source was first observed within the recent new-peer window rare-port The source's dominant destination port is outside the well-known allowlist beaconing Interval-regularity score in [0,1] over the source's flow arrival times; higher is more clock-like and can indicate a C2 beacon The service is lazy and consumer-refcounted, so it costs nothing until a consumer attaches. It aggregates on a one-second tick and bounds memory with per-source cardinality and idle-eviction caps. Operators can read it directly: show traffic feature show traffic feature 203.0.113.7 // one source The output lists the top source IPs by activity with their feature vector and a degraded flag when no data has arrived yet. How detection scores a source Each tick, the detector folds one traffic-feature snapshot into per-source, per-feature baselines and scores every source in two ways: Self-deviation. A z-score of the current value above the source's own running mean, in units of standard deviation, from an EWMA baseline. Below-baseline values score zero because only excess is anomalous. Each feature has a standard-deviation floor so a near-constant feature does not produce a divide-by-tiny-variance spike. Cohort rarity. How far the value sits above the source's cohort, other sources in the same source-prefix bucket. It is computed leave-one-out so an outlier is never compared against a baseline it dominates. Rarity is scored only once the cohort has at least min-cohort-size other members. A continuous feature fires at the larger of its self-deviation and cohort-rarity score when that reaches deviation-threshold. The binary features, new-peer and rare-port, each contribute exactly one unit of evidence, enough to satisfy the correlation gate without dominating a continuous signal. Correlation into one incident A source is anomalous for a tick only when at least min-features-to-correlate features fire together. The fired z-scores are fused into one incident score: the strongest at full weight plus a discounted sum of the rest through corroboration-weight. The score is capped so a benign multi-feature move cannot saturate into a critical incident. The incident carries a graded severity derived from the score. Confirm and clear lifecycle An incident is confirmed only after confirm-duration consecutive anomalous ticks and cleared only after clear-consecutive consecutive normal ticks. This drives an AnomalyDetected, AnomalyOngoing, and AnomalyCleared event stream plus a bounded recent-incident ring. Poisoning and false-positive guards Freeze-learn. The per-source baseline is updated with the current tick only when the source is not anomalous, or while it is still warming up. A sustained attack cannot drift the source's baseline upward until it looks normal again. No first-sight false positive. A newly seen source has no baseline to deviate from. Self-deviation is suppressed until the baseline has accumulated a short warmup of samples. Early values seed the baseline before the detector can flag the source. Viewing anomaly incidents show anomaly detect The command reports whether the detector is enabled and lists the recent-incident ring. Each incident includes the entity, cohort, fused score and severity, timestamp, and fired features with their z-scores. The detector records confirmations, so the ring says when each incident started and never says when it ended. Incident lifecycle store The anomaly-observe plugin keeps the other half: it opens a record when an incident is confirmed and closes it with an end time when the incident clears, so a finished incident has a readable duration. anomaly { observe { incident-ring-size 1000; // incidents retained in memory stale-incident-timeout 3600; // seconds before an open incident is closed anyway } } The store is always on when the plugin is loaded, and an empty observe {} block takes both defaults. Three properties matter to an operator: A finished incident stays visible. Finalized records remain in the ring with their end time until the ring evicts them, which is what makes a duration readable at all. The ring is bounded. At most incident-ring-size records are held. When it is full the oldest finalized record is dropped first, so the incident still in progress is never the one lost. An incident that never clears is still closed. A source that goes silent is evicted by the detector without a clear event. Any record left open longer than stale-incident-timeout is finalized by a one-second sweep, so the active count cannot climb forever. Read the lifecycle with: show anomaly observe The output reports whether the plugin is running, how many incidents are still active, and the ring newest-first. Each record carries the entity, cohort, fired features, score, severity, start time, active flag, and, once the incident is over, its end time. Shadow-first responder The anomaly-shape responder can act on confirmed incidents. It defaults to shadow mode, where it logs the action it would take and installs nothing. Set it explicitly to armed before it can alter traffic. anomaly { shape { mode shadow; // default; armed installs live per-source rules action limit; // rate-limit (default) or drop limit-rate 1000; limit-unit second; auto-revert-ttl 300; blast-radius-cap 16; allowlist [ 192.0.2.0/24 ]; } } When armed, it installs a per-source firewall rule, a rate limit by default or a drop, for the anomalous source. Its safety properties are: Per-entity arming. Each source is armed independently as a whole owner set. Re-arming an already armed source refreshes its timer without reinstalling or double-counting. Timed auto-revert. Every armed rule carries an auto-revert-ttl. The rule is withdrawn when the TTL elapses regardless of any clear event, and an ongoing incident extends the deadline. A cleared incident withdraws the rule early. Blast-radius cap. At most blast-radius-cap sources are armed at once. Beyond the cap, arming is refused and logged. Kill switch. Engaging the kill switch reverts every armed rule and forces the responder back to shadow. Allowlist. Sources in the allowlist are never armed. Inspect the responder state with: show anomaly shape The output reports the mode, configured action, kill-switch state, armed count, and armed sources. Configuration reference anomaly detect Parameter Default Range Description enabled false bool Enable the detector deviation-threshold 3.0 1.0-100.0 Sigma at or above which a feature fires min-features-to-correlate 2 1-6 Features that must fire together to form an incident min-cohort-size 4 2-1024 Minimum other cohort members before rarity is scored cor

title: REST and gRPC API
text: REST and gRPC API Ze exposes a programmatic API over REST (HTTP/JSON) and gRPC. Both transports share one engine -- they produce identical command output and support the same commands. Quick Start Enable REST in your config: environment { api-server { rest { enabled true; server { ip 127.0.0.1; port 8081; } } } } REST uses plaintext HTTP and only binds loopback addresses. Use authenticated gRPC with TLS for management from a non-loopback address. Or via environment variable: ze.api-server.rest.enabled=true ze.api-server.rest.listen=127.0.0.1:8081 Query the API: curl http://localhost:8081/api/v1/commands curl -X POST http://localhost:8081/api/v1/execute \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"command":"show bgp"}' Open interactive docs: http://localhost:8081/api/v1/docs Authentication Ze selects one of three API authentication modes: Mode User or token source Client credentials Per-user A zefs user or a system.authentication.user entry Authorization: Bearer username:password Single token ze.api-server.token or YANG api-server { token "secret"; } Authorization: Bearer <secret> No auth No users and no token No header, with read-only authority Per-user mode has precedence. If at least one user exists, the shared token does not act as a fallback for a failed per-user login. The per-user source merges managed-store users with system.authentication.user entries from the running config. A config user replaces a stored user with the same name. Only stored users that survive this merge keep the recovery profile. A successful login carries its authorization view with the authenticated request. Concurrent requests with the same username cannot replace each other's resolved profiles. At boot, Ze reads the merged user source once after it populates the config provider. Ze refuses startup before management listeners bind if that read fails. An environment.ssh block is not required for API users or no-BGP AAA. Each request uses the current accepted authentication generation. A successful reload publishes one generation that adds, changes, or removes API users and authorization policy atomically. The generation includes profile definitions and user-profile assignments. A failed reload keeps the prior credentials and policy. The zefs user list stays the boot snapshot. Per-user requests keep the authenticated username and the authorizer from that authentication result. Single-token and no-auth requests use a reserved server-injected identity. A valid shared token has write authority. A no-auth request stays read-only, so Ze denies writes before command authorization. Startup output and remedies Ze writes one of these exact lines when an API server is configured: API auth mode: per-user (1 users) API auth mode: single-token (shared bearer) warning: API auth mode: NONE (no users, no token) -- set ze.api-server.token or run ze init The per-user count includes surviving zefs users and config users. To leave single-token or NONE mode, add a config user or run ze init. To keep shared credentials, set ze.api-server.token. REST Endpoints Command execution Method Path Description GET /api/v1/commands List all commands with metadata GET /api/v1/commands/{path} Describe one command (e.g., /bgp/summary) POST /api/v1/execute Execute any command GET /api/v1/execute/stream?command=... Stream a registered streaming command, for example monitor event, as Server-Sent Events. It uses the same handler registry, authorization, and accounting path as SSH monitor commands. GET /api/v1/complete?partial=... Tab completion (future) A plugin command registered with Hidden true is absent from /api/v1/commands, as it is from completion, from help, and from the MCP tool list. buildCommandMeta is the one source those surfaces read, so the flag has one meaning everywhere. Each command in the list, and the object that /api/v1/commands/{path} returns, carries the keys name, short-help, description, read-only and params. Each entry in params carries name, type, short-help, description, required, anchor and flag: anchor names the command-path keyword the value follows, and flag is true when the keyword alone supplies the argument. Empty short-help, description, params and anchor values, and a false flag, are omitted. read-only and required are always sent. { "name": "show bgp rib", "short-help": "Show routes", "read-only": true, "params": [{"name": "family", "type": "string", "required": false}] } POST /api/v1/execute body: { "command": "show bgp rib", "params": {"family": "ipv4/unicast"} } The optional pipe list applies pipe operations to the answer, in order, as if typed after the command. This body answers what show bgp rib | received | count answers: { "command": "show bgp rib", "pipe": [{"name": "received"}, {"name": "count"}] } Each element holds a name and an optional args array, one word per element ({"name": "match", "args": ["link down"]} matches the two words as one). A name that is not one of the command's pipe operations is refused, and the refusal lists the valid ones; show command help "<command>" lists them too. An element key other than name and args is refused. Response: { "status": "done", "data": { ... } } Convenience routes Most convenience routes map to the generic Execute endpoint internally. The refresh row gives the required generic Execute command instead. Method Path Maps to GET /api/v1/peers show bgp GET /api/v1/peers/{name} show bgp peer {name} detail DELETE /api/v1/peers/{name} request peer {name} teardown POST /api/v1/peers/{name}/refresh Use /api/v1/execute with request peer {name} refresh {family} GET /api/v1/rib/{family} show bgp rib | family {family} GET /api/v1/rib/{family}/best show bgp rib best | family {family} GET /api/v1/system/version show version GET /api/v1/system/status show status POST /api/v1/system/reload request reload Config editing Method Path Description GET /api/v1/config/running The configuration the daemon applied, from memory (show config running). After a refused reload it still answers the config in force, not the file. Secret values are replaced with a placeholder POST /api/v1/config/sessions Start a candidate session, returns {"session-id": "..."} PUT /api/v1/config/sessions/{id} Set a value: {"path":"bgp.router-id","value":"10.0.0.1"} DELETE /api/v1/config/sessions/{id}/{path} Delete a config path GET /api/v1/config/sessions/{id}/diff Preview pending changes POST /api/v1/config/sessions/{id}/commit Apply changes DELETE /api/v1/config/sessions/{id} Discard session Sessions are owned by the authenticated user. Another user cannot access a session they did not create (returns 403 Forbidden). Idle sessions expire after 30 minutes. While a commit confirmed window is open, a session commit is refused for every user with the window's refusal naming its owner and the seconds left, and the session stays open for a retry once the window is accepted or aborted (config-editor.md, "Commit Confirmed"). Session commits apply one at a time. A commit that arrives while another is being applied waits its turn, then applies as its own commit with its own version in the config history, so two commits land in arrival order and both answer {"status":"committed"}. Each session commits the whole candidate it built, so the later commit replaces what the earlier one changed wherever the two sessions edited the same value. No-auth REST/gRPC callers cannot create config sessions. Configure a token or per-user authentication for API-driven config changes. A session refuses a new list key that its YANG type does not accept before changing the candidate. The answer lists the accepted keys with their help and ends with the complete corrected set command, including the setting and value after the key. For example, setting ospf.redistribute.bogus.nssa-propagate to true proposes fix: set ospf redistribute <connected|static|kernel|bgp|isis> nssa-propagate true. REST answers HTTP 400, and gRPC answers InvalidArgument. gNMI Set uses the same editor and answers InvalidArgume

title: VM Appliance
text: VM Appliance Build a bootable VM image with Ze baked in using gokrazy. The default target is x86_64, and image.arch in appliance.json selects another architecture for ./ze-host appliance build. At runtime, the appliance is minimal: Linux kernel, gokrazy init, and Ze as the only application, with no package manager, no general shell (except authenticated emergency serial console), no unused distro daemons, and automatic process supervision. Suitable for N100-class mini PCs, Proxmox VMs, or QEMU testing. Prepare the build-host command Work from the Ze source checkout with Go and Git installed. Build the native host driver and select the patched Go environment before the image commands: ./le build host-driver GOROOT="$(./le go stdpatch goroot)" export GOROOT GOTOOLCHAIN=local PATH="$GOROOT/bin:$PATH" The examples below use ./ze-host, which runs on the build machine and carries the appliance and PXE provisioning commands. The ordinary ./ze launcher builds the Linux daemon; it does not carry appliance. Build kernels and cold-cache images on a host matching the image architecture. Binaries can be cross-built, but selecting another image.arch does not make a foreign kernel build possible. What's in the image Component Purpose Linux kernel Boot and hardware drivers gokrazy init Starts Ze, supervises it, seeds entropy, sends watchdog heartbeat Ze BGP daemon with DHCP client and all internal plugins ze-serial-shell Authenticated emergency shell on serial console (login required) Ze owns network configuration in the appliance. The gokrazy default DHCP and NTP packages are excluded from the image; the shipped Ze seed template enables interface DHCP auto-discovery with set interface dhcp-auto true and leaves Ze NTP disabled (set environment ntp enabled false) until the operator enables it in Ze config. The root filesystem is read-only (SquashFS). Persistent data lives on a separate ext4 partition mounted at /perm. Prerequisites Install once on the build machine. macOS: brew install e2fsprogs # ext4 filesystem tools brew install qemu # VM runtime (testing only) Linux: sudo apt-get install -y e2fsprogs qemu-system-x86 # Debian, Ubuntu sudo dnf install -y e2fsprogs qemu-system-x86 # Fedora The build needs mkfs.ext4 and debugfs from e2fsprogs. If e2fsck is available, the builder also checks ext4 structure; otherwise it warns and skips that check. The native builder resolves each tool independently from the Homebrew keg, standard sbin directories, and PATH. For appliance ISO creation, install grub-mkstandalone (or grub2-mkstandalone) with the GRUB EFI modules for the target (x86_64-efi or arm64-efi), plus xorriso. ./ze-host appliance iso checks those tools and modules before it stages an ISO. On macOS, build the ISO on a Linux host: see ISO prerequisites. The vendored gokrazy command (github.com/gokrazy/tools/gok) runs in process. ./ze-host appliance build calls it directly. A developer runs it with ./le build gokrazy <gok args>, which uses the checked-in module cache, forbids network module lookups, and builds overwrite from a prepared copy of the instance under tmp/. No separate gokrazy installation or first-party script is required. The image's ze compiles only against Ze's patched standard library, so the build runs under the patched GOROOT. ./le build gokrazy inherits it from le. ./ze-host appliance build refuses unless its environment already selects it: GOROOT set to the tree, GOTOOLCHAIN=local, and $GOROOT/bin/go first on PATH. The refusal ends with the command line that sets all three: GOROOT="$(./le go stdpatch goroot)" && export GOROOT GOTOOLCHAIN=local PATH="$GOROOT/bin:$PATH" && ./ze-host appliance build <name> First-time setup Initialize the named appliance before its first build: ./ze-host appliance init edge-01 The build resolves pinned system packages through the Go module graph. Runtime Kernel Requirements The runtime kernel is pinned by two manifests, gokrazy/kernel/kernel.require and gokrazy/kernel/runtime.require. Each is checked against the resolved config after the build, and enforce_required_symbols accepts =y alone. A Kconfig answer of m therefore fails the BUILD rather than shipping an appliance where a feature Ze accepts in config cannot work. Runtime images also package the matching module tree; a module from a stock distribution is not a substitute for that kernel's modules. Each symbol has a producer in Ze rather than a test that wanted it. Group Symbols Producer in Ze Subscriber PPP, PPPOL2TP, PPPOE, L2TP, L2TP_V3 The L2TP LNS, and the PPPoE server and client Firewall NF_TABLES, NF_TABLES_INET, NF_TABLES_IPV4, NF_TABLES_IPV6, NF_CONNTRACK, NF_NAT, NFT_CT, NFT_NAT, NFT_MASQ, NFT_REDIR, NFT_LIMIT, NFT_LOG, NFT_REJECT, NF_FLOW_TABLE, NF_FLOW_TABLE_INET, NFT_FLOW_OFFLOAD The nftables backend, and translatePolicy (internal/plugins/copp/translate.go), which returns FamilyInet unconditionally. Without NF_TABLES_INET the kernel answers EOPNOTSUPP, Apply's flush fails, the firewall plugin fails startup, and the daemon exits. The three flowtable symbols carry a table's flowtable and a term's flow-offload action (applyFlowtable); without them the kernel answers ENOENT and refuses the whole table Tunnels NET_IPGRE_DEMUX, NET_IPGRE, IPV6_GRE, NET_IPIP, IPV6_TUNNEL, IPV6_SIT, VXLAN The nine tunnel kinds ze-iface-conf.yang models. Six symbols plus the GRE demux gate. Measured cost: vmlinuz 16352256 to 16450560 bytes, +0.60% SRv6 IPV6_SEG6_LWTUNNEL The kernel FIB backend's Service SID routes: buildSEG6Encap (internal/plugins/fib/kernel/nexthop_linux.go) installs each RFC 9252 service route as a seg6 encap-mode lightweight tunnel. Without it the kernel answers EOPNOTSUPP and no SRv6 service route is installed Policy routing IP_MULTIPLE_TABLES, IPV6_MULTIPLE_TABLES, IP_ROUTE_MULTIPATH The policy-routing engine. Without IPV6_MULTIPLE_TABLES the kernel folds every table id into the main table and says nothing Traffic control NET_SCH_HTB, TBF, FQ_CODEL, HFSC, FQ, SFQ, NETEM, PRIO, INGRESS, NET_CLS_U32, NET_CLS_FW, NET_CLS_MATCHALL, NET_ACT_MIRRED, NET_ACT_POLICE Class of service, rate limiting, and mirroring; subscriber upload rates use the police action through shaper.applyTC and ingressPolicerFilter Interfaces and VPN DUMMY, VETH, MACVLAN, VLAN_8021Q, INET_ESP, INET6_ESP, XFRM_STATISTICS, HUGETLBFS, BPF_SYSCALL, BPF_JIT Interface creation, IPsec, VPP hugepages, and the eBPF surfaces IPsec and WireGuard XFRM_USER, XFRM_INTERFACE, XFRM_MIGRATE, INET_AH, INET6_AH, WIREGUARD, CRYPTO_CBC, CRYPTO_DES, CRYPTO_NULL, CRYPTO_GCM, CRYPTO_CHACHA20POLY1305, CRYPTO_SHA1, CRYPTO_SHA256, CRYPTO_SHA512 Every SA install (XFRM netlink), route-based IPsec, MOBIKE, OSPFv3 authentication, WireGuard links, and one symbol for each ESP transform Ze can install, so every cipher Ze accepts in config is carried by the kernel CONFIG_NET_UDP_TUNNEL and CONFIG_TUN are =y in the config fragment and are not pinned in a manifest. Hardware drivers The appliance kernel holds some drivers in the kernel itself and loads the others from the image when the device is present. Kind Where the driver is Examples Virtual NICs and disks In the kernel virtio network and block devices, the Xen guest network and block devices Storage and boot devices In the kernel NVMe, SATA/AHCI, SCSI disks, USB storage, the console Every networking feature Ze configures In the kernel Routing, firewall, IPsec, WireGuard, MPLS, traffic control, PPP/L2TP, tunnels Physical hardware Loaded when the device is present Physical NICs and their PHYs, wireless, sound, Intel graphics, board sensors A networking feature never waits for a driver to load. A virtual machine loads no driver for hardware it does not have. The load happens one time, when Ze starts. Ze reads which devices are present, loads the driver of each one, and only then lists the interfaces. Ze does not watch for new devices after that: A card added while the appliance runs has no driver and no interface. Its driver loads the next time Ze starts. A device that r

title: AS112
text: AS112 Ze's as112 plugin runs an AS112 anycast DNS node: an authoritative sink for misdirected RFC 1918 and link-local reverse-DNS queries (RFC 7534), plus the EMPTY.AS112.ARPA DNAME-redirection sink (RFC 7535). It answers on four fixed anycast host addresses, so the plugin config never needs an operator-supplied service IP. Quick Start service { as112 { enabled true hostname "node1.example.net" } } This is the full config for the DNS node. The four canonical addresses (192.175.48.1, 192.31.196.1, 2620:4f:8000::1, 2001:4:112::1) are Go constants, registered against the interface address-ownership registry and bound on lo automatically, so they are not typed into config. as112 must run as an internal plugin (the default auto-load path, or an explicit plugin { internal as112 { use as112; } }). It must not run as plugin { external as112 { ... } }. The address-ownership registration is a same-process call into the iface engine; as a forked subprocess, it would register against its own copy of that state and never reach the kernel. as112 refuses to start and logs an error if it detects it is not running in-process. Configuration Reference All leaves go under service { as112 { ... } }. Leaf Type Default Description enabled boolean false Enable the AS112 anycast DNS node. address-family enumeration both both, ipv4-only, or ipv6-only. Restricts the service to one address family (RFC 7534 §3.4 / RFC 7535 §3.1 single-stack option). hostname string (0-63) (empty) Node-identification string surfaced in HOSTNAME.AS112.NET/ARPA TXT answers, so operators can tell which anycast instance answered a query. Empty omits the TXT string. facility string (0-100) (empty) Facility/site name surfaced alongside location in the HOSTNAME TXT answer. location string (0-100) (empty) City/country surfaced alongside facility. allow-from leaf-list (ip-prefix) (empty = answer all) Optional client-source access list. When non-empty, only queries from a listed prefix are answered; the rest are silently dropped. Loopback/on-box sources are always permitted, so request as112 healthcheck is never blocked. Setting this makes the node non-public, which is correct for a local-use mirror and wrong for a globally-reachable AS112 contributor. asn asn (1-4294967295) 112 Origin AS the covering prefixes carry when redistributed into BGP (import as112). Defaults to the well-known AS112 number 112, since the source models an AS112 virtual router. Set an operator or RFC 6996 private ASN to originate under a coordinated or local-use AS. Ignored unless import as112 is configured. community leaf-list (string) (empty) Optional BGP communities on the redistributed covering prefixes. Accepts AA:NN and well-known names (no-export, nopeer; RFC 1997/3765), the values RFC 7534 §3.4 recommends for restricting AS112 route propagation. Ignored unless import as112 is configured. watchdog boolean true Health-gate the BGP announcement on DNS serving state (RFC 7534 §3.3). true (default) announces only while the node is serving and withdraws on serving loss, enabled false, or shutdown; false announces as soon as enabled and imported. Ignored unless import as112 is configured. The combined hostname+facility+location TXT payload is bounded so the assembled HOSTNAME.AS112.* response always fits 512 octets with TC=0, even at every field's maximum length (RFC 7534 §3.5). allow-from is the recommended way to restrict a local-use mirror to known client ranges. Set it directly in service { as112 { ... } } rather than hand-authoring firewall section rules matching UDP/TCP port 53 across all four anycast addresses (two per family). Keeping access control in the plugin avoids splitting one policy decision across two subsystems, and the loopback/on-box carve-out is never blocked, which a hand-authored firewall rule would have to replicate correctly. The on-box carve-out recognises both loopback and the node's own four anycast addresses as sources. The healthcheck probe deliberately queries the real anycast address rather than loopback; see BGP Integration. Unlike loopback, the anycast addresses are ordinary public IPs that a remote sender could forge as a UDP source, so a query claiming to originate from the node's own address bypasses allow-from. This does not enable data exfiltration because replies go to the real address rather than the spoofed one, but allow-from should not be the only access control against a source willing to spoof the node's own addresses. Answer Policy Every AS112 zone holds its records at the apex and nothing below it (RFC 7534 §3.5), so where the query name sits decides the response code. Query RCODE AA Authority section Opcode other than a standard query (inverse query, server status, notify, update) 4 Not Implemented (RFC 1035 §6.4) set empty Name under no served zone 5 Refused (RFC 1035 §4.1.1) clear empty Name inside a served zone, below its apex 3 Name Error (RFC 1035 §4.1.1) set zone SOA Zone apex, query type the zone holds no record for 0 No Error, empty Answer set zone SOA Sinking the reverse-DNS query for a private address is exactly the statement that the name does not exist, which is what RFC 7534 §3.5 has these empty zones make. A Refused reply carries no authority, because the node holds no zone for that namespace. The SOA in the Authority section is what RFC 2308 §3 requires so a resolver can cache the negative answer for the 1W the SOA MINIMUM field gives it, which is the point of an AS112 node. The non-query opcode is refused before any zone lookup, so an opcode ze does not serve costs one header. Reply shape and size The shared authoritative harness owns the reply shape for as112 and geodns alike. Recursion is never advertised (RA clear), the reserved Z field and the AD bit go out zero (RFC 1035 §4.1.1, RFC 4035 §3.1.6), and no answer path can change them. A reply on a datagram transport is bounded and gets TC when it is shortened. The bound is 512 octets (RFC 1035 §2.3.4) or the larger reassembly buffer the requestor advertised in an OPT record (RFC 6891 §6.2.3). An advertisement below 512 does not lower the bound. A reply on TCP, DoT or DoH is written whole and never carries TC: RFC 1035 §4.2.1 bounds UDP only, and §4.2.2 puts no length ceiling on a stream. CLI Commands Command Description show as112 Node status: enabled, address-family, hostname/facility/location, allow-from count, served zone count, current SOA serial, and the address-registry's health (address-registry-ok; when false, address-registry-error/address-registry-error-at explain the most recent failure to apply the anycast addresses to a kernel interface). request as112 healthcheck [target <ip>] One-shot authoritative query against an anycast service address (or the given target; defaults to the address-family-appropriate loopback). Exit 0 when the expected AS112 answer comes back. This is the tool a healthcheck probe or monitoring script calls, since dig is not on the gokrazy appliance and ze resolve dns cannot target a specific server. BGP Integration (Conditional Origination) AS112 covering prefixes (the /24s and /48s per RFC 7534 §3.4 / RFC 7535 §3.1, NOT the /32,/128 host addresses bound on lo) can be originated into BGP two ways. Both preserve the layering rule: as112 never reads bgp {} config and BGP hardcodes no AS112 knowledge. Path When to use Origin-AS / community control Health gate Redistribute Use when the same ASN, community, and service-state gate should apply to every BGP peer. One import as112 line plus source-level asn/community in the as112 block. Source-level (asn, community leaves), identical on every peer. Process serving-state (watchdog leaf, default true): announce while the DNS node serves. Hand-authored Use when per-peer origin-AS/community, dedicated peer-group policy, or end-to-end anycast-path liveness matters. Per-peer, per-update-block (as-path, community, replace-as). healthcheck probe gating a watchdog update block, which can probe the real anycast path as well as loopback. Redistribut

title: Audit Trail
text: Audit Trail Ze keeps a local structured audit log for operator actions that change state or fail authentication. The log is append-only from the user's point of view: there is a query command, but no command to delete or truncate records. What Is Recorded Action Surfaces config-commit SSH/CLI config editor, web config editor, REST config sessions, gRPC config sessions, gNMI Set config-discard SSH/CLI config editor, web config editor (the Discard button, the web terminal and the CLI bar, discard <path> included), REST config sessions, gRPC config sessions. A rollback in the SSH editor or the web terminal also writes one config-download web GET /config/download config-upload web POST /config/upload, once the uploaded config is applied daemon-reload SIGHUP, and request reload through the daemon on any surface data-key-change delete data key and update data key through the daemon on any surface, which ze data rm and ze data write also send while ze runs data-config-import update data config through the daemon on any surface, which ze data import also sends while ze runs. The detail holds the name and the placeholder in place of the content auth-fail SSH, web, REST, gRPC, gNMI, MCP Each entry has timestamp, actor, remote-addr, surface, action, detail, and outcome fields. detail carries the config diff for commit and discard records when Ze has one. The web terminal's commit confirmed and the CLI bar's commit now record one successful config-commit entry after publication. The detail is the same path-qualified, secret-masked review shown before committing. A refused commit keeps the pending changes and records no successful commit entry. A daemon command records an entry only when it succeeds: a refused or failed command records nothing. Its detail is the command line as typed, with every credential value and the value after content replaced by <redacted>, so a key's bytes never reach the log. A discard record's detail lists only the changes that discard dropped. discard <path> keeps your changes outside that path, so they are not in its record, and they appear in the commit record that later applies them. One exception: the SSH editor's diff lines carry no path, so when two places hold the same pending line (two peers both changed to the same hold time, say) and discard <path> drops one of them, the SSH record can also name the line you kept. The web records are exact. A whole discard run with nothing pending still writes a record, with an empty detail, on every surface, so the trail shows every discard an operator ran. A rollback record's detail is the rollback itself (the command in the web terminal, rollback <backup> in the SSH editor), a download record's is the file name, and an upload record's is uploaded configuration. Before a whole web discard, Ze opens the user's saved changes to prepare its audit detail, including after idle eviction. If that open fails, discard stops without dropping changes or recording a successful action. For a whole web discard, an empty detail means a successful read found no pending intent for that user. Storage For a daemon started from a real config file, the audit log is stored next to that file as <config-base>.audit.jsonl. For stdin configs (ze -) and web-only test mode, Ze uses an in-memory audit log. The in-memory query cache keeps the newest records up to the configured retention limit in code. The default is 10,000 entries, with accepted bounds from 100 to 100,000. Each record rewrites the file. When a write fails (a full disk, a directory ze cannot write), the action still goes ahead and the record stays in memory; show doctor reports doctor-audit-record-failed with the file, the error, the time and how many writes failed, whichever surface wrote. The next write that lands rewrites the file with every record still held, and the row clears. Querying Use show audit from the daemon CLI or ze show audit from the shell: ze show audit ze show audit action config-commit ze show audit actor alice ze show audit surface web count 20 ze show audit since 2026-05-24T10:00:00Z until 2026-05-24T11:00:00Z The response is structured data with entries and count. Filters can be combined. Time filters use RFC 3339 timestamps. Authorization Notes Web config mutations now use the same profile authorizer as SSH, API, and MCP command dispatch. A read-only user can still open /show/ pages, but POST /config/set/, add, delete, rename, commit, and discard are denied before the draft is changed. REST and gRPC without a configured token or per-user authenticator use the built-in api identity in read-only mode. Read commands work. Command writes and config sessions return 403. Likewise, unauthenticated loopback gNMI allows Capabilities, Get, and Subscribe, and refuses Set with PermissionDenied.

title: Authentication
text: Authentication Ze supports local operator users defined in the daemon configuration, in addition to the bootstrap super-admin written to the database/ store by ze init. This guide covers adding configured users, hashing their passwords, and connecting with the ze CLI. Two sources of users Source Where stored Created by Used for Bootstrap super-admin database/ store (meta/auth/local/{username,password,authorized-keys}) ze init or named appliance initialization Bootstrap and recovery -- the operator who set the box up YANG users system.authentication.user <name> Config edit Day-to-day operators, auditors, scripts At boot, the daemon resolves both sources and publishes the merged users with their authorization policy as one accepted generation. SSH, web, REST, and gRPC read that live generation. During reload, the old generation remains active through every fallible step; a failed candidate is never published. When a YANG user has the same name as the zefs super-admin, the YANG entry takes precedence and the zefs entry is dropped. This lets operators override the bootstrap password via configuration without a stale zefs hash remaining as a backdoor. Named appliances accept SSH public keys in credentials.ssh-authorized-keys. Each value is a complete plain OpenSSH public-key line for the bootstrap username. Assembly stores them with the local recovery credential, and the daemon reads them into the same accepted identity as its password. A missing or comment-only key file leaves password recovery available. Bootstrap keys must have no authorized_keys options. Ze refuses malformed lines, SSH certificates and restrictions such as from=, command= or restrict. Bootstrap login does not validate certificate expiry, permitted users or critical options. Generate a dedicated plain public key with ssh-keygen -y -f <recovery-private-key> and supply its complete output. Diagnosing bootstrap credentials ze doctor reports doctor-local-admin-credentials when the same credential reader used at boot refuses the local recovery account. An explicitly disabled account is not a fault. Boot also logs the code and repair command and keeps one active warning until a successful read or explicit disable clears it. Keep console access or another working login while repairing credentials. Restore the affected meta/auth/local/ frame from a known backup, then restart the daemon. Select the device's database explicitly: ze data --path <database> write <credential-key> <credential-backup-file> The daemon need not be stopped for the write. While it runs, ze data write sends the frame to it as update data key <key> content <base64>, which writes it through the daemon's own store and records <redacted> in place of the bytes in the audit log and the SSH exec log. That route needs a login the daemon still accepts, and carries at most 195,840 bytes, far more than a credential frame holds. With no working login, stop the daemon and run the same command: it then writes the store directly. The password frame contains a bcrypt hash, not a plaintext password. Restoring an unrelated frame does not repair the reported credential. A store that could not be opened is reported as unchecked rather than as a usable recovery account. Disabling the super-admin Setting meta/instance/admin-disabled to "true" in the database/ store (via admin-enabled: false in the appliance config) disables the super-admin on all surfaces: SSH, web, API, and serial console. The serial console returns "local admin login disabled" and denies access (fail-closed), unlike the missing-database case which grants access for emergency recovery. A backend that will not build is dropped, and the others still answer The table above is about who CAN log in. This is about a backend that never starts. A TACACS+ server declared with no shared secret is one case, and any error while the AAA chain is built is another. That backend is dropped and the rest of the chain composes without it. A user who exists locally still logs in, against the local backend, and the local authorization profiles still govern what they run. The daemon logs the drop at ERROR and keeps running. Which backend answers is the chain's ordinary rule, and it does not change here: The remote backend is asked first, because it sits ahead of local in priority. A REJECT stops the chain. A wrong password at a reachable server does not fall through to your local hash. Any other failure tries the next backend, so an unreachable or unbuildable server reaches the local account. The local password must be right. The fallback is an ACCOUNT, never an open door. No user, no login. Where every backend fails to build there is no chain at all, so nothing can authenticate. ssh is not started: a listener that authenticates nobody is a port rather than a service. Every command is refused for the same reason. When What happens ze config commit, with a chain already running REFUSED. The commit is rolled back and the running chain is kept The same, after a boot that composed no chain Nothing. The rebuild is skipped, so a corrected config needs a restart Boot The broken backend is logged and dropped. What composed answers So a config error you commit is caught, while the same error already in the file at boot is not. Keep a local account that works on a box whose logins come from a central server. ze doctor says so before you find out the hard way: ze doctor --json config router.conf ze show diagnostic doctor-aaa-no-local-fallback It warns where a RADIUS or TACACS+ server is configured and no system.authentication.user is. docs/architecture/aaa-tacacs.md carries the mechanism. Adding a user Step 1: hash a password ze passwd takes plaintext on stdin or via interactive prompt and prints a bcrypt hash to stdout. The hash uses cost 10 (the same as ze init). $ echo "secret" | ze passwd $2a$10$abcdefghijklmnopqrstuABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ012345678 Interactive use prompts twice for confirmation. ze passwd writes a warning to stderr when the password is weak, and prints the hash to stdout anyway with exit code 0: $ echo "secret" | ze passwd warning: weak password (shorter than 8 characters) $2a$10$abcdefghijklmnopqrstuABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ012345678 Step 2: declare the user in YANG Three ways to set the password: Form When to use password "$2a$10$..." You already have a hash (from ze passwd, fleet automation, or a backup) password "$6$..." You migrate an account from another system and keep its SHA-crypt hash (see below) plaintext-password "secret" You want to type the plaintext and let Ze hash it (Junos style) Example using the plaintext form: system { authentication { user alice { plaintext-password "secret" } } } After commit (or ze config set), the persisted file contains only the bcrypt hash; the plaintext-password leaf is removed and never written to disk. This matches Junos's plain-text-password behavior. Migrated accounts keep their SHA-crypt hash An account copied from another system keeps the password its user already has. Put the system's stored hash on password as it is: system { authentication { user alice { password "$6$rounds=656000$examplesalt$..." } } } Ze recognises the format by the hash's prefix: Prefix Format Ze writes it $2a$, $2b$, $2y$ bcrypt yes, from plaintext-password and ze passwd $6$ SHA-crypt with SHA-512, the format of a Linux shadow file no, it only verifies it $5$ SHA-crypt with SHA-256 no, it only verifies it A SHA-crypt hash has the form $6$[rounds=N$]salt$digest. Without a rounds= field the hash uses 5000 rounds. With one, N is between 1000 and 999999999, the salt holds at most 16 characters, and the digest holds 86 characters for $6$ and 43 for $5$. That is the form crypt(3) writes, so a hash copied from a shadow file fits it. Ze stores the hash as given and never hashes it again. ze config validate warns about a value that is neither a bcrypt hash nor a well-formed SHA-crypt hash, and that account cannot log in. Each login runs all of the hash's rounds. A has

title: Authorization
text: Authorization Ze uses profile-based command authorization (RBAC) to control which commands each user can execute. Profiles are defined in the daemon configuration alongside user accounts. Each user is assigned one or more profiles; each profile contains ordered rules that allow or deny commands. Authorization is separate from authentication. Authentication (covered in authentication.md) decides who the user is. Authorization decides what they can do. Concepts Profiles A profile is a named set of authorization rules. Each profile has two sections: Section Governs ReadOnly flag run Operational (read-only) commands: the read verbs show, monitor and resolve, plus the noun-first roots validate, help, system, plugin and rib true edit Configuration (write) commands: clear, set, delete, request, commit, update, create, send, debug, cache, and everything else false The dispatcher classifies commands automatically by their leading verb. You do not choose which section a command falls into. The read verbs are not listed twice. IsReadOnlyPath asks command.IsReadOnlyVerb, which reads the verb's role out of command.Verbs, so a verb whose role changes there changes the section its commands land in. The five noun-first roots predate the verb-first grammar and are the only names this decision holds of its own. Entries Each section contains an ordered list of numbered entries. Each entry has: Field Type Description number uint32 Sequence number controlling evaluation order (lowest first) action allow or deny What to do when this entry matches match string The pattern to match against the command regex boolean If true, match is a Go regular expression. If absent or false, match is a prefix. Default action Each section has a default-action (allow or deny). When no entry matches the command, the default action applies. Evaluation order The dispatcher resolves the command and determines which section applies (run or edit). Entries are evaluated in ascending number order. The first matching entry wins. Its action is the verdict. If no entry matches, default-action applies. When a user has multiple profiles, the profiles are evaluated in assignment order. The first profile with a matching entry wins. If no profile has a matching entry, the first profile's default-action applies. What happens when a backend will not build The rules above assume a chain. Where a BACKEND failed to build, it is dropped and the chain composes from the rest. These rules then still apply. The first authorizer any surviving backend contributed decides. Where the local backend survived, that is the local RBAC store this page describes. A TACACS+ server declared with no shared secret puts a daemon in that state. So does any other error while the chain is built. Where EVERY backend failed there is no chain, and then every command is refused. Nothing was installed to consult, and no session exists to ask: ssh is not started either, because nothing can authenticate. Matching rules Prefix matching (default) When regex is absent or false, the match string is compared as a case-insensitive prefix with word-boundary enforcement. A match string of "show bgp peer" matches: show bgp peer (exact) show bgp peer list (prefix + space boundary) show bgp peer list 10.0.0.1 (prefix + deeper arguments) SHOW BGP PEER list (case insensitive) It does not match: show bgp peering (no word boundary after "peer") show bgp (match string is longer than the command) show bgp peers ("peers" is not "peer" + space) The key insight: prefix matching authorizes the command stem, not the arguments. When you allow "show bgp peer", all arguments that follow (peer names, IP addresses, keywords like detail or routes) are implicitly permitted. This is the standard network OS approach: authorize the command, not every parameter. Regex matching When regex is true, the match string is a Go regular expression (the regexp package syntax). The regex is tested with MatchString, meaning it matches anywhere in the command unless you anchor it with ^ and $. Examples: Pattern Matches Does not match "^show bgp peer (list|summary)( |$)" show bgp peer list, show bgp peer summary, show bgp peer list 10.0.0.1 show bgp peer detail, show bgp peer routes "peer .* show" peer 10.0.0.1 show, peer myrouter show peer 10.0.0.1 list "^restart$" restart restart now "^clear (bgp|counters)" clear bgp peer1, clear counters all clear l2tp session Regex entries are compiled and validated at config load. An invalid regex causes a config validation error. Use prefix matching when you can. It is simpler, faster, and covers most real-world policies. Use regex only when you need to restrict which sub-commands are allowed under a common prefix, or when the command structure requires non-prefix patterns. What string gets matched The authorization check receives the full command as typed by the user, including all arguments, before the dispatcher strips selectors or validates argument types. For peer-scoped commands dispatched through the typed command system, the canonical authorization string prepends "peer" to the command tokens (but not the peer selector value itself). For example, if a plugin dispatches command "show routes" scoped to peer "10.0.0.1", the authorization string is "peer show routes", not "peer 10.0.0.1 show routes". For operational commands entered at the CLI (the common case), the authorization string is exactly what the user typed: show bgp peer list, clear counters, etc. Configuration mode is different, and the next section covers it. Every command now starts with its verb, so profile entries must too. The bare forms that once worked without a verb (bgp summary, system memory, daemon reload) were removed from the command tree. Prefix matching is anchored at the start of the typed string, so an entry whose match is bgp no longer covers show bgp. Review any denylist entry keyed on a bare form: it silently stops covering the command it was written for. Write show bgp, show system, and request reload instead. Configuration mode A configuration change is never authorized by what the user typed. Each change is authorized by a permission string from a fixed table, judged in the edit section. The SSH session editor, the web editor, the web terminal and the REST and gRPC config sessions use the same strings, so one profile entry governs a change on every surface. Editor verb Permission string set, activate config set delete, deactivate config delete commit config commit discard, disconnect config discard rollback config rollback rename config rename copy, insert config add save, load config save configure is never authorized: it only switches the CLI into configuration mode, and an entry that matches configure matches nothing Ze checks. Navigation and display (edit, up, top, show, who, option, help) are not checked, so a read-only user can browse the configuration. run <command> is authorized as the operational command it runs. top <command> is judged as the command it runs, so top set ... needs config set. When the profiles load, Ze logs the warning authz match entry does not match any known command for each prefix entry that matches neither a command nor one of these permission strings, such as a misspelled confg set. An entry config, config commit or config commit client-edge.conf is known and logs nothing. An SSH session that edits another stored configuration than the daemon's own, such as a hub editing a client's configuration with ze config edit client-edge.conf, adds the configuration's name to the string: config commit client-edge.conf. Prefix matching keeps an entry config or config commit covering it, and an entry that names the file restricts that file alone. This profile lets its user change the daemon's configuration and edit client-edge.conf, but refuses a commit of client-edge.conf: edit { default-action allow entry 10 { action deny match "config commit client-edge.conf" } } A refused change prints command restricted by access control: followed by

title: Benchmarking
text: Benchmarking Ze includes le perf, a tool for measuring BGP route propagation latency through a device under test (DUT). It works with any BGP implementation, including Ze. le perf send runs one benchmark against a DUT, le perf compare compares result files, and le perf track follows the history. Every word after the verb reaches the program unchanged, and the program's exit code is le's. Architecture +-----------+ le perf send | | le perf send (sender) ----> | DUT | ----> (receiver) AS 65001 | AS 65000 | AS 65002 +-----------+ The sender establishes a BGP session with the DUT, injects routes, and the receiver measures when those routes arrive. Both sessions are managed by le perf send in a single process. Timing starts when the sender writes the first UPDATE and stops when the receiver has collected all expected prefixes. Quick Start Run a benchmark against Ze on localhost: # Start ze with a config that accepts peers from 127.0.0.1 and 127.0.0.2 ze start test-config.conf & # Run the benchmark ./le perf send --dut-addr 127.0.0.1 --dut-asn 65000 --dut-name ze --routes 1000 With JSON output saved to a file: ./le perf send --dut-addr 127.0.0.1 --dut-asn 65000 --dut-name ze \ --routes 1000 --output result-ze.json Running Benchmarks For a complete flag reference, see le perf send. Encoding Modes Three encoding modes measure different code paths through the DUT: Mode Flag What It Tests IPv4 inline NLRI --family ipv4/unicast (default) Standard IPv4 unicast path with NLRI at the end of the UPDATE IPv4 force-MP --family ipv4/unicast --force-mp IPv4 encoded via MP_REACH_NLRI attribute (exercises multiprotocol path) IPv6 MP --family ipv6/unicast IPv6 unicast via MP_REACH_NLRI (standard for non-IPv4 families) Multi-Iteration By default, le perf send executes 5 iterations with 1 warmup run. The warmup run is discarded, and outliers beyond 2 standard deviations from the median convergence time are removed (minimum 3 iterations kept). Final results report median and standard deviation across the kept iterations. Flag Default Purpose --repeat 5 Total iterations (including warmup) --warmup-runs 1 Warmup iterations discarded from results --iter-delay 3s Pause between iterations for clean separation More iterations improve statistical confidence. For reliable results, use at least --repeat 10: ./le perf send --dut-addr 172.31.0.2 --dut-asn 65000 --repeat 10 --warmup-runs 2 Timing Flag Default Purpose --warmup 2s Delay after session establishment before injecting routes --connect-timeout 10s TCP connection timeout --duration 60s Maximum wait time for convergence per iteration --iter-delay 3s Delay between iterations --reconnect-wait 0 How long to keep dialing a DUT that refuses the next iteration's session The --iter-delay flag controls whether iterations run back-to-back or with a pause. Longer delays give the DUT time to settle between measurements. Every iteration ends its sessions with a Cease and opens new ones. A DUT may hold a peer in Idle after a reset, as RFC 4271 Section 8.1.1 allows: OpenBGPD holds it 30 s after the second reset and doubles the hold after each later one, closing every connection the peer opens meanwhile. With --reconnect-wait, le perf send dials such a DUT again every second until it accepts the session or the wait runs out; timing starts only once the session is up, so the wait is not measured. With the default 0, the run fails at the first connection the DUT closes before its OPEN, and the error names the flag. ./le perf run passes --reconnect-wait 10m. Cross-Implementation Comparison Automated Docker Runner The included test runner benchmarks all eight supported implementations in Docker: DUT Image Config Forwarding mechanism Ze ze-interop (built) test/perf/configs/ze.conf bgp-rs plugin, import and export final accept (RFC 8212 refuses an EBGP direction with no policy) FRR quay.io/frrouting/frr:10.7.1, pinned by digest (interoplab.FRRImage) test/perf/configs/frr.conf route-map PERMIT BIRD bird-interop (built) test/perf/configs/bird.conf import/export all GoBGP gobgp-interop (built) test/perf/configs/gobgp.toml default accept policy rustbgpd rustbgpd-interop (built from source) test/perf/configs/rustbgpd.toml route_server_client rustybgp rustybgp-interop (built) test/perf/configs/rustybgp.toml default accept policy FreeRtr freertr-interop (built) test/perf/configs/freertr-sw.txt eBGP + redistribute connected OpenBGPD openbgpd-interop (built) test/perf/configs/openbgpd.conf allow from/to any The Ze DUT runs on the Docker daemon's kernel, so a run that tests it first builds test/interop/ze-linux, the ze the image carries, for the daemon's architecture, then checks that kernel with it and refuses one that lacks any feature Ze enrolls, naming each. The check and its routes are in docs/architecture/testing/interop.md, "The Docker host kernel check". # Build every DUT image, measure every DUT, and record the run. ./le perf run # Measure one DUT, or several. ./le perf run dut ze ./le perf run dut "ze bird rustbgpd" # Run one step: build the images only, or measure with the images that exist. ./le perf run step build DUT_ROUTES=10000 DUT_REPEAT=5 ./le perf run step test dut ze # Append the results of the last measurement to the committed NDJSON history. ./le perf record history # The release evidence gate: measure ze, append the result, fail on a regression. ./le perf record evidence A run with no step keyword builds the images and measures. step build records nothing, because it measured nothing. Any other step value exits 2 and names the value. A run that measured and passed records the commit, so the perf nudge (./le perf suggest) stops asking for one. A run that failed, for any cause below, records nothing. An image that fails to build or pull fails the run, and the run prints an error naming the DUT and the cause. In a step build run the image is the whole answer, so the run names every DUT that has no image, prints the rebuild command, exits 1, and never reports the images as built. In a run that also measures, the test step still measures every DUT whose image was made, but it never measures a DUT whose build failed, even from an image an earlier run left. The summary line reads FAIL, counts that DUT as failed, gives its cause, and the run exits 1. A DUT is skipped only when the run built no image (NO_BUILD=1, or step test) and none exists. The summary names the skipped DUTs and the ./le perf run step build dut "..." command that builds them. Under NO_BUILD=1 that command is env -u NO_BUILD ./le perf run step build dut "...", because the plain form would build nothing. Skips beside a measured DUT still pass, but a run that measured no DUT prints FAIL no DUT was measured and exits 1, because a run of skips has no result. A DUT whose measurement lost a route is failed, because its timings describe the routes that arrived, or nothing, and a DUT that forwarded nothing reads as the fastest. After each le perf send pass the runner reads the result file and judges it with the same check that sets le perf send's own exit code: every route sent must reach the receiver, and a result that sent none measured nothing. The ze DUT's propagation pass (ze-propagation.json) is judged the same way. For a pass that lost routes the run prints the DUT's last log lines under its name, while the DUT still runs. The summary line reads FAIL, counts the DUT as failed, and names the pass and the count, as in ze: the measurement lost routes: 0 of 100000 routes reached the receiver. It then prints the ./le perf run dut "..." command to run once the DUT is fixed, and the run exits 1. A result file that does not read or parse fails the pass the same way. A pass that lost routes is left out of the comparison table, the HTML report and the doc snapshot, so no row of 0ms values reads as a fast result, and a DUT left with no rendered pass is named on the run's no result for line. A complete pass of the same DUT is still rendered, and when both passes of ze are complete the co

title: BFD: Bidirectional Forwarding Detection
text: BFD: Bidirectional Forwarding Detection BFD monitors connectivity between two systems so routing protocols can react to a forwarding failure before their own hold timers expire. Ze runs BFD as a plugin whose session service is used by BGP, OSPF, and static-route monitors. The transport uses GTSM, outbound IP_TTL=255, SO_BINDTODEVICE for single-hop and multi-VRF sockets, and RFC 5880 §6.8.7 transmit jitter. You can inspect sessions with show bfd sessions and show bfd session address <peer>, view profiles with show bfd profile, and monitor Prometheus ze_bfd_* metrics. Adding bfd { ... } inside a bgp peer connection block opens a per-peer BFD session on Established and tears the BGP session down with RFC 9384 Cease subcode 10 ("BFD Down") when BFD reports the forwarding path lost. Adding strict true to that block runs draft-ietf-idr-bgp-bfd-strict-mode instead: capability 74 is negotiated, the BFD session opens before the BGP FSM starts, and the BGP session is held out of Established until BFD is Up. When to use it Scenario BFD value eBGP transit session Sub-second failure detection without waiting for BGP hold time (default 90 s) iBGP over a loopback Multi-hop BFD can accelerate route reconvergence if the IGP alone is too slow Static route to a gateway Withdraw the route when the gateway stops forwarding, even if the physical link is up OSPF adjacency Detect a forwarding failure before the OSPF dead timer expires Do not use BFD between two routers where the IGP already runs fast BFD; the redundant sessions double the packet rate and can amplify instability. Basic configuration Profiles Profiles are named bundles of timer and feature parameters. Sessions reference a profile by name and inherit every leaf from it. Profiles are optional: sessions can carry their parameters inline. bfd { profile fast-link { desired-min-tx-us 50000; # 50 ms required-min-rx-us 50000; # 50 ms detect-multiplier 3; # 150 ms detection time } profile lan-default { desired-min-tx-us 300000; # 300 ms required-min-rx-us 300000; detect-multiplier 3; } profile ibgp-loopback { desired-min-tx-us 300000; required-min-rx-us 300000; detect-multiplier 5; } } All interval fields are in microseconds because RFC 5880 expresses every interval in microseconds. A future release may add -ms aliases. Leaf Range Default Meaning desired-min-tx-us 1 – 4 294 967 295 300 000 Local target transmit rate. RFC §6.8.3 enforces a 1 000 000 µs floor while the session is not Up. required-min-rx-us 0 – 4 294 967 295 300 000 Minimum inter-packet gap the local end can handle.
