text: Configuration Editor Ze includes an interactive configuration editor with YANG-driven tab completion, rollback history, and live validation. Usage ze config edit # Edit default config ze config edit myconfig.conf # Edit specific file Stored editing runs inside the owning daemon over an SSH terminal session. When no daemon answers, the editor starts an ephemeral daemon and connects to it. Once connected, the local process holds no writable store handle. Terminal resizing and input travel over the SSH PTY, and the daemon persists drafts and command history. Three more surfaces reach the same editor against a running daemon. An SSH session opens in configuration mode. The web interface gives each authenticated user an editor of their own. The console of ze start --cli opens at the operational prompt, where configure enters configuration mode. A commit now from any of the three reloads the daemon. Command history is immediately available to Up/Down after Enter. A session-owned worker publishes detached whole snapshots without holding up input, timers or delivered command results. It keeps only the newest waiting snapshot for each of the two modes, plus the active write. The model owner MUST close the model before releasing its editor or borrowed store: graceful close cancels dispatch, drains and joins history, then closes the transcript. SSH (including no-PTY refusal), attached consoles, local loose-file/backup programs and headless restarts use that lifetime. Construction alone starts no history worker. Each SSH channel holds its own model closer, even when channels share one authenticated connection. The SSH model owner's Server.Stop seals new model admission and joins all admitted factories/model cleanup before its caller may close the borrowed store. Its network deadline does not cancel this history drain: a network error closes remaining connections, then Stop still waits for accepted history. Expiry of the network grace permits forced closure; successful closure and history cleanup complete a normal stop. Independent listener, transport or close failures remain stop failures. A storage call that has stopped answering holds Stop for at most 5 seconds, a share of the teardown margin the service manager's stop timeout allows. Stop then logs an error naming the storage and returns, so the daemon's teardown continues without that write, and that session's history or unsaved edit may be lost: a write it has not begun yet fails once the store closes. The stuck write still holds the store's own lock, so closing the store waits for it after everything else has stopped, and a second stop signal or the service manager's stop timeout forces the exit. Server.Start refuses a new generation while such a session is still running. Server.Start waits for every bound listener's actual Serve registration, so an immediate Stop cannot miss a primary/extra listener still starting. Hook-built daemon SSH is retained by the actual plugin server's OnStop callbacks. runYANGConfig immediately defers one sync.OnceFunc stop owner and uses that same owner at explicit shutdown sites. Normal shutdown and startup failure therefore both join SSH cleanup before the outer caller releases its store. A private hook-admission seal also joins a constructor already running; a just-built server refused by the stopping owner is closed synchronously. This does not depend on stop-callback ordering or a live editor Update loop. Abrupt process death can lose queued command history; draft, configuration and commit durability are unchanged. Slow draft I/O can still delay a command's own result. Separate sessions keep independent whole snapshots, not merged history. Missing history is an empty successful read. A history storage failure instead shows recovery instructions and disables publication for that mode until the session is reopened; diagnostic commands remain usable. Recall and newly published snapshots mask credentials using the shared schema-aware command display producer, including records written by older sessions. Completed publication failures remain visible when the model closes. A final write status is meaningful only after that close has joined the history worker; the absence of an earlier error does not prove an outstanding write succeeded. An editor resolves these assignments against its own schema before either mode is loaded, so ordinary values remain usable when the editor's schema differs from the process-wide schema. Recalled credentials contain a display marker; commit refuses that marker in a secret leaf and asks for the real value. A set entered at a relative configuration address is recalled as the equivalent absolute top set <address> ... command. This retains its original target after reconnecting or moving to another configuration context. Safe nonsecret values remain usable after reopening; an older relative record whose address was not stored is masked conservatively. Mode snapshots are detached, bounded by the configured entry count, and deduplicate consecutive displayed commands. Who may change the configuration On a daemon with system.authorization configured, an SSH session, and ze config edit in session mode, checks every change against the user's profile before it runs. Each verb that changes the candidate, the store or the running configuration (set, delete, commit, rollback, load and the others) is judged in the profile's edit section by its permission string, such as config set or config commit. Browsing is never checked: edit, up, top, show, who, option and help work for every user. A refused line changes nothing and answers: command restricted by access control: config commit ask an administrator for a profile whose edit section allows `config commit` To allow the change, an administrator adds an allow entry for that string, or for config, to the edit section of one of your profiles. Authorization, "Configuration mode", lists every verb's string, and the configuration name a session on another stored configuration adds to it. The console of ze start --cli, and the file and backup modes of ze config edit, authenticate nobody and are not checked. Editor Commands In an SSH session, load file reads only a regular configuration file inside the daemon's configured configuration directories. Paths through symlinks are checked against the same directories; the configuration store's private files are excluded. The opened file must remain regular, and opening refuses any path component replaced by a symlink after validation. Remote file imports accept up to 4 MiB. To import a file held elsewhere, use load terminal absolute merge and paste its configuration, or choose the file in the browser. Local loose-file editors retain the local operator's filesystem permissions. Relative SSH import paths are resolved beside the active configuration; a stored configuration name uses the configured store directory as its base. The graphical web editor's Import into candidate forms use the same load producer as these editor commands. A local file or pasted text can merge into or replace the root or selected subtree. Import stages changes for your account; review and commit them separately to publish them. A refused import leaves your candidate intact. See Web interface. Command Description set <path> <value> Set a configuration value delete <path> Delete a configuration value or section show Display current configuration show <path> Display a specific section show | blame Annotate with authorship show | changes [all] Pending changes (session or all) show | compare Diff against committed config; shows only the parts that differ show | errors Validation issues show | history List rollback revisions commit now Save changes and notify daemon commit now force Commit even though validation reports warnings (never errors) commit confirmed <N> Commit with N-second auto-revert window (1-3600) commit accept Make a pending confirmed commit permanent commit abort Roll back a pending confirme

title: Configuration
text: Configuration Ze uses a JUNOS-like hierarchical configuration format. Syntax Rules Element Syntax Example Blocks name { ... } bgp { ... } Values key value or key value; router-id 1.2.3.4 Comments # to end of line; ze config fmt keeps each one beside its statement, and so does an editor commit with no editing session, which writes the hierarchical form; a commit from an editing session writes the set-meta form, which drops them # this is a comment Lists [ item1 item2 ] receive [ update state ] Strings Unquoted or "double quoted" run "/usr/bin/my-plugin" Terminators ;, or automatic after a value token at a newline, EOF, or before } Both edit { default-action deny } and edit { default-action deny;} work Inline blocks name { key value; key value; } remote { ip 10.0.0.1; as 65001; } Indentation is not significant. Unknown keys are rejected with a suggestion for the closest valid key. A block written twice, such as two filter { ... } blocks, is read as one. A list both blocks set, such as filters [ a b ] and then filters [ b c ], holds the members of both: [ a b c ]. An ordered list keeps every copy in order, so it can hold a member twice. A member deactivated with inactive: in either block stays deactivated. Ze refuses the file when an ordered list ends up holding a deactivated member more than once, because it cannot tell which copy you meant to deactivate. Write that list once, in one block, or remove its inactive: line. The rules and the error text are in the configuration syntax reference. A plugin that registers no schema at build time has its schema selected at startup with --plugin, for example ze --plugin ze.<name> .... The schemas of the internal plugins, bgp-ls-export and bgp-epe among them, are always loaded, so their configuration needs no selection. Reload verification retains that selection, including when a configuration removes and later restores the plugin's root. It does not enable schemas for other optional plugins. Commands that assign a schema-marked secret are masked before they enter a CLI transcript, command accounting, or the dispatcher's refusal and audit output. The mask covers the entire value, including quoted words, while execution and authorization receive the original arguments. A configuration path the schema cannot resolve is redacted in full after set. File Format # Global BGP settings bgp { router-id 1.2.3.4; session { asn { local 65000; } } # Peer group with shared defaults group upstream { timer { receive-hold-time 180; } connection { local { ip auto; } remote { connect false; # passive: do not initiate outbound } } session { capability { asn4 enable; route-refresh enable; } family { ipv4/unicast { prefix { maximum 1000000; } } ipv6/unicast { prefix { maximum 250000; } } } } filter { import { final accept; } export { final accept; } } attach process bgp-rib { receive [ update-received state refresh ]; send [ update ]; } peer transit-a { connection { remote { ip 10.0.0.1; } } session { asn { remote 65001; } } } peer transit-b { connection { remote { ip 10.0.0.2; } } session { asn { remote 65002; } } timer { receive-hold-time 90; # overrides group value } } } # Standalone peer (no group) peer internal { connection { remote { ip 192.168.1.1; } local { ip 192.168.1.2; } } session { asn { remote 65000; } router-id 192.168.1.2; family { ipv4/unicast { prefix { maximum 1000000; } } } } } } The upstream group deliberately permits route exchange in both directions. Its peers inherit those explicit policies. Without an import or export policy at any level, EBGP rejects routes in that direction, but the session can still establish. The internal peer needs no policy to preserve its existing behavior. By default, every peer sends the global router-id as its BGP Identifier. A peer or group can set session { router-id ... } to select another non-zero identifier. Only the affected peers send that override in their OPEN messages. This option differs from RFC 6286 Section 2.1, which defines one identifier for every local interface and peer. RFC conformance is assessed separately on the default path, with no overrides or requested identifier changes. By default Ze enforces AS-wide BGP Identifier uniqueness: the first peer of an AS to present a router-id holds it, and a second peer of the same AS presenting the same router-id is rejected with a Bad BGP Identifier NOTIFICATION (RFC 6286 Section 2.1 makes this only a SHOULD). The identifier is claimed while the peer's OPEN is validated and released when that connection ends, so which peer wins does not depend on which one establishes first. An incumbent and its one admitted incoming candidate hold separate claims; closing either cannot release the other's identifier. Removing the peer releases all its connection claims. A candidate's validated identifier becomes the peer's published identifier only when that same Session is selected. Set bgp { session { allow-shared-router-id true; } } to accept the duplication when it is intentional, for example one anycast speaker (AS112) peering over both IPv4 and IPv6 with the same router-id. When enabled, Ze performs no AS-wide router-id uniqueness check at all. allow-shared-router-id does not relax RFC 6286 Section 2.2, which Ze always enforces on reception: an OPEN whose BGP Identifier is 0.0.0.0, or whose BGP Identifier is Ze's own router-id when the peer is in the same AS (an internal peer), is answered with OPEN Message Error / Bad BGP Identifier and the connection is closed. The same identifier from an external peer is accepted, as the RFC requires; if that leads to a connection collision, Section 2.3 preserves the connection initiated by the speaker with the larger AS number. Ze also refuses to start with its own router-id 0.0.0.0, since Section 2.1 defines the BGP Identifier as a non-zero integer and every conformant peer would reject such an OPEN. Two facts decide "internal peer" for that check, and neither is taken from the OPEN alone. The AS is the configured session { asn { remote } } when the session has one, and the AS the peer advertises only for a dynamic peer that has none. That AS is internal when it equals Ze's own AS, and also when it equals a configured session { asn { migration } }: RFC 7705 Section 4.2 makes a peer reached under either ASN of a migrating pair an iBGP peer, so the Section 2.2 identifier check binds it exactly as it binds a peer in the same AS. Loc-RIB Import Filters isis, ospf, static and connected each accept a filter { import { filters [ ... ]; final accept|reject; } } block that judges the routes the protocol offers to the Loc-RIB. The same block under rib judges routes from every source, after the protocol's own chain. The names in filters are filter instances defined under policy {}, such as a prefix-list. A filter's accept passes the route to the next filter, and final decides a route that passed them all. A rejected route is kept as a hidden path: it is not selected and does not reach the FIB, while the protocol's LSDB keeps it. A commit that relaxes the chain installs it again with no protocol event. A chain with no final, a <plugin>:<filter> reference, or a filter type that cannot run at the Loc-RIB is refused at load. See Route Policy at the Loc-RIB. OSPF The top-level ospf block enables Ze's native OSPF engine. The root container configures OSPFv2 for IPv4; ospf { address-family ipv6 { ... } } enables the OSPFv3 IPv6 instance on the same engine. Interface and neighbor state, LSDB flooding, SPF, inter-area logic, NSSA policy, redistribution, and route installation are shared. The wire codec, raw transport, and prefix strategy are address-family specific. For IPv4, the engine opens active non-passive broadcast and point-to-point interfaces through the raw IPv4 transport. For IPv6, it uses the OSPFv3 raw IPv6 transport (ff02::5 / ff02::6) and the OSPFv3 prefix model (Intra-Area-Prefix, Link, AS-External, and NSSA LSAs). Both families install selected routes through the shared Loc-RIB -> sysrib -> fibker

title: Features by Data Plane: Linux Kernel and VPP
displayTitle: Features by Data Plane: Linux Kernel and VPP
text: Features by Data Plane: Linux Kernel and VPP Ze can forward packets through the Linux kernel or through VPP. Most of Ze is control plane and is the same on both. The features that write forwarding state are different: each one has a kernel implementation, a VPP implementation, or both. This page lists them, so that you can see what a VPP deployment keeps and what it loses before you select it. For how Ze starts and supervises VPP, see the VPP guide. How the data plane is selected No single switch selects VPP. Four parts of the configuration each select their own backend. Configuration Values Default What it selects interface backend netlink, vpp netlink Who creates and configures interfaces. PPPoE subscriber sessions and the automatic route writer follow this leaf. firewall backend nft, vpp nft Who carries the firewall and NAT rules: nftables, or VPP ACL and NAT44. traffic control backend tc, vpp tc Who shapes traffic: Linux queueing disciplines, or VPP policers. fib kernel, fib vpp a block for each writer none Who writes routes. Without a fib block, Ze loads the writer for the data plane that interface backend names. The vpp value of each leaf exists only in a build that has the ze_vpp tag. A build without the tag refuses the configuration and names the tag. Ze checks each selection against the features under it. Ze does not compare the selections with each other. For example, a configuration with interface backend vpp and the default firewall backend nft commits. The section Features that only program the kernel says what that combination does. Summary "Refused" means that the commit, the daemon start and ze config validate all refuse the configuration and name the path. "Not built" in the VPP column means that the feature has a kernel implementation only. Ze accepts its configuration and programs the kernel, whichever interface backend is selected. Feature Linux kernel VPP Detail Ethernet, dummy, loopback, VLAN units Yes Yes Interfaces Bridge, veth Yes Refused Interfaces GRE, GRETAP, IPIP, VXLAN tunnels Yes Yes, without the outer TTL leaf Interfaces IP6GRE, IP6GRETAP, SIT, IP6TNL, IPIP6 tunnels Yes Refused Interfaces WireGuard Yes Yes, with the VPP WireGuard plugin Interfaces XFRM interface, PPPoE client Yes Refused Interfaces Port mirroring Yes Yes Interfaces DHCP client, SLAAC, router advertisements, reverse path check Yes Refused Interfaces VRRP Yes Refused Interfaces Container networks Yes Refused Interfaces VRF on an interface unit Not built Not built Interfaces IPv4 and IPv6 route install Yes Yes Routes and MPLS MPLS push, swap and pop Yes Yes, without the path MTU Routes and MPLS SRv6 service routes Yes Yes, one Service SID for each policy Routes and MPLS Stateless packet filter Yes Yes, a subset Firewall and NAT Connection tracking matches and helpers Yes Refused Firewall and NAT NAT Yes IPv4 only, a subset Firewall and NAT Traffic shaping Yes HTB and TBF as policers Traffic control Ingress policer Yes Refused Traffic control PPPoE subscriber access Yes Yes, in a ze_vpp build Subscriber access L2TP Yes Not built Features that only program the kernel IPsec Yes Not built Features that only program the kernel Flow export packet sampling Yes Not built Features that only program the kernel Policy routing Yes Not built Features that only program the kernel Kernel tunables (sysctl) Yes Yes, applied to the Linux kernel Features that only program the kernel Interfaces interface backend selects the backend. The schema marks each node that only some backends implement, and the commit refuses a marked node that the selected backend does not implement. Feature netlink vpp Limits ethernet, dummy, loopback, VLAN units, addresses, MTU, MAC address Yes Yes On VPP a dummy interface is a VPP loopback. bridge Yes Refused veth Yes Refused tunnel with gre, gretap, ipip Yes Yes The ttl leaf is refused on VPP: the VPP GRE and IPIP calls that Ze uses carry no hop limit. tunnel with vxlan Yes Yes tunnel with ip6gre, ip6gretap, sit, ip6tnl, ipip6 Yes Refused wireguard Yes Yes VPP needs vpp plugins wireguard true. The commit does not check that leaf. ze doctor reports doctor-vpp-wireguard when it is off. xfrm Yes Refused pppoe-client Yes Refused mirror on a unit Yes Yes The kernel mirrors with tc. VPP mirrors with SPAN, as a port mirror of the device. mpls enable on a unit Yes Yes dhcp, dhcpv6, delegated-prefix on a unit Yes Refused autoconf, accept-ra on a unit Yes Refused router-advertisement on a unit Yes Refused rpf-check on a unit Yes Refused vrrp on a unit Yes Refused VRRP needs macvlan devices and raw sockets. Native VPP VRRP is not built. vrf on a unit Not built Not built Ze refuses the leaf on both backends. Container network Yes Refused A network with masquerade, and a container that publishes a port, also need firewall backend nft. A refusal names the path, the selected backend and the backends that implement the node: <path>: feature not supported by backend "vpp" (supported: netlink) On VPP, BGP still uses Linux sockets. The VPP Linux Control Plane plugin shows each VPP interface to Linux as a TAP device, and BGP binds on that device. The VPP guide describes the namespace limit of that arrangement. Routes and MPLS One plugin writes routes for each data plane: fib-kernel for the kernel and fib-vpp for VPP. Ze refuses a second writer for the same data plane. fib p4 is in the schema and reaches no data plane today. Feature Kernel (fib-kernel) VPP (fib-vpp) Limits IPv4 and IPv6 routes from the system RIB Yes Yes VPP routes go to the table that fib vpp table-id names. Automatic writer for static, OSPF, IS-IS, LDP, RSVP-TE and BGP EPE routes Yes Yes Ze loads the writer for the selected interface backend. A build without that writer refuses to start. MPLS label push on an IP route Yes Yes The kernel must have MPLS support. Ze refuses to start when it does not. MPLS transit swap and pop Yes Yes VPP uses MPLS table 0. VPP has no MTU for each route, so Ze does not install the path MTU of an entry and logs one warning. MPLS push into a private table (RSVP-TE facility backup) Yes Refused when the entry arrives VPP has no packet mark context. SRv6 service routes Yes Yes VPP: one encapsulation policy for each Service SID. Ze allocates no egress Service SID and installs no remote endpoint behavior. show mpls forwarding Yes Yes The command reads the data plane that interface backend selects. fib vpp needs interface backend vpp. fib-vpp resolves each next-hop interface to a VPP interface index, and that lookup refuses while another interface backend is active. The commit does not check this pair, so the refusal comes when a route is installed. Firewall and NAT firewall backend selects the backend. The vpp backend translates filter chains to VPP ACL rules and NAT chains to VPP NAT44. It refuses at commit every rule that it cannot translate exactly, and the refusal names the table, the chain and the term. Feature nft vpp Limits on VPP Match on source or destination address, protocol, ICMP type, ICMPv6 type, TCP flags Yes Yes Match on source or destination port Yes Yes One port range in a term. accept, drop Yes Yes Rate limit in a term Yes Yes IPv4 addresses and exact ports only. connection-state, connection-mark Yes Refused notrack, flow-offload, flowtable Yes Refused mark-set, connection-mark-set, mark match Yes Refused tcp-mss-clamp-to-pmtu, TCP MSS set, DSCP match, DSCP set Yes Refused reject, redirect, counter, log Yes Refused VPP ACL denies without a response and has no named counter for a rule. jump, goto, return, chains that are not base chains Yes Refused A VPP ACL is a flat list of rules. Named sets Yes Refused Match on input or output interface Yes Refused A VPP ACL is bound to an interface. Match on destination-local, link-layer unicast, IPsec transform Yes Refused Conntrack helpers (system conntrack module) Yes Refused snat, masquerade Yes IPv4 only No destination or protocol match. A source address match is accepted and has no effect: VPP NAT44 applies to al

title: DDoS Detection and Auto-Mitigation
text: DDoS Detection and Auto-Mitigation Ze can automatically detect volumetric DDoS attacks on its interfaces, mitigate them locally or upstream, and report incidents to the Flowtriq cloud. Overview The system has four independent components, each enabled separately: Component Plugin What it does Detector ddos-detect Watches interface rates, learns a baseline, triggers when traffic exceeds the dynamic threshold Local responder ddos-local Installs an nftables drop rule on the host when an attack is detected FlowSpec responder ddos-flowspec Announces a surgical FlowSpec (or RTBH) rule upstream via BGP Flowtriq reporter ddos-flowtriq Reports incidents to the Flowtriq cloud API for dashboarding and server-driven mitigation Each component subscribes to the detector's events independently. You can run any combination: detector alone (monitoring only), detector + local (on-host protection), detector + flowspec (upstream mitigation), or all four. Quick Start Alert-only mode (monitoring, no mitigation) ddos { detect { enabled true } local { response-level alert } } The detector watches interface rates and emits events. The local responder logs what it would do but installs no rules. Check the logs for ddos-local: alert mode, would mitigate. Local mitigation mode ddos { detect { enabled true policy { default-action deny rule 10.0.0.0/8 { action allow; match destination; scope mitigation } rule 192.168.0.0/16 { action allow; match destination; scope mitigation } } } local { response-level enforce } } traffic { usage { enabled true track-ip true interfaces { interface eth0 { enabled true } } } } On attack detection the detector identifies the victim by querying on-box flow data, then emits the target so the local responder installs an nftables drop rule for it. The ddos detect policy allow rules prevent auto-mitigation from ever blocking management, DNS, or other critical prefixes. Target identification needs a flow source. The detector reads the attacked destination from traffic-usage (with track-ip enabled on the exposed interfaces). Without a reachable flow source-ipv4 the detector still fires but emits a generic signal with no target, and the local responder cannot install a targeted rule. The coarse rule matches the destination prefix; characterization (below) then narrows it in place to the attack's protocol, ports, and TCP flags. The flow sources are the traffic-usage plugin (build tag ze_trafficusage) and flow-export (ze_flowexport). A build that carries neither refuses ddos detect enabled true at ze config validate, at commit, at daemon start and at SIGHUP reload, naming both tags as alternatives in its fix line. A build that carries either accepts it, and whether that source is configured stays the doctor-ddos-detect-no-flow-source warning of ze doctor. Enabling detection starts no flow source: the source you configure (flow-export or traffic-usage) starts from its own config block, and one you do not configure does not run. anomaly detect enabled true gets the same treatment, for the same two sources. ddos flowspec response-level enforce announces through the BGP subsystem, so a build without ze_bgp refuses it the same way, naming ze_bgp; response-level alert announces nothing and is accepted in every build. The drop rule is removed automatically when the attack stops (the detector observes RxPps falling below threshold, which works because nftables drops occur after the kernel NIC RX counter), when it reaches max-mitigation-duration, and when a commit turns mitigation off, and when a commit deletes the ddos local block or the ddos block that holds it. The table under "When the clear never comes" gives each case. Attack characterization (Stage 2) With flow-export conntrack enabled, the detector runs a second, finer pass on the trigger: it queries the flow-export recent-flow ring for flows to the victim, classifies the attack, and emits a characterized signal so responders install a surgical rule and then narrow the local drop in place: reflection -- UDP with a dominant amplifier source port (DNS 53, NTP 123, SNMP 161, CLDAP 389, SSDP 1900, Memcached 11211, ...): matches proto + source port. syn-flood -- TCP dominated by half-open conntrack states: matches proto + SYN flag. icmp-flood -- ICMP dominant: matches proto. udp-flood -- UDP dominant without a reflector: matches proto (and dominant dst port). generic-flood -- no clear signature (includes fragment floods, which have no on-box conntrack signal): coarse destination-prefix drop. The recent-flow ring is IPv4 and IPv6 capable, so IPv6 victims (invisible to the IPv4-only traffic-usage map) are resolved from the ring. Characterization runs off the detection hot path with a bounded timeout and degrades to the coarse target when no flow source-ipv4 is reachable. Characterization refreshes the ring on demand. The recent-flow ring is normally refreshed only at each conntrack dump (every flow-export active-timeout seconds, default 60s). To avoid classifying against a pre-attack ring, detection forces the refresh: ddos-detect emits AttackDetected, flow-export responds with an immediate out-of-band conntrack dump, and the classifier then polls the ring for up to characterize-timeout until it reflects the attack. So a just-started flood is characterized promptly regardless of active-timeout; if the ring still never yields discriminating flows within the budget, ddos local keeps the coarse destination drop it installed on the fast signal (still protective, just not narrowed). ddos-flowspec has no such fallback: see "When characterization does not happen" below. Lowering active-timeout is no longer required for responsive characterization (it still governs NetFlow/IPFIX export cadence). Inspect the ring directly: show flow recent # all recent conntrack flows (bounded to recent-flow-ring) show flow recent dst 203.0.113.42 # flows to a destination prefix or address Each signal carries a graded severity from the peak-to-threshold ratio: medium (>=1x), high (>=2x), critical (>=5x). The FlowSpec responder can use critical to engage an immediate blackhole (below). The severity is graded once, when the detector triggers, from the highest rate seen above the threshold up to that moment. It is not revised while the attack continues: the AttackOngoing events that follow carry the current rates and no severity. Upstream FlowSpec mitigation ddos { detect { enabled true policy { default-action deny rule 10.0.0.0/8 { action allow; match destination; scope mitigation } } } flowspec { response-level enforce action rate-limit rate-limit-bytes 1000000 hold-down 300 probe-interval 60 } } Once the attack is characterized, a surgical BGP FlowSpec rule is announced to the configured upstream peer, matching the attack's protocol, ports, and flags. The FlowSpec responder waits for characterization by default rather than acting on the fast signal: announcing upstream blinds the box behind the filter, so the rule must be right the first time. Once a flowspec block is present, its action is mandatory (no default, because neither choice is universally safe); a ddos block without flowspec needs none: rate-limit announces an RFC 8955 traffic-rate of rate-limit-bytes bytes/sec (preserving legitimate traffic up to that rate), while discard drops the whole characterized flow. A rate-limit-bytes of 0 is valid and is equivalent to discard; action rate-limit without a rate-limit-bytes is a configuration error (no rate is fabricated). Blackhole fallback. With blackhole-fallback true, a critical-severity attack (peak >= 5x threshold) engages an immediate upstream discard on the fast signal without waiting for characterization -- the escape hatch when local filtering cannot hold the flood. Because the grade is fixed when the detector triggers, an attack that triggers below five times the threshold and then grows is not treated as critical, and blackhole-fallback does not fire for it. With characterization enabled, the characterized announcement still f

title: ZeBGP Debugging Tools
text: ZeBGP Debugging Tools This document describes the debugging tools available in ZeBGP for troubleshooting config parsing, BGP message encoding, and session issues. Quick Reference Tool Purpose Usage ze config dump Inspect parsed config ze config dump config.conf, or ze cli -c "show config dump config.conf | json" le test peer --decode Decode BGP messages le test peer --decode --sink ze.log.* Per-subsystem logging ze.log.bgp.routes=debug ze bgp server config.conf Functional test diff Test failure analysis Automatic on message mismatch --server N / --client N Interactive test debugging le test bgp encode --server 1 1. Config Dump Command Location: internal/component/config/cli/cmd_dump.go Parses a config file and displays the interpreted values. Useful for verifying that config parsing works correctly. Usage # Human-readable output ze config dump config.conf # JSON output (for scripting) ze cli -c "show config dump config.conf | json" Example Output Warnings: line 5: freeform 'flow' contains nested block 'route match' - data may be lost router-id: 1.2.3.4 local-as: 65000 peer 10.0.0.1: local-as: 65000 peer-as: 65001 static-routes: - prefix: 192.168.0.0/24 next-hop: 10.0.0.254 local-preference: 100 When to Use Config not being parsed correctly Static routes not appearing Verifying attribute values after parsing Checking for parser warnings about data loss 2. BGP Message Decoder Decodes raw BGP messages (hex) into human-readable format. Used automatically by functional tests and available via --decode flag. Usage # In ze-peer, show decoded messages le test peer --decode --sink --port 1790 Example Output msg recv FFFFFFFF...:0030:02:00000014400101004002060201000000014003040A000001... UPDATE (len=48) ORIGIN: IGP AS_PATH: [1] NEXT_HOP: 10.0.0.1 NLRI: 192.168.0.0/24 Decoded Attributes Code Name Decoded Format 1 ORIGIN IGP, EGP, INCOMPLETE 2 AS_PATH [1 2 3] or [{1 2}] for AS_SET 3 NEXT_HOP IP address 4 MED Integer 5 LOCAL_PREF Integer 8 COMMUNITIES high:low format 16 EXT_COMMUNITIES Hex (0x...) 3. Test Failure Diff When a functional test fails with "message mismatch", the output now includes a decoded diff showing exactly what differed. Example Output failed: message mismatch --- Expected vs Received --- Expected: UPDATE (len=64) ORIGIN: IGP AS_PATH: [] NEXT_HOP: 10.0.0.1 LOCAL_PREF: 100 NLRI: 193.0.2.1/32 Received: KEEPALIVE (len=19) Differences: - ORIGIN: IGP (missing) - AS_PATH: [] (missing) - NEXT_HOP: 10.0.0.1 (missing) - LOCAL_PREF: 100 (missing) ~ NLRI: expected=193.0.2.1/32, got= Diff Symbols - Missing attribute (expected but not received) + Unexpected attribute (received but not expected) ~ Different value (both present but values differ) 4. Per-Subsystem Logging (ze.log.*) Environment variables that enable structured logging at key points in the pipeline. Usage # Enable all subsystems at debug level ze.log=debug ze bgp server config.conf # Enable specific subsystems ze.log.bgp.config=debug ze.log.bgp.routes=debug ze bgp server config.conf Subsystems Names follow <domain>.<component> convention. Run ze env for the full list. Variable What it logs ze.log Base level for ALL subsystems ze.log.bgp.config Config parsing and loading ze.log.bgp.routes Static route handling, UPDATE sending ze.log.bgp.reactor.session BGP session handling ze.log.bgp.reactor.peer Peer FSM transitions, session events ze.log.bgp.reactor Reactor operations (reload, etc.) ze.log.plugin.server Plugin RPC server ze.log.plugin.relay Plugin stderr relay Levels: disabled, debug, info, warn, err (case-insensitive) Example Output time=2024-01-15T13:53:41.182Z level=DEBUG msg="config parsed" subsystem=bgp.config warnings=0 time=2024-01-15T13:53:41.183Z level=DEBUG msg="config loaded" subsystem=bgp.config peers=1 time=2024-01-15T13:53:41.183Z level=DEBUG msg="peer routes configured" subsystem=bgp.config peer=127.0.0.1 routes=2 time=2024-01-15T13:53:41.184Z level=DEBUG msg="FSM transition" subsystem=bgp.reactor.peer peer=127.0.0.1 from=OPENSENT to=OPENCONFIRM time=2024-01-15T13:53:41.184Z level=INFO msg="session established" subsystem=bgp.reactor.peer peer=127.0.0.1 localAS=1 peerAS=1 time=2024-01-15T13:53:41.184Z level=DEBUG msg="route sent" subsystem=bgp.routes peer=127.0.0.1 prefix=193.0.2.1/32 nextHop=10.0.0.1 Hierarchical Priority Most specific wins: ze.log.bgp.reactor.peer=warn - Peer logging at WARN ze.log.bgp.reactor=debug - All reactor.* at DEBUG ze.log.bgp=info - All bgp.* at INFO ze.log=debug - All subsystems at DEBUG Shell-compatible: ze_log_bgp_routes=debug also works (dot→underscore) Logging Locations Currently instrumented: internal/component/config/loader.go: Config parsing, peer routes (configLogger) internal/component/bgp/reactor/peer.go: FSM, session, route operations (peerLogger, routesLogger) internal/component/bgp/reactor/session.go: RFC 7606 handling (sessionLogger) internal/component/bgp/reactor/reactor.go: Reload, route operations (reactorLogger, routesLogger) 5. Parser Warnings The parser now collects warnings for potentially problematic patterns, accessible via Parser.Warnings(). Warning Types Pattern Warning Nested block in Freeform freeform 'X' contains nested block 'Y' - data may be lost Viewing Warnings # config-dump shows warnings ze config dump config.conf # Output: # Warnings: # line 5: freeform 'flow' contains nested block 'route match' - data may be lost # Also visible with debug logging ze.log.config=debug ze bgp server config.conf 5. Granular Debug (runtime) Set debug per-module with filters and named profiles (verb-first, VyOS-style): ze set debug module bgp.reactor # Enable debug ze set debug module bgp.reactor flag update # Add a flag filter ze set debug module bgp.reactor scope neighbor 192.0.2.1 # Add a scope filter ze delete debug module bgp.reactor # Disable debug ze show debug profile name default # Show stored profile (offline) show debug # Show live daemon state (YANG RPC) ze set debug profile name deep-trace # Save named profile ze set debug active name deep-trace # Apply a saved profile after restart show debug profile name <name> reads from debug.zefs (works offline). show debug queries the running daemon's actual slogutil state (requires daemon). Debugging Workflow 1. Config Issues # Step 1: Check parsed config ze config dump config.conf # Step 2: Look for warnings ze config dump config.conf 2>&1 | grep -i warning # Step 3: Check JSON for exact values ze cli -c "show config dump config.conf | json" | jq '.Neighbors[0].StaticRoutes' 2. Route Not Being Sent # Step 1: Enable route logging ze.log.bgp.routes=debug ze.log.bgp.config=debug ze bgp server config.conf # Expected output when working: # level=DEBUG msg="peer routes configured" subsystem=bgp.config peer=X routes=2 # level=DEBUG msg="route sent" subsystem=bgp.routes peer=X prefix=10.0.0.0/24 nextHop=192.168.0.1 3. Session Issues # Step 1: Enable session + peer logging ze.log.bgp.reactor.peer=debug ze.log.bgp.reactor.session=debug ze bgp server config.conf # Look for FSM transitions and session establishment A session closed because the peer stopped reading Ze logs this line at WARN, with no debug logging needed, when it closes a session whose peer accepted no data: level=WARN msg="BGP session closed: the peer accepted no data for the write budget; ze connects to it again by itself" subsystem=bgp.reactor.session peer=192.0.2.1 budget=30s fix="..." code=doctor-bgp-peer-not-reading What it means: ze had data to send, and for the whole write budget the peer took none of it while it kept the TCP connection open. Its BGP process is not reading. Ze closed the connection with no NOTIFICATION, because the peer could not have read one, and connects again by itself. The routes are sent again when the session is Established. A hold timer, a send hold timer or an operator can end the session before the write budget passes. The blocked route write then still holds the session, and ze logs this line at ERROR instead, with the code doctor-bgp-write-path-held: level=ERROR msg="no NOTIFICATION was sent t

title: Docker
text: Docker Run Ze in Docker for BGP evaluation or a daemon deployment where the host owns the network interfaces. This guide starts from the repository root and uses the supplied Compose file. Docker and its Compose plugin must already be installed. Ze is pre-release software. For an immutable VM or hardware image, see VM Appliance. For a native Linux service, see Linux installation. To compare every route, see Choose a deployment path. Two images Ze builds two container images. They carry the same daemon features and differ in the base. Local image Recipe Target Base ze:local docker/Dockerfile Deployment scratch: no shell, no libc, no package manager netlab/ze:latest docker/Dockerfile.lab Labs under netlab and containerlab alpine:3.24.3 with tini and iproute2 These are local build tags, not public registry downloads. Use the deployment image for a daemon and the lab image with netlab/containerlab. Lab tools execute sh and ip inside nodes to assign topology addresses; the scratch image has neither. For the lab image, see netlab. The preview artifact builder instead packages its inspected native binary through docker/Dockerfile.runtime. Those prepared images carry the binary's exact tags, including ze_distro; the source-building commands below keep their own feature selection. Both images include system CA certificates for outbound HTTPS requests, including ze init --from https://.... Both deployment recipes also provide an empty /tmp with mode 1777 for temporary files during provisioning and configuration reload. Build the deployment image docker build -t ze:local -f docker/Dockerfile . Choose another repository or tag with the normal Docker tag argument: docker build -t myregistry/ze:v1 -f docker/Dockerfile . The Dockerfile derives the default tag set from feature-gates.txt. ZE_TAGS adds tags on top of that set: docker build --build-arg ZE_TAGS=maprib -t ze:maprib -f docker/Dockerfile . That command builds the default feature set plus maprib. Build the lab image docker build -t netlab/ze:latest -f docker/Dockerfile.lab . This produces netlab/ze:latest. The image runs ze under tini, which forwards SIGHUP and SIGTERM. See netlab. Initialize persistent state Use the supplied Compose file in place, from the repository root. Its build context is the repository; copying the file elsewhere changes that context. Initialization, offline configuration commands and the daemon all mount the same named volume at /etc/ze and use the same ZE_CONFIG_DIR. docker compose -f docker/compose.yaml build docker compose -f docker/compose.yaml run --rm ze init Choose a username and strong password at the prompt. Keep the default host 127.0.0.1, port 2222 and instance name ze; the Compose hostname makes that name stable. There is no password in the image or Compose file. Initialization creates a private store in the volume and refuses to replace an existing store. Run it once, before first start. For this newly initialized volume, import the supplied management configuration in place of the ze.conf seed that initialization generated. --yes confirms replacement of that seed; the initialized credential store persists. The configuration enables SSH without taking over host interfaces. The input is streamed into the image; no shell is needed inside it. docker compose -f docker/compose.yaml run --rm -T ze config import --yes --name ze.conf - < docker/ze.conf docker compose -f docker/compose.yaml up -d Verify and configure docker compose -f docker/compose.yaml logs ze docker compose -f docker/compose.yaml exec ze /ze status docker compose -f docker/compose.yaml exec ze /ze cli -c "show bgp peer list" ssh -p 2222 YOUR_USERNAME@127.0.0.1 The initial configuration enables management and defines no BGP peer. Add a peer through the SSH editor using BGP peering, commit the change, and check the peer and received routes. For a complete two-peer example, start with the local quickstart or netlab. Compose publishes SSH on the host's loopback port 2222, and BGP on port 179. To allow remote operator access, publish SSH on your management address and apply the host's access policy. Web/API listeners need their own explicit configuration and port publication. Exposing a Docker port does not enable a service in Ze. Persistence, updates and removal Configuration commits and credentials live in the named volume. Recreating the container keeps them. Bare start reads the active config from that store, so there is no bind-mounted file competing with the committed configuration. # Recreate without discarding the store, then verify your configuration. docker compose -f docker/compose.yaml up -d --force-recreate docker compose -f docker/compose.yaml exec ze /ze cli -c "show bgp peer list" # Stop and remove the container; retain its volume. docker compose -f docker/compose.yaml down Before an update, export or back up the configuration using the lifecycle guide, record the running image ID, and retain the previous image. Build a new image from the selected source revision, recreate the container during a maintenance window, and verify login, peers and routes. Roll back by selecting the retained image and restoring a compatible config if the syntax changed. Do not use the daemon's binary self-update inside a container. docker compose -f docker/compose.yaml down --volumes also deletes this Compose project's named state volume. Use it only to discard the installation, after exporting anything you need. Ordinary down keeps the volume. Run without Compose Use the same image entrypoint and explicit config-directory mount in plain Docker. This first-start sequence uses a new volume and replaces only the seed configuration generated by initialization, keeping its credential store: docker volume create ze-data docker run --rm -it --hostname ze -e ZE_CONFIG_DIR=/etc/ze -v ze-data:/etc/ze ze:local init docker run --rm -i -e ZE_CONFIG_DIR=/etc/ze -v ze-data:/etc/ze ze:local config import --yes --name ze.conf - < docker/ze.conf docker run -d --name ze --hostname ze --restart unless-stopped \ --ulimit memlock=-1 -e ZE_CONFIG_DIR=/etc/ze -v ze-data:/etc/ze \ -p 179:179 -p 127.0.0.1:2222:2222 ze:local start Everything after the image name is a Ze command because the entrypoint is /ze. An explicit configuration path belongs after start. When using that form, mount a writable directory containing both the file and its store; a single read-only file mount prevents the editor from saving commits back to the file. Limitations The deployment container runs on a scratch base. Features that require kernel access do not work without extra privileges. The same capability table applies to the lab image: Feature Requirement Interface configuration --cap-add NET_ADMIN or --privileged VPP data plane Not supported in containers (use VM Appliance) L2TP tunnels --cap-add NET_ADMIN + host networking nftables / firewall --cap-add NET_ADMIN + --cap-add NET_RAW Binding port 179 Works by default (container runs as root) Locking the executable in memory (memlock plugin) --ulimit memlock=-1 or --cap-add IPC_LOCK. Docker grants neither by default, so the lock fails, ze doctor warns under doctor-memlock-rlimit-low, and show plugin list reports the memlock row as soft-failure For BGP peering without interface management (route server, looking glass, policy testing), no extra capabilities are needed. Troubleshooting Container exits immediately: inspect docker compose -f docker/compose.yaml logs ze. Bare start needs the initialized store and imported active configuration. A bare config path without the start keyword is not a daemon command. Cannot connect to CLI: verify initialization, the imported SSH listener, and the 127.0.0.1:2222:2222 publication. Use the username and password you chose. The scratch image has no shell: use /ze directly with docker exec. Peer won't connect: If peering with the host, use --network host or the Docker bridge gateway IP. Container-to-container peering works on a shared Docker network.

title: Environment Variables
text: Environment Variables Ze reads environment variables for daemon-wide settings and BGP protocol tuning. Config-backed keys have matching paths under environment { }. Bootstrap, safety, and test keys can be environment-only. See environment.md for the authoritative list. Priority for Config-Backed Keys OS environment variable (shell, systemd EnvironmentFile, container runtime) Config file environment { ... } block Built-in default An OS env var is never overwritten by a config value. Common Variables Variable Purpose ze.user User to drop to after binding privileged ports ze.pid.file Path to PID file written at startup, removed at clean shutdown ze.pprof Bind pprof HTTP server (e.g. :6060). Empty disables ze.hide-version Keep the X-Ze-Version build banner off every HTTP response. Default false ze.bgp.openwait Seconds to wait for peer OPEN after TCP connect ze.bgp.announce.delay Duration to block between reactor Ready and first UPDATE exabgp.api.ack ExaBGP bridge: emit done/error ack lines on plugin stdin ze.web.certificate PKI store entry the web HTTPS listener serves. Empty means self-signed ze.looking-glass.certificate PKI store entry the looking glass serves. Empty means self-signed Config Block Syntax The same knobs can be expressed in the config file: environment { daemon { pid "/run/ze.pid" user "zeuser" } bgp { openwait 60 announce-delay 5s } pprof ":6060" hide-version true exabgp { api { ack false } } chaos { seed 0 rate "0.1" } reactor { cache-ttl 60 } log { level INFO bgp.routes debug } } Discoverability Shell completion offers env-key suggestions after ze env get and ze env registered using canonical dot-form keys. Concrete ze.log.<subsystem> keys (visible in ze env list) are completable and inspectable via ze env get. In the interactive CLI operational mode, show env get and show env registered also offer env-key completion through the shared command tree. wireEnvHints spells the show in those two paths as command.VerbShow, the verb registry's own constant, so renaming the read verb moves the completion paths with it. Changes in 2026-04 The ExaBGP compatibility surface was trimmed. Every ze.bgp.daemon.*, ze.bgp.log.*, ze.bgp.tcp.*, ze.bgp.api.*, and ze.bgp.debug.* variable was either renamed, dropped, or plumbed from a YANG leaf to a new env key: Old New / Action ze.bgp.daemon.pid Plumbed to ze.pid.file (YANG leaf kept) ze.bgp.daemon.user Plumbed to ze.user (YANG leaf kept) ze.bgp.daemon.daemonize, drop, umask Dropped (use systemd unit file) ze.bgp.log.level, destination, short Dropped (slogutil owns ze.log.*) ze.bgp.tcp.attempts Dropped (test harness sends SIGTERM) ze.bgp.tcp.delay Dropped; new ze.bgp.announce.delay duration ze.bgp.tcp.port Renamed ze.test.bgp.port (test infrastructure only) ze.bgp.tcp.acl Dropped (experimental, unimplemented) ze.bgp.bgp.openwait Renamed ze.bgp.openwait ze.bgp.cache.attributes Dropped (caching is architectural) ze.bgp.debug.pprof Renamed ze.pprof (process-wide) ze.bgp.debug.* (pdb/memory/rotate/etc.) Dropped (use go tool pprof, ze.log) ze.bgp.api.ack Dropped; exabgp.api.ack handles bridge ack ze.bgp.api.chunk, encoder, respawn, ... Dropped (Ze manages plugins) The ze exabgp migrate --env tool converts surviving keys to Ze YANG blocks and emits # <key> -- no longer supported comments for dropped ones so an operator can audit an ExaBGP env file before commit.

title: Firewall
text: Firewall Ze manages nftables packet filter and NAT rules from a single firewall { } YANG section. The abstract data model describes matches (from) and actions (then); the nft backend lowers them to nftables kernel expressions. Backend Backend Platform Default Mechanism nft Linux yes google/nftables netlink library vpp Linux with VPP no GoVPP ACL classify pipeline and NAT44-ED firewall { backend nft; } backend vpp needs the VPP component, which only a build with the ze_vpp tag carries. Selecting it starts that component with the firewall and orders the firewall after it; backend nft does not start it, though the firewall still starts after VPP when a vpp {} block runs it. In a build without ze_vpp, ze config validate, a commit and daemon boot all refuse firewall backend vpp before anything is applied, naming the leaf and the ze_vpp tag, where the config used to pass validation and fail at apply. Clean-shutdown teardown flush-on-shutdown controls whether stopping the ze process removes ze-owned tables from the kernel. It defaults to true: an orderly stop (SIGTERM, e.g. systemctl stop ze) tears the tables down so a stopped daemon leaves no rules behind. It keys off how the process exits, and is unrelated to BGP graceful restart -- that concerns only RIB/FIB route retention while a peer re-establishes and never restarts the daemon, so it never reaches this path. Set it to false to use ze as a one-shot provisioner: apply the firewall (and interface) configuration, let the process exit, and leave the rules running in the kernel -- the way nft -f programs a ruleset and returns. Nothing is torn down when ze quits. firewall { backend nft; flush-on-shutdown false; # one-shot: program the rules, exit, leave them running } A crash (SIGKILL, panic, power loss) never runs the shutdown path, so ze-owned tables always persist across a crash regardless of this setting. The option governs every ze table producer that shares the backend -- the firewall component, control-plane-protection, policy-routes, and ddos-local -- and the firewall component performs the teardown as a single ordered actor so plugin table removal never races the backend close. The reconcile deadline Ze serializes the whole firewall reconcile: a snapshot of every owner's tables followed by one Backend.Apply, under one process-wide lock. The owners are the firewall component, control-plane-protection, policy-routes, and ddos-local. A dataplane call that never returns therefore does not stall one owner, it stalls all of them. Each backend bounds one dataplane round-trip. Neither bound can be turned off. A value below the floor or above the ceiling clamps, and an unparseable value falls back to the default, because an unbounded call is the failure this guard exists to prevent. The ceiling is one shared constant, firewall.MaxBackendDeadline, which the latency histogram's last finite bucket is also derived from. Backend Bounds Environment variable Default Range nft One nftables netlink round-trip ze.firewall.nft.netlink-timeout 10s 1s to 60s vpp One VPP binary-API round-trip ze.firewall.vpp.reply-timeout 10s 1s to 60s The VPP backend previously ran with no bound at all. govpp's default reply timeout is 0, which govpp documents as disabling the timeout, and Channel.ReceiveReply has no context arm, so a wedged VPP held the process-wide reconcile lock indefinitely. When the deadline expires the apply fails, and ze logs an error saying the dataplane did not answer within the backend deadline and its ruleset is now behind the registry. That log sits outside the metrics path, so it is written whether or not telemetry is enabled. A dataplane that is ABSENT is a different condition and is deliberately not reported as a timeout: VPP not running, or a connect wait that ran out, means the reconcile failed for a reason with a different fix, and there is no ruleset to be behind. Metric Type Labels Meaning ze_firewall_apply_duration_seconds histogram result Time spent in Backend.Apply. result is ok, timeout, error, or panic. ze_firewall_apply_timeout_total counter Reconciles that failed because the dataplane did not answer within the backend deadline. ze_flowspec_rules_refused_total counter reason FlowSpec routes received from a peer that did not become a firewall rule. reason is unknown-protocol, unsupported-component, unsupported-action, parse, or max-rules. The result label is what separates a healthy-but-slow apply from one that gave up: a backend deadline of 10s and a 10s successful reconcile land in the same latency bucket, and only the label tells them apart. Both signals derive from one result value, so they cannot drift apart. A backend that panics is recorded as panic rather than lost or filed as healthy. A refused FlowSpec route is otherwise invisible: it is never registered, so no reconcile fails and show firewall has nothing to render. The peer believes ze filters the traffic and ze does not, which is what the counter reports. Tables and Chains Ze owns all tables whose kernel name starts with ze_. A table contains one or more chains; a base chain has a type, hook, priority, and default policy. firewall { backend nft; table wan { family inet; chain input { type filter; hook input; priority 0; policy drop; term allow-ssh { from { destination-port 22; protocol tcp; } then { accept; } } } } } Tables another feature installs A ze_ table is not always one the firewall { } section declared. A feature that needs kernel state of its own publishes a table through the same backend, so it appears beside yours in show firewall ruleset <name> and is withdrawn with the configuration that asked for it. system conntrack module <helper> is another: each listed helper publishes ze_conntrack_helpers (family inet) or ze_conntrack_helpers_ip (family ip, for helpers the kernel registers for IPv4 only). Each holds one ct helper object per kernel helper and transport, and prerouting and output chains at priority -5 that assign it by destination port, so the assignment runs before your own chains at priority 0. A chain of yours at a priority below -5 sees the connection before the helper is attached. The per-helper ports are in the configuration guide, system conntrack. One example: a BGP peer configured with connection { ttl { max N; } } (RFC 5082 GTSM) gets ze_gtsm, an input chain with two kinds of term for that peer. Term Matches Why dangerous-<peer>-listen TCP from the peer to Ze's listen port with a TTL (IPv4) or hop limit (IPv6) below the peer's floor, then drop The SYN reaches the listener before the accepted socket carries its own floor, so a spoofed SYN would otherwise cost a SYN-ACK and a request socket dangerous-<peer>-type<N>-quoted-<side> (IPv4 only) An ICMP error which quotes that peer's BGP session and arrives below the floor The related messages RFC 5082 Section 6.1 covers A GTSM dynamic group gets one listen term per range, named dangerous-<address>-<length>-listen, with the range as its source and the group template's floor. A SYN to the listen port from any other source, or from the peer to any other port, matches no term: RFC 5082 Section 3 forbids dropping a packet GTSM classifies as Unknown. A session source inside a wider GTSM range on the same port (a static peer, or a dynamic group whose range is longer) owns its own SYNs, because the listener gives the connection to that session. It gets a claimed-<source>-listen term that accepts its TCP to the listen port, after its own drop term when it has a floor and before the wider range's drop, so the range never judges it by the range's floor. The accept ends only the ze_gtsm chain; every other table still sees the packet. A prefix two sources share is judged only by the one the listener picks: a static peer before a group range of the same address, and the first of two groups whose ranges are the same prefix. Every term carries a packet counter (the nft backend adds one to each rule), so show firewall ruleset gtsm shows how many below-floor SYNs each dangerou

title: Fleet Configuration
text:
Fleet Configuration One Ze, the hub, holds the full configuration of every other Ze, the managed clients. Each client connects to the hub over TLS, fetches its own configuration and applies it. When you change a client's configuration on the hub, the hub tells that client, and the client fetches and applies the change. Status: Implemented. The hub serves each client its configuration, and a client fetches, applies, caches and reconnects. Hub Managed clients ┌──────────────┐ ┌─────────────┐ │ ze │ ◄──── TLS ──────── │ ze edge-01 │ │ │ └─────────────┘ │ client-edge-01.conf ┌─────────────┐ │ client-edge-02.conf ◄─── TLS ──── │ ze edge-02 │ └──────────────┘ └─────────────┘ What you get, and what you do not: Fleet configuration does Fleet configuration does not Keep one full configuration for each client, on the hub Build a configuration from a template: each client has its own file Push a change to the one client it belongs to Roll a change out to a group of clients in stages Keep a client running when the hub is down Record which version each client runs This guide follows the order of a first deployment: Set up the hub Write each client's configuration Provision a client Start the client Then the daily work: change a client's configuration, what happens when the hub is down, how a client leaves and rejoins the fleet, what to do when a client holds and troubleshooting. The reference is at the end. 1. Set Up the Hub The hub is an ordinary Ze. It becomes a hub when one server block of its configuration lists the clients it accepts. plugin { hub { server local { ip 127.0.0.1; port 1790; secret "local-plugin-secret-of-32-characters"; } server central { ip 0.0.0.0; port 1791; secret "remote-plugin-secret-of-32-character"; client edge-01 { secret "edge-01-secret-of-at-least-32-chars"; } client edge-02 { secret "edge-02-secret-of-at-least-32-chars"; } } } } Three rules apply to this block: One entry and one secret for each client. The name is the client's identity. The secret belongs to that name only: the hub refuses it under another client's name. A secret has 32 characters or more. The clients need their own port. The first server block is the one the hub's local plugins use. The block that lists clients is a different block with a different port, 1791 here. A client connects to the block that lists it. With two blocks that list clients, the hub refuses a client on the address of the other block. List a client under both blocks if it must reach both. Start the hub with ze start. It also needs the root of its certificate authority later, in step 3. Print it now and save it to a file: ze show pki local-ca pem > hub-root.pem The hub makes this authority at its first start and keeps it. The root is public: it holds no private key. 2. Write Each Client's Configuration The hub stores one full configuration for each client, under the name client-<name>.conf. Write it as you write any Ze configuration, and add the client block that tells the client where its hub is: plugin { hub { server local { ip 127.0.0.1; port 1790; secret "local-secret-of-at-least-32-characters"; } client edge-01 { host 10.0.0.1; port 1791; secret "edge-01-secret-of-at-least-32-chars"; } } } bgp { ... } The client block must be there. The name and the secret are the ones in the hub's client edge-01 entry. A client that applies a configuration with no client block stops following its hub. Give the file to a running hub, on the hub's own host: ze data import client-edge-01.conf The hub keeps it as a new version of that client's configuration. It refuses a name that has no client entry in step 1, because no client would fetch it. 3. Provision a Client On the new client, ze init --managed asks for what the first start needs. It asks for the usual SSH login, then for three things about the hub: Prompt What to enter name The client's name on the hub, edge-01 hub address The hub's address and port, 10.0.0.1:1791 hub token The secret of this client's entry on the hub You also choose how the client makes sure that it talks to your hub and not to something else. The client checks the hub before it sends its secret. Choose one of these: Choice Command When to use it Give the hub's root ze init --managed --hub-ca hub-root.pem The safe choice. Copy hub-root.pem from step 1 to the client first Trust on first use ze init --managed --hub-trust-first-use When you cannot copy a file to each device, and you trust the network during provisioning Neither ze init --managed Only when a public certificate authority issued the hub's certificate Give the hub's root. The client checks every connection, the first one included, against that root. It refuses a hub that the root did not issue. Trust on first use. The first start accepts the hub that answers, one time. It keeps the certificate authority that this hub presents and prints its SHA-256. It checks every later connection against the authority it kept. To be sure of what it kept, compare the printed SHA-256 with the hub's root. First use never happens a second time. To trust a different hub, run ze init --managed --force again. With either choice, the client keeps the root in its store. Its configuration then needs no certificate settings at all. To provision with no prompt, give the seven answers on standard input: echo -e "admin
secret
127.0.0.1
2222
edge-01
10.0.0.1:1791
edge-01-secret-of-at-least-32-chars" \ | ze init --managed --hub-ca hub-root.pem The seven lines are: SSH user, SSH password, SSH address, SSH port, client name, hub address, hub token. 4. Start the Client ze start On this first start the client connects to the hub, checks it, fetches its configuration, checks the configuration, keeps a copy and starts. Every later start is the same command. You can leave the hub address and the token empty at ze init. Then give them at the first start. The flags go before start: ze --server 10.0.0.1:1791 --token "edge-01-secret-of-at-least-32-chars" start When the first start lacks a value, it stops and names the value and the flag that gives it. Change a Client's Configuration Edit the client's file and give it to the running hub again: ze data import client-edge-01.conf The hub tells edge-01 at once. The client then does four things: It fetches the new configuration. It checks it with the same checks as ze config validate. It applies it. It tells the hub the result. A client that refuses the configuration keeps the one it runs. The hub shows the refusal and its reason in show doctor. A change made on the client while it fetches yours is kept. The client applies your configuration only over the one it ran when it fetched. When its configuration changed in between, it applies nothing, fetches once more, and holds (see "When a Client Holds"). A change reaches the client it belongs to and no other. To change ten clients, import ten files. A client that is not connected gets the change the next time it connects. To move a client to another hub, or to change its secret, change the client block in its configuration. The client applies the configuration and reconnects with the new values. It needs no restart. Change the secret in the hub's client entry at the same time, or the client cannot come back. To restore a client's configuration from a backup, on a running hub: request data restore path /var/backups/edge-01.zefs config client edge-01 The hub pushes the restored configuration as it pushes any change. To edit with the configuration editor, on the hub's own host, in the folder that holds the hub's store (its ze.config.dir): ze config edit client-edge-01.conf The command opens the store of the folder its path names, so a bare name typed in another folder finds no store there. The editor runs inside the running hub. When you commit, the hub records a new version of that client's configuration and pushes it to the client, as it pushes an import. The file must exist first: give the hub the first version with ze data import. The hub refuses to open the editor

title: Flow Export
text: Flow Export Ze exports interface counters and per-flow records to external collectors over UDP. The flowexport component is a registered component: it loads only when a flow-export { } section is present in the config. Counter polling is driven by the interface rate tracker's snapshot callback; per-flow records come from packet sampling and from periodic conntrack table dumps. Because counter export consumes the interface rate tracker, configuring flow-export { } automatically pulls in the interface plugin (a registered dependency). You do not need to add a separate interface { } section just to get counter datagrams flowing. Three export protocols are supported, selected per collector: Protocol Reference Carries sflow sFlow v5 Interface counters, packet samples (flow samples) netflow9 NetFlow v9 (RFC 3954) Interface counters, per-flow records (template-based) ipfix IPFIX (RFC 7011) Interface counters, per-flow records (template-based) Configuration All flow export configuration lives under a single flow-export { } section. Collectors A collector is an export endpoint. Each collector names one protocol; you may configure several collectors at once (for example one sFlow and one IPFIX). Field Default Description name - Collector name (list key) address - Collector IP address (mandatory) port 6343 Collector UDP port protocol - sflow, netflow9, or ipfix (mandatory) polling-interval 20 Maximum time between two counter polls, in seconds (1-3600). Snapshots arrive once a second, so Ze polls from one second before the interval ends template-refresh 600 Template refresh interval in seconds, NetFlow v9 / IPFIX (1-86400) sub-agent-id 0 sFlow sub-agent identifier. Every sflow collector exports every interface, so all sflow collectors MUST name the same value observation-domain 0 IPFIX / NetFlow v9 observation domain ID agent-address - sFlow agent address (the device's own stable IP, for example a loopback). Mandatory for sflow. 0.0.0.0 and :: are refused, and all sflow collectors MUST name the same address. Ze compares the parsed addresses, so 2001:db8::1 and 2001:DB8:0::1 are one address. Ze logs a warning when no interface holds the address, or when the router has more than one routed interface and the address is not on a loopback or dummy interface source-address - Local source IP for the collector's UDP socket max-datagram-size 464 Maximum UDP payload bytes, including protocol padding (464-1400) The default reserves IPv6 and UDP headers within a 512-byte packet when the path MTU is unknown. Raise it only when the path MTU is known, after subtracting all IP, UDP and tunnel headers. Encoders split batches or cap sampled headers to this bound. Oversized sends return an error. sFlow uses expanded counter and flow samples for every interface, preserving full-width interface indexes without mixing compact and expanded formats. An sFlow counter collector: flow-export { collector edge-sflow { address 192.0.2.10; port 6343; protocol sflow; polling-interval 20; sub-agent-id 0; agent-address 198.51.100.1; } } The agent address is how a collector tells this router from every other agent. sFlow v5 asks a router with several routed interfaces to use a loopback address, which does not go away when one interface goes down. When the plugin applies the config, it compares the address with the router's interfaces and logs a warning that names the fix: flow-export: sflow agent-address 203.0.113.1 is on routed interface eth0, not on a loopback interface. ... flow-export: sflow agent-address 198.51.100.1 is not configured on any interface. ... A dummy interface counts as a loopback, so create interface dummy name agent0 address 198.51.100.1/32 silences both. The warning never refuses the config: the export runs either way. A NetFlow v9 collector plus an IPFIX collector on the same device: flow-export { collector nf9 { address 192.0.2.20; port 2055; protocol netflow9; polling-interval 30; template-refresh 600; observation-domain 1; } collector ipfix { address 192.0.2.21; port 4739; protocol ipfix; polling-interval 30; template-refresh 600; observation-domain 1; } } Sampling Packet sampling uses the Linux tc sample action plus the kernel psample module and exports sampled packet headers as sFlow flow samples. Field Default Description name - Interface to sample (list key) rate - Sampling rate, 1-in-N packets (1-1000000) trunc-size 128 Bytes of each sampled packet header to capture (64-1500) group 1 psample group ID (1-2147483647) flow-export { sampling { interface eth0 { rate 1024; trunc-size 128; group 1; } } } Conntrack Conntrack-based per-flow records are exported via NetFlow v9 and IPFIX. The exporter walks the conntrack table on a fixed interval and emits one record per tracked flow. Field Default Description enabled false Export per-flow records from the conntrack table active-timeout 60 Seconds between conntrack table dumps (1-3600) flow-export { conntrack { enabled true; active-timeout 60; } } Enrichment Flow records can be enriched from the BGP RIB. With bgp true, the exporter consumes the RIB best-change event and attaches the next-hop for each flow's destination prefix. Field Default Description bgp false Enrich flow records with the BGP next-hop flow-export { enrichment { bgp true; } } The BGP RIB is the bgp-rib plugin, which only a build with the ze_bgp tag carries. Turning bgp true on starts it when the build has it, even with no bgp {} block; with enrichment off, flow export never starts it. A build without ze_bgp still runs flow export, and refuses bgp true at ze config validate, at commit, at daemon start and at SIGHUP reload, before any plugin starts. The refusal names the setting, says why, and gives the fix on its own line. ze config validate prints: configuration invalid: flow.conf Errors: config: "flow-export enrichment bgp true" needs plugin bgp-rib, and this build does not include it flow-export cannot act on this setting without it, so ze refuses the config rather than run a setting that does nothing fix: rebuild ze with build tag ze_bgp added to its -tags list, or remove "flow-export enrichment bgp true" from the config Set bgp false (or leave the leaf out) to run flow export on that build. Before this refusal existed, such a build accepted the setting and the exporter silently received no RIB data. Operational Command show flow export [name <collector>] reports per-collector export statistics. With no argument it lists every collector; with name <collector> it returns that one collector, or an error if the name is not configured. When no flow-export section is configured the command returns {"status": "not-configured"}. ze cli -c 'show flow export | json' The | json pipe asks for that shape. Without it the answer is rendered in the format environment cli format default names, whose registered value is text. [ { "name": "edge-sflow", "address": "192.0.2.10", "port": 6343, "protocol": "sflow", "datagrams-sent": 1842, "bytes-sent": 1325760, "errors": 0, "sequence": 1842, "last-export-time": 1748430000 } ] Field Description name Collector name address Collector IP address port Collector UDP port protocol Export protocol datagrams-sent UDP datagrams sent to this collector bytes-sent Total bytes sent to this collector errors Send errors sequence Shared collector sequence: successful data records for IPFIX, successful packets for NetFlow v9, generated datagrams for sFlow last-export-time Unix timestamp of the most recent successful counter poll (omitted before the first successful poll) The command answers structured data, rendered in the format environment cli format default names. The registered value is text. The full set of pipe operators selects another one. Datagram and byte totals include successfully sent templates and any packets sent before a later error in the same batch. A failed template blocks its data batch until a subsequent template attempt succeeds. Counter and flow exporters share the sequence; a configuration reload creates a new transport

title: FlowSpec protected router
text: FlowSpec protected router Use this when a Ze router receives BGP FlowSpec rules and should turn them into nftables filters, while also protecting its own BGP control plane from connection floods. The example enables the nft firewall backend, starts the flowspec-firewall bridge plugin, accepts FlowSpec from an iBGP route reflector, and adds a conservative control-plane policing rule for TCP/179. 1. Start from an installed Ze node Follow Build and install Ze on Ubuntu through the systemd step. This page assumes /usr/local/bin/ze, /etc/ze, and active config name edge-01.conf. Example topology: Node Role IP AS edge-01 protected Ze router 192.0.2.10 65010 flowspec-rr FlowSpec route reflector 203.0.113.1 65010 flowspec-rr-b second trusted source 203.0.113.2 65010 2. Update the active stored config Keep the active configuration in the database/ store. The commands below read the current active config, normalize it to set format, append the FlowSpec protection settings, render the import file, validate the result, import it back into the store, and reload the daemon. They do not create /etc/ze/edge-01.conf. set -euo pipefail umask 077 CONFIG_SET="$(mktemp)" CONFIG_IMPORT="$(mktemp)" trap 'rm -f "$CONFIG_SET" "$CONFIG_IMPORT"' EXIT sudo /usr/local/bin/ze config cat edge-01.conf | /usr/local/bin/ze config migrate -o "$CONFIG_SET" - cat >>"$CONFIG_SET" <<'EOF' set plugin internal flowspec-firewall use flowspec-firewall set firewall backend nft set control-plane-protection bgp rate 100/second set control-plane-protection bgp burst 20 set control-plane-protection bgp protected-port 179 set control-plane-protection bgp trusted-source [ 203.0.113.1/32 203.0.113.2/32 ] set control-plane-protection bgp over-limit-policy drop set ddos flowspec response-level enforce set ddos flowspec action rate-limit set ddos flowspec rate-limit-bytes 1000000 set ddos flowspec hold-down 300 set ddos flowspec probe-interval 60 set ddos flowspec probe-window 10 set ddos flowspec probe-rate 1000000 set ddos flowspec announce-rate-limit 10 set ddos flowspec max-mitigation-duration 3600 set ddos flowspec backoff-cap 3600 set ddos flowspec blackhole-fallback disable set ddos flowspec allowlist [ 192.0.2.0/24 2001:db8::/32 ] set bgp router-id 192.0.2.10 set bgp session asn local 65010 set bgp peer flowspec-rr description "FlowSpec route reflector" set bgp peer flowspec-rr connection remote ip 203.0.113.1 set bgp peer flowspec-rr connection local ip 192.0.2.10 set bgp peer flowspec-rr connection md5 password change-this-md5-secret set bgp peer flowspec-rr connection ttl min 255 set bgp peer flowspec-rr session asn local 65010 set bgp peer flowspec-rr session asn remote 65010 set bgp peer flowspec-rr session family ipv4/flow mode enable set bgp peer flowspec-rr session family ipv4/flow prefix maximum 1000 set bgp peer flowspec-rr session family ipv4/unicast mode enable EOF /usr/local/bin/ze config migrate -o "$CONFIG_IMPORT" format hierarchical "$CONFIG_SET" /usr/local/bin/ze config validate "$CONFIG_IMPORT" sudo /usr/local/bin/ze config import --yes --name edge-01.conf "$CONFIG_IMPORT" sudo systemctl reload ze.service Expected validation output: configuration valid: /tmp/tmp.XXXXXXXXXX What each block does: Config Purpose plugin internal flowspec-firewall Starts the bridge and subscribes to validated BGP RIB best-path changes. firewall backend nft Uses Linux nftables as the firewall backend. control-plane-protection bgp Accepts TCP to the protected BGP port from configured BGP neighbors only, drops every other source, and rate-limits new connections from the neighbors. trusted-source Accepts a source that is not a configured BGP neighbor, such as a monitoring host, and never rate-limits it. family ipv4/flow Negotiates IPv4 FlowSpec with the route reflector. ddos flowspec Optional automatic upstream mitigation policy for the DDoS pipeline. over-limit-policy drop is the default. During first turn-up you can set accept to observe the rate without dropping, then remove it after counters and logs look correct. Neither setting admits a source that is not a configured neighbor or a trusted-source. The bridge receives selected routes from bgp-rib. Received UPDATE events do not program the firewall.
