The RIB validates FlowSpec against unicast reachability and removes rules when authorization is lost. Startup requests replay the current selected rules, including their action communities. The same peer must also supply eligible unicast reachability covering the protected destination, or reflect it with the matching ORIGINATOR_ID. With no covering unicast route, a received external FlowSpec rule cannot authorize itself. Enabling the unicast family above supplies that validation input. The firewall applies an attribute-only replacement to the same rule and removes the old action even when the replacement cannot be enforced. Native NLRI length encoding does not create a second rule. VPN FlowSpec remains a BGP validation and propagation capability; this global firewall bridge installs SAFI 133 only. At initial configuration, after the firewall backend is ready, the bridge clears any ze_flowspec table left by a previous process before requesting replay. Live plugin removal suspends selected-route callbacks while it withdraws the table. A failed reconcile restores the previous desired rules and returns an error without disabling delivery, so the running configuration remains usable and removal can be retried. Successful removal stops delivery. Daemon shutdown remains governed by firewall { flush-on-shutdown ...; }; the bridge does not flush separately. A compensating Configure after failed removal preserves that live subscription and selection; it does not repeat the startup sweep. Initialization is complete only after replay succeeds. A failed initial replay removes its partial rules and subscription instead of treating that partial view as configured. Enabling a FlowSpec family derives a bgp-rib receive binding for every BGP peer, including unicast-only peers and dynamic group templates. An explicit binding must grant update-received and state; a narrower binding is refused at configuration load because it would hide routes needed for authorization. This does not grant the RIB permission to send routes. FlowSpec authorization requires an internal bgp-rib. A bgp-rs, bgp-rr or bgp-adj-rib-in process that receives a FlowSpec peer's state and has send [ update ] permission must also run internally: its peer-up replay reads the same process-local selecting RIB. Process aliases do not change this requirement. An Adj-RIB-In that normally delegates replay still needs access, because it resumes replay when the forwarder's per-peer ownership is absent. External processes attached only to unicast peers, or without the state and UPDATE-send grants needed for replay, remain supported. Execution mode comes from the effective plugin declaration: use bgp-rib runs in-process even inside an external stanza, while run "ze plugin bgp-rib" forks a subprocess. Validation and derived receive bindings use that same resolved declaration. Replay admission identifies FlowSpec from each configured family's registered SAFI, including VPN FlowSpec, rather than from a fixed list of family names. A configured name absent from the registry is refused. 3. Check the firewall backend export XDG_RUNTIME_DIR=/run/ze /usr/local/bin/ze cli -c "show bgp peer list" /usr/local/bin/ze show warnings sudo nft list ruleset | sed -n '/table inet ze_flowspec/,+80p' The FlowSpec bridge generates an nft table named ze_flowspec. The ze_ prefix is what tells the firewall backend the table is ze's, so a route the peer withdraws takes its rules out of the kernel with it. show firewall ruleset and the web pages strip the prefix, so the name you type there stays flowspec. The bridge creates base chains for forwarded traffic and local input traffic when rules exist: Chain Hook Used for flowspec-fwd forward Transit packets matching any selected FlowSpec rule. flo

title: FlowSpec route reflector
text: FlowSpec route reflector Use this when you want one Ze node to receive FlowSpec routes from mitigation systems or edge routers and reflect them to iBGP clients. The example is a single AS with one Ze route reflector, one upstream FlowSpec receiver, and two edge clients. It enables the bgp-rr runtime plugin, negotiates ipv4/flow, marks the edge peers as route-reflector clients, and binds the peers to the reflector plugin. 1. Start from an installed Ze node Follow Build and install Ze on Ubuntu through the systemd step. Keep the same active file name, edge-01.conf, or replace it in the commands below. This page uses these addresses: Node Role IP AS fs-rr Ze FlowSpec route reflector 10.0.0.1 65000 mitigation-upstream upstream or mitigation controller 10.0.0.2 65000 edge-a Ze or router client 10.0.0.11 65000 edge-b Ze or router client 10.0.0.12 65000 2. Update the active stored config Keep the active configuration in the database/ store. The commands below read the current active config, normalize it to set format, append the route-reflector settings, render the import file, validate the result, import it back into the store, and reload the daemon. They do not create /etc/ze/edge-01.conf. set -euo pipefail umask 077 CONFIG_SET="$(mktemp)" CONFIG_IMPORT="$(mktemp)" trap 'rm -f "$CONFIG_SET" "$CONFIG_IMPORT"' EXIT sudo /usr/local/bin/ze config cat edge-01.conf | /usr/local/bin/ze config migrate -o "$CONFIG_SET" - cat >>"$CONFIG_SET" <<'EOF' set plugin internal bgp-rr use bgp-rr set bgp router-id 10.0.0.1 set bgp session asn local 65000 set bgp peer mitigation-upstream description "Upstream FlowSpec receiver" set bgp peer mitigation-upstream connection remote ip 10.0.0.2 set bgp peer mitigation-upstream connection local ip 10.0.0.1 set bgp peer mitigation-upstream connection ttl min 255 set bgp peer mitigation-upstream session asn local 65000 set bgp peer mitigation-upstream session asn remote 65000 set bgp peer mitigation-upstream session route-reflector-client disable set bgp peer mitigation-upstream session cluster-id 10.0.0.1 set bgp peer mitigation-upstream session next-hop unchanged set bgp peer mitigation-upstream session family ipv4/flow mode enable set bgp peer mitigation-upstream session family ipv4/flow prefix maximum 1000 set bgp peer mitigation-upstream attach process bgp-rr receive [ update-received state open-received ] set bgp peer mitigation-upstream attach process bgp-rr send [ update ] set bgp peer edge-a description "FlowSpec client edge-a" set bgp peer edge-a connection remote ip 10.0.0.11 set bgp peer edge-a connection local ip 10.0.0.1 set bgp peer edge-a session asn local 65000 set bgp peer edge-a session asn remote 65000 set bgp peer edge-a session route-reflector-client enable set bgp peer edge-a session cluster-id 10.0.0.1 set bgp peer edge-a session next-hop unchanged set bgp peer edge-a session family ipv4/flow mode enable set bgp peer edge-a session family ipv4/flow prefix maximum 1000 set bgp peer edge-a attach process bgp-rr receive [ update-received state open-received ] set bgp peer edge-a attach process bgp-rr send [ update ] set bgp peer edge-b description "FlowSpec client edge-b" set bgp peer edge-b connection remote ip 10.0.0.12 set bgp peer edge-b connection local ip 10.0.0.1 set bgp peer edge-b session asn local 65000 set bgp peer edge-b session asn remote 65000 set bgp peer edge-b session route-reflector-client enable set bgp peer edge-b session cluster-id 10.0.0.1 set bgp peer edge-b session next-hop unchanged set bgp peer edge-b session family ipv4/flow mode enable set bgp peer edge-b session family ipv4/flow prefix maximum 1000 set bgp peer edge-b attach process bgp-rr receive [ update-received state open-received ] set bgp peer edge-b attach process bgp-rr send [ update ] EOF /usr/local/bin/ze config migrate -o "$CONFIG_IMPORT" format hierarchical "$CONFIG_SET" /usr/local/bin/ze config validate "$CONFIG_IMPORT" sudo /usr/local/bin/ze config import --yes --name edge-01.conf "$CONFIG_IMPORT" sudo systemctl reload ze.service Expected validation output: configuration valid: /tmp/tmp.XXXXXXXXXX What matters: Config Why plugin { internal bgp-rr { use bgp-rr; } } Starts the in-process route reflector plugin. attach process bgp-rr { receive [ update-received state open-received ]; send [ update ]; } on each peer Feeds the reflector what it declares it handles, and lets it reflect back. The received direction is not a preference: reflecting an UPDATE raises the sent event the reflection is waiting on, so a plain update deadlocks it. family ipv4/flow Negotiates FlowSpec NLRI with the peer. route-reflector-client enable on edge clients Routes from clients are reflected to all clients and non-clients. next-hop unchanged Keeps the mitigation next-hop unchanged. Change this only when your design requires next-hop rewrite. cluster-id 10.0.0.1 Uses a stable route reflector cluster ID. The plugin dependency bgp-adj-rib-in is added by the plugin dependency resolver. There is no separate route-reflector config root. 3. Verify sessions and reflector state export XDG_RUNTIME_DIR=/run/ze /usr/local/bin/ze cli -c "show bgp peer list" /usr/local/bin/ze cli -c "show rr status" /usr/local/bin/ze cli -c "show rr peers" Each row of an established peer carries families: the address families the reflector recorded from that peer's OPEN, sorted (ipv4/unicast alone when the OPEN carried no Multiprotocol capability). A row whose peer is down, or whose OPEN the reflector could not read, has no families key. show bgp rs peers carries the same key for the route server. If a peer does not show the FlowSpec family, check the remote router address-family configuration first. Ze cannot reflect a family that was not negotiated. 4. Inject a test FlowSpec rule The reflector only reflects FlowSpec it receives, so originate the test rule from a peer that announces toward the reflector, not from the reflector itself. The rule below matches TCP traffic to 10.0.0.0/8 with destination port 80. If the source peer (mitigation-upstream, 10.0.0.2) is itself a Ze node, announce toward the reflector (10.0.0.1) with the required peer <selector> prefix: export XDG_RUNTIME_DIR=/run/ze /usr/local/bin/ze cli -c "send bgp 10.0.0.1 update text extended-community discard mp ipv4/flow add destination-ipv4 10.0.0.0/8 protocol tcp destination-port =80" The peer <selector> prefix is required; the update command does not dispatch without it. On a non-Ze source, use that router's FlowSpec origination syntax instead. Withdraw it with the same match components: /usr/local/bin/ze cli -c "send bgp 10.0.0.1 update text mp ipv4/flow del destination-ipv4 10.0.0.0/8 protocol tcp destination-port =80" Then confirm edge-a and edge-b received the reflected rule with show rr peers or the client's own FlowSpec table. The bgp-rr plugin forwards cached UPDATEs and the reactor applies the route-reflection rules, including source exclusion, client to all, non-client to clients only, ORIGINATOR_ID, CLUSTER_LIST, and next-hop policy. 5. Router-side shape On a conventional router, configure the Ze node as an iBGP route reflector and enable the FlowSpec address family. Vendor syntax differs, but the intent is always the same: neighbor 10.0.0.1 remote-as 65000 neighbor 10.0.0.1 update-source LOOPBACK0 address-family ipv4 flowspec neighbor 10.0.0.1 activate If the router expects TTL security, match the Ze ttl min 255 policy on the router. If the router uses TCP MD5, add the same connection md5 password block to each Ze peer. 6. Operations export XDG_RUNTIME_DIR=/run/ze /usr/local/bin/ze cli -c "show rr status" /usr/local/bin/ze cli -c "show rr peers" /usr/local/bin/ze cli -c "monitor event" /usr/local/bin/ze show warnings source bgp Common mistakes: Symptom Check Peer up but no FlowSpec routes Confirm ipv4/flow was negotiated on both sides. Updates are reflected back to the origin Confirm the source peer is bound to attach process bgp-rr and is visible in show rr peers. Clients do not receive non-clie

title: gNMI Guide
text: gNMI Guide Ze includes a gNMI (gRPC Network Management Interface) server that exposes YANG-modeled configuration over the industry-standard gNMI protocol. This allows management by tools like gnmic, Ansible, and network controllers that speak gNMI. Default feature-tag lists include ze_gnmi. A custom minimal build that needs gNMI must include -tags "ze_core ze_gnmi". Enabling gNMI gNMI is disabled by default. Enable it via environment variables or YANG config. Environment variables: ze.gnmi.enabled=true ze.gnmi.listen=0.0.0.0:9339 ze.gnmi.token=your-secret-token ze.gnmi.tls.cert=/path/to/cert.pem ze.gnmi.tls.key=/path/to/key.pem YANG config (in ze.conf): environment { gnmi { enabled true; token your-secret-token; tls { cert /path/to/cert.pem; key /path/to/key.pem; } server default { ip 0.0.0.0; port 9339; } } } Authentication When ze.gnmi.token is set, every gNMI request must include a Bearer token in the authorization gRPC metadata header. The token is compared using constant-time comparison (SHA-256 hash with subtle.ConstantTimeCompare) to prevent timing attacks. When no token is configured, gNMI may bind only to a literal loopback address (127.0.0.1 or ::1) and runs in read-only mode: Capabilities, Get, and Subscribe succeed, while Set is refused with PermissionDenied (matching REST and gRPC read-only loopback enforcement). Non-loopback listeners without a token are refused. Failed bearer token checks record auth-fail audit entries (without logging any rejected token bytes) and committed Set operations record config-commit audit entries under the gnmi audit surface. TLS TLS is required on every non-loopback gNMI listener: both the boot-time management-listener guard and Server.Serve refuse to start a non-loopback listener without both a token and TLS credentials so credentials and configuration never cross the network in clear text. Loopback listeners (127.0.0.1 or ::1) may run without TLS. To enable TLS on the gNMI gRPC transport: ze.gnmi.tls.cert=/path/to/cert.pem ze.gnmi.tls.key=/path/to/key.pem Or in YANG config: environment { gnmi { tls { cert /path/to/cert.pem; key /path/to/key.pem; } } } TLS certificates are loaded once at startup. Certificate rotation requires restarting the gNMI server. Naming either file asks for TLS, and gNMI then serves TLS or nothing. It never falls back to clear text. When only one of the two files is set, when a file cannot be read, or when the certificate and key are not a valid pair, gNMI does not start: nothing listens on its port, and Ze logs an error naming the file, why, and the fix. The rest of the daemon keeps running. Restore the file or correct environment gnmi tls cert / key (or ze.gnmi.tls.cert / ze.gnmi.tls.key), then restart ze: sudo systemctl restart ze only when ze runs under ze.service, otherwise ze signal stop, then a start the way ze was started. A reload does not restart gNMI. The error carries the code doctor-gnmi-tls-material, and ze doctor reports the same cause before the daemon starts: its gnmi-tls-material check loads the pair gNMI would serve, environment overrides included, and names the file, why, and the fix. It also reports a certificate that is expired or not yet valid as an error, and one within 30 days of expiry as a warning. It reports nothing when gNMI does not start or names no TLS file. ze show diagnostic doctor-gnmi-tls-material explains the code. Supported RPCs RPC Description Capabilities Returns supported YANG models, encodings (JSON and JSON_IETF), and gNMI version Get Reads config state from the running tree by path Set Applies config modifications atomically (update, replace, delete) Subscribe ONCE Snapshot of current config for requested paths Subscribe STREAM Continuous change notifications (from gNMI Set and external commits) Sensitive values A leaf the YANG model marks ze:sensitive (a BGP MD5 password, a TACACS+ or RADIUS shared key, the gNMI token) never reaches a client in clear. Get, Subscribe ONCE and the STREAM notification that echoes a Set all carry it in its reversible $9$ form, the form ze config fmt and the CLI write to the config file. A value the config file already holds in $9$ form is answered with that same text. The echo goes to every subscriber, so the key one client sent is never shown to another. Set accepts a sensitive value either in clear or in the $9$ form a Get returned. A $9$ value is decoded to the key the daemon uses, and the config keeps the $9$ text exactly as written, so a value read with Get and sent back with Set leaves the config file unchanged. When Set is refused An update the session refuses (a path the schema does not hold, a list key outside its type) ends the Set with status InvalidArgument, and nothing it carried is applied. A refused key's message is the refusal Ze prints on every surface, unchanged, so its last line is the fix. A session refusal that carries no fix of its own is answered with the path, the cause, and a fix that says to send the Set again with a path and a value the schema accepts. A value the schema refuses (outside an enumeration, a range, a length or a format) is refused when the Set commits: the status is Aborted, the message starts commit: config validation failed:, and each refusal follows as its own block, ending with the set command from the root that fixes it. The shape of each block is Value refusals. When a call meets an internal defect Every call and every Subscribe stream runs behind a panic boundary, outside the token check. If a Ze defect is reached while one is served, only that call or stream ends, with status Internal and a message that says so and names the ze show crashes command that finds its crash record. A Set that ends this way discards its uncommitted edits, so nothing it changed is applied. The listener and every other call and stream keep running. The panic is logged, crash recorded, and counted in ze_task_panics_total{component="gnmi",task="rpc"} and ze_gnmi_errors_total{code="Internal"} (monitoring). CLI Status Check gNMI server status from the SSH CLI when ze_gnmi is compiled in: show gnmi Returns JSON with: enabled, listen address, token configured, TLS configured, and active subscriber count. Prometheus Metrics Metric Type Labels Description ze_gnmi_requests_total counter rpc Total gNMI RPC requests ze_gnmi_subscribe_active gauge -- Active Subscribe STREAM connections ze_gnmi_errors_total counter rpc, code gNMI RPC errors by gRPC status code Usage with gnmic Example using gnmic to get the full config tree: gnmic -a 192.0.2.1:9339 --token your-secret-token get --path / Example to subscribe to config changes: gnmic -a 192.0.2.1:9339 --token your-secret-token subscribe --path / --mode stream Limitations Subscribe POLL mode is not implemented Telemetry SAMPLE mode (periodic counter streaming) is not supported gNMI path target field (multi-target) is not supported TLS certificates are loaded at startup only; no hot rotation External config commits (web/CLI) send a generic config-changed notification, not per-path diffs

title: Graceful Restart
text: Graceful Restart Graceful Restart (RFC 4724) preserves forwarding state across BGP session restarts. When a peer goes down and comes back, routes are held during the restart window instead of being immediately withdrawn, preventing traffic black-holes. Configuration plugin { internal gr { use bgp-gr } internal rib { use bgp-rib } } bgp { peer upstream1 { remote { ip 10.0.0.1; as 65001; } ... capability { graceful-restart { short-lived { restart-time 120; } } } attach process gr { receive [ open state eor ] send [ update ] } attach process rib { receive [ update state refresh ] send [ update ] } } } Config Reference Path Type Default Description graceful-restart / short-lived / restart-time uint16 120 Seconds to hold stale routes during conventional GR (0-4095); omitting short-lived sends code 64 with Restart Time 0 and no family tuples graceful-restart / short-lived / family list (name) -- Address families code 64 names when short-lived is present. Absent: every family the peer carries; present: only the listed families graceful-restart / long-lived / family / stale-time uint32 -- Per-family Long-Lived Stale Time in seconds (0-16777215, mandatory per entry) advertised in code 71 How It Works What Ze Advertises The code-64 capability Ze sends carries the Restart Time, then one <AFI, SAFI, Flags> tuple for each address family the peer carries. A peer configured for ipv4/unicast and ipv6/unicast with the default restart time receives 0078 00010100 00020100. The family list defaults to the peer's own family configuration (narrowed when short-lived / family is written); code 71 (LLGR) is configured separately under long-lived / family. RFC 9494 Section 4.2 reads a family that code 64 omits as a Restart Time of zero. A tuple tells the peer that Ze can preserve that family across a restart, and what Ze keeps is the RIB plugin's copy of the routes, which it sends again once the session is back. RFC 4724 Section 4: "A BGP speaker MAY advertise the Graceful Restart Capability for an address family to its peer if it has the ability to preserve its forwarding state for the address family when BGP restarts." So code 64 lists a family only when the RIB plugin can store it, which is when an NLRI splitter frames that family. bgp-gr always loads bgp-rib, and every family compiled into Ze has a splitter, so the check removes nothing from a stock build. A family an external plugin registers at runtime with no splitter is left out, and Ze logs a warning naming the peer and the family. When no family is left, Ze still sends the capability, with no tuple. The graceful-restart short-lived family list narrows code 64 alone: capability { graceful-restart { short-lived { restart-time 120; family { ipv6/unicast } } } } That peer receives 0078 00020100, whatever else its family configuration carries. Omitting short-lived altogether (writing graceful-restart { } or configuring only long-lived { ... }) makes Ze send code 64 with Restart Time 0 and no address family tuple (0000), which RFC 4724 Section 3 reads as a speaker that runs the Receiving Speaker procedures and preserves nothing of its own, and RFC 9494 Section 4.1 uses to skip the conventional GR phase. Writing short-lived with no family list is the default for conventional GR, naming every family the peer carries. The list only narrows: a family the RIB plugin cannot store is left out with the same warning, never added. A family under short-lived family or long-lived family that the peer's own family list does not carry is refused, because RFC 4724 Section 3 and RFC 9494 Section 3.1 scope a tuple to routes "advertised with the same AFI and SAFI" and the session carries none of them. Ze names the family in the error. The refusal runs at offline ze config validate, at config commit, and at startup rather than leaving the daemon running without Graceful Restart. The families the peer carries include the ones it inherits from its group, and exclude any entry written mode disable. Both are what the session really negotiates. Omitting short-lived while configuring long-lived is how an operator asks for LLGR with no conventional GR phase. RFC 9494 Section 4.1: "the conventional GR phase can be skipped by omitting all AFIs/SAFIs from the GR Capability, advertising a Restart Time of zero, or both". short-lived family and long-lived family govern code 64 and code 71 independently. The Two Bits Ze Sets at Connection Time The payload above is built when the configuration is loaded, so it carries what the operator configured and nothing about a restart. Two bits say what happened to Ze, and both are written on the way to the OPEN. The Restart State bit says Ze has restarted. ze signal restart writes the restart marker, and the reactor sets the bit while that marker is live. Outside the window a new connection gets 0, which is a cold start. The Forwarding State bit of an address family says the routes of that family were still being forwarded while Ze was down. Ze sets it inside the same window, and only when the forwarding plane kept its routes. The kernel FIB does keep them by default: fib { kernel { } } leaves every route it installed in place as Ze stops, marks them on the way back up and removes only the ones that do not return (flush-on-stop, sweep-delay). Writing flush-on-stop true, or configuring no FIB at all, means nothing was preserved and the bit stays 0. The bit decides what the peer does the moment Ze comes back. RFC 4724 Section 4.2: if it "is not set in the newly received Graceful Restart Capability ... then the Receiving Speaker MUST immediately remove all the stale routes from the peer that it is retaining for that address family". So a peer holds Ze's routes while the session is down either way, and a clear bit makes it drop them at re-establishment rather than waiting for Ze to re-advertise. Normal Session Peer session establishes, GR capability negotiated in OPEN Routes received and installed in RIB normally Peer Restarts Peer goes down -- unless the session ended by a NOTIFICATION, sent or received. RFC 4724 Section 4 says "the normal BGP procedures MUST be followed when the TCP session terminates due to the sending or receiving of a BGP NOTIFICATION message", so that down (reason notification) retains nothing. Ze never advertises the RFC 8538 N bit, so no NOTIFICATION is graceful. A session whose received UPDATEs Ze could not publish to its plugins retains nothing either: Ze ends it with a Cease (Out of Resources), and when that Cease did not reach the peer, or the session had already ended, the down carries reason adj-rib-in-invalid, because the routes it holds are known to be incomplete or already withdrawn. For any other down (tcp-failure, local-close) the GR plugin sends retain-routes with the received GR families plus exchanged LLGR families whose received LLST is nonzero RIB marks routes as stale -- routes kept in forwarding but flagged Restart timer starts -- countdown from restart-time seconds Peer reconnects -- new session established, fresh routes received. A family whose Forwarding State bit is clear in the new OPEN, a family the new capability omits, and every family when the new OPEN carries no Graceful Restart Capability at all, are purged with purge-stale at once (RFC 4724 Section 4.2) Fresh routes replace stale -- each new route implicitly clears its stale flag End-of-RIB received -- GR plugin sends purge-stale to RIB Remaining stale routes removed -- any route not refreshed is withdrawn The RIB retains only those families: a negotiated family with neither a GR period nor an enabled LLGR period is removed from the received inventory as well as withdrawn from its recorded destinations. GR supplies the explicit on-down argument so RIB applies the family list before its DOWN event but leaves nonretained-family wire withdrawals to the forwarding DOWN owner (RS); no second retained-route inventory is kept. The operator form request bgp rib retain-routes <selector> remains peer-wide. Supplying [famil

title: Native IKEv2 and IPsec
text: Native IKEv2 and IPsec Pre-Alpha. This page describes behavior that may change. Ze implements native IKEv2 in Go for route-based IPsec VPN tunnels. It does not require strongSwan, libreswan, or another external IKE daemon. The IKE engine, cryptographic primitives, wire codec, and XFRM dataplane integration are all in-tree. The Ze binary negotiates IKE SAs, installs XFRM policies and states, and programs routes through XFRM interfaces from the same YANG config tree as every other subsystem. Live IPsec demonstration The recording loads IKE, ESP, peer authentication and selectors, then XFRM routing into one SSH candidate on a running router. A hidden Ze responder protects the other host. Kernel SPIs and increasing packets-in after a protected-host ping distinguish installed forwarding from negotiated state. The failure changes only ESP to a cipher the responder does not offer. show vpn ipsec peer name responder can still report established IKE with no Child SA. show log recent level warn | match NO_PROPOSAL_CHOSEN | last 1 | yaml shows the latest refusal with notify: NO_PROPOSAL_CHOSEN and peer: responder in the same entry's structured attributes, without unrelated warnings scrolling it out of view. Empty dataplane drift means the expected SA identities are present, not that a tunnel exists or that every forwarding policy is installed. The repair restores the ESP group, clears that peer's SAs and proves protected traffic again. For Junos operators, the equivalent observations are show security ike security-associations for IKE and show security ipsec security-associations for the installed IPsec SAs and SPIs. Demo: Build and repair a native IPsec tunnel live Commit IKE, ESP, selectors and XFRM routing over SSH, prove kernel SPIs with protected traffic, diagnose an ESP mismatch, and restore the tunnel. Download the asciicast recording · Plain-text transcript Recorded with Ze 26.11.20 in a Linux namespace lab using Ze recorder. Duration: 3 minutes 37 seconds. Native IKEv2 and Linux IPsec, configured live Lab: shown Ze 172.30.0.1 initiates to a hidden Ze responder at 172.30.0.2. Protected hosts 10.78.1.2 and 10.78.2.2 live behind different routers. The shown daemon starts with no VPN configuration or XFRM interface. $ ze-demo card topic-ipsec lab $ ze-demo card topic-ipsec overview In one SSH candidate, load topics/ipsec/1-ike.conf, 2-esp.conf, 3-peer.conf, and 4-xfrm.conf with load file absolute merge. Review show | compare and commit now. The sections define IKE, ESP, authenticated peer and selectors, and the route through vpn-xfrm (if-id 42). $ sshpass -e ssh ze-demo ze# load file absolute merge topics/ipsec/1-ike.conf ze# load file absolute merge topics/ipsec/2-esp.conf ze# load file absolute merge topics/ipsec/3-peer.conf ze# load file absolute merge topics/ipsec/4-xfrm.conf ze# show | compare ze# commit now ze# exit ze> exit $ ze-demo card topic-ipsec proof $ ze cli -c 'show vpn ipsec status | no-more' $ ze cli -c 'show vpn ipsec sa | no-more' $ ze cli -c 'show vpn ipsec dataplane sa | no-more' $ ze-demo run showcase-lab control vpn ping $ ze cli -c 'show vpn ipsec sa | no-more' The kernel SPIs must match the negotiated Child SA. The protected ping must succeed and the same inbound SA's packets-in must increase. Failure: load 5-mismatch.conf and commit. It changes only ESP to AES-128; the far end offers AES-256. IKE can stay established while no Child SA exists. $ ze-demo card topic-ipsec failure $ sshpass -e ssh ze-demo ze# load file absolute merge topics/ipsec/5-mismatch.conf ze# show | compare ze# commit now ze# exit ze> exit $ ze-demo card topic-ipsec diagnosis $ ze cli -c 'show vpn ipsec peer name responder | no-more' $ ze cli -c 'show log recent level warn | match NO_PROPOSAL_CHOSEN | last 1 | yaml | no-more' $ ze cli -c 'show vpn ipsec dataplane sa | yaml | no-more' $ ze cli -c 'show vpn ipsec dataplane drift | yaml | no-more' The same log entry carries peer responder and notify NO_PROPOSAL_CHOSEN under attributes beside the message that IKE remains established. An empty drift result means the engine and kernel agree, not that a tunnel carries traffic. Load 2-esp.conf, review and commit, then clear vpn ipsec sa peer responder. Verify the new kernel SPIs, successful protected ping and increasing packets-in. The shown Ze process is never restarted. $ sshpass -e ssh ze-demo ze# load file absolute merge topics/ipsec/2-esp.conf ze# show | compare ze# commit now ze# exit ze> exit $ ze cli -c 'clear vpn ipsec sa peer responder | no-more' $ ze-demo run showcase-lab control vpn ping $ ze cli -c 'show vpn ipsec sa | no-more' $ ze cli -c 'show vpn ipsec dataplane sa | no-more' $ ze-demo card topic-ipsec recap Vendor mapping: Junos show security ike security-associations reads IKE state; show security ipsec security-associations reads the IPsec SAs and their SPIs. https://www.juniper.net/documentation/us/en/software/junos/cli-reference/topics/ref/command/show-security-ike-security-associations.html https://www.juniper.net/documentation/us/en/software/junos/cli-reference/topics/ref/command/show-security-ipsec-security-associations.html https://www.juniper.net/documentation/us/en/software/junos/cli-reference/topics/ref/statement/security-edit-proposal.html Architecture The IPsec stack is split across several packages: Package Role internal/component/ike/wire IKEv2 wire format codec for RFC 7296 payloads internal/component/ike/crypto DH groups, PRFs, integrity, encryption, and key derivation internal/component/ike/transport UDP transport with NAT-T keepalives and port 4500 encapsulation internal/core/eap EAP-MSCHAPv2, EAP-TLS and EAP MD5-Challenge authentication internal/component/ike/engine IKE_SA_INIT, IKE_AUTH, CREATE_CHILD_SA, and INFORMATIONAL state machines for initiator and responder roles, rekeying, and DPD internal/component/ike/ipsec YANG schema, configuration, and validation internal/component/ike/dataplane XFRM policy and state programming through netlink internal/component/pki X.509 certificate and private-key store Configuration IPsec is configured under vpn { ipsec { } }. Named ike-group and esp-group blocks hold the IKE and ESP proposals and lifetimes. Each site-to-site peer references a group pair, sets its authentication, and binds to an XFRM interface for route-based forwarding. A peer's and remote-access's ike-group and esp-group are leafrefs: commit, a SIGHUP reload and ze config validate refuse a name no group declares, naming the groups that exist, and the editor completes the names. pki { ca my-ca { certificate "-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----..."; } certificate my-cert { certificate "-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----..."; private { key "-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----..."; } } } vpn { ipsec { interface eth0; ike-group site-b-ike { key-exchange ikev2; lifetime 28800; proposal 1 { encryption aes256gcm; hash sha256; dh-group 14; } dead-peer-detection { interval 30; timeout 120; } } esp-group site-b-esp { lifetime 3600; pfs enable; proposal 1 { encryption aes256gcm; } } site-to-site { peer site-b { ike-group site-b-ike; esp-group site-b-esp; connection-type initiate; local-address 198.51.100.2; remote-address 198.51.100.1; authentication { mode x509; certificate my-cert; ca-certificate my-ca; } vti { bind vti0; } } } } } Traffic selectors constrain which protected networks a peer negotiates. Route-based forwarding also needs a route through the bound XFRM interface. The generated configuration reference documents the XFRM interface leaves. In the live demonstration, the route is 10.78.2.0/24 with next { interface vpn-xfrm {} }. The empty next-hop entry is meaningful: it selects the XFRM interface without a gateway or another leaf. The editor records this as an owned entry, not as a side effect of configuring the nearby interface leaves. It must survive the SSH candidate commit and appear in the kernel routing table. Established IKE, installed SAs and an up XFRM interface do not substitute for that route. If the protected ping receives Destination Ne

title: Filter BGP Imports with IRR
text: Filter BGP Imports with IRR Ze can build a BGP import prefix-list from an ASN or IRR AS-SET. The irr plugin resolves the AS-SET through an IRR whois server and stores the resulting IPv4 and IPv6 prefixes, and the bgp-filter-irr plugin rejects received routes that are not in that stored list. Use this for a customer or peer that should only announce prefixes registered to its network. It replaces a separate bgpq4 job and static prefix-list deployment. Complete example This example accepts registered routes from customer AS 65001. Replace the addresses, ASN, and AS-CUSTOMER with values for your network. plugin { internal bgp-adj-rib-in { use bgp-adj-rib-in } internal bgp-filter-irr { use bgp-filter-irr } } system { irr { server whois.radb.net refresh-interval 3600 } peeringdb { url https://www.peeringdb.com } } bgp { router-id 192.0.2.1 session { asn { local 65000 } } peer customer-a { connection { remote { ip 198.51.100.2 } local { ip 198.51.100.1 } } session { asn { local 65000 remote 65001 } family { ipv4/unicast { prefix { maximum 1000 } } ipv6/unicast { prefix { maximum 1000 } } } irr { as-set AS-CUSTOMER } } filter { import { filters [ bgp-filter-irr:65001 ]; final accept; } } attach process bgp-adj-rib-in { receive [ update-received state ] } } } The two plugin blocks load the filter and Adj-RIB-In. The Adj-RIB-In plugin is not required to make the filter decision, but it provides show bgp adj-rib-in so you can verify which routes passed. The suffix in bgp-filter-irr:65001 is the peer's remote ASN. It selects the dynamic list associated with AS 65001. Use the corresponding ASN in each peer's filter reference. Prefixes that do not match that list are rejected by the implicit deny. No attach process bgp-filter-irr block is needed. A filter reference invokes the plugin directly through the BGP import filter chain. Add it to an existing stored configuration If the stored ze.conf already contains the BGP peer but no IRR filter, stop Ze and add these settings to the stored configuration. An offline ze config set writes the file path it is given and never resolves a stored name, so the stored configuration travels through stdin: ze config cat reads it, one ze config set - stage applies each setting, and ze config import stores the result as a new version. $ sudo systemctl stop ze.service $ ze config cat ze.conf | > ze config set - plugin internal bgp-filter-irr use bgp-filter-irr | > ze config set - system irr server whois.radb.net | > ze config set - system irr refresh-interval 3600 | > ze config set - bgp peer customer-a session irr as-set AS-CUSTOMER | > ze config set - bgp peer customer-a filter import filters bgp-filter-irr:65001 | > ze config set - bgp peer customer-a filter import final accept | > ze config import --yes --name ze.conf - $ sudo systemctl start ze.service The import replaces the stored ze.conf only because --yes confirms it; the previous version stays available to ze config rollback. Nothing here contacts the daemon, which is stopped anyway. Starting Ze loads the plugin; the irr plugin fetches the AS-SET in the background the first time and stores it. An UPDATE that arrives before the list is rejected at once and kept for another evaluation, as After a restart describes. Replace ze.conf, customer-a, AS-CUSTOMER, and 65001 with the stored configuration key, peer name, AS-SET, and remote ASN for your deployment. Run ze config cat ze.conf before and after these commands to review the stored changes. This offline workflow is separate from the live SSH workflow in the demonstration below. Choose the AS-SET Set session { irr { as-set AS-CUSTOMER; } } when you know the correct AS-SET. This is the most predictable production configuration. Tab completes the name. On the peer's session irr as-set, on the firewall's AS-SET leaves, and after update irr as-set and clear irr as-set, Ze offers every AS-SET the irr plugin knows: each name a consumer references and each name it has stored, in upper case, marked "AS-SET with a stored IRR dataset" or "AS-SET a consumer references, nothing stored yet". The suggestion refuses nothing, so an AS-SET nothing references yet stays valid: writing it is how you ask for it. If you omit as-set, Ze queries PeeringDB with the remote ASN. It uses the registered irr_as_set value when one exists, then falls back to the origin object AS<number> if PeeringDB does not return an AS-SET. For a peer that must bypass this policy, set: session { irr { enable disable } } Changing IRR settings on a running router A commit that changes a peer's as-set or a peer's filter import filters reference takes effect on the running filter. A changed as-set does not inherit the list of the old one: when the new set is stored the filter enforces it at once; when it is not, the irr plugin fetches it right after the commit, and an UPDATE from that peer before it arrives has its announced routes rejected and kept, and the filter asks the peer for them again once the new list arrives. Deleting the as-set counts as a change: the filter then enforces the set the irr plugin's PeeringDB answer for the remote ASN names, as for a peer that never named one. The irr plugin stores that answer, so a restart queries the same set without asking PeeringDB, and asks PeeringDB again when the set is due for a refresh; if PeeringDB does not answer, the stored set is kept. Where and when the irr plugin fetches is system irr and system peeringdb url (command reference, "show, update and clear irr"). Verify before carrying traffic After committing the configuration and establishing the BGP session, check the generated list: $ ze cli -c 'show bgp irr | no-more' $ ze cli -c 'show bgp irr prefix customer-a | no-more' These commands use the CLI's default text format. Its indented key/value layout can resemble YAML, but it is not YAML. text is the default unless environment { cli { format { default ... } } } changes it. Select another format explicitly with | yaml, | json, or | table. The prefix command takes the configured peer name. Confirm that the status is ok, the resolved AS-SET is correct, and the prefix counts are plausible. Test both a registered and an unregistered route without changing policy: $ ze cli -c 'show bgp irr check customer-a 203.0.113.0/24 | no-more' $ ze cli -c 'show bgp irr check customer-a 192.0.2.0/24 | no-more' Each result reports accepted: true or accepted: false. Use show bgp adj-rib-in to confirm that only accepted routes entered the inbound RIB. Refresh and failure behavior The irr plugin refreshes each stored list when system irr refresh-interval says it is due, counted from the last time the server answered. You can also fetch every set a consumer names, the set of one ASN, or one AS-SET at once; the filter enforces each stored list when the irr plugin announces it: $ ze cli -c 'update irr all' $ ze cli -c 'update irr asn 65001' $ ze cli -c 'update irr as-set AS-CUSTOMER' A refresh that returns prefixes is stored by the irr plugin, and the filter replaces the list it enforces atomically when it reads the stored copy (see "After a restart" below). Three other outcomes keep the last known good list instead, and each records the reason in show bgp irr: The refresh failed: the server was unreachable, refused the query, or sent a truncated reply. The refresh returned more than 500000 prefixes across both families. The BGP filter refuses the list whole rather than cutting it, because a cut kept the IPv4 half and lost IPv6; the error gives the IPv4 and IPv6 counts. Narrow the AS-SET. The refresh succeeded and returned no prefixes at all. Ze treats "I have nothing" the same as a failure, because an empty allow-list rejects every route the peer sends. A server that answers D (key not found), answers with no records, or reports an error can therefore not empty a live list. The prefixes an empty answer left in place are still enforced. show bgp irr and show firewall irr mark the entry stale and give the age of the data, so enforcing data no

title: IS-IS
text: IS-IS Ze implements IS-IS (Intermediate System to Intermediate System, ISO/IEC 10589 as updated by RFC 1195 / RFC 5305 / RFC 5308 / ...) as a native link-state interior gateway protocol that runs directly over Layer 2. This guide collects the user-facing behaviour; the wire format is documented in docs/architecture/wire/isis.md. Interface names are logical. interface <name> in an isis { } block refers to the Ze logical interface name, not necessarily the kernel device name. By default the logical name equals the kernel device, but an interface configured with an os-name selector binds a logical name to a different kernel device; IS-IS resolves the name to its kernel device through the shared iface resolver. See Logical Name and the os-name Selector. Routing capabilities The instance level limits every interface, including passive interfaces. With level l2, an interface whose level is omitted or set to l1-l2 uses only L2. On an l1-l2 instance, an interface can select l1 or l2. An enabled interface with no level in common with the instance is refused at startup or commit. Set its level to l1-l2 to use the instance's levels. show isis interface reports the effective level of each interface. IPv4 Protocols Supported (0xCC) is advertised on every circuit. Enabling IPv6 on any enabled interface, including a passive one, adds 0x8E to every Hello and LSP fragment zero. A commit updates both advertisements even when no active circuit changes; individual interfaces still control their addresses and prefixes. Connected and passive-interface prefixes are refreshed on activation and each commit, including interface, family, metric and level changes. Point-to-point links send and receive ISO 9542 ISHs as well as IS-IS Hellos. An ISH starts discovery but cannot establish or sustain an Up adjacency. Ze does not require one either: a neighbor that sends only IS-IS Hellos still forms its adjacency through the Hello exchange. Ze accepts narrow IPv4 reachability in TLV 128 and TLV 130 and preserves its internal or external metric type through SPF and inter-level leaking. Local connected and redistributed IPv4 prefixes use wide TLV 135 under the default metric-style wide, and narrow TLV 128 under narrow or transition (see "Narrow and wide metrics" below). An adjacent router's next-hop address can be on another logical subnet; forwarding retains the outgoing interface and marks the gateway on-link. Equal-cost originators contribute their capable next hops to the same route. If none of those selected next hops can forward an address family, the route is installed as unreachable rather than falling through to a default route. These rejected routes are withdrawn from redistribution until their selected adjacency can forward that address family again. The owner decisions recorded on 2026-09-21 are: "Keep standard fragment sets", "Keep specific prefixes", and "Do not originate IDRPI". Ze therefore uses one standard 256-fragment LSP set per source, leaks specific prefixes without manual summaries, and has no IDRPI producer or consumer. RFC 3786 extended-set modes and RFC 1195 manual-summary discard routes are not enabled features. The same day's TE path-computation decision was "Keep configured routes". RSVP-TE follows configured explicit routes and bypasses; no CSPF or TE shortest-path consumer is enabled. This leaves the wire requirements for any advertised TE information unchanged. Narrow and wide metrics metric-style picks the TLVs every LSP this router originates, its pseudo-node LSPs included, uses for its links and IPv4 prefixes: Style Links IPv4 prefixes Metric range wide (default) TLV 22 TLV 135 circuit 1 to 16777215 narrow TLV 2 TLV 128 circuit 1 to 63 transition TLV 2 and TLV 22 TLV 128 and TLV 135 circuit 1 to 63 A router that only understands narrow metrics cannot read TLV 22 or TLV 135, so it never computes a path through a wide-only Ze. RFC 3787 section 5 states that "If not all devices in the IS-IS domain support wide metrics, narrow metrics MUST continue to be used." Set narrow while any router in the domain is narrow-only: isis { net 49.0001.0000.0000.0001.00 metric-style narrow interfaces { interface eth0 { metric 20 } } } To migrate, RFC 3787 section 5.1 moves every router to transition one by one, then to wide once every router advertises wide metrics. Ze's SPF already reads both families from every LSP and keeps the lower cost of a link described twice. Under narrow and transition a circuit metric, or a level-1 / level-2 metric, above 63 is refused at commit, because the 6-bit narrow metric cannot carry it: isis: interface "eth0" metric 100 does not fit metric-style narrow, whose narrow metric is 1 to 63 (RFC 3787 section 5): set "isis interfaces interface eth0 metric 63" or lower, or set "isis metric-style wide" once every router in the domain supports wide metrics A prefix metric Ze did not take from a circuit, such as the fixed redistribution metric of 100 or an inter-level leak's sum, is advertised as 63 in TLV 128. IPv6 prefixes stay in TLV 236 in every style. A commit that changes only metric-style re-originates every own LSP at once. The dynamic hostname hostname names this router in the IS-IS network. Ze floods it in the Dynamic Hostname TLV 137, and a peer renders it wherever it would otherwise print a 6-octet system ID. isis { net 49.0001.0000.0000.0001.00 hostname core-1.example.net } Accepted shape. RFC 5301 section 3 encodes the value in 7-bit ASCII and calls its content a domain name. Ze enforces both at the config boundary: Rule Limit Character set Printable ASCII only, from space (0x20) to tilde (0x7e) One label 1 to 63 octets (RFC 2181 section 11) The whole name 1 to 255 octets, separators included Trailing dot One is permitted, and it marks the root The character rule bounds octets, not vocabulary. RFC 2181 section 11 forbids restricting WHICH characters a label carries. RFC 5301 section 3 says the value can be any string an operator wants. So core_1 and a name with spaces are both accepted. A name outside that shape is REFUSED, not repaired. ze config validate and a commit both fail, and the error names the offending octet or label: isis: isis/hostname: "café.example" is not a valid IS-IS hostname for isis/hostname: octet 4 is 0xc3. RFC 5301 section 3 encodes the value in 7-bit ASCII, so each character must be a printable ASCII character from space (0x20) to tilde (0x7e) Ze does not apply the IDNA ToASCII algorithm to a Unicode name. Converting it would put xn--caf-dma.example on the wire while the config file still read café.example. A name a peer sees must be the name an operator wrote. Use the ASCII form directly if that is the name you want advertised. A hostname a PEER advertises is treated as untrusted. It is accepted whatever its octets, and it is only filtered for display. RFC 5301 section 4 permits that. Rejecting a peer's LSP over its hostname would hand any neighbor a way to break this router. Changing an interface parameter on a running router A commit reaches the circuit that is already up. Ze does not wait for a link flap, a disable, or a restart. Adding the first NET to an idle daemon also starts receive processing, aging, flooding, and link monitoring; no daemon restart is required. Most parameters are written into the running circuit and cost no adjacency: metric, priority, hello-interval, hold-multiplier, the same four under level-1 and level-2, and the per-level auth-key-chain. A new hello interval takes effect with one IIH sent at the moment of the commit, before the new period starts. That IIH carries the new holding time, so the neighbor re-arms its adjacency timer from the new value: raising hello-interval from 3 to 30 seconds keeps the adjacency up, where a silent 30-second gap after a 9-second holding time would have dropped it. Three parameters decide what the circuit IS rather than what it advertises, and changing one closes the circuit and opens it again. That FLAPS every adjacency on the link, so plan it li

title: L2TPv2 LNS subsystem
text: L2TPv2 LNS subsystem Ze includes a native L2TPv2 (RFC 2661) LNS/LAC implementation used as a BNG (Broadband Network Gateway) component: it terminates L2TP tunnels over UDP, runs PPP negotiation (LCP, authentication, IPCP/IPv6CP), assigns peer IPs, and hands the kernel data plane to the l2tp_ppp module via netlink. Subscriber routes are tracked for redistribution into the protocol RIB. This page covers operator-facing use: configuration, the CLI surface, PPP negotiation, authentication, IP pools, traffic shaping, RADIUS, metrics, the web UI, reload semantics, and how subscriber routes flow out to BGP. Configuration The l2tp {} container carries protocol settings; listener endpoints live under environment { l2tp { server ... } }: l2tp { enabled true; shared-secret <secret>; // CHAP-MD5 tunnel auth (RFC 2661 S4.2) auth-method chap-md5; // PPP Auth-Protocol first advertised allow-no-auth false; // explicit opt-in required for no-auth proxy-lcp accept; // LNS: accept the LAC's proxy LCP, or renegotiate mru 1500; // Information-field octets; 68..1500, IPv6 needs 1280 lcp { restart-timer 3000; // milliseconds, 100..60000 max-terminate 2; // transmissions, including the first max-configure 10; // transmissions without a valid reply max-failure 5; // Naks before rejecting unacceptable options } authentication { allow [ chap-md5 ]; // ordered permitted methods; optional } hello-interval 60; // seconds of peer silence before HELLO hello-retries 2; // unanswered HELLO intervals before dead-peer teardown (0 disables) max-retransmit 5; // retransmissions of an unacknowledged message before the tunnel is cleared max-tunnels 1024; // 0 explicitly means unbounded max-sessions 1024; // per-tunnel, 0 explicitly means unbounded } environment { l2tp { server main { ip 0.0.0.0; port 1701; } } } Presence of l2tp {} with any content implies the subsystem is enabled. Set enabled false to disable explicitly. Listener endpoints use the standard zt:listener grouping (ip, port) with port conflict detection via ze:listener. A session that ended keeps its place under max-sessions until Ze has confirmed that its PPP and kernel resources are released, and a tunnel that closed with such sessions keeps its place under max-tunnels. A failed cleanup therefore cannot pile up resources without limit: once those places fill a tunnel, a new call on it is refused with a CDN, Result Code 4, as at the session limit, and a new tunnel is refused as at the tunnel limit. The log line and ze doctor (doctor-ppp-cleanup) say how many places unconfirmed cleanup holds, and show warnings lists the cleanup failures to repair. A limit of 0 then reads as the 16-bit ID space. shared-secret is also the secret a LAC hides AVPs under (RFC 2661 Section 4.3). Ze reveals a hidden AVP, a hidden Calling Number or proxy authentication field for instance, with the tunnel's secret and the Random Vector before it, and uses its value as if it had come in clear. Without a secret, or when the hidden value cannot be read, Ze logs hidden AVP left hidden with the reason and the fix; a mandatory hidden AVP then refuses its message (a CDN for a session, a StopCCN for the tunnel), and an optional one is ignored. The line names the peer, and ze doctor reports it under doctor-l2tp-hidden-avp-unrevealed with the same fix, at most once a minute per peer. The lcp settings control RFC 1661 retransmission on local PPP sessions. Each limit accepts 1 through 255. The Restart timer is restarted by each Configure-Request or Terminate-Request transmission, and by the Zero-Restart-Count action after the peer stops LCP. A silent peer receives exactly max-configure requests before negotiation ends. The defaults give a 30-second budget. max-failure counts Configure-Naks sent since the last Configure-Ack. After that many Naks, Ze rejects unacceptable options. An accepted proxy LCP starts already Opened and sends no initial requests. It retains the configured request budget for a later peer-triggered LCP renegotiation. Its Restart timer stays stopped while Opened. A responding peer can renew the request budget with valid negotiation replies. Each LCP negotiation therefore has a convergence deadline of twice the Restart timer times max-configure, or 60 seconds at the defaults. A new negotiation after Opened gets a new deadline. Replies within one negotiation do not extend that deadline. Initiator: dial targets and outgoing calls Beyond answering tunnels, ze can INITIATE them (send SCCRQ) toward a configured remote. A remote list under l2tp {} declares dial targets; declaring one grants no dial by itself. An operator action (RPC) or a PPPoE relay binding drives the dial. l2tp { enabled true; remote lns-retail { address 203.0.113.10; // control-plane IP to dial (SCCRQ destination) port 1701; // remote UDP port (default 1701) shared-secret <secret>; // per-remote CHAP-MD5 (empty = no Challenge) outgoing-calls true; // permit `request l2tp outgoing-call` to this remote } relay <service-name> { // PPPoE Service-Name -> L2TP incoming call (LAC) remote lns-retail; // must reference an l2tp/remote above } } Place an LNS-side outgoing call (RFC 2661 S10.4) with: request l2tp outgoing-call remote lns-retail called <number> The command dials the remote if no tunnel is up, sends an OCRQ, and blocks until the call establishes (returning the local/remote session IDs) or fails (returning the cause and RFC 2661 Result Code: tunnel auth reject, tie-breaker loss, peer CDN, or timeout). The remote must have outgoing-calls true. A dialed tunnel sends from the L2TP listener socket, so the listener's ip is the tunnel's source address (RFC 2661 Section 8.1 requires the addresses and ports to stay static for the life of the tunnel). Every dial, from this command or from a relay, uses the first environment l2tp server. When that listener is on a loopback address it cannot reach another host, so Ze refuses a config that pairs it with an off-host remote: Ze does not start with it, and a reload that adds such a remote is refused and changes nothing. ze config validate does not check this yet. A dial that still meets the case is refused at once. Each error names the remote, the listener and the fix: bind environment l2tp server <name> ip to an address that reaches the remote, or to the wildcard of the remote's family (0.0.0.0 for IPv4, :: for IPv6) to let the route choose it. Ze binds a listener only when it starts, so after a reload that moves the listener, a dial asks for a restart instead. The relay binding is the LAC path: a PPPoE subscriber whose Service-Name matches is relayed into an L2TP incoming call (ICRQ) toward the bound remote instead of terminating PPP locally. The subscriber-PPP↔L2TP kernel channel bridge that carries frames at the LAC is Linux-only. TestLACChannelBridge shows only that the bridge ioctls reach the kernel, and ./le test deployment l2tp-ppp has xl2tpd dial Ze as an LNS with no PPPoE and no Ze LAC, so it never reaches the bridge. The end-to-end proof of the relay data path is the topology scenario access-up (./le test integration interop-topology scenario access-up): a Ze CPE dials with no Service-Name, a Ze LAC relays it with relay "" to a Ze LNS, and the CPE pings the LNS across the session. It runs on a Docker host running Ze's kernel, and it goes red when the LAC skips the bridge: the LNS then logs an LCP negotiation timeout and the CPE never holds its address. access-pool proves the LNS pool fallback and access-accounting the RADIUS Start, Interim-Update and Stop over the same chain. Initiator tunnel interop is proven against xl2tpd in test/interop-l2tp/scenarios/03-ze-lac-xl2tpd-lns. Relay by realm (wholesale LAC) A relay-realm binding selects the LNS from the realm of the PPP username, the way a wholesale access network does: l2tp { relay-realm example.net { // username realm -> L2TP incoming call remote lns-retail; // must reference an l2tp/remote above } } The realm is the text after the last @ of the username, compared exactly once ca

title: Lifecycle, Rollback, and Recovery
text: Lifecycle, Rollback, and Recovery Use this guide for routine daemon control and configuration recovery. Ze separates configuration reload, process restart, and host reboot because they have different routing consequences. Before first start ze init ze config validate ze.conf ze doctor ze start ze.conf ze init creates the local credential and blob database. Validation checks the candidate configuration without applying it. ze doctor checks host capabilities and dependencies. See Operations and Installation for systemd and appliance-specific setup. Choose the right action Intent Action Routing effect Apply a validated configuration change ze signal reload Transactional subsystem reload, with the current config retained on failure Stop normally ze signal stop Graceful shutdown, peers receive a normal teardown Restart with BGP GR signalling ze signal restart Writes the restart marker used by the Graceful Restart path Inspect process state ze signal status No configuration or routing change Capture goroutines and exit ze signal quit Diagnostic termination, not a routine stop Check liveness ze status TCP liveness check only A failed reload clears the candidate and keeps the previous active configuration. Do not replace reload with a process restart merely to apply a normal edit. Review and commit configuration The CLI and web editor maintain a candidate separate from the active configuration: Enter an edit session. Make the smallest change. Validate and review the diff. Commit. Verify live state and health. Use show config dump <file> for the fully resolved configuration of a file and show config diff before rollback or commit. show config running asks the daemon for the configuration it applied, from memory. A reload the daemon refused leaves that answer unchanged, while the config file already holds the refused text, so this is the command that says what is in force. Secret values are replaced with a placeholder. REST (GET /api/v1/config/running) and gRPC (GetRunningConfig) answer the same command. Archive and rollback Ze stores configuration revisions in the configured storage backend. The archive guide covers revision pointers, named archive destinations, schema evolution, and recovery. Useful commands include: Copy the snapshot key returned by show config history before running cat: ze cli -c "show config history" ze cli -c "show config diff" ze cli -c "show config cat <snapshot-key>" ze cli -c "request config archive" See Configuration archive for the current archive and rollback workflow. Review the selected revision before moving the active pointer. A syntactically valid historical revision can still be unsuitable after a schema or topology change. Logging and reports Start with bounded operational views: ze cli -c "show warnings" ze cli -c "show errors" ze cli -c "show event recent" ze cli -c "show health" Raise a subsystem's log level only while investigating: ze cli -c "request log level bgp.fsm debug" Persistent log configuration and destinations are described in Logging. Use structured command output for automation rather than scraping human log messages. Software updates The update mechanism is platform-aware. Standard Linux, systemd, and appliance deployments do not all use the same backend. Follow Self update, then decide whether the BGP restart path is required for the maintenance window. Before updating: Archive the active configuration. Confirm the current version and health. Confirm peers negotiated the resilience mechanisms the maintenance plan assumes. Record peer and RIB counts. Keep the previous binary or appliance slot available for rollback. After updating: Confirm the process is running. Check warnings, errors, and component health. Compare peer and RIB counts with the pre-change snapshot. Confirm stale routes were purged and no replay remains in progress. Exercise one representative management path. Recovery order When a change fails, recover in this order: Preserve warnings, errors, events, and crash output. Determine whether the failure is configuration, one subsystem, or the process. Discard or roll back the candidate when configuration caused the failure. Reload if the process remains healthy. Restart only when process state must be rebuilt. Reboot the host only for kernel, dataplane, or appliance failures that require it. See Production diagnostics for symptom-led checks and support bundle collection. Related guides Operations Configuration archive Logging Self update BGP resilience Production diagnostics

title: Logging
text: Logging Ze uses hierarchical, structured logging with runtime-configurable levels per subsystem. Log Levels Level Description disabled No output debug Detailed diagnostics (FSM transitions, wire events, plugin IPC) info Informational messages (peer up/down, config reload) warn Warnings and errors (default) err Errors only Configuration Config File environment { log { level warn # base level for all subsystems backend stderr # output destination bgp.reactor debug # subsystem-specific override bgp.routes info # another override plugin.relay warn # plugin stderr relay level } } Environment Variables Environment variables take precedence over the config file: # Set base level export ZE_LOG=debug # Set per-subsystem level export ZE_LOG_BGP_FSM=debug export ZE_LOG_PLUGIN=info # All notation forms are equivalent: ze.log.bgp.fsm ZE_LOG_BGP_FSM ze_log_bgp_fsm CLI Flag ze -d example.conf # shorthand for ze.log=debug + ze.log.relay=debug Runtime Change Change log levels on a running daemon without restart: ze cli -c "request log level bgp.fsm debug" ze cli -c "request log level bgp.reactor info" ze cli -c "request log level bgp.reactor disabled" # silence one subsystem ze cli -c "show log levels" # show current levels disabled silences the subsystem until a later request log level sets a level again. show log levels reports it as disabled, and a subsystem that started disabled through ze.log.<subsystem>=disabled is listed the same way, so the runtime command can enable it. A level set at runtime is lost on restart. Priority Order Most specific wins, environment beats config: Environment variable ZE_LOG_BGP_FSM (most specific) Environment variable ZE_LOG_BGP (parent) Environment variable ZE_LOG (base) Config file bgp.fsm debug (most specific) Config file level warn (base) Default: warn Backends Backend Config Description stderr backend stderr Standard error (default). Color auto-detected on TTY. stdout backend stdout Standard output. Color auto-detected on TTY. syslog backend syslog Syslog: the local daemon, a Unix socket or a UDP collector, set with destination. Syslog example: environment { log { level info backend syslog destination 192.0.2.100:514 } } Syslog facility and severity Each syslog record carries the severity of its level: debug is sent as debug, info as info, warn as warning and err as err. A collector can select records by facility and severity. Every subsystem goes out on the daemon facility unless the syslog container names another one. The facility leaf changes the facility for all subsystems. Any other name in the container is a subsystem, and its value is the facility that subsystem and its children go out on. Ze reads the longest matching name first, as it does for levels, so bgp covers bgp.server until bgp.server is named too. The name facility is reserved for the leaf, so a subsystem called facility cannot be mapped here. Facility names are kern, user, mail, daemon, auth, syslog, lpr, news, uucp, cron, authpriv, ftp and local0 to local7. The level of a facility is the level of the subsystems it carries. To send everything at info on daemon, and the BGP subsystems at debug on local7: environment { log { level info bgp debug backend syslog destination 192.0.2.100:514 syslog { bgp local7 } } } To send everything on one facility, set only the leaf: environment { log { level info backend syslog syslog { facility local7 } } } The environment variable ze.log.syslog.facility overrides the leaf, and ze.log.syslog.<subsystem> overrides a subsystem name (ZE_LOG_SYSLOG_BGP=local7). A word that names no facility is refused with a warning on stderr, and the subsystem keeps the facility of the next shorter name. Plugin Stderr Relay External plugins (forked processes) write to stderr. Ze captures this output and relays it through the logging system tagged with subsystem plugin.relay. export ZE_LOG_PLUGIN_RELAY=debug # see all plugin stderr export ZE_LOG_PLUGIN_RELAY=disabled # silence plugin output Default relay level: warn. The relay keeps the LAST line a plugin wrote. Ze attaches a parent-owned pipe to the child and drains it after reaping the process, with a bounded grace period, so a verdict written immediately before the plugin exits still reaches the log. A grandchild holding the descriptor open cannot hold the drain open forever. A quoted value in a relayed line arrives decoded. The parser reads the escapes the structured logger wrote, so a backslash no longer doubles at every relay hop. A value that ends in a backslash no longer runs the scan past its own closing quote and into the attributes after it. A fatal diagnostic from a dying process goes to the real stderr rather than to the crash-capture pipe. Crash capture redirects os.Stderr into a pipe whose reader goroutine dies with the process, so a fatal message written there existed, was written, and reached no one. The last thing a dying process says now reaches the terminal. Naming Convention Subsystem names follow <domain>.<component>[.<concern>]: Domain Covers bgp BGP protocol (config, filter, reactor, routes, server) chaos Chaos fault injection cli CLI and editor hub Hub process management plugin Plugin infrastructure web Web UI Setting a parent level applies to all children. ze.log.bgp=debug enables debug for every bgp.* subsystem. ze.log.plugin=info enables info for every plugin.* subsystem. Subsystems Run ze env to see the full list with descriptions. Below is the complete inventory: Subsystem Description bgp.config Configuration parsing and loading bgp.filter Route filtering (AS loop, originator-ID) bgp.filter.community Community-based route filtering plugin bgp.gr Graceful restart marker handling bgp.reactor Reactor event loop and peer management bgp.reactor.cache UPDATE cache gap-based eviction bgp.reactor.forward Per-peer forward worker pool bgp.reactor.peer Peer lifecycle and FSM transitions bgp.reactor.session Session wire protocol handling bgp.routes Route processing and announcements bgp.server TCP server and connection handling bgp.watchdog Watchdog timer plugin chaos Chaos fault injection orchestration chaos.peer Chaos testing simulated peers cli.editor.draft Config editor draft persistence hub.managed Managed mode client connection hub.reload Configuration reload handling plugin Plugin process lifecycle and event delivery plugin.coordinator Plugin startup stage coordination plugin.manager Multi-plugin coordination and respawn plugin.relay Plugin stderr relay to engine log plugin.server Plugin RPC server and stage protocol web.auth Web UI authentication web.server Web UI HTTP server Inspecting Current Configuration ze env list -v # show all env vars with current values ze env get ze.log # show specific var details ze cli -c "show log levels" # show runtime log levels

title: Looking Glass
text: Looking Glass Ze includes a built-in looking glass that provides public, read-only access to BGP session state and route information. It runs as a separate HTTP server from the authenticated web UI. Configuration Add the looking-glass block under environment in your Ze config: environment { looking-glass { enabled true server main { ip 0.0.0.0 port 8443 } next-hop-range 198.51.100.0/24 { name ams-ix-lan } next-hop-range 2001:db8:100::/64 { name ams-ix-lan } } } Setting Default Description enabled false Enable the looking glass server. server <name> { ip } 0.0.0.0 Listen address. Set to 127.0.0.1 to restrict to local access. server <name> { port } 8443 Listen port. Must differ from the web UI port. server <name> { tls } true This endpoint serves HTTPS. Set false to serve plain HTTP on it. See HTTP and HTTPS. certificate (empty) Name of a pki { certificate <name> } entry to serve on every HTTPS endpoint. Empty selects a self-signed certificate in the live store. token (empty) Bearer token. When set, every /api/ and /lg/ route needs Authorization: Bearer <token>. Empty leaves the looking glass open. next-hop-range <prefix> { name } (none) A name for one range of next-hop addresses, shown beside a next hop inside it. See Names for next hops and peers. Environment variable overrides: ze.looking-glass.listen=ip:port, ze.looking-glass.enabled=true, ze.looking-glass.token=<token>, ze.looking-glass.certificate=<name>. No environment variable chooses HTTP or HTTPS: write tls in the server entry. HTTP and HTTPS What a looking glass publishes is public, so you choose for each endpoint whether it serves HTTPS or plain HTTP, and one looking glass serves both at the same time: environment { looking-glass { enabled true server public { ip 0.0.0.0 port 80 tls false } server secure { ip 0.0.0.0 port 8443 } } } Rule Detail Default An endpoint serves HTTPS unless its entry says tls false. Plain HTTP Write tls false in the entry, for port 80 or behind a proxy that terminates TLS. The other entries are not affected. No certificate to present HTTPS needs a named certificate or the live store, where Ze keeps its self-signed certificate. With neither, an entry that left tls unset serves plain HTTP, and Ze prints a warning that names the entry: run ze init and restart for HTTPS, or write tls false to serve HTTP on purpose. An entry that says tls true cannot be served: the looking glass does not start, and a reload is refused, with the same message. An explicit-file start creates a live store. Reload Change tls on an entry, add an entry, or remove one, and reload. An endpoint that stays keeps its socket: open connections finish on the protocol they started with, and the next connection takes the new one. A reload serves what a restart with the same config serves. ze.looking-glass.listen An address from this variable has no entry, so it serves HTTPS. Write the server entry to serve HTTP on it. RFC 8522 API /.well-known/looking-glass/ answers on HTTPS endpoints only. See RFC 8522. Serve your own certificate A visitor to a public looking glass has not installed your root, so a self-signed certificate gives them a browser warning. Set certificate to the name of a pki { certificate <name> } entry and the listener serves that leaf and every intermediate the entry holds, on every endpoint that serves HTTPS: environment { looking-glass { enabled true certificate lan } } Rule Detail Default No certificate leaf means Ze generates and serves a self-signed certificate, which is the behavior of every release before this leaf existed. Fail closed A name the store does not hold, or an entry with no private { key }, refuses the start: Ze exits and names the missing certificate. A reload that names one is rejected as a whole, and the running looking glass keeps the chain it is serving. Ze never falls back to a self-signed certificate for a name you configured. Rotation Load new material under the same name and reload: the listener serves the new chain from the next handshake, with no rebind, so a viewer's open connection survives. Removal Delete the certificate leaf and reload: the listener serves its self-signed certificate from the next handshake, with no rebind, as a restart would. Without a database/ store there is no self-signed certificate to return to. An entry that left tls unset then serves plain HTTP from its next connection, with a warning, and an entry that says tls true refuses the reload: run ze init and restart, or name a certificate. TLS off When every entry says tls false no endpoint presents a certificate, so the leaf is inert. Neither the start nor a reload reads the name. One HTTPS entry is enough for the name to be read. HTTP for want of a certificate A daemon with no live store took the TLS default and serves an entry over plain HTTP. Name a certificate and reload: that endpoint serves the named chain over HTTPS from its next connection, with no restart. No live store needed A named certificate comes from the pki {} container. Only the self-signed certificate needs the live store. Name 1 to 255 characters, A-Z a-z 0-9 . _ -. It is a store key, never a file path. Own leaf The looking glass and the web UI have separate certificate leaves, so each listener serves the certificate that matches its own hostname. Env override ze.looking-glass.certificate takes precedence over the config file. Optional bearer token A looking glass is normally public and read-only, so token is off by default. Set it to require a bearer token on every route. Ze compares the token constant-time over SHA-256 digests. A request with no token, a wrong token, or an Authorization header that is not Bearer <token> gets 401. When the looking-glass block is absent, no HTTP server is started and no resources are consumed. Web UI The HTMX web UI is available at https://<host>:<port>/lg/ (http:// on an endpoint whose entry says tls false). No authentication is required unless you set token. Tab / View URL Description Peers tab /lg/peers All peers with state, session history, remote AS, route counts. The remote AS cell shows the number; its AS name (from Team Cymru, through resolve cymru asn-name) shows when the pointer rests on the cell. An AS it names nothing for, such as a private AS number, or a lookup that failed, has no name to show. Live SSE updates. Lookup tab /lg/lookup Prefix/IP lookup with inline all-peers AS path topology graph (SVG). Search tab /lg/search Unified search: prefix, AS path, or community. Type selector. Per-peer routes /lg/peer/{address} Routes received from a specific peer (inline below peers table). Route detail /lg/route/detail Expanded route attributes and the route's age (HTMX fragment, click-to-expand). AS path graph /lg/graph?prefix=X Server-side SVG topology from all peers (auto-loaded on lookup). Each AS is labelled AS<n>, and its name, when Team Cymru gives one, shows on mouse-over only, so a name never widens a node. The text form (format=text), read by scripts, still writes the name, as it always did. Session history on the peers page Uptime says nothing about a session that is down, and a session that drops every hour shows an uptime of an hour. The peers table therefore carries two history columns, and the header of a peer's own page carries a third value: Shown Where What it is Read from show bgp Last Change A column of the peers table, and the header of /lg/peer/{address} The time the session last changed state, as the engine writes it (RFC 3339, such as 2026-07-15T10:30:00Z). It is the most recent transition of the session's state machine, so a session that keeps retrying shows the time of its last attempt state-changed Drops A column of the peers table, and the header of /lg/peer/{address} How often the session has dropped. A peer that never dropped shows 0 connections-dropped Last error The header of /lg/peer/{address}, which a click on the peer's row opens below the table Why the session last closed: the NOTIFICATION code and subcode by name, such as Cease/Adminis

title: Chaos MCP Server
text: Chaos MCP Server ./le chaos run includes an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server that lets AI assistants query chaos test state, detect problems, and control the chaos scheduler. Starting ./le chaos run --mcp :8001 --web :8000 --peers 4 --routes 1000 The --mcp flag starts an HTTP MCP server on the given address. The --web flag is required because the MCP server reads from the web dashboard's shared state. Use --ai-help to print the tool definitions as JSON (for configuring AI clients): ./le chaos run --ai-help Ze MCP Injection To inject an MCP server into the Ze daemon started by ./le chaos run: ./le chaos run --ze-mcp 9718 ... This adds environment { mcp { port 9718; } } to the generated Ze config. Tools chaos_status Full snapshot of the chaos test state: peer counts, route counts, convergence statistics (min/avg/max/p50/p90/p99 with histogram), per-family convergence, throughput, property results. chaos_problems Filtered list of actionable issues. Returns an empty JSON array when healthy. Problem types: missing-routes, peer-stuck-down, route-plateau, slow-convergence, dropped-events, property-violation. chaos_peers Per-peer detail. Omit the peer argument for a summary of all peers. Provide a peer index for full detail including recent chaos history (last 5 actions). chaos_scenario Static scenario metadata: seed, peer count. chaos_control Control chaos scheduling.
