Configuration A VRRP group lives under the interface unit's address family, next to the addresses it backs: interface { backend netlink; ethernet eth0 { unit 0 { ipv4 { address [ 192.0.2.251/24 ]; vrrp { group uplink { vrid 10; virtual-address [ 192.0.2.1 ]; priority 200; } } } } } } group uplink is a name you choose, for your own readability: it names the group in show vrrp output, in log lines, and in the group metric label. It carries no protocol meaning. The protocol identity is vrid, which is mandatory, must be 1..255, and must match on every router in the group. The two routers in a group differ only in priority. Give the router you want to win the higher number. Leaf Default Meaning vrid none (mandatory) Virtual Router ID, 1..255. The same value on every router in the group. virtual-address none (at least one) The address(es) the group backs. A leaf-list: [ 192.0.2.1 192.0.2.2 ]. priority 100 1..254. Highest wins. 255 is reserved for the address owner and is assigned by ze, never by you. preempt true Whether a higher-priority router takes mastership back when it returns. preempt-delay-seconds 0 0..3600. How long a returning higher-priority router waits before preempting. Useful when a router's uplinks converge more slowly than it boots, so it does not take the gateway back before it can forward. accept-mode false VRRPv3 only. Whether a non-owner Active accepts packets addressed to the virtual IP. False is the RFC default and means a ping to the virtual IP gets no reply from a non-owner. Forwarding, ARP and Neighbor Discovery are unaffected. advertise-interval-milliseconds 1000 How often the Active router advertises. version 3 2 opts this group into VRRPv2. checksum rfc9568 IPv4 VRRPv3 only. rfc5798-compatible computes the checksum over the IPv4 pseudo-header as RFC 5798 did, which keepalived requires. See Running beside keepalived. track absent Interfaces whose loss lowers the priority this group advertises. See Tracking an interface. Tracking an interface A group can watch other interfaces and lower the priority it advertises while one of them is down. That is how a router hands the gateway over when an uplink fails, rather than only when VRRP itself stops. vrrp { group uplink { vrid 10; virtual-address [ 192.0.2.1 ]; priority 200; track { interface eth1 { priority-decrement 150; } } } } While eth1 is down this router advertises 50 instead of 200, so a Backup configured at 100 takes the gateway. When eth1 returns, the router advertises 200 again and takes it back (subject to preempt). The decrement changes preference, not eligibility. Ze remains Active until it receives a winning advertisement; it does not resign merely because an uplink went down. The higher-priority Backup must have preemption enabled to take over. If that peer then disappears while the tracked interface is still down, Ze can take the gateway at priority 50. A returning peer at 100 takes it back, and restoring the tracked interface lets Ze preempt at 200. Leaf Default Meaning interface <name> none The interface to watch. Up to 16 for one group. The name is an interface from the interface tree, or a kernel device name. priority-decrement none (mandatory) 1..254. The priority subtracted while this interface is down. Four rules decide what tracking does: Decrements add up. Two tracked interfaces down cost the sum of their decrements. The result never falls below 1. RFC 9568 Section 5.2.4 keeps a Backup router in 1..254, and 0 says the Active router stopped participating, so a decrement at or past the configured priority leaves this router at 1. A name Ze cannot resolve counts as DOWN. An uplink Ze cannot find is not carrying traffic. Ze logs the resolver error, so a typo shows up in the log rather than in an unexplained priority. Tracking is refused on the address owner. That router advertises 255 (RFC 9568 Section 5.2.4), so no decrement could take effect. Ze rejects the configuration rather than accepting it and ignoring it. Ze reads the tracked interface's OPERATIONAL state and nothing else. An interface that is up while it blackholes traffic still counts as up. show vrrp reports effective-priority beside the configured priority, and lists the tracked interface

title: Web Interface
text: Web Interface Ze provides an HTTPS web interface for browsing configuration, editing values, and running commands through a browser. The web UI uses the same YANG schemas, user database, and command grammar as the SSH CLI. Starting the Web Server Command Line ze start --web 8443 # Start daemon + web on port 8443 ze start --web 8443 --insecure-web # No authentication (forces 127.0.0.1) When no certificate is configured, ze generates an ECDSA P-256 self-signed certificate automatically. The certificate includes SANs for localhost, 127.0.0.1, ::1, and the listen address. WebCertHosts builds that list, and a listen address of 0.0.0.0 adds every non-loopback interface address of the machine. When no config file is named, the daemon reads the config name from the store. If the store's instance name cannot be read, ze start exits 1 with an error naming ze doctor, and a web server started with no config path stays off and prints warning: web server disabled: with the reason. Flag Description --web <port> Start web interface on 0.0.0.0:<port> (requires config) --web-only Start web UI only, no daemon (config editing only, default port 3443) --insecure-web Disable authentication (forces 127.0.0.1, requires --web or --web-only) Choosing an Interface The default YANG editor uses Finder columns to browse the configuration and edit its schema-backed fields. The CLI link opens /cli, where commands use the shared configuration editor and the daemon's command dispatcher through the browser, without an SSH connection. Workbench (experimental) remains available as an unfinished alternative. Its purpose-built pages use the same authentication and candidate configuration, but some Workbench workflows are still incomplete. The controls at the top of the page switch between the graphical editor, CLI and Workbench; an explicit selection of Workbench remains selected for that browser. The startup setting is environment web ui-mode, with values finder (the default) and workbench. The equivalent environment key is ze.web.ui-mode: env ze.web.ui-mode=workbench ze start --web 8443 Configuration The web server listen address can also be set in the ze configuration file: environment { web { enabled true; server main { ip 0.0.0.0; port 8443; } } } Offline backup workspace Choose Services → Backup workspace, or open /backups/, to edit a .zefs backup independently of the running configuration. This page uses a full-text configuration editor. It requires an account with configuration edit access, because the artifact can contain credentials. To make a new backup of the system serving this page, choose Create backup of this system. The browser downloads system-backup.zefs, containing the complete store: configurations, history, saved drafts, credentials and other stored keys. Creating the backup does not commit pending edits or change uploaded workspaces. The system must have an open device store, and the complete snapshot must fit the workspace's size and temporary-storage allowance. A refused creation returns an explanation instead of a partial backup. Before opening the new download in the Ze CLI on Unix, run chmod 600 system-backup.zefs. Keep the backup private because it contains credentials. You can upload it here to inspect or edit its configuration. The server keeps its private backup working copies under the platform data directory's backups folder: /var/lib/ze/backups on an installed Linux system and /perm/var/lib/ze/backups on the appliance. To choose a different folder: environment { backup { directory "/srv/ze-backups"; } } Use an absolute path the daemon user can create or write to, then commit the change. Ze normalizes separators and . components to keep private roots stable and refuses any .. component; name the intended absolute folder directly. The ze.backup.directory environment override takes priority over this leaf. The commit creates a missing folder and checks write access as the running daemon account. A successful commit selects it for new workspaces and downloads without restarting Ze. A failed commit keeps the previous folder. Existing workspaces and downloads keep their private files until they close or expire; empty retired roots are then removed. Removing the leaf restores the platform default unless the OS override is set. Ze preserves an existing parent's permissions and unrelated files and refuses an unusable explicit location. An unconfigured development binary whose platform data directory cannot be resolved keeps the operating system's temporary folder. Browser downloads go to the location chosen in the browser's download settings. The backup workspace also runs with ze start --web-only. It uses the same artifact commands as the configured daemon; opening it starts no routing protocol. Stop the web process only after downloading the changes you need. Full-store restore also uses the normal recovery lifecycle in web-only mode. It waits for web requests and the original store owner to finish before replacing the store. A cleanup failure prevents replacement and returns a failure with the recovery instructions. Applying only the running configuration requires a loaded daemon; web-only mode refuses that operation before staging any configuration candidate. Select a backup file and choose Open backup. Choose its Configuration, then Open configuration. The editor starts with the committed configuration. Existing saved drafts and pending candidates remain in the artifact and are not resumed. Edit the text and choose Validate. A refused edit keeps your text available for correction. Validation covers the checks available in this Ze process; it does not prove acceptance on the target host or running system. Choose Review changes, then Save into backup. Changing the text after review requires another review. A form opened before another tab saved the same configuration must be reviewed against the newer saved configuration. Choose Download saved backup. The download is a complete artifact with the edited configuration, its history and the original backup's other keys. Unsaved text is not included. Before opening the downloaded backup in the Ze CLI on Unix, restrict access to your account: chmod 600 updated-backup.zefs Choose Close workspace when finished. Each workspace has its own URL and is available only to the account that uploaded it. Uploaded copies are private temporary files; the original file on your computer is unchanged. An artifact can be at most 64 MiB, and configuration text can be at most 4 MiB. The server retains at most 32 workspaces, eight per account, with a shared 256 MiB artifact allowance. Workspaces expire after one hour without use and are removed when the daemon stops. Download the edited backup before closing the workspace or stopping the daemon. The same private artifact can be used from the command surface. The artifact identity comes from upload completion and belongs to your authenticated account. The browser's Admin Commands forms derive these commands and their fields from the command model: Operation Command Stored configurations show config artifact config list artifact <id> Masked committed source show config artifact source artifact <id> name <config> Resolved comparison show config artifact diff artifact <id> name <config> other <config> Compare a revision show config artifact diff artifact <id> name <config> revision <number> Stored history and draft state show config artifact history artifact <id> name <config> Set, activate or deactivate request config artifact <operation> artifact <id> name <config> text <transfer> Complete replacement request config artifact replace artifact <id> name <config> text <transfer> Publish a history revision request config artifact rollback artifact <id> name <config> revision <number> For a statement or replacement, upload the text with request config artifact text begin, the declared upload append operation and upload finish. Keep the returned text-transfer identity until the operation end

title: Installation
text: Installation Choose a deployment path for the environment you want to evaluate. Ze is pre-release software; start with an isolated lab. Choose a deployment path Goal Guide Success check Exchange routes on one Linux host Two-peer quickstart Both peers establish and each received RIB contains the other peer's prefix. This checks the control plane. Run a Linux service Local installation and build prerequisites The service is active, authenticated management connects, and repeat installation retains configuration and credentials. Run a daemon in Docker Docker Compose A committed configuration change and the same login survive container recreation on the same named volume. Install a VM or dedicated router Appliance build and ISO installation After removing installer media, the written disk boots and authenticated SSH reports the selected image. Run a protocol topology netlab and containerlab The live check passes adjacencies, kernel routes, traffic between all three nodes and teardown. It last passed on arm64 on 2026-11-14. Completed deployment checks covered native systemd installation and removal, two-peer route exchange, and container configuration retention after recreation. The container check used a prepared runtime image without verified source identity. A separate private preview run prepared and checked Linux amd64 and arm64 binaries and archives, plus amd64 deployment and lab container exports, with source identity and checksums. That artifact check does not extend the container recreation proof to those images. See preview preparation; these pages do not provide a public release download. The appliance installation and update checks passed on amd64 with KVM. They covered selected-disk installation, preservation of an extra disk, installed-disk SSH access, and an image update followed by recovery to the previous root slot. Configuration and login survived the update and recovery. Arm64 boot and physical hardware installation remain unverified by these checks. See appliance updates for retention and recovery checks. Once ze is installed, ze create agent skill sets Claude Code or Codex up to test it: see Use Ze with an AI agent. Local Installation Run ze install for the complete Linux installation. It installs the running binary, initializes absent state, and starts the service when systemd is available. Existing configuration and credentials are preserved. Quick Start sudo ze install Build the command with the Linux installation guide, or use a privately supplied preview bundle. From a built source checkout or extracted preview, use sudo ./ze install. The default installed binary is /usr/local/bin/ze and its private state is /etc/ze. A fresh installation asks for management credentials and creates a loopback-only SSH configuration. It does not configure the host's interfaces. Follow the connection command printed by the installer, then run ze doctor and inspect the service with systemctl status ze.service. Choose a prefix or foreground operation explicitly: sudo ze install --prefix /opt/ze sudo ze install --no-service sudo ze install --dry-run Flags Flag Default Description --prefix /usr/local Installation prefix (binary goes to <prefix>/bin/ze) --no-service Install for foreground operation without a service --dry-run Print what would be done without making changes Without systemd, installation prints the foreground start command. Repeat ze install to replace the binary while keeping state and compatible service customizations. Conflicting paths or service definitions are refused before binary replacement. See Upgrading for the steps and checks, and Operations for upgrades and recovery. What It Does Checks the selected paths and service before changing the installation. Initializes the private store only when it is absent. Installs the binary and starts the systemd service when available. The config directory is resolved from the binary path following GNU prefix conventions: Binary location Config directory /usr/local/bin/ze /etc/ze /usr/bin/ze /etc/ze /opt/ze/bin/ze /opt/ze/etc/ze The installer creates a missing config parent with mode 0755, so the service account can traverse it after ownership of the private 0700 config directory transfers. Existing parent permissions are preserved. The explicit ze install local command remains available for a binary-only installation. That lower-level path requires ze init and service setup as separate steps. Systemd Service The default ze install command handles systemd setup. For an existing manual installation, ze install systemd remains available: sudo ze install local --prefix /usr/local sudo ze init sudo ze install systemd --start The generated service-management unit file: [Unit] Description=Ze Network OS After=network-online.target Wants=network-online.target [Service] Type=simple User=ze Group=ze ExecStart=/bin/sh -c 'trap "" HUP; exec <prefix>/bin/ze start' ExecReload=/bin/sh -c 'kill -HUP $MAINPID' Restart=on-failure SuccessExitStatus=75 RestartForceExitStatus=75 RestartSec=5 TimeoutStopSec=90 KillMode=mixed LimitNOFILE=65536 LimitCORE=infinity LimitMEMLOCK=infinity WorkingDirectory=<config-dir> Environment=ZE_CONFIG_DIR=<config-dir> Environment=XDG_RUNTIME_DIR=/run/ze AmbientCapabilities=CAP_NET_ADMIN CAP_NET_RAW CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE CAP_BPF CapabilityBoundingSet=CAP_NET_ADMIN CAP_NET_RAW CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE CAP_BPF # Host tuning may need CAP_SYS_NICE. Future VRF/netns support may need CAP_SYS_ADMIN. # Add those capabilities only when the configured feature requires them. NoNewPrivileges=true ProtectSystem=true ProtectHome=true RuntimeDirectory=ze [Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target An intentional daemon restart exits 75 after teardown. SuccessExitStatus=75 keeps it from being reported as a daemon failure, and RestartForceExitStatus=75 starts the next process even with Restart=on-failure. Ordinary shutdown exits 0 and stays stopped; startup and plugin failures still exit 1 and restart under the failure policy. This describes the generated policy; a supervisor restart roundtrip must be verified on the deployment host. ze doctor checks the effective restart properties, including drop-ins, under doctor-service-restart. An older unit missing this policy needs sudo ze install systemd --force followed by sudo systemctl daemon-reload; remove any overriding drop-in shown by systemctl cat ze.service. CAP_BPF lets ze load the eBPF programs of the IPsec ESP form fast path, the IPsec application override guard and traffic-usage; without it the kernel refuses each load, so a unit written by an older ze is rewritten with sudo ze install systemd --force while the daemon is stopped. TimeoutStopSec=90 and KillMode=mixed serve the stop drain. On a stop, ze first drains its routing protocols for up to 60 s, then tears down for up to 30 s, so systemd waits 90 s before its SIGKILL. mixed sends the stop SIGTERM to ze alone, so ze can drain its external plugins before it stops them; the SIGKILL at the timeout still reaches the whole unit. ze doctor reads the values systemd actually applies, drop-ins included, and warns under doctor-service-stop when either is weaker. The shell in ExecStart starts ze with SIGHUP ignored, then execs it, so ze keeps the main PID. A systemctl reload during the first few hundred milliseconds, before ze can register a handler, is then lost instead of killing the daemon (docs/architecture/behavior/signals.md). ExecReload sends that SIGHUP with the same shell's builtin kill, so the unit runs no program beyond /bin/sh and ze: /bin/kill comes from procps, which a minimal host does not install. ze doctor checks the programs ExecStart and ExecReload run, and reports a missing one under doctor-service-executable. The install refuses a binary or config path holding a character that systemd or /bin/sh interprets: a quote, a backslash, $, %, ;, &, |, <, >, parentheses, a backtick, or a glob character. ze install systemd requires <config-dir>/database/ and refuses while another process owns the stor

title: Testing labs.
text: Testing labs Testing labs. Each lab runs Ze on your own machine so you can examine its behavior and repeat the checks. Labs run against real third-party daemons (xl2tpd, accel-ppp, strongSwan), or boot Ze in a VM using Docker or QEMU. Some need Docker with host-kernel features Docker Desktop on macOS doesn't provide; a QEMU path is noted where one exists. The lab pages describe what each run checks and its limitations. Measurements of speed are covered under Performance. Available labs BGP Protocol Interop Daemon Docker BGP sessions with FRR, BIRD, and GoBGP 425 scenarios across core protocol and extensions netlab Topology Lab Daemon Docker QEMU Three Ze nodes under containerlab, started by netlab Live check of BGP, OSPF, IS-IS and BFD, kernel routes and traffic L2TP PPP/NCP Interop Daemon Docker QEMU Ze as LNS vs real xl2tpd/pppd LAC FRR tests BGP redistribution from a live PPP session PPPoE Interop Daemon Docker QEMU Ze's PPPoE client vs real accel-ppp access concentrator Discovery and PPP negotiation checked against the access concentrator IPsec / IKEv2 Interop Daemon Docker Ze as IKE initiator vs real strongSwan/charon FRR redistribute scenarios over the tunnel VLAN QoS Packet Tests Daemon AF_PACKET Packet captures check 802.1p PCP tags nftables counters check ingress priority classification Looking Glass Graph Demo Daemon Browsable Realistic UK topology, real external ASNs A browser graph for inspecting AS paths Appliance Installer Evidence Appliance QEMU Installer boots and completes for real: HTTP/PXE, ISO, Ventoy Plus failure-path, fault, pin, and rescue scenarios VPP Dataplane Evidence Daemon Docker Ze programs FIB, traffic, and firewall into a real VPP daemon Backs the production numbers in the VPP guide

title: Appliance Installer Evidence
text: Appliance lab Appliance Installer Evidence Run the installer in QEMU through HTTP/PXE, ISO, or Ventoy-on-FAT paths, with separate failure-path and rescue scenarios. A successful action verifies its selected path; a skipped action supplies no boot evidence. Appliance Four native QEMU actions exercise the installer end to end: the PXE/HTTP chain boots the installer kernel and initrd, serves the image over HTTP, and asserts serial success markers before rebooting into the written disk and logging in over SSH. The ISO path wraps the same image in a bootable ISO and also verifies GPT layout and power-off-not-reboot behavior. The Ventoy path checks that the installer finds the appliance ISO as a file on a FAT/exFAT data partition rather than as burned boot media. The scenarios action covers what the other three do not: a forced mid-init panic recovering cleanly, MAC-based install pinning on multi-homed boxes, and rescue console access. Until a release publishes an appliance image, build one with the appliance guide. The current amd64 installation ISO is under 150 MB. The prod build with the hardware kernel profile on October 1, 2026 produced ze-20261001-142644.iso: 128,933,888 bytes (128.93 MB) for the complete ISO. From the source checkout, prepare the build-host command with ./le build host-driver, then use ./ze-host appliance kernel to build the installer kernel. Set ZE_INSTALL_KERNEL to its printed path for these QEMU tests. The appliance guide covers the image and native-architecture build prerequisites. What this lab tests: A passing action verifies its selected install, fault, pinning, or rescue path in QEMU Environment: The boot checks use QEMU; building their kernel or image also needs a supported build backend. The installer initrd is pure Go. Requires: A matching native-architecture installer kernel with the selected media, network, and disk drivers built in; see the installer profiles in the guide Source: docs/guide/ze-install.md # HTTP/PXE install chain $ ./le test qemu installer # bootable ISO chain $ ./le test qemu installer-iso # Ventoy ISO-on-FAT path $ ./le test qemu installer-ventoy # fault/pin/rescue scenarios $ ./le test qemu installer-scenarios Prerequisites QEMU and an operator-supplied installer kernel (ZE_INSTALL_KERNEL=/path/to/vmlinuz); each native QEMU action reports a clear skip when none is usable. internal/le/test/qemu native QEMU evidence

title: BGP Protocol Interop
text: Protocol lab BGP Protocol Interop These scenarios test Ze's BGP engine by exchanging routes with FRR, BIRD, and GoBGP. Two ways to test Ze. Use the Ze interop harness for protocol assertions, or netlab for reusable multi-node topologies. Ze harness Protocol interop scenarios The shared routing and network-service suite has 261 scenarios, including 157 primary BGP cases. BGP external-peer scenarios start only the required FRR, BIRD, or GoBGP daemons and check behavior through each peer's own CLI. 261 shared-suite scenarios FRR BIRD GoBGP Use the Ze harness scenario assertions netlab Reusable topology lab Describe a three-node topology in YAML. netlab renders Ze configuration and starts each daemon node under containerlab. YAML containerlab BGP OSPF IS-IS BFD Use netlab three-node topology Daemon A Docker orchestrator launches Ze and one or more peer daemons on an isolated network, establishes real BGP sessions, and asserts correct behavior through each daemon's own CLI (vtysh, birdc, gobgp). Daemons start conditionally per scenario, so each run only spins up what it needs. The shared suite’s 261 routing and network-service scenarios include eBGP/iBGP, 4-byte ASN, IPv6, Add-Path, Route Refresh, Graceful Restart, Route Server, standard and extended communities, MD5 auth, BGP Roles, EVPN, VPN, FlowSpec, multihop, BFD and BFD strict mode, update delay, ECMP, SRv6, RPKI, BMP, max-prefix, GTSM, AS112, VRRP against keepalived, and OSPF/IS-IS interop with FRR. What this lab tests: BGP session and route behavior observed through the peer daemons' own commands Peers: Real FRR, BIRD, and GoBGP, in Docker containers Requires: Docker on a kernel with Ze's required features; see the kernel setup in the interop guide Source: docs/architecture/testing/interop.md # all BGP interop scenarios $ ./le test integration interop # single scenario, verbose $ INTEROP_SCENARIO=bgp-ebgp-ipv4-frr ./le test integration interop Prerequisites Docker runs the peer containers. On Linux, the harness checks the daemon kernel before starting Ze. On macOS, it uses Ze's Colima profile. The interop guide explains these prerequisites and the QEMU Docker guest. Set FRR_IMAGE to pin a different FRR version, or NO_BUILD=1 to skip rebuilding images on repeat runs. test/interop/ lab source

title: IPsec / IKEv2 Interop
text: Protocol lab IPsec / IKEv2 Interop Ze as an IKE initiator against real strongSwan/charon, with FRR redistribute scenarios over the resulting tunnel. Daemon A peer-isolated Docker lab runs Ze as an IKEv2 initiator against strongSwan/charon as the responder, with FRR available as a BGP peer for redistribute scenarios over the established tunnel. The native Go runner owns Docker lifecycle, scenario discovery, and protocol checks. The checked-in lab tree supplies container definitions, PKI material, and scenario fixtures. What this lab tests: IKEv2 negotiation and tunnel establishment against a real, independent IKE implementation Peer: Real strongSwan/charon (IKE responder), optional FRR for redistribute scenarios Requires: Docker, privileged containers Source: internal/le/interoplab/ipsec/ # all scenarios $ ./le test integration interop-ipsec # a single named scenario $ IPSEC_INTEROP_SCENARIO=name ./le test integration interop-ipsec Prerequisites Docker with privileged containers (IKE/IPsec needs kernel XFRM access). test/interop-ipsec/ scenario fixtures

title: L2TP PPP/NCP Interop
text: Protocol lab L2TP PPP/NCP Interop Ze as an LNS against a real xl2tpd/pppd LAC, with FRR checking that a subscriber route makes it all the way into BGP. Daemon A peer-isolated Docker lab runs Ze as an LNS, a real xl2tpd/pppd LAC, and FRR as a BGP peer in separate privileged containers on an isolated bridge network. It tests the complete path from L2TP control tunnel through PPP LCP/IPCP, kernel pppN interface creation, dataplane connectivity, and BGP route redistribution from a live PPP session. Two scenarios: end-to-end PPP/IPv4 dataplane tests with cleanup verification, and a subscriber /32 BGP redistribution scenario -- advertised to FRR when the session comes up, withdrawn on teardown. What this lab tests: Full L2TP control tunnel, PPP LCP/IPCP negotiation, kernel pppN creation, BGP redistribution Peer: Real xl2tpd/pppd (LAC), optionally FRR as BGP peer Requires: Docker and a host kernel with PPPoL2TP support (Docker Desktop on macOS typically lacks this -- use the QEMU path instead) Source: docs/labs/l2tp-interop.md # Docker lab, all scenarios $ ./le test deployment docker-l2tp-ppp # single scenario, verbose $ ZE_L2TP_INTEROP_SCENARIO=01-ppp-ipv4 ./le test deployment docker-l2tp-ppp # QEMU path instead of Docker (needs tmp/kernel/vmlinuz) $ ./le test deployment gokrazy-l2tp-ppp Prerequisites Docker for the primary path. The QEMU path uses the runtime kernel built by ze appliance kernel --target runtime --arch arm64 and works where Docker Desktop's VM lacks the PPPoL2TP kernel module. test/interop-l2tp/ lab source

title: L2TP PPP/NCP Docker Interop Lab
text: L2TP PPP/NCP Docker Interop Lab Peer-isolated Docker lab for full L2TP PPP/NCP/kernel dataplane evidence. Overview The lab runs Ze as an LNS, a real xl2tpd/pppd LAC, and optionally FRR as a BGP peer in separate Docker containers on an isolated bridge network. No container runs privileged: Ze and the LAC hold NET_ADMIN and the host's /dev/ppp device, and neither loads a kernel module. It proves the complete path from L2TP control tunnel through PPP LCP/IPCP, kernel pppN interface creation, dataplane connectivity, and BGP route redistribution from a live PPP session. Layout test/interop-l2tp/ Dockerfile.ze Ze LNS image (Alpine + tini + iproute2 + ppp; copies the ze-linux the suite preflight cross-compiles) ze-linux the staged daemon, git-ignored and rewritten each run Dockerfile.ze-scale maintained Ze runtime with the scale-only staged daemon ze-scale-linux isolated allocator build, git-ignored avp-relay-linux host-staged relay package, git-ignored Dockerfile.lac LAC image (Alpine + xl2tpd + ppp + iproute2) daemons FRR daemons config (zebra + bgpd) vtysh.conf FRR vtysh config scenarios/ 01-ppp-ipv4/ PPP IPv4 dataplane proof 02-ppp-bgp-redistribute-frr/ BGP route redistribution proof 03-ze-lac-xl2tpd-lns/ ze as initiator (LAC) vs real xl2tpd LNS 04-radius-acct-attrs/ subscriber attributes in RADIUS auth and accounting dns-resolver-l2tp-subscriber/ IPCP DNS to Ze's LAN resolver, then a lookup l2tp-unknown-mandatory-avp-xl2tpd/ unknown AVP, M=0 then M=1, through the relay ppp-code-reject-xl2tpd/ unknown LCP and IPCP Codes injected through the relay lcp-restart-timer-pppd/ configured retry interval and request budget after live LCP restart l2tp-lns-pppd-ipv6cp-rejected-by-lns/ stock pppd's IPv6CP and an injected CCP Protocol-Rejected, IPv4 kept l2tp-lns-pppd-noip-rejects-ipcp/ pppd noip rejects IPCP, Ze stops IPCP and ends at the no-NCP bound l2tp-lns-pppd-ipcp-terminate-redistribute/ relay and FRR: IPCP Terminate withdraws and reinstalls the /32 l2tp-many-sessions-kl2tpd/ three LACs, sixteen PPP sessions per tunnel l2tp-lns-mru-xl2tpd/ configured MRU, CHAP, live daemon output, and traffic l2tp-lns-omitted-mru-xl2tpd/ default peer MRU and Ze-side transmit cap l2tp-lns-negotiated-mru-xl2tpd/ unequal configured/negotiated session output l2tp-lns-chap-only-xl2tpd/ PAP Nak refused before authentication l2tp-proxy-mru-transmit-cap/ accepted proxy AVPs, kernel MTU, and ICMP l2tp-radius-acct-wire-fixture/ original accounting fixture regression internal/le/interoplab/l2tp/ l2tp.go Native topology, images, selection, and lifecycle checkers.go Typed protocol assertions for the scenarios dns_resolver.go The dns-resolver-l2tp-subscriber assertions mandatory_avp.go The l2tp-unknown-mandatory-avp-xl2tpd assertions ppp_code_reject.go The ppp-code-reject-xl2tpd assertions ppp_ipcp_reopen.go Its IPCP withdrawal and reopen after the Terminate-Request ncp_lifetime.go The three NCP lifetime scenarios' assertions lns_policy.go MRU and CHAP-only typed assertions and daemon queries scale_overlay.go guarded allocator candidate substitution for scale only scale.go ordered launch, full-population proof and exact teardown scale_evidence.go typed daemon, FRR and accounting evidence scale_kernel.go point-to-point interfaces, routes and IPCP evidence scale_window.go independent control trace and reliable-window proof avprelay/ UDP relay between the LAC and Ze, on 172.29.0.4 radiusmock/ Independent Go RADIUS peer Each scenario registers its checker, plan, kernel prerequisite and image selection in the owning L2TP lab. Discovery and the catalog read that same registry. Existing scenarios retain their established preparation; the scale scenario declares three kl2tpd LACs and three relays, plus Ze, FRR and FreeRADIUS. Its cleanup container list and failure diagnostics derive from those peer declarations. The selected image declarations determine which host binaries are staged. Ordinary scenarios use the normal Ze daemon. The scale image reuses the same runtime image and replaces only its daemon with ze-scale-linux. That binary uses a temporary Go overlay to choose the lowest unused nonzero session ID within each tunnel. It retains the allocator's random read and error handling, zero and collision guards, and retry bound. The complete parsed allocator method must match the expected source shape before the overlay is written; allocator drift stops staging for review. The original source is unchanged, and the replacement is removed after compilation. This instrumentation forces legal repeated Ze-local IDs across tunnels. The scenario measures session isolation under that collision. The relay is compiled from its Go package by the same host staging action and copied into its Alpine image. An RFC recorder overlay therefore reaches the relay that runs, including the PPP framing producer. Staging composes the scale overlay with an inherited recorder overlay, refuses conflicting source replacements, and never changes process-global GOFLAGS. The scale, relay, xl2tpd and kl2tpd builds send only their Dockerfiles, image-specific ignore files, and any declared staged binaries to the builder. Many sessions in each tunnel l2tp-many-sessions-kl2tpd runs three kl2tpd v0.1.8 containers using the maintained pppd 2.5.5 image. Each has one tunnel and sixteen configured PPP sessions. Each session has its own username, pppd interface, link name, log and read-only argument-file mount. The containers initially wait under Suite ownership. The checker launches a configured LAC through detached exec only when it is ready to measure that tunnel's control window, then starts the next LAC after the first sixteen sessions have established. The scale configuration enables CQM explicitly. After the original complete FRR route census and before either existing teardown, a selector check reads two real subscribers with equal local SIDs on different tunnels. Their detail, FSM history, observer events and all eight traffic counters must carry the selected original identity and listener. An unqualified read or clear must report ambiguity. A guard copied from the other admission must be refused. Those refusals must retain every original subscriber identity and native interface, all 48 FRR routes, independent event histories, the original Accounting-Starts and no Accounting-Stop. The existing selected RADIUS disconnect, 47-survivor proof, peer CDN and 46-survivor/accounting tail then run unchanged. On 2026-11-19 the full scenario passed in Ze's Linux 7.3 arm64 guest. After both selector refusals preserved all 48 subscribers, the exact-ID RADIUS Disconnect left 47 and the independently selected peer CDN left 46. At each stage the checker verified the exact subscriber routes, accounting records and interface-bound traffic. The pinned kl2tpd release uses cgo for its Linux PPPoX socket bindings. Its builder installs GCC, musl development headers and Linux headers, then enables cgo for this third-party peer. The runtime remains the maintained Alpine LAC image. Ze and the relay retain their own build settings. The v0.1.8 peer includes one build-time diff for autonomous HELLOs. Upstream sendHelloMessage bypasses the ACK queue, so a genuine ACK cannot complete the send. The stock peer retried an acknowledged HELLO and closed its sessions after three retry attempts in the real guest. The diff sends HELLO through the existing reliable queue. The five-second HELLO inputs, retry settings and all scale assertions remain required. The builder checks the original and patched source hashes, applies the diff with zero fuzz, and builds from that source. The runtime image retains the diff and pinned module-download identity under /usr/local/share/ze/. Pinned peer source. The independent control decoder requires the omitted Receive Window Size AVP in each SCCRQ. Three genuine cumulative ACK advances warm the window before the relay holds Nr alone. The assertion requires five distinct response-producing ICRQs behind that hold, four distinct outsta

title: Looking Glass Graph Demo
text: Demo lab Looking Glass Graph Demo Ze's looking glass, replayed from a real run: Ze collects routes from eleven simulated BGP speakers, and every page and graph below is the answer it gave. A second lab checks the graphs against a hand-built UK network with real AS names. Daemon The replay comes from a functional test. It generates a network from a seed: five routers of AS65000, one of them a route reflector, and six external peers on eBGP. Each speaker holds a real BGP session to Ze and announces the routes a model of the network computed for it. The test asks the looking glass for its pages and its three graphs and compares every answer with the model, router by router, before the recorder keeps a copy for this page. The UK lab injects 36 routes for a small network: a core ring (Telehouse, Leeds, Manchester, Birmingham) with edge sites (Slough, Bradford) under AS65000, peered with NTT and Cogent for transit and Cloudflare and Akamai for peering. It checks the AS path and next-hop drawings byte for byte, AS names included, which a stub name server supplies. As that stub listens on port 53, this lab runs on Linux only. What this lab tests: The looking glass pages and its three graphs (AS path, next hop, trace) over real BGP sessions, compared with what a model of the network computed Topology: Replay: five routers of AS65000 with a route reflector, six external peers. UK lab: AS65000 core ring and edge sites, peers NTT, Cogent, Cloudflare and Akamai Requires: Go toolchain. The UK lab also needs Linux and permission to bind port 53 Source: test/plugin/lg-simulated-network.ci, internal/le/interoplab/bgp/ The looking glass, replayed Below is the looking glass itself, not a picture of it: its own pages, stylesheet and scripts, answering from the answers a real ze gave while it served the simulated network. Click a peer, a route or a graph button, or play the tour. Only the recorded questions have an answer, so a search for anything else shows a notice that names the request. The replay runs in your browser and needs JavaScript. Read the transcript of the tour. The tour The peers page: every simulated router and external neighbor, each holding a real BGP session to ze, with its uptime, its last state change and how often the session dropped. GET /lg/peers One peer's routes: what the external neighbor 203.0.113.1 announced, and how long ago each route last changed. GET /lg/peer/203.0.113.1 (asked by the page, answered with a fragment) The search page. GET /lg/search (asked by the page, answered with a fragment) Search by prefix: every speaker that announced 198.18.0.0/24, with each route's next hop, AS path and age. POST /lg/search prefix=198.18.0.0/24 (asked by the page, answered with a fragment) The AS path graph of 198.18.0.0/24: the ASes its routes cross. GET /lg/graph?prefix=198.18.0.0/24&mode=aspath (asked by the page, answered with a fragment) The next-hop graph of 198.18.0.0/24: which router hands the traffic to which. Routers of the AS show by address, the neighbors outside by AS number only. GET /lg/graph?prefix=198.18.0.0/24&mode=nexthop (asked by the page, answered with a fragment) The trace of 198.18.0.0/24: each router's BGP next hop followed router to router to the exit, then the AS it is handed to and the AS path to the origin. From 198.51.100.1 it crosses three routers of the AS. GET /lg/graph?prefix=198.18.0.0/24&mode=trace (asked by the page, answered with a fragment) The trace as text, the form a test reads. GET /lg/graph?prefix=198.18.0.0/24&mode=trace&format=text The AS path graph as text. GET /lg/graph?prefix=198.18.0.0/24&mode=aspath&format=text The next-hop graph as text. GET /lg/graph?prefix=198.18.0.0/24&mode=nexthop&format=text Route detail: the route 203.0.113.1 sent for 198.18.0.0/24, with every attribute and its age. GET /lg/route/detail?prefix=198.18.0.0/24&peer=203.0.113.1 (asked by the page, answered with a fragment) Search by address: the routes that cover 198.18.0.1. POST /lg/search prefix=198.18.0.1 (asked by the page, answered with a fragment) Search by AS path with the end anchor: 64499$ lists the routes AS 64499 originates. POST /lg/search aspath=64499$ (asked by the page, answered with a fragment) Recorded by ./le site lg-replay record from commit bad92271a4 (2026-11-19): a real ze, 11 simulated BGP speakers generated from seed 7, 84 recorded answers. 234 values that change from run to run (session uptimes, state-change times, the listener address) are fixed values the recording declares. None of the networks shown is a real one: the prefixes come from 198.18.0.0/15, the range RFC 2544 reserves for benchmarking, the speakers use documentation addresses (RFC 5737), and the AS numbers are private or documentation numbers (RFC 6996, RFC 5398). Transcript of the tour. # the simulated network behind the replay, on any machine $ ./le test bgp plugin --pattern lg-simulated-network # the UK lab, Linux only $ ./le test bgp plugin --pattern lg-graph-lab Good first lab The simulated network needs no Docker, no QEMU and no root. If you want to see Ze's looking glass before running anything else, start here. Looking Glass docs peer and route viewer

title: netlab Topology Lab
text: Topology lab netlab Topology Lab netlab starts three Ze nodes under containerlab from the supplied topology. A live check tests the routing protocols, the kernel routes and the traffic between them, then tears the lab down. Daemon The reference topology in contrib/netlab/topology.yml has three nodes. r1 and r2 share an internal link in AS 65001 and run iBGP, OSPF, IS-IS and BFD. r3, in AS 65002, is an eBGP peer of r1 on its own link, because netlab runs an IGP on internal links only. r1 also carries two static routes. To start the same topology by hand with netlab, check it, rebuild it and remove it, follow the netlab guide. What this lab tests: Every declared BGP, OSPF, IS-IS and BFD adjacency, both static routes in the kernel FIB, and sourced loopback pings between every pair of nodes, when ./le test netlab run exits 0 after teardown Environment: Three Ze nodes under containerlab on a Docker host; netlab and containerlab run in a tool container Requires: Docker access to a Ze Docker host, or QEMU for the disposable Ze Docker host Source: contrib/netlab/ # live check against a Ze Docker host $ ./le test netlab run # the same check in the disposable QEMU Docker host $ ./le test qemu docker-lab lab "test netlab run" # render the templates and compare with the golden files; # this one needs netlab installed on the machine that runs it $ ./le test netlab check Prerequisites Docker access from a Ze source checkout. For the two live runs, Python, netlab and containerlab run in the tool container. The template check is different: it runs the netlab installed on the machine that invokes it, or the one named by NETLAB=/path/to/netlab, and a missing netlab is an error. internal/le/test/netlab/live.go live check contrib/netlab/ daemon definition and templates What has been tested. The render check covers template rendering and parsing. The functional profile check covers one daemon's SSH login. The live command checks adjacencies, kernel routes and traffic across the topology; it must finish successfully before those properties can be claimed for a run. Statement Evidence netlab accepts the daemon definition and finds a template for each module netlab create exits 0 on the reference topology, in ./le test netlab check The render is valid ze configuration ze config validate exits 0 on each file under contrib/netlab/golden/ A daemon runs one of those renders and answers the show command with JSON test/plugin/netlab-lab-profile.ci Every declared protocol reaches its healthy state, static routes reach the kernel FIB, and sourced loopback pings pass ./le test netlab run exits 0 after teardown Each declared feature passes netlab's own upstream integration suite Not verified: no run here executes netlab's upstream integration suite. This is separate from the native reference-lab test The live command passed on 2026-11-14 on arm64, in Ze's QEMU Docker host under HVF, with netlab 26.10 and the committed templates. It reached every BGP, OSPF, IS-IS and BFD adjacency, found both static routes in the kernel FIB, passed all six sourced loopback pings, and tore the lab down with no container left. No amd64 run from the committed templates is recorded. Ze also sends and receives no LLDP frame, so a netlab validation that reads LLDP data cannot pass. containerlab does not need LLDP, because the topology names the veth links. Run the automated live check. To run the automated live checks from the source checkout against an existing Ze Docker host, run: ./le test netlab run The automated run stages the node binary once for the Docker daemon's architecture, then packages it with the lab target in docker/Dockerfile.runtime. Its node build context contains only that binary and the runtime recipe; it does not compile Go inside Docker or send the source checkout. The manual source-building command in the netlab guide remains available. If Docker currently uses the distribution's kernel, use the disposable QEMU Docker host instead. This boots Ze's own system, forwards its Docker endpoint, and runs the same lab against it: ./le test qemu docker-lab lab "test netlab run" The QEMU route needs QEMU and the native-architecture Ze Docker-host image; its first run builds missing image and kernel inputs. Building the Docker-host image from scratch also needs the Docker CLI and a reachable build daemon for its static administration tools. A native kernel build needs Docker or QEMU and network access to its pinned sources. See the QEMU integration guide. The command builds the local lab image and a tool image with the versions the netlab guide lists. The tool build prints its Python and tool versions and checks Python dependency compatibility. The host needs Docker access; Python, netlab and containerlab run in the tool container, and Ansible configures the nodes from it. That container shares the Docker host's network and PID namespaces, which also supports Ze's QEMU Docker host transport. Running host containerlab against a remote Docker socket alone cannot provide those namespaces. The runner waits for every declared BGP, OSPF, IS-IS and BFD adjacency, verifies both static routes in the kernel FIB, and sends sourced loopback pings between every pair of nodes. It tears the topology down on success and failure, and a cleanup failure fails the command. Artifacts stay in session scratch for diagnosis. Each run binds its nodes to the image tag retained for that build and verifies that tag still resolves to the built image ID before startup. A host-runtime run holds an exclusive directory lease and refuses an existing deployment, so a second invocation cannot tear down another run's topology. When a run fails. Files saved when a test fails Before cleanup, a failed test run saves a private diagnostics-* directory inside the retained lab directory. It contains startup output, the topology snapshot, generated node files, Docker inspection, and each node's last 200 log lines. It also saves addresses, kernel routes, BGP and BFD state, OSPF and IS-IS interfaces, neighbors, databases and routes, the system RIB, and plugin state. Address, kernel route and adjacency queries run across every node before the more detailed routing queries. Capture has a two-minute total deadline and a five-second deadline for each command. A failed query leaves an .error.txt artifact with its command, failure and process output, so unavailable state cannot appear as an empty successful result. Cleanup still runs after capture. JSON artifacts keep stdout and use private .stderr.txt sidecars for stderr. The runner explicitly adds netlab.snapshot.yml to netlab's normal outputs before startup. netlab 26.10 writes a pickle snapshot by default; the added YAML inventory supplies node names for live checks, failure capture, and cleanup. Keeping the templates from drifting. ./le test netlab check It renders the templates with a real netlab, compares the result with contrib/netlab/golden/, and runs ze config validate on each golden file. A missing netlab is an error exit, never a skip. Use ./le test netlab update to rewrite the golden files. test/plugin/netlab-lab-profile.ci is the other half and needs no netlab: it starts a daemon from a golden file and parses the show command output.

title: PPPoE Interop
text: Protocol lab PPPoE Interop This lab connects Ze's PPPoE client to the accel-ppp access concentrator. Daemon In this pairing, accel-ppp is the PPPoE server (access concentrator) and Ze is the client. Their L2TP implementations both take the LNS responder role, so they cannot form an L2TP tunnel with each other. PPPoE gives them complementary roles for testing discovery and PPP negotiation. A peer-isolated Docker lab tests Ze's PPPoE client discovers, negotiates PPP, and establishes a session against a real accel-ppp AC. What this lab tests: RFC 2516 PPPoE discovery and PPP negotiation with accel-ppp Peer: Real accel-ppp access concentrator Requires: Docker, or Linux root with accel-ppp and PPPoE kernel support Source: docs/labs/pppoe-interop.md # Docker lab $ ./le test deployment docker-pppoe-accel # native Linux network-namespace path $ ./le test qemu pppoe-accel # Ze as the access concentrator on VPP, in a Ze-kernel guest $ ./le --name session test qemu docker-lab \ lab "test deployment vpp-pppoe product" timeout 3600s Prerequisites Docker for the peer-isolated lab. The native Linux action uses paired network namespaces and needs ip, ping, accel-pppd, and PPPoE kernel support. test/interop-pppoe/ lab source

title: PPPoE Docker Interop Lab
text: PPPoE Docker Interop Lab This peer-isolated Docker lab proves both Ze PPPoE roles against independent implementations. Ze acts as a client against accel-ppp, then as an access concentrator against pppd with the rp-pppoe plugin. Overview Each scenario runs its containers on an isolated bridge because PPPoE uses Ethernet discovery and session frames (EtherTypes 0x8863 and 0x8864). No container runs privileged: Ze, accel-ppp and the pppd client each hold NET_ADMIN and the host's /dev/ppp device, and the discovery sockets use the NET_RAW Docker grants by default. The host kernel must provide /dev/ppp and the pppoe pppox module, built in or loaded by the host: no container loads a kernel module. The client scenario requires PADI/PADO/PADR/PADS discovery, LCP, CHAP-MD5, IPCP, one kernel device named after the pppoe-client key (pppoe0), traffic to the access concentrator, the accel-ppp session view, and clean teardown. The access-concentrator scenario requires the same discovery and NCP path from an independent pppd trace. It also dials a wrong credential and requires CHAP refusal before proving that all session state disappeared. Two clients on one native VLAN pppoe-shared-access-two-clients runs the real Ze daemon and two independent pppd clients on VLAN 100. Both clients use the maintained pppd 2.5.5 image, with separate credentials, container namespaces, PPP interface names, PID files and logs. The checker requires each client's discovery exchange to carry its own MAC and admitted session ID, both directions of LCP acknowledgment, CHAP success, distinct IPCP addresses, matching kernel PPP devices and routes, and traffic bound to each PPP interface in both directions. The checker terminates the first client's exact PID from its own pppd PID file. It requires that client's daemon row and native PPP interfaces to disappear while the second client's original row, assignment and traffic remain. It then terminates the second client and requires both sessions to be gone while the configured access VLAN remains unchanged. Suite teardown owns all three containers and their capture/log files, including failed runs. This is a classless fixture foundation; it does not test CoS maps, original Snapshot counts, native fences or retirement receipts. On macOS, select this scenario through the registered lab route: CGO_ENABLED=0 ./le --name session test qemu docker-lab lab 'test deployment docker-pppoe-accel' env 'ZE_PPPOE_INTEROP_SCENARIO=pppoe-shared-access-two-clients' timeout 3600s This route resolves Ze's own runtime kernel and image and checks their identity. Its kernel must provide /dev/ppp, PPPoE and VLAN support; the native preflight is mandatory. Explicit kernel and image keywords belong to the separate command mode and are refused with lab. Layout test/interop-pppoe/ Dockerfile.ze Ze image used in both roles (copies the ze-linux the suite preflight cross-compiles) ze-linux the staged daemon, git-ignored and rewritten each run Dockerfile.accel accel-ppp access-concentrator image Dockerfile.client pppd and rp-pppoe client image scenarios/ 01-pppoe-chap-ipv4/ Ze client, accel-ppp concentrator 02-ze-ac-pppd-client/ Ze concentrator, pppd client pppoe-omitted-mru-ze-ac/ Ze concentrator, peer MRU omitted, measured Ze transmit cap pppoe-chap-rechallenge-ze-client/ Ze client, native accel-ppp reauthentication pppoe-named-device-reconnect-ze-client/ Ze client as a CPE: pppoe0, static default, masquerade, reconnect pppoe-peer-terminate-ze-ac/ Ze concentrator, pppd LCP termination without incoming PADT pppoe-chap-only-pap-client/ Ze concentrator, CHAP-only default, PAP-only pppd client pppoe-empty-service-name/ Ze concentrator, pppd client, no service-name configured pppoe-padr-replay/ Ze concentrator, pppd client, max-sessions-per-mac 1 ipv6cp-zero-identifier/ Ze concentrator, pppd session, zero IPv6CP identifier replayed ipv6cp-missing-option/ Ze concentrator, pppd client whose IPv6CP request carries no identifier option internal/le/interoplab/pppoe/ pppoe.go Native images, preflight, selection, and lifecycle scenarios.go Role-selected container plans and mounts check_client.go Ze client assertions check_ac.go Ze access-concentrator assertions check_named_device.go pppoe-named-device-reconnect-ze-client: device name, route and NAT across a reconnect check_service_name.go pppoe-empty-service-name: wire-level Service-Name proof check_auth_allow.go pppoe-chap-only-pap-client: session-correlated policy refusal and resource cleanup check_padr_replay.go pppoe-padr-replay: wire-level replay and per-MAC cap proof check_ipv6cp.go ipv6cp-zero-identifier, ipv6cp-missing-option: wire-level IPv6CP proof, BLOCKED until plan/post-release/features/spec-l2tp-ipv6-subscriber.md lands (see the file's own header comment) The Dockerfiles keep their small amount of peer initialisation in the image entrypoint command. There are no separate runner or entrypoint scripts. Prerequisites The native preflight probes /dev/ppp and the pppoe module from a temporary container that holds the peers' grants and nothing more. It exits non-zero when either is absent, names what is missing, and prints the host command that loads it: sudo modprobe -a ppp_generic pppoe Ze's kernel builds both in, so ./le test qemu docker-lab needs neither. Setting ZE_PPPOE_SKIP_KERNEL_PROBE or ze.pppoe.skip-kernel-probe causes an immediate refusal. The probe decides whether Docker can carry the proof. Docker Desktop on macOS was measured on 2026-08-01 and its Linux VM supplied both requirements on that machine. The QEMU action remains available for a host where the probe refuses. The client image pins pppd 2.5.5 from the official GitHub tag archive with a SHA256 checksum. The archive contains autotools inputs, not configure. Upstream autogen.sh generates the build system and runs configure with the image's existing installation paths. Build-only autotools dependencies do not enter the runtime image. Native runs against pppd 2.5.5 passed pppoe-chap-only-pap-client, pppoe-pap-ze-ac and 02-ze-ac-pppd-client on 2026-11-04. The CHAP-only scenario also failed against a rebuilt producer with the old broad authentication default and passed again after restoration. Running VPP mechanism image ./le --name session build vpp run builds the pinned, patched VPP image for the PPPoE data-plane mechanism lab. Its recipe and patch provenance live in third_party/vpp-patches. The image includes the af_packet, Linux CP and PPPoE plugins, with one compile worker for the small Docker VM. The answer names its immutable image ID. The optional variant missing-frame-metadata keyword builds a separate proof image that omits parsed metadata; the answer records its variant and immutable ID. This counterfactual must fail the same runtime oracle the baseline passes. This builds a lab dependency; the existing scenarios below still exercise the kernel backend. The complete native mechanism proof passed on 2026-11-16, including its separate missing-metadata image. VPP mechanism proof The native Phase 0 proof is ./le --name session test deployment vpp-pppoe run. It starts three separate peers: patched VPP with a scratch control helper, pppd 2.5.5 from the existing client image, and an independent IP traffic host. The helper opens a PPPoX datagram socket without opening /dev/ppp or creating a PPP unit. Its deliberately fixed, unauthenticated LCP/IPCP exchange tests the transport mechanism; it is not Ze's subscriber control plane. The proof runs plain, named-namespace and VLAN access topologies. It requires a VPP session before PADS, reciprocal LCP over the raw socket, IPCP service, positive traffic through VPP, a measured 1492-byte session MTU boundary, increases in both VPP session packet counters across the controlled ping, and RS/DHCPv6 delivery to the control socket. The VPP access MAC is set explicitly and checked against the injection destination. The checker waits for pppd's actual PPP interface and assigned address, then installs and reads back a specif

title: VLAN QoS Packet Tests
text: Wire lab VLAN QoS Packet Tests Packet captures and counters check how VLAN QoS maps translate packet priority into 802.1p tags and back. Daemon Two network namespaces are joined by a veth pair. One side has a VLAN sub-interface with egress/ingress QoS maps; the other is a raw capture/inject endpoint. On egress, the lab sends UDP with a given SO_PRIORITY, the egress map stamps the matching PCP bit in the 802.1Q header, and a capture on the peer side confirms it. On ingress, a raw 802.1Q frame with a given PCP arrives, the 8021q module strips the tag, and the ingress map translates PCP back to skb->priority, verified with an nftables counter. The lab checks software veth pairs; physical NICs with hardware VLAN offload need separate testing. It covers single-tag 802.1Q, with QinQ outside its scope. Its assertions check marking correctness; QoS scheduling, throughput, and latency remain untested by this lab. What this lab tests: 802.1p PCP tagging/classification actually on the wire (AF_PACKET capture + nftables counters) Scenarios: Egress (PCP on the wire), Ingress (PCP classification), Full chain (DSCP to PCP) Requires: Linux with network namespace support, root (CAP_NET_ADMIN), iproute2, nftables Source: internal/plugins/iface/netlink/vlanqoslab_integration_linux_test.go # run the packet-level Go integration test (requires Linux root) $ sudo -E env "PATH=$PATH" go test -tags integration -count=1 ./internal/plugins/iface/netlink -run TestVLANQoS Prerequisites Linux with network namespace support and root (CAP_NET_ADMIN). No Docker, no QEMU needed. VLAN QoS integration test Go producer and assertions

title: VPP Dataplane Evidence
text: Dataplane lab VPP Dataplane Evidence Ze programs FIB, traffic, and firewall state into a real VPP daemon over GoVPP -- the evidence behind the production numbers quoted in the VPP guide. Daemon Runs a real VPP (FD.io Vector Packet Processor) daemon in Docker and tests Ze's fib-vpp plugin programs routes from Ze's system RIB directly into VPP's FIB via the GoVPP binary API, that per-interface and system-wide stats come back through the VPP stats segment, and that firewall state applies correctly. This is the evidence behind the numbers already published in the VPP guide: on the reference hardware IPng Networks runs in production on AS8298, VPP forwards at roughly 35 Mpps on a 4-core Xeon D-1518 -- line rate where the default kernel-FIB path would be dropping packets. What this lab tests: FIB, traffic, and firewall state applied to the VPP daemon through GoVPP Peer: Real VPP daemon in a Docker container Requires: Docker with a privileged container Source: docs/guide/vpp.md # real VPP daemon in Docker, privileged container $ ./le test deployment vpp Prerequisites Docker with a privileged container (VPP needs DPDK-class access to devices). VPP deployment reference IPng Networks production numbers

title: Performance.
text: Benchmarks Performance. Measured, not claimed. Benchmark numbers need context: these numbers measure one scenario, on one machine, under artificial conditions. They show relative differences between implementations, not absolute performance. If it matters to you, run le perf on your own hardware with your own workload. BGP benchmark le perf establishes two BGP sessions with a device under test: a sender injects 100,000 routes, a receiver times their arrival. The same harness runs unmodified against BIRD, FRR, GoBGP, RustyBGP, freeRtr, rustbgpd, and OpenBGPd, all in Docker on the same host. Go carries an estimated 10-15% CPU overhead against C/Rust implementations. That number comes from code-path analysis, not a measured benchmark -- Ze has not been benchmarked at DFZ scale (1M+ prefixes). title: Performance Comparison
text: Performance Comparison Benchmark numbers need context. These numbers measure one specific scenario (route propagation latency through a single DUT with two peers) on one specific machine under artificial conditions. They do not predict real-world performance. Different hardware, different route counts, different address families, different policies, different network conditions will all produce different results. Use these numbers to understand relative differences between implementations, not as absolute performance claims. If performance matters to you, run le perf on your own hardware with your own workload. Methodology Ze-perf establishes two BGP sessions with a device under test (DUT): a sender and a receiver. The sender injects routes and records when each was sent. The receiver parses incoming UPDATEs and records when each prefix arrived. Propagation latency = time received minus time sent, matched by prefix. Each benchmark runs multiple iterations. Results show the median across iterations with standard deviation. Outlier iterations (beyond 2 stddev from median convergence time) are automatically discarded. Comparisons require every raw input row to have zero routes lost and a recorded convergence measurement before selecting the latest sample or writing output. Missing or null convergence is not zero; an explicitly measured zero is valid. An older lossy sample cannot be hidden by a newer clean one. This publication rule does not retrospectively establish the provenance of historical figures. Environment Field Value Platform darwin/arm64 Virtualization Docker (Colima VM, 8 GB RAM / 4 vCPU) Date 2026-11-22 Commit 6803c60c8a Pass live-forwarding Routes 100,000 Seed 42 Iterations 3 measured, 1 warmup These results were collected on a development laptop using Docker containers via Colima. A dedicated server with bare-metal networking would produce different (likely faster and more consistent) numbers. DUT Setup All DUTs run in Docker containers on the same host. Each DUT is configured with two passive BGP peers (sender AS 65001, receiver AS 65002) and AS 65000 as the local AS. The benchmark tool (le perf send) establishes both sessions, injects routes via the sender, and measures when they arrive at the receiver. Ze -- Go BGP daemon, goroutine-based, kernel TCP stack. Config: passive peers, route-reflector plugin (bgp-rs), 1M prefix limit per family. Transport: kernel TCP (standard Docker networking). BIRD -- C BGP daemon, kernel TCP stack. Config: passive peers, import/export all (no filtering). Transport: kernel TCP (standard Docker networking). FRR (Free Range Routing) -- C BGP daemon, kernel TCP stack. Config: passive peers, PERMIT route-maps in/out (no filtering). Transport: kernel TCP (standard Docker networking). GoBGP -- Go BGP daemon, kernel TCP stack. Config: passive peers, default accept policy. Transport: kernel TCP (standard Docker networking). RustyBGP -- Rust BGP daemon, kernel TCP stack. Config: passive peers, default policy. Transport: kernel TCP (standard Docker networking). freeRtr -- Java BGP daemon with its own TCP/IP stack. Config: passive peers, 256KB buffer-size, extended-update enabled, advertisement-interval-tx 0, incremental bestpath (1M limit), no safe-ebgp. JVM: 2GB heap with ZGC (low-pause garbage collector). Transport: rawInt bridge (UDP encapsulation between Docker eth0 and freeRtr's virtual interface layer) -- adds latency vs kernel TCP used by other DUTs. DUT Convergence +/- Throughput (r/s) +/- p99 +/- bird 50ms 0ms 2,000,000 32,675 26ms 0ms ze 91ms 27ms 1,098,901 461,693 81ms 27ms rustbgpd 179ms 5ms 558,659 15,247 151ms 12ms rustybgp 252ms 14ms 396,825 20,283 233ms 13ms frr 537ms 10ms 186,219 3,764 532ms 10ms gobgp 1,147ms 13ms 87,183 1,031 1,118ms 14ms freertr 2,294ms 146ms 43,591 7,872 1,992ms 619ms Reading the Results Convergence is the time from the first UPDATE sent to the last UPDATE received. Lower is better. This is the primary metric: the time until all routes are propagated. Throughput is routes received per second, averaged over the convergence window. Higher is better. Zero means all routes arrived in a single burst (sub-second convergence with coalesced TCP delivery). p50/p99 are per-route latency percentiles. p50 is the median route's latency; p99 is the slowest 1%. The gap between p50 and p99 shows how consistent the DUT's forwarding is. +/- columns show standard deviation across iterations. Small stddev means consistent performance; large stddev means the measurement is noisy. Withdrawal is the time from sending route withdrawals to the receiver going idle. Lower is better. Measures how fast the DUT propagates route removals. Lost must be zero for a comparison. Any lost routes mean the DUT failed to forward some prefixes, so its convergence cannot be ranked. Raw result JSON and NDJSON retain the loss for diagnosis; comparison and trend renderers refuse it. Reproducing This document is auto-generated by le perf compare --doc. To regenerate with fresh results: # Build all DUT Docker images, then run benchmarks ./le perf run # Or test specific DUTs (available: ze, bird, frr, gobgp, rustbgpd, rustybgp, freertr, openbgpd) ./le perf run dut "ze bird" # Regenerate this document from existing results ./le perf compare --doc test/perf/results/*.json > docs/performance.md Requires Docker (Colima on macOS). See Benchmarking Guide for details on enviro

title: Project overview
text: Project overview Follow Ze from its ExaBGP roots to a network operating system: what works today, what is changing, and what remains before the first release. Where Ze stands Ze brings routing protocols, Linux networking and operator tools together around one configuration. It grew from ExaBGP's programmable BGP model, with a broader job: configure the network, inspect its state, and expose the same operations to people and automation. Ze is pre-release. You can explore it in a lab today; the available capabilities and their test evidence vary by feature. Why Ze, and where it fits Recent work Latest development 2026-11-09 – 2026-11-23 (15 days) BGP accepts RPKI Invalid routes unless told otherwise and sets itself as next hop towards eBGP peers, gNMI… Read the latest update Browse all update reports Pre-release Before the first release The remaining work includes correctness fixes, validation of existing behavior, and release delivery. The roadmap separates these from later features and proposals. Work-item counts describe the backlog. They do not measure effort or production readiness. Release roadmap Inspect the test evidence A recorded session on a real lab router See Ze running Watch an ExaBGP migration, inspect BGP peers, then configure, diagnose and repair services while the same router keeps running. The recordings include the commands and their output, with transcripts you can read at your own pace. Watch Ze in action Try the BGP quickstart Open the continuous configuration recording and transcript Ze's terminal dashboard showing BGP peers, session states and message counters Preview from Ze's published terminal recording. Open the player to watch. Recorded achievements How we got here These recent landmarks mark capabilities that arrived in Ze. The full timeline and project history explain how the system developed. 2026-10-25 LAN caching DNS resolver service dns-resolver answers DNS queries from allowed LAN and subscriber prefixes over UDP and TCP, caches answers, and forwards cache misses to configured upstream servers. DNSSEC validation is still pending. 2. 2026-10-25 Shared route policy Named filters move into a shared policy tree, with import chains at the Loc-RIB and export chains for IS-IS and OSPF redistribution. 3. 2026-10-05 Ze appliance kernel Appliance images boot Ze's own Linux kernel, with the routing and VPN support the system needs, packaged with each image. Explore the milestone timeline From ExaBGP to Ze How Ze is built AI coding agents write most of Ze's code within a framework of specifications agreed before implementation, tests written before code, independent reviews and commit checks. That process is iterative: code and the checks that exercise it improve as problems are found. Checking a first version against every requirement takes time and resources, so published code can still be imperfect. Most of this site's information is generated from the code. Its free text has more room for mistakes than protocol behavior defined by an RFC, so reports of unclear or incorrect information help improve it. How Ze is developed with AI Engineering blogLonger accounts of the design and development. TalksPresentations about Ze and ExaBGP. Development activityRepository history and the scope of the code. Get involved Try Ze in a lab and report a failure with its configuration, trace or transcript. Documentation corrections, interoperability results, tests and focused code changes all help the project move forward. Contribute to Ze
