It now refuses and points at ze init. ze signal stop over SSH left the daemon running. 🛰️ Routing New: Administrative distance now lives in the Loc-RIB under rib { distance { } }. Changing it re-ranks installed routes, and the FIB follows. ze_bgp_open_rejected_bad_peer_as_total counts OPENs refused for AS 0 or an unexpected peer AS (RFC 7607, RFC 4271 Section 6.2). Fixed: Adding a receive-only process, such as RPKI, to an established BGP peer no longer resets the session when the peer supports route refresh. Changes to the IRR filter took effect only after a restart. Peers made with create bgp peer were lost on the next reload, and a removed peer's routes stayed in the RIB. The looking glass showed an empty best-routes table, and counted routes sent to a peer as learned from it. RSVP-TE refuses a path MTU below what an MPLS packet needs, which could hang a stock kernel. A repaired LSP now stays on its bypass when refreshed (RFC 4090 Section 6.4.3). 💿 Appliance and VPN The appliance now boots only Ze's own kernel, Linux 7.2.9, with WireGuard and every IPsec transform built in. Each image carries the kernel's GPL source notice. IKEv2: a refused Child SA no longer tears down the IKE SA. Ze keeps it and retries the Child SA later (RFC 7296 Section 2.21.2). IKEv2: a refused rekey was resent every second until the SA expired. It now waits, and never re-offers a group the peer refused. 📚 Standards programme Ze is being checked against every RFC it implements, one MUST at a time. The work continues. 175 RFCs are on the list. Of 6,452 requirements, 4,524 are MUST-level and 4,147 are checked. 218 still owe a test, down from 248 last week. Each test is also being read again against the RFC sentence it checks. Fixes from that second reading are finished for four of its eight areas and are being checked: https://ze-software.net/quality/rfc-compliance/ 🔭 Coming up Under way: Fixing the remaining defects the second reading found in BGP and OSPF. Finishing the appliance kernel: VPN support proven on a running image, and the test hosts booting the same kernel. Enabling BFD on an established BGP peer without resetting the session, as FRR and BIRD do. Deeper route decision and FIB programming, and a third round of hot-path performance work. Ready to start: BGP DelayOpen and automatic start (RFC 4271 Section 8). BGP EPE peer segments and SRv6 PeerNode SIDs (RFC 9086, RFC 9514). A choice of when a fetched IRR change takes effect: at once, on a schedule, or only when the operator applies it.

title: 2026-10-12 – 2026-10-25 (2 weeks)
text: 2026-10-12 – 2026-10-25 (2 weeks) This update covers two weeks. Many settings that Ze used to accept and then silently ignore are now refused, so please read the changes below before upgrading. The release queue is now sorted into correctness fixes, validation and delivery work. It holds 240 required items and 273 nice-to-have, up from 202 and 224. 79 required items joined, most of them defects found by reviewing the code area by area, and 41 left, either finished or moved to after the release. The counts compare the two ends of the period, so an item added and finished in between is missed, and they count work items rather than readiness: https://ze-software.net/project/roadmap/ ⚠️ Changes to check IPsec: traffic that matches no IPsec policy is now dropped by default (RFC 4301 Section 5). A config saved by an older release is rewritten to vpn ipsec unmatched bypass at start, with a warning. A new config drops it too, so it needs bypass policies for BGP, SSH, DNS and NTP, or unmatched bypass. BGP filters: every configured import or export must now end with final accept or final reject, as in filter { import { filters [ a b ]; final accept; } }. An accept from one filter now passes the route on to the next one. The old import [ ... ] list is refused. Config: a missing mandatory value is refused at load, validate and commit. A flag takes no value, so disable false;, which used to disable the interface, is refused. A setting that needs a feature this build leaves out is refused, naming the line to remove. Run ze config validate before upgrading. CLI: commands that clear everything need an explicit all, as in clear ospf neighbor all, clear vpn ipsec sa all or clear dns cache all. clear bgp rib in and out need a peer. ⚠️ More changes to check CLI: five commands were renamed. explain is now show diagnostic, skills is show skills, support is request support archive, generate wireguard keypair is request wireguard keypair, and validate config is show config validation. API: in FlowSpec update text, values listed one after another now mean OR, and & means AND, matching ExaBGP 6.0. destination-port =80 =443 now matches 80 or 443, where it used to mean both. update text takes nlri add|del|eor for IPv4 unicast and mp <family> add|del|eor for other families. FlowSpec: a redirect-to-IP action from an eBGP peer is now dropped unless the route to that address comes from the peer's own AS. The rest of the rule still applies. flowspec-redirect-check { enabled false; } turns the check off. VRRP over IPv4 now uses the RFC 9568 checksum. A group that shares a link with keepalived needs checksum rfc5798-compatible. L2TP RADIUS accounting now goes to the new accounting-port, default 1813, instead of the authentication port. IPv6 rpf-check was accepted and ignored on Linux. It is now enforced. The DHCPv6 client now builds its DUID from the interface MAC, so a DHCPv6 server treats each client as new after the upgrade. 🛰️ Routing New: BGP shutdown { message "..." } holds a peer down, and sends the message when it closes the session (RFC 9003). request peer <peer> disable [message] and request peer <peer> enable do the same at runtime. BFD can be added, changed or removed on an established BGP peer without resetting the session, as FRR and BIRD do. OSPF over unnumbered point-to-point links: ipv4 unnumbered <donor> borrows the address of the named interface. Tested against FRR. clear bgp rib advertised <peer> withdraws everything sent to a peer, and show bgp peer * detail gains fsm-state. ExaBGP 6.0: the bridge handles neighbor disable/enable, ping and flush adj-rib out, and migration handles as-set and tunnel-encapsulation. Fixed: A configured med 0 was never sent, and local-preference 0 went out as 100. Received BLACKHOLE routes were passed to eBGP peers that had not agreed to them (RFC 7999 Section 3.1). Routes from a route-server client were sent on to providers and peers (RFC 9234 Section 3.1). LDP timed out a silent neighbour at three times the agreed KeepAlive (RFC 5036 Section 3.5.3). 🔒 VPN, access and DHCP New: Integrity-only ESP, with encryption null in an esp-group. An intermediate-certificate list for EAP-TLS clients that do not send their full chain. Fixed: IKEv2 tunnels now follow a peer when a NAT changes its address or port, and later rekeys go to the new address (RFC 3948 Section 2.1). The DHCPv4 client dropped its address after the first renewal. It now renews and rebinds for the life of the lease (RFC 2131 Section 4.4). DHCPv6 pd now requests a delegated prefix; before, it did not. A commit no longer strips DHCP, SLAAC or link-local addresses. The DHCP server now applies a reloaded config, and subnets that did not change keep their leases. 📚 Closing the RFC gap A requirement counts as covered once it has a test, and the code behind it has been deliberately broken to confirm that the test then fails. The number of requirements covered this way grew from 253 in mid-September to 867 at the end of September, 1,844 by 11 October and 2,108 by 25 October. These two weeks went into the tests that were hardest to prove. The tool that breaks the code can now run tests that need Ze's own kernel inside a virtual machine, break the Ze side of an interop test against another implementation, and prove requirements that only fail when two faults are combined. The defects the tests exposed were fixed as they were found, among them the BLACKHOLE and route-server leaks above. Today 1,994 of the 4,680 MUST requirements are covered: https://ze-software.net/quality/rfc-compliance/

title: 2026-10-25 – 2026-11-09 (16 days)
text: 2026-10-25 – 2026-11-09 (16 days) This update covers two weeks, and a number of the changes can break a working configuration. Following RFC 8212, an eBGP peer with no policy configured no longer receives or announces any route, and the routing policy which lived under BGP is now shared by every protocol. Please read the changes below before upgrading. The work left is kept as a list of items, each either required before the first release or planned for after it. 298 items are now required, up from 240, and 348 are planned for later, up from 273. Most of the 71 new required items came from searching the code for errors which were ignored rather than reported, and 12 left the list. The numbers compare both ends of the period, so an item added and completed in between is not counted, and they count work items, not how close the release is: https://ze-software.net/project/roadmap/ ⚠️ Changes to check BGP: an eBGP peer without an import or export policy no longer takes or sends routes (RFC 8212 Section 3), iBGP is not affected. Should you want the old behaviour, add filter { import { final accept; } export { final accept; } }. Both ze config validate and the session warn, giving the command to run. Policy: bgp { policy { ... } } moved to a top-level policy { ... }, used by BGP, IS-IS, OSPF, static, connected and the RIB. The old form is refused and should be moved by hand. Policy: a chain can no longer name a prefix-list (or any other list) directly. The list goes in a match instance, policy { match customers { prefix-list CUSTOMERS; } }, which the chain then uses with filters [ customers ]. Redistribution: the family and tag leaves of a redistribute import, as well as OSPF's redistribute metric, metric-type and tag, are replaced by filters, and the old leaves are refused. ADD-PATH limit N; is now limit { receive N; }. ⚠️ More changes to check RADIUS: every request is now signed with a Message-Authenticator, and any answer without one is dropped (CVE-2024-3596, "BlastRADIUS"). A server which can not sign its answers should be upgraded, require-message-authenticator false is there for when it can not be. IPsec: only Ze is now allowed to install per-socket IPsec policies (vpn ipsec application-override deny, the default). It requires Linux 6.10 and CAP_BPF, and the commit fails without them, so a container needs CAP_BPF or application-override allow. Connection tracking helpers are only attached when listed in system conntrack module [ ... ], which is empty by default (RFC 4787). L2TP and PPPoE: auth-method chap-md5 now means CHAP only, where a subscriber could previously negotiate down to PAP. The allowed methods are listed with authentication { allow [ ... ] } or pppoe authentication-allow. DHCP, router advertisements and L2TP pools now give out the DNS servers learned on the WAN when none are configured. dns-source { source [ configured ]; } keeps the previous behaviour. 🔒 Security RADIUS: without the signature, anyone between Ze and the RADIUS server could forge an Access-Accept, for a system login or for a subscriber. Configurations without RADIUS were not exposed. gNMI returned BGP passwords, RADIUS and TACACS+ keys in clear, and a Set echoed them to every subscriber. They are now sent in $9$ form. Configurations without gNMI were not exposed. GTSM: for a peer using it, SYNs below the TTL floor are now dropped by the firewall before reaching BGP (RFC 5082 Section 3), and ze doctor checks the rule is installed. 🏠 Home router Ze can now replace the router of a home FTTP line, using PPPoE carried to the LNS over L2TP. The PPPoE client learns its DNS servers (RFC 1877), runs IPv6 with DHCPv6 prefix delegation, and has new keepalive and reconnect options. A LAN interface takes a /64 of the delegated prefix with ipv6 delegated-prefix <client>. It was tested against accel-ppp, xl2tpd and strongSwan; reports from other access networks are welcome. service dns-resolver is a caching DNS forwarder for the LAN, with show dns resolver. It does not validate DNSSEC yet. show system dns shows which DNS servers each service uses and where they were learned. 🛰️ Routing New: timer { delay-open N; } delays sending the OPEN, for peers which need it with BFD. PATHS-LIMIT is enforced in both directions, counted by ze_bgp_paths_limit_refused_total. Tested against FRR and BIRD. show rib candidates lists the paths hidden by a policy, and which chain hid them. IS-IS metric-style narrow|transition|wide, wide by default (RFC 3787 Section 5). IKEv2 supports Ed25519 and Ed448 signatures (RFC 8420), and a second authentication round (RFC 4739). Fixed: A policy prepend created a new AS_PATH segment rather than extending the first one (RFC 4271 Section 5.1.2). A peer with asn4 disable and remote AS 23456 was refused with Bad Peer AS (RFC 6793 Section 4.1). The 14 September update said preference ordered RPKI cache failover. It did not correctly until now (RFC 8210 Section 8.3). The 18 May update announced IKE virtual IP pools, but no address was handed out until now. OSPFv3 installed no IPv4 next hop (RFC 5838), and IS-IS point-to-point links to FRR only worked on FRR's first circuit. 📚 Closing the RFC gap A requirement counts as proven when its test fails once the code behind it is broken on purpose. There were 1,844 on 11 October, 2,108 on 25 October and 2,388 today. Most of the work went into running these proofs on Ze's own system in a virtual machine, which let test suites run that could not start before. A requirement Linux meets for Ze now has a test checking the state Ze installs, and a requirement only the kernel can decide is reported on its own rather than counted as proven. 2,239 of the 5,367 MUST requirements written down are now covered, against 1,994 of 4,680 last time: https://ze-software.net/quality/rfc-compliance/

title: 2026-11-09 – 2026-11-23 (15 days)
text: 2026-11-09 – 2026-11-23 (15 days) This update covers two weeks, and several BGP defaults changed to follow the RFCs, so please read the changes below before upgrading. The work left is kept as a list of items, each either required before the first release or planned for after it. 307 items are now required, up from 298, and 373 are planned for later, up from 348. 49 required items were added, 39 left the list and one moved to the later list. The numbers compare both ends of the period, so an item added and completed in between is not counted, and they count work items, not how close the release is: https://ze-software.net/project/roadmap/ ⚠️ Changes to check: BGP RPKI: an Invalid route is no longer dropped unless asked for (RFC 6811 Section 2). For the old behaviour, add bgp { rpki { action { invalid reject; } } }. next-hop auto, the default, now sets Ze as next hop on routes sent to an eBGP peer (RFC 4271 Section 5.1.3). Route server clients and iBGP keep the received next hop, as does next-hop unchanged;. A route whose next hop can not be resolved is no longer selected (RFC 4271 Section 9.1.2). show bgp rib marks it next-hop-unresolvable. Graceful restart is now written graceful-restart { short-lived { restart-time; family ...; } long-lived { family ... { stale-time; } } }, and the old leaves are refused. A bare graceful-restart { } now only helps restarting peers (RFC 4724 Section 3), short-lived { } restores the 120 second restart. The Origin Validation State community is removed from routes received over eBGP (RFC 8097 Section 2), unless the peer sets session { accept-origin-validation-state true; }. ⚠️ More changes to check Ze no longer rewrites a config written in its own older syntax, at start or with ze config migrate, so such a config is refused and should be edited by hand. ExaBGP configs still convert with ze exabgp migrate. The 12 October update said an IPsec config without an unmatched line was rewritten to vpn ipsec unmatched bypass. It now gets the default discard, which drops clear-text management traffic, so add the line before upgrading. gNMI on a non-loopback address now needs a token and TLS, and without a token it is read-only. MCP on a non-loopback address needs TLS. IKEv2 refuses a certificate issued without the IPsec IKE purpose, such as a Let's Encrypt one (RFC 4945 Section 5.1.3.12). It should be reissued. IRR settings moved to system irr { server; refresh-interval; }, and the fetched lists now survive a restart. Refused at commit: a firewall prefix with host bits set (10.10.10.1/30), a tunnel whose remote is 0.0.0.0 or ::, and an interface named by a mirror, bridge, tunnel or PPPoE which is not declared. show bgp gives the peer group under a new group key, description is the peer's own. RIB words such as received and count are now pipes: show bgp rib | received | count. ze config validate shows each refusal with its fix before moving to the new build. 🔒 Security SSH config editor: a user whose system authorization profile denied editing could still set and commit. Each change is now checked. Routers without authorization profiles were not exposed. Appliance web UI: any logged-in account, read-only ones included, could install software or reboot through the /gokrazy/ page. Linux installs were not exposed. MCP: the scope of a bearer-list identity was not enforced, so a read-only identity could run write tools. IPsec: a gateway forwarding for protected hosts sent their traffic from ports 500 and 4500 in clear text (RFC 4301 Section 5.2). Hosts protecting only their own traffic were not exposed. IKEv2: a revoked certificate was accepted, now each pki ca crl is checked. The 7 September update said revocation was checked, which held for EAP-TLS only. IKEv2: a forged message during the handshake could end it (RFC 7296 Section 2.21.2). Established SAs were not exposed. IPsec on VPP installed inbound bypass and discard entries backwards. The kernel backend was not exposed. Fleet: a hub accepted a device claiming an unknown name with an empty token. 📡 Access New: the PPPoE access concentrator runs on VPP, with interface backend vpp. It was tested with pppd, 100 subscribers, a VLAN and RADIUS framed routes, but subscribers on VPP are not rate limited yet. New: clear l2tp session user <name> and clear l2tp session address <ipv4>. Fixed: the 11 May update said RADIUS framed routes are announced in BGP. They were, but no route was installed through the session, so their traffic was dropped. Fixed: WireGuard peers no longer lose their session when Ze restarts. 🛰️ Routing New: BGP aggregation with bgp { aggregate <prefix> { ... } } (RFC 4271 Section 9.2.2.2), not yet tested against another implementation. New: after a restart, route selection waits for End-of-RIB from restarting peers (RFC 4724 Section 4.1). Fixed: the 5 January update said Enhanced Route Refresh was supported, but the markers received were ignored (RFC 7313 Section 4). Fixed: a peer which stops reading no longer holds its session for ever (ze.fwd.write.deadline, 30 seconds). 📚 Closing the RFC gap Each MUST in the RFCs Ze implements gets a test. When the test is written, the code behind it is broken on purpose to see the test fail, and that check is repeated only when the test itself changes. 53.6% of all the MUSTs have a test checked this way (2,779 of 5,188). This counts every MUST of every RFC Ze implements, including the 1,539 for parts of an RFC Ze does not build today, which need no test until they are built. 76% of the MUSTs for what Ze builds have a test checked this way. This leaves those 1,539 out, so it shows how well the features Ze ships are tested. The second figure is new. The MUSTs without such a test are now split more precisely, between those the operating system meets for Ze, those with a test still to be checked, and those for parts Ze does not build. The split changes none of the counts of tested MUSTs. Most of this period's new tests are for IKEv2 (RFC 7296), followed by BGP (RFC 4271 and RFC 7606): https://ze-software.net/quality/rfc-compliance/

title: Project History
text: Project History Ze grew from the operational lessons of ExaBGP. ExaBGP made BGP programmable by treating routes and protocol events as input and output for ordinary processes. That model proved that a routing tool did not need to imitate a traditional router CLI to be useful. From ExaBGP to Ze ExaBGP remained deliberately focused on BGP and process integration. Over time, operators needed the surrounding system as well: a validated configuration model, route storage, policy, interface and FIB management, health, telemetry, secure operator access, and a consistent way to expose every command to automation. Ze keeps the programmable event model and builds those surrounding responsibilities into one system. Its native BGP engine, YANG configuration, plugin registry, CLI, web interface, APIs, MCP server, Looking Glass, telemetry, and optional dataplane integrations share the same runtime state and command dispatcher. The first development period The first tracked development week began in December 2025 with the BGP wire engine, capability negotiation, path attributes, address families, RIB work, session state, and ExaBGP interop. The project then expanded through configuration and plugin architecture, route server and reflector paths, policy, operator surfaces, interfaces, FIB backends, routing protocols, access services, security, diagnostics, packaging, and interoperability. The update reports retain the detailed chronological record. Milestones selects the larger product changes, while the roadmap describes what remains before a stable release. What remained familiar The ExaBGP migration path preserves two useful ideas: Existing ExaBGP configuration can be converted into Ze's configuration model. Existing process scripts can continue through the compatibility bridge before being ported to the native plugin SDK. This allows a routing-engine migration and an application rewrite to happen separately. The ExaBGP migration example documents that path. Why the architecture changed Ze needs to support both a small programmable speaker and a more complete Linux network system. Plugins provide that boundary. BGP, policy, RIB storage, interfaces, FIB backends, routing protocols, services, and operator features register what they own. A deployment loads only the components selected by configuration and build tags. The shared registration model also keeps operator surfaces aligned. A command registered by a component can be discovered and dispatched through the CLI, web interface, REST, gRPC, and MCP without each surface building a separate implementation. Current state Ze remains pre-release. Capability and maturity claims are generated from current source and evidence where possible. Use the feature inventory, RFC status, quality evidence, and roadmap for current decisions rather than treating this history as a readiness statement.

title: Why Ze / Why Not Ze
text: Why Ze / Why Not Ze Ze is a network operating system (NOS) with programmable routing. It combines its own BGP engine with Linux networking and network services, managed through one configuration and plugin engine. You can use it as a route controller, or evaluate it as the software that configures a router and its services. Ze is pre-release software. This assessment was reviewed on November 16, 2026. APIs and configuration syntax can change. The feature inventory records implementation scope and maturity, including partial and experimental features. Corrections are welcome through the issue tracker. Reasons to consider Ze Programmable routing, with control of the device around it Ze keeps ExaBGP's controller model: a process can receive BGP events and inject routes. Your controller can remain a separate program, written in a language that can read and write the process protocol. The Go plugin SDK provides another way to integrate custom logic. That controller can run alongside the device functions Ze provides. The code includes interface configuration, routing-table installation, firewall rules and IPsec, plus access services such as L2TP and PPPoE. Each has its own scope and maturity record. A route-injection deployment can use the BGP functions without configuring those services. For an existing ExaBGP deployment, ze exabgp migrate converts configuration and ze exabgp plugin bridges process scripts. The migration guide explains the differences to check with your own configuration and scripts before replacing a deployment. Operator tools that share the configuration model Ze uses YANG to describe configuration. Its CLI and web editor use that schema, so operators can inspect and edit the same configuration through either interface. The editor provides completion, comparisons and commit validation. The configuration editor guide shows the workflow. Operational tools include a live BGP dashboard, a looking glass and ze doctor for configuration and runtime diagnostics. These are useful when the task is to understand the device as well as exchange routes. The operations guide describes the diagnostic commands. Automation through native APIs and MCP REST and gRPC are implemented command transports. They share an execution engine and expose command discovery and execution, with streaming for registered streaming commands. The gRPC service also provides configuration sessions. The API guide documents authentication and listener requirements. Ze's Model Context Protocol (MCP) server builds tools from command metadata, so an AI assistant can discover commands and call the daemon. This gives an assistant access to the operator's tools. The MCP guide explains the connection and access controls. API compatibility still matters when you choose an implementation. Ze's gRPC service uses Ze's command model, so an integration written for another daemon's protobuf service needs an adapter. API completion is unimplemented, and the REST/gRPC feature remains experimental. gNMI is a separate configuration and telemetry interface. Deployment as a service or an appliance Ze can run as a Linux daemon or in a container. There is also an immutable appliance image built with Linux and gokrazy, with a read-only root filesystem and persistent storage under /perm. The appliance guide and Docker guide describe those deployment choices. Optional subsystems have build tags, so you can compile a focused service or include the wider network OS. An omitted subsystem's code and schema are excluded from the build. The available functions therefore depend on both the build and its configuration. Routing policy, monitoring and protocol tools BGP functions include route-server and route-reflector plugins, routing information base (RIB) storage, graceful restart and filter plugins. Custom plugins can extend policy through the same plugin interfaces. The plugin guide explains those interfaces and their configuration requirements. For monitoring and analysis, Ze includes BGP events, a looking glass and MRT recording. The MRT recorder can write UPDATEs, all BGP messages and periodic TABLE_DUMP_V2 RIB snapshots. MRT recording is experimental. The MRT guide also describes tools to inspect and replay recorded data. Standalone tools include ze bgp decode, ze bgp encode and ze config validate. They are useful for protocol debugging and offline configuration checks, even when you do not run Ze as the router. Reasons to choose another implementation Your deployment requires a released, operationally established NOS Ze has no published release. Its test suites and interoperability labs provide evidence about specific behavior, but they do not establish a history of production operation. A network that requires an established release and support process needs an implementation that already meets those requirements. The distinction applies across the network OS. OSPFv2, OSPFv3 and IS-IS exist, and the code includes BFD, MPLS, IPsec and subscriber access functions. OSPF, IS-IS and PPPoE remain experimental and partial. Their presence in the binary is a reason to evaluate the documented behavior in a lab, rather than assume that the whole routing suite is ready for your network. You need a feature Ze does not provide The feature inventory records what each feature implements and the evidence behind its maturity. The comparison identifies gaps such as BGP confederation support and PIM multicast routing. Check the behavior your deployment depends on, including the selected dataplane, rather than infer support from a protocol name. The standards coverage pages describe what has been tested and what is missing. They list tests that still need checking separately from behavior Ze does not implement. A feature label or a large test count alone does not tell you whether Ze meets your network's requirements. Your project requires a different license or maintenance model Ze is licensed under AGPL-3.0-only. If your project requires a permissive license, Ze does not meet that requirement. The license and contribution policy describe the project terms and contribution requirements. Ze is developed with AI coding assistants, with Thomas Mangin directing the architecture and development decisions. Specifications, tests and independent review constrain that process. If your organization requires a larger maintainer team or a contracted support arrangement, evaluate those requirements separately from the feature list. Engineering tradeoffs Plugins share a contract, with a choice of process boundary Ze separates BGP functions such as RIB storage and route-server behavior into plugins. Internal plugins run inside the daemon and use DirectBridge for typed calls after startup. External plugins run in separate processes and communicate through the process protocol. The separation lets a plugin be replaced without moving its policy into the BGP engine. Internal plugins share the daemon's address space. External processes provide a process boundary, with transport and serialization costs. Both forms still need correct lifecycle handling and event ordering. Performance depends on the workload Ze is written in Go and uses pooled data and lazy wire parsing to reduce allocation and decoding costs. WireUpdate retains the supplied payload and parses sections when needed. These techniques reduce particular costs, and their effect on throughput depends on the workload. The performance results describe measured scenarios, with their dates and environments. They cannot establish a general percentage cost for Go, a plugin boundary or another implementation. For a deployment decision, use the benchmarking guide to test your route counts, policies and peer topology, and check that all expected routes arrive. Process IPC and management APIs serve different callers External plugins use a multiplexed text protocol, while operators and automation can use REST, gRPC or MCP. A custom plugin therefore needs to implement the plugin contract even

title: Code Quality
text: Code Quality Ze uses different tests for package logic, running daemons, and behavior that depends on Linux or another router. This page explains which test fits a change and how a failure points to the next check. Quality model A package test can check a parser without starting Ze, but it cannot show that the daemon applies a new configuration or sends a route to another router. Functional transcripts exercise those operations through the running program. QEMU provides the Linux environment for kernel-dependent tests, while interoperability tests exchange messages with other implementations. Fuzzing extends the inputs a Go test tries, and mutation testing with gomu checks whether its assertions detect a deliberate code change. A parser failure can then become a saved regression case. If a mutation survives, the reviewer must establish whether the changed code behaves equivalently or whether the test missed a defect. Local: Go tests, race checks, coverage, generated-input tests, and gomu run before checks that need more time or resources. Process: .ci, .wb, and .et files run Ze the way an operator, peer, browser, or editor would use it. Linux: QEMU runs the same tests where netlink, nftables, eBPF, PPP, and namespaces exist. Release: Interop, deployment, performance, and chaos runs check behavior that package tests cannot establish. The flow Step 1 Test package behavior Start with a small Go test that names the case and expected result. Use fuzzing when one or two examples cannot cover the input space. Use gomu when the code is covered but the assertion may still be too loose. Step 2 Test visible behavior When the behavior crosses a process boundary, use a functional transcript. .ci drives commands, peers, files, HTTP, and daemons. .wb drives the browser. .et drives the editor. Step 3 Test Linux behavior Tests that depend on the Linux kernel run on Linux. From macOS, a functional file marked option=needs-linux can run in QEMU using Ze's kernel and system image. Step 4 Run release checks Release checks include peer daemons, deployment tests, performance measurements, and chaos scenarios. Together these exercise interactions and failure conditions beyond the fixtures used in package tests. Local tests are one layer Example tests A normal Go test gives the case a name and states the exact result. It checks a parser rule, encoder rule, state transition, validation, or error message. Fuzz targets A fuzz target is a Go test with generated inputs. It starts from known examples, tries variations, and saves any input that causes a crash or an incorrect result so it can be tested again. gomu mutation checks gomu changes production code in small ways and runs the same tests. If the tests still pass, the changed code was equivalent or the assertions did not check that behavior tightly enough. Which guide to open What you are testing Use this Guide Package behavior, parser rules, encoders, races, fuzzable inputs, or weak assertions go test, race, fuzz, coverage, gomu mutation checks Local Go tests, fuzzing, and gomu Daemon startup, CLI output, BGP wire output, HTTP, syslog, files, or process exits .ci under test/<suite>/ Functional .ci tests Rendered web UI behavior or interactive editor behavior .wb under test/web/, .et under test/editor/ Browser and editor tests Linux kernel behavior, compatibility with other routers, deployment, or release evidence QEMU, Docker interoperability tests, deployment scripts, performance checks QEMU, interop, and release evidence A failing verify run that needs a clear rerun command Verify stages, failure groups, trace output, debug logs Verify and debugging workflow Whether the suite would catch a regression What assertions check, tests that cannot fail, tests nothing runs, checks against declining coverage, and results over time Testing health RFC requirement coverage, known omissions, or checks on AI changes to tests ./le rfc check, links from requirements to tests, agreement with published status, and current reviews RFC compliance Commands that matter Edit loop Use one focused command while changing code. go test -race -run TestName ./internal/component/config/... FUZZ=FuzzParseNLRI PKG=./internal/component/bgp/wire/ TIME=30s ./le test fuzz run go run github.com/sivchari/gomu/cmd/gomu run --incremental --base-branch=main --fail-on-gate=false ./le test bgp plugin 42 -v Release verification GitHub CI runs full verification on pushed commits. The maintainer can also schedule a release check; day-to-day changes use the tests they reach. ./le verify current ./le verify current fast ./le repo check Linux and release Use these checks when the behavior depends on Linux, another router, or the release environment. ./le test qemu netns ./le test qemu run command '...' keep-alive ./le test integration interop ./le verify evidence release-candidate How a failure becomes useful ./le verify current writes per-stage logs under tmp/, groups related failures, and prints the rerun commands. Its lock prevents overlapping verification runs. The functional runner adds per-step traces for .ci, .wb, and .et files. BGP expectations decode wire messages before showing differences, so a failed UPDATE is reported as protocol fields that can be compared. The rule A failure needs a test that can observe the required behavior. After correcting the cause, rerun that test while preserving its assertions. Wider verification belongs in CI and the release check. File formats Ze currently has three functional formats. Use .ci for process, protocol, command, HTTP, syslog, file, and daemon behavior. Use .wb for rendered browser behavior. Use .et for the headless interactive editor. There is no .wt parser in the current tree; notes using that extension should be read as web tests only if a new parser is later added.

title: Browser .wb and Editor .et Tests
text: Browser .wb and Editor .et Tests Ze has two formats for testing its interfaces. A .wb file drives the web interface through a browser session, while an .et file drives the interactive configuration editor through the CLI testing harness. Both exercise the actions a person takes and the responses they see. There is no .wt parser in the current tree. Web tests use .wb; editor tests use .et. Browser tests A .wb file is a short browser script. The runner starts Ze, opens an isolated agent-browser session, runs actions, waits for browser activity to settle, and evaluates expectations against the rendered page. The point is to test the behavior after templates, HTMX, handlers, and client-visible state have all interacted. Use .wb when navigation, form behavior, HTMX replacement, visible copy, page title, URL, or accessibility-visible elements are the contract. Use a Go unit test for pure handler logic and use .ci for simple HTTP status checks. ./le test web --list ./le test web -p config -v ./le test functional web Browser syntax Line Meaning Example action=open Navigate to a path action=open:path=/config action=click Click by visible text or id action=click:text=Save action=fill Fill an input selected by label, text, or id action=fill:text=Hostname:value=router1 action=press Press a key after optional focus action=press:text=Search:key=Enter action=wait Wait for a small explicit condition when auto-waiting is not enough action=wait:ms=100 expect=element Assert visible text in the accessibility snapshot expect=element:text=Routes expect=url Assert current browser URL expect=url:contains=/config expect=html Assert markup when markup itself is the contract expect=html:contains=hx-get Prefer id= for stable controls and text= when the visible label is the contract. A .wb test should assert after state-changing actions so the failure points at the first broken transition. Avoid fixed sleeps except for behavior that genuinely has no observable readiness signal. Editor tests An .et file is a replay script for the interactive configuration editor. The runner creates a temporary config root, starts the editor model, sends key and text input, and checks the prompt, context, completions, dirty state, validation messages, and persisted files. It is headless, which makes it fast, but it still exercises the editor input model rather than a single parser function. ./le test editor --list ./le test editor -p completion -v ./le test functional editor Editor syntax Line Meaning Example session= Create or reuse a named editor session session=main input=type Type text into the editor input=type:text=set interfaces input=key Send a named key input=key:name=tab input=enter Submit the current line input=enter expect=prompt Assert the prompt or context expect=prompt:contains=interfaces expect=completion Assert completion candidates expect=completion:contains=neighbor expect=dirty Assert whether pending changes exist expect=dirty:value=true expect=file Assert saved config content expect=file:path=config.conf contains=router bgp restart= Restart the editor and reopen persisted state restart=session=main Use editor tests for completion, validation, path context, commit and discard behavior, session persistence, and lifecycle bugs. Use .ci when the behavior is already visible through a non-interactive command. Failure reading Both runners emit per-step trace records. The human output shows action and expectation lines with source locations. The machine output emits VERIFY STEP JSON so ./le verify current can group failures without scraping prose. ./le test web config-menu -v ./le test editor completion-basic -v ZE_TEST_KEEP_TMP=1 ./le test editor completion-basic -v For web failures, read the snapshot before changing selectors. For editor failures, read the prompt, context, and buffered text before changing parser code. Most flaky UI tests come from checking too early; prefer an observable wait such as URL, element text, validation state, or command completion.

title: Functional .ci Tests
text: Functional .ci Tests .ci is Ze's process and protocol test format. Use it when correctness is visible through a real command, daemon, socket, HTTP request, syslog line, file artifact, process exit, or BGP wire message. A .ci file is an executable transcript. The runner reads key-value directives, creates a temporary workspace, writes embedded files, allocates ports, starts foreground and background commands, waits for readiness, and checks the observable result. That makes the test close to the debugging session a developer would run by hand, and repeatable enough to run automatically during verification. Where it belongs Behavior Files Narrow run Native suite BGP encode and route output test/encode/*.ci ./le test bgp encode NAME -v ./le test functional encode BGP plugin behavior test/plugin/*.ci ./le test bgp plugin NAME -v ./le test functional plugin Config parsing test/parse/*.ci ./le test bgp parse NAME -v ./le test functional parse Decode command output test/decode/*.ci ./le test bgp decode NAME -v ./le test functional decode Reload behavior test/reload/*.ci ./le test bgp reload NAME -v ./le test functional reload CLI output test/ui/*.ci ./le test ui NAME -v ./le test functional ui L2TP, firewall, policy, LDP, RSVP-TE, IS-IS, OSPF, OSPFv3, static, traffic, VPP, and install flows test/<suite>/*.ci ./le test <suite> NAME -v ./le test functional <suite>-test Run ./le test bgp plugin --list or the equivalent suite command before picking an id. The list output gives the exact test name, id, status, and command for running it again. Execution model The runner has five stages. It parses the file into records, writes embedded files in a temporary directory, starts background processes, waits for readiness, and then executes foreground commands and expectations in order. Each test has its own temporary directory and ports, so parallel runs cannot change each other's files or connections. Background commands are for daemons and peers. Foreground commands are for assertions that should complete, such as ze cli, ze config, curl, helper scripts, or packet checks. A foreground process can assert stdout, stderr, exit code, files, JSON, HTTP, and BGP messages without adding a second test harness. A small example file=config.conf<<EOF router bgp 65000 neighbor 127.0.0.1 remote-as 65001 EOF cmd=background:ze:bin/ze config.conf cmd=background:peer:le test peer --as 65001 --listen 127.0.0.1:$PORT1 cmd=foreground:show:bin/ze cli -c "show bgp peer list" expect=stdout:show:contains=Established Use embedded files for configs, fixtures, plugin payloads, and helper scripts. Use variables such as $TMP, $PORT1, and $ZE rather than hard-coded paths and ports. That keeps the test parallel-safe and portable. Expectations Expectation Use it for Example expect=stdout and reject=stdout CLI-visible text contains=Established expect=stderr Warnings and validation errors contains=invalid prefix expect=exit Process status code=1 expect=file Generated files and state dumps path=$TMP/out.json contains=neighbor expect=json Decoded JSON with volatile fields normalized json={...} expect=http HTTP readiness and body checks url=http://127.0.0.1:$PORT1/health code=200 expect=bgp Exact BGP messages seq=1 hex=... Prefer the narrowest expectation that expresses the contract. For BGP, assert the decoded protocol behavior or the exact wire message. For JSON, remove known volatile fields instead of asserting a loose substring. For CLI output, assert the user-visible line that would catch a regression. Linux behavior A .ci file that needs netlink, nftables, eBPF, PPP, L2TP, namespaces, kernel routing, or Linux-only sockets should say so directly: option=needs-linux On macOS that test reports SKIP. Inside QEMU the option is inert and the same file runs for real. Use ./le test qemu netns for the curated Linux kernel suites. For one command or an interactive investigation, use ./le test qemu run command '...' keep-alive. Failure reading A good .ci failure tells you the file, step, line, assertion, process output, temporary directory, and rerun command. With -v, the runner keeps enough detail to see command stdout and stderr. BGP mismatches are decoded before display, which turns a wire failure into protocol fields. ./le test bgp plugin 42 -v ZE_TEST_KEEP_TMP=1 ./le test bgp plugin 42 -v ze.log.bgp.reactor.peer=debug ./le test bgp plugin 42 -v If the failure only reproduces under Linux, rerun it through ./le test qemu run rather than adding sleeps or Darwin-only skips.

title: Testing Health
text: Testing Health GENERATED by ./le test health update -- do not edit. Source: internal/le/test/health.Answer. How current is this? The structural facts -- which test files nothing runs, which RFCs have no test pair, and every metric's status -- are checked by ./le verify current and cannot lag the tree. The volume counters are as of the last ./le test health update and may lag by a few tests; they deliberately do not fail the check, because a check that fired on most commits that add a test would be routed around rather than read. Ratchets are enforced from the tree itself, not from this page. These measures help assess whether Ze's tests would catch a regression. A growing suite can cover a smaller share of the program as the code changes, so its test count alone says little about the faults it would detect. Each measure addresses one of the three questions below. Needs attention Metric Question Value What to do RFC MUST requirements proven by test, by ze or as OS verified, over the RFCs ze implements Q2 2671 / 4633 (attention) Write a test for a {gap} requirement, or for one carrying no test and no annotation, then record its break with ./le rfc record: a requirement counts as proven only when a discrimination record still verifies on a walked summary. Not-applicable needs no test. Enrolled RFCs with zero test-proven requirements Q2 21 / 200 (attention) Pick the largest and complete a pair, or accept it is a single-polarity claim. Logged known-failing tests Q3 1 (attention) Fix or delete the oldest entry; a permanently logged failure is a deleted test with extra steps. 6 further metric(s) are within threshold and are listed in full below. Sensitivity If the code were wrong, would something go red? Tests with no reachable failure call 108 / 53587 (floor 108) (ok) These execute code and pass unconditionally. Breaking the code under test would not turn them red. Action if this degrades: Add a real assertion, or annotate with // test-asserts-nothing: <why> when the oracle is genuinely implicit (a must-not-panic smoke test). file test internal/chaos/chaos_test.go TestChaosConcurrency internal/chaos/watchdog/watchdog_test.go TestWatchdogRouteRegression internal/component/bfd/api/registry_test.go TestSetGetService_ConcurrentNoRace internal/component/bfd/metrics_test.go TestMetricsHookStateChangeCounters internal/component/bfd/metrics_test.go TestRefreshSessionsGauge internal/component/bgp/plugins/healthcheck/hooks_test.go TestHookFailureNoEffect internal/component/bgp/plugins/nlri/evpn/plugin_test.go TestSetEVPNLogger internal/component/bgp/plugins/rib/rib_metrics_test.go TestUpdateMetricsNilRegistry internal/component/bgp/plugins/rib/rib_pipeline_test.go TestShowPipelineConcurrentChurn internal/component/bgp/plugins/rib/storage/sizeof_test.go TestRouteEntrySizes time.sleep() calls in .ci tests 0 (floor 0) (ok) A sleep is a guess about timing that hides the race it was added to mask. The ratchet allows the count to fall, never rise. Action if this degrades: Replace a sleep with a payload-predicate wait (wait_until, dispatch_until), then lower the floor in the same change. Intent coverage Are the things that matter checked, or only the happy path? RFC MUST requirements proven by test, by ze or as OS verified, over the RFCs ze implements 2671 / 4633 (attention) 57.7% of the 4633 MUST rows ze and the OS owe in the walked RFCs ze implements are proven with a recorded break: a discrimination record that still verifies against this tree. 2668 of them are proven by ze, and 3 are performed by the OS with a verified test (OS verified), whose record broke the state ze installs for that layer. Of the rest, 232 are performed by the OS with no verified test yet (a tag alone, a stale record, or a no-break or kernel-producer escape), and 1730 are owed by ze and not proven: proof pending 408 (a tagged test and no recorded break yet), exclusion unchecked 21 (a not-owed claim whose evidence fails its check), not assessed 0 (no tagged test covers the row, so nothing yet says whether ze meets it), not built 1301 (the summary or the audit says the obligation is unmet). 74 further MUST rows are not owed (not applicable, declined, OS blocked) and are in neither count. Until 2026-10-31 this figure was taken over every MUST row of those RFCs but rollups, annotated rows included, so a row that does not bind ze counted against it; until 2026-11-13 its numerator held the rows ze proves alone, and an OS verified row was counted only in the denominator. 0 of the 191 RFCs ze implements are not walked yet: their requirement lists are unbounded, so they are left out of every count rather than measured. The gate holds a wider set -- 4739 MUST rows across 199 enrolled RFCs -- and of the 2218 of those not proven in both polarities: 99 not-applicable (recorded as not binding ze, and counted not owed only once its evidence passes: one whose evidence fails stays among the rows ze owes, as exclusion unchecked), 1337 known gap (unimplemented, genuinely untested), 33 partial (scoped evidence with a remaining gap; subset of annotated, zero whole-requirement credit), 511 single-polarity -- those DO have a passing tagged test, just one side of the pair, and the RFC gate fails if that test is missing -- 235 met by a layer under ze on state ze installs, which the annotation names with the producer that installs it: those are owed by the stack, so they count in the MUST rows owed above, and in the proven rows only once a record that broke that producer verifies (OS verified), never in the rows proven by ze, 0 conditional on an optional feature ze does not offer, each quoting the RFC sentence that makes it optional: the condition is false, so the row is counted not owed only once its evidence passes, and otherwise stays among the rows ze owes, as exclusion unchecked, 0 blocked by a Linux kernel limitation: no proof credit, and counted not owed as OS blocked only once its register entry verifies, because ze cannot meet it on Linux; one whose entry fails stays among the rows ze owes, as not built, and 0 with no test and no annotation at all, which is what ./le rfc check is red about. Apart from every figure above, 15 rows carry {rollup}: each derives its state from rows already counted here, and none is in any count above. In-repo test inventory 53633 test functions (ok) 11412 Go test files, 121 fuzz targets, 161 benchmarks, 3223 .ci scenarios, 210 .et editor tests. Counts cover internal, cmd, pkg, test only: vendor/ and gokrazy/modcache/ are third-party module trees and are excluded. Action if this degrades: This is volume, not health. It is here to state the counting boundary, because a count that silently includes vendored tests inflates by ~6x. title: QEMU, Interop, and Release Evidence
text: QEMU, Interop, and Release Evidence Some behavior can only be checked with a Linux kernel, another routing daemon, or a service outside Ze. This page explains the QEMU, Docker, live-data, and performance tests used for those cases, and how their results contribute to release verification. Day-to-day changes use the tests that exercise the affected behavior. When that behavior depends on Linux or another implementation, the relevant QEMU or interoperability test is part of that work. Full verification runs in GitHub CI on pushed commits and during release checks. When QEMU is required On a non-Linux host, QEMU provides the environment for tests that depend on Linux behavior. That includes netlink, nftables, network namespaces, veth pairs, PPP, L2TP, eBPF, kernel route state, raw sockets, Linux-only build tags, and tests marked option=needs-linux. Need Command Run curated Linux-only functional files ./le test qemu netns Run the full suite inside a prepared guest ./le test qemu run command '<guest-le> le test qemu all' Rerun one failing command inside the VM ./le test qemu run command '...' Keep a VM alive for manual inspection ./le test qemu run command '...' keep-alive The QEMU guest uses Ze's kernel and system image. It provides Linux features that Docker Desktop on macOS cannot provide reliably. During a debug run, you can inspect ip, nft, dmesg, temporary files, process state, and generated logs inside the guest. Linux-only .ci files A functional file that needs Linux says so explicitly: option=needs-linux On macOS, the functional runner reports that test as skipped. The same file runs inside the Linux QEMU guest, so its assertions can be checked on either a Linux host or a Mac with QEMU. Integration Go tests Go integration tests that require Linux use the integration and linux tags. The QEMU integration targets run these tests inside the guest. //go:build integration && linux This format suits a kernel API wrapper or package integration test. A .ci transcript is useful when the test must start a daemon, apply configuration, or run an operator command. Docker interop Docker interop tests protocol behavior against real implementations. Ze runs BGP scenarios against FRR, BIRD, GoBGP, OpenBGPD, RustyBGP, freeRouter, and related peers. Other labs cover IPsec, L2TP, PPPoE, deployment, and live checks where the target behavior depends on an external daemon or service. Evidence Command What it tests BGP interop ./le test integration interop Ze exchanges real protocol messages with third-party BGP daemons. IPsec interop ./le test integration interop-ipsec strongSwan and Ze agree on the deployed behavior. L2TP and PPPoE ./le test deployment docker-l2tp-ppp, ./le test deployment docker-pppoe-accel Access protocol behavior works against real peers. Deployment evidence ./le test deployment l2tp, ./le test deployment vpp Exercises the deployment scripts with the services they configure. A .ci transcript can isolate a Ze behavior and make its failure easy to reproduce. An interoperability test adds another implementation, which can expose a protocol mistake shared by Ze and its own test peer. Both kinds of test are useful. Performance and live evidence Performance checks are used when a change can reduce throughput, slow convergence, or affect packet forwarding. Tests with live services are used when the behavior depends on external data, such as an RPKI cache. These checks are separate from the default verification run because they depend on time, host capacity, Docker, root privileges, or the internet. ./le perf record ./le test integration live-rpki Release evidence Release evidence runs verification over a clean checkout in a container. The command checks its prerequisites before it starts testing each supported build. ./le verify evidence release-candidate Release evidence supports claims across the system. For a single failure, the useful starting point is the test that reproduces it; a wider environment is needed when the behavior depends on it.

title: RFC Compliance Report
text: RFC Compliance Report How far Ze meets each RFC it implements, and the tests that check it. Source: internal/le/rfc, rfc/short/*.md, and rfc/audit/*/*.json. How to read this page This page shows how far Ze meets the standards (RFCs) it implements, and how that is tested. For each RFC, Ze keeps a summary of the requirements identified so far and links them to their tests. Automatic checks read those summaries and tests, and the figures on this page are computed from the same summaries and tests. If you are evaluating Ze for one role, start with Coverage by profile. To check one RFC, find it in the RFCs included in automatic checks table and open its own page, which lists each requirement and the tests behind it. The glossary below explains the results and notes the corresponding terms in Ze's source. Summary: Ze's file for one RFC: it lists the RFC's requirements, the tests behind each one, and the support status Ze publishes for the RFC. Requirement: one obligation an RFC states, kept in the summary with an identifier such as RFC4271-8.2.2-12 that names the RFC and its section. MUST-level (mandatory): a requirement stated with MUST, MUST NOT, REQUIRED, SHALL, SHALL NOT. The optional levels are MAY, NOT RECOMMENDED, OPTIONAL, RECOMMENDED, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT. Included in automatic checks: an RFC whose mandatory requirements are checked against its summary and tests. Other RFC summaries are listed at the end of the page with the reason they are excluded. The repository calls this enrollment. Automatic compliance check: the check reads RFC requirement summaries and tests to find missing evidence or unsupported claims. The repository calls it a gate. Positive and negative test (polarity): a positive test checks that Ze does what the requirement demands; a negative test checks that Ze refuses what the requirement forbids. Tested both ways means both exist. Test linked to a requirement: one test that names the requirement it checks in a source annotation. One requirement can have several tests. Recorded fault test: evidence that a test can detect a fault: the code under the test was broken once on purpose, the test was seen to fail, and a record stores what the test, its claim and the code looked like. The break is not run again. Ze's source calls this a discrimination record. No fault test recorded: a test record states that no deliberate code change could demonstrate the test failing. The source calls this escaped, and it does not verify that the test can detect a fault. Outdated fault test: a test, its stated claim, or the code it checks has changed since the fault test was recorded. The source calls this lapsed, and the fault-detection check is no longer current. Gap: a requirement the summary openly declares Ze does not meet yet. Every gap is work Ze owes. Annotation: a note on a requirement, written in braces, that says why it needs no ordinary pair of tests. {single-polarity}: the requirement admits no counter-case, so one direction plus a recorded reason is the complete test coverage required. {not-applicable}: the obligation does not bind Ze. {feature-declined}: the obligation applies only to a feature the RFC makes optional and Ze does not offer. {lower-layer}: a layer under Ze performs the behavior, on state Ze installs into that layer. {gap}: a declared gap. A partial requirement has tests for part of it; the rest is unmet or unverified and earns no credit. Linux cannot do this: a verified kernel limitation prevents the required primitive. The annotation names the Linux Limitations Register entry. The row is OS blocked: a limit of the kernel, never counted against Ze, so it sits with the rows not owed and in no section of the MUST bar. Requirements reviewed: a reviewer read the original RFC sentence by sentence and checked the requirement list against it. The review record documents that check. Requirements not reviewed means that this check has not been completed, so the RFC is excluded from the coverage figures. Excluded sentence: a sentence of the RFC that the review decided not to turn into a requirement, with a kind and a reason. Test review: a reviewer's recorded judgment of whether the tests check what the requirement says. Fresh means still current. Shifted means the test is unchanged and only the surrounding file moved. Stale means the reviewed code or requirement changed. Ze verified, Ze MUST verified (bar segment): a MUST row Ze's own code performs, with a tagged test whose recorded break was seen to fail. OS verified (bar segment): a row a layer under Ze performs (the Linux kernel Ze ships, or a Go library Ze links), with a tagged test that checks that layer's behavior on the state Ze installs, and a recorded break. Tests awaiting verification (bar segment): a row with a tagged test and no recorded break checking fault detection, that neither the summary nor a test review says Ze does not meet. OS testing gap (bar segment): a row a layer under Ze performs, with no verified test of that behavior yet. It is a gap in testing, not in correctness. Exclusion unchecked (bar segment): a row claimed not to bind Ze whose evidence is still to be checked. Until it is, the row stays among the rows Ze owes. Not assessed (bar segment): a row no tagged test covers and that neither the summary nor a test review says Ze does not meet, so nothing yet says whether Ze meets it. Not built (bar segment): a row the summary or a test review says Ze does not meet, including a row built only in part. SHOULD verified (bar segment): a SHOULD or MAY row Ze's code performs, with a tagged test whose recorded break was seen to fail. Not owed (bar segment): a row that does not bind Ze, shown by checked evidence: it binds a role Ze does not fill, it applies only to an optional feature Ze does not offer, or Linux cannot provide its primitive (OS blocked). It is left out of the MUST bar. How compliance is calculated Two headline percentages: Ze publishes two percentages over mandatory (MUST / MUST NOT / SHALL / REQUIRED) requirements of reviewed RFCs it implements. The overall figure is (Ze verified + OS verified) divided by all applicable MUST requirements, including optional or unfinished parts of an RFC Ze does not build yet. The built-features figure leaves out those unbuilt parts, showing (Ze verified + OS verified) divided by (all applicable MUST requirements minus not built). What counts as verified: A requirement counts as verified only when a test checks it and that test was observed to fail when the underlying behavior was deliberately broken. That fault check runs when the test is written and again whenever the test changes, not on every test run. Behavior handled by the Linux kernel or a linked library counts as OS verified once a test verifies that behavior on the state Ze installs. Default behavior vs. custom operator configuration: Compliance is judged on Ze's default configuration path. Operators can still configure custom routing policy, raw wire attributes, or explicit overrides that depart from an RFC; those controls are kept by design and do not count as compliance failures when default behavior follows the standard. Superseded RFCs: When a newer RFC obsoletes an older one and Ze implements the newer standard, an obsoleted requirement counts as validated and complete once its replacement in the newer RFC is verified (or dropped by the newer RFC). Requirements that are still unimplemented in the newer RFC remain open gaps. What is left out of the denominator: Requirements that bind a role Ze does not fill (such as a DNSSEC zone signer, an RPKI cache server, or a route reflector), obligations that apply only to a human operator's deployment or network topology, IANA/IETF registry rules, optional features Ze explicitly declines, and requirements blocked by a documented Linux kernel limit are excluded from the denominator. Internet-Drafts (draft-*) are not published RFCs and are counted separately from RFC conformance figures and release targets until

title: Local Go Tests, Fuzzing, and gomu
displayTitle: Local Go Tests, Fuzzing, and gomu
text: Local Go Tests, Fuzzing, and gomu This page covers package tests in Go and ways to examine their coverage and assertions. Named _test.go cases establish expected results, fuzz targets try more inputs, and gomu changes the code to see whether the tests detect a mistake. Race runs check for unsafe concurrent access. The local test loop Start with a normal Go test. It names the behavior and fixes the expected result. If the input space is too large for a few named cases, add a fuzz target for the same behavior. If the code is covered but the assertion may still be weak, run gomu and see whether a deliberate code change survives. Mode Question Command Example test Does this named input produce the exact expected behavior? go test -race -run TestName ./path/... Fuzz target Does the same rule hold for generated inputs and saved corpus entries? FUZZ=FuzzParseNLRI PKG=./internal/component/bgp/wire/ TIME=30s ./le test fuzz run gomu mutation run Would the tests fail if the implementation made a small wrong decision? go run github.com/sivchari/gomu/cmd/gomu run --incremental --base-branch=main --fail-on-gate=false Race run Does the behavior still hold when goroutines are scheduled differently? ./le test unit Coverage report Which branches ran without a strong assertion attached? go test -coverprofile coverage.out ./path/... Fuzzing needs an assertion that should hold across its generated inputs. Mutation testing needs assertions that distinguish correct behavior from the deliberate mistake. A named example test is a useful starting point for both. Example tests A normal unit test is the right tool when the behavior sits inside one package or a small group of production types. Good targets are wire encoders, parsers, state machines, validation helpers, route selection, command formatting, and error paths. If the behavior only exists after a daemon starts, a browser renders, or the Linux kernel answers, use .ci, .wb, .et, or QEMU instead. Scope Command When to use it One test go test -race -run TestName ./path/... Fast edit loop for one named behavior. BGP group ./le test unit bgp Wire, FSM, peer, and BGP component changes. Core group ./le test unit core Core libraries and shared infrastructure. Plugin group ./le test unit plugins Runtime plugin logic and plugin boundaries. Config group ./le test unit config YANG, config parsing, validation, and rendering. CLI group ./le test unit cli Command parsing and user-visible formatting. All unit groups ./le test unit Run every unit test group. Fuzz targets are still tests A Go fuzz target is a test function with generated inputs. It should start from useful seed cases, call the same parser or decoder a normal unit test would call, and assert a stable rule. For Ze, good fuzz targets are BGP attributes, communities, capabilities, AS paths, L2TP control packets, TACACS packets, and other parsers that must survive malformed external input. ./le test fuzz run FUZZ=FuzzParseNLRI PKG=./internal/component/bgp/wire/ TIME=30s ./le test fuzz run Keep the target deterministic and small. Be strict about accepted errors and round trips. When fuzzing finds a crash or semantic bug, keep the corpus entry. That saved input becomes the named regression case that explains the failure. gomu checks assertion strength gomu is the mutation-testing tool Ze uses to test the tests. It changes Go code in small ways and reruns the same test suite. If the tests fail, the mutation is killed. If the tests still pass, the mutation survived. A survived mutation usually means the changed code was equivalent or the test did not check the decision tightly enough. go run github.com/sivchari/gomu/cmd/gomu run --incremental --base-branch=main --fail-on-gate=false go run github.com/sivchari/gomu/cmd/gomu run --incremental=false --fail-on-gate=false ./internal/core/textbuf/ go run github.com/sivchari/gomu/cmd/gomu run --incremental=false --fail-on-gate=false ./le test mutation record report mutation-report.json Fuzzing and mutation testing expose different weaknesses. Fuzzing may find an input the author overlooked, while gomu may show that an existing assertion accepts an incorrect result. Using both helps reviewers examine what the tests actually establish. gomu result Meaning Response Killed The test suite noticed the changed behavior. No action needed. Survived The tests still passed after a code mutation. Add a stronger assertion, add a functional test, or classify the mutation as equivalent. Timed out The package or test is too slow for the current mutation settings. Test a smaller package or skip mutation testing where it provides no useful result. gomu runs through go run, so no separate install is needed. .gomuignore excludes paths where mutation testing produces misleading results or is not useful. Full mutation runs are slower than unit tests and do not determine whether a release passes, but a change that the tests fail to detect still needs review. Choosing the test Change Starting test Strengthen it with Pure parser or encoder Normal test with exact input and output. Fuzz target for malformed inputs and gomu for assertion strength. State machine or route decision Normal test for transition or selected result. Race run if goroutines are involved. Error handling Normal test that checks the error type and message. gomu if changing a condition could silently pass. Malformed external input Fuzz target seeded with known examples. Corpus regression when a failure is found. Process or UI behavior Functional transcript. Normal tests for the helper functions used by the process or interface.

title: Verify and Debugging Workflow
text: Verify and Debugging Workflow When a test fails, its failure report should identify the next command to run. This page explains how to read those reports and enable logging for the part of Ze under investigation. ./le verify current is a release check, also run by GitHub CI on pushed commits. It runs checks in stages, prevents overlapping verification runs, and reports commands for reproducing failures. During development, a change is checked with the tests for the affected packages and behavior; a full verification run is scheduled by the maintainer. ./le verify current fast ./le verify current What verify does Stage Purpose Typical rerun Lint and architecture checks Formatting, code analysis, generated docs, component registration, and project rules. ./le go lint run or the printed check command. Unit and race checks Package behavior, affected test groups, and concurrent memory access. go test -race -run TestName ./path/... Functional suites .ci, .wb, and .et behavior that an operator or browser can observe. ./le test <suite> NAME -v Compatibility checks ExaBGP and related protocol compatibility checks included in this verification run. The command printed by the failure group. The verify runner writes logs under tmp/, keeps an index of failures, and groups related failures in its report. The job scheduler in internal/le/job/job.go (./le job run) prevents resource-intensive verification runs from overlapping and interfering with shared temporary files or their reports. Reading the failure Start with the first failing group. It tells you the stage, summary, related files, and rerun command. If the failure came from a functional transcript, rerun exactly that test with -v. If it came from a Go package, rerun one test or one package before rerunning a group target. ./le test bgp plugin 42 -v go test -race -run TestName ./internal/component/bgp/... If the rerun prints a temporary directory, keep it only when you need the artifacts. If the test is Linux-only, go straight to QEMU rather than trying to make Darwin behave like Linux. ZE_TEST_KEEP_TMP=1 ./le test bgp plugin 42 -v ./le test qemu run command 'le test bgp plugin 79 -v' keep-alive Trace output Functional runners emit per-step trace records. Human output shows the line and status. Machine output uses VERIFY STEP JSON so failure grouping can stay stable even when prose changes. 12 ✓ action open 13 ✗ expect element -> expected element with text "Routes" not found VERIFY STEP: {"file":"test/web/foo.wb","step":13,"kind":"expect","status":"fail"} Trace output is available for .ci, .wb, and .et. The first broken transition usually explains later assertion failures, so it is the useful place to begin. Debug logging Ze logging is controlled per subsystem through environment variables. Enable the log for the subsystem involved in the failure. Area Example BGP peer behavior ze.log.bgp.reactor.peer=debug ./le test bgp plugin NAME -v Plugin server behavior ze.log.plugin.server=debug ./le test bgp plugin NAME -v Config parsing ze.log.config=debug ./le test bgp parse NAME -v Linux diagnosis ./le test qemu run command '...' keep-alive, then inspect ip, nft, dmesg, and temp files. Do not turn on every log by default. Broad logs can hide the one line that matters and can change timing in concurrent tests. Skipped and intermittent tests A skipped test supplies no result. option=needs-linux marks functional behavior that requires Linux. .wb has an explicit skip option for external browser fixtures. Go tests should skip only when an optional capability is absent and another check covers the required behavior. Intermittent failures need their cause fixed. Replace timing guesses with readiness checks, process waits, observable browser state, or protocol synchronization. If increasing a delay makes the test pass, the runner needs to check when the operation has finished. Debugging order The failure index gives you a command for reproducing the problem. If its output is insufficient, enable logging for the affected subsystem. A kernel-dependent failure needs Linux, while a disagreement with another daemon needs the interoperability lab. After the fix, rerun the failing test and the other tests reached by the change; CI supplies the full verification.

title: Reference
text: Reference These pages describe Ze's commands, configuration, plugins, and standards support. Where possible, the reference is generated from the definitions in the code so that a change appears in the documentation on the next site build. CLI reference: every generated Ze command in one searchable catalog. Configuration reference: the complete YANG configuration tree. Command equivalents: Ze syntax beside Junos, IOS XR, SR OS, and VyOS. Plugin catalog: available plugins, their dependencies, configuration sections, and source files. RFC status: implemented RFCs, partial support, and remaining gaps. Feature status: what each feature implements and how thoroughly it has been tested. Dependencies: direct Go packages and why Ze uses them. Glossary: routing, policy, configuration, operator, and testing terms. Deprecated options: removed syntax and its replacement. For procedures, start with the guides. For system design, use architecture.

title: delete data key
text: delete data key Remove one runtime-state key from the daemon's store. Ze command Registry path: delete data key Usage: delete data key <key> Mode: Daemon Wire method: ze-config:data-key-delete Backends: any backend Task support: optional: the MCP call is synchronous, which is the default Subcommands: none: this command takes no subcommand Answer shape: not declared Address fields: none Column order: none Pipes, always: json, ndjson, table, text, yaml, raw, no-more, save Pipes, when the answer has rows: match, count, first, last, display, fill Pipes, while streaming: log Pipes, local process only: save Command pipes: none Pipe aliases: none Removes one runtime-state key (a key under meta/ outside meta/config/) through the store the daemon owns, so it works while ze runs. A configuration key (under file/ or meta/config/, or outside both) is refused before the store is touched, because a raw removal bypasses its versions, pointers and history. A key a plugin is granted is refused while that plugin runs, because the plugin manages the key while it runs; the refusal names the plugin and its restart. Until the daemon has started its plugins, such a key is refused, because the daemon cannot tell yet whether the plugin runs. A key the store does not hold is an error. text: request data backup Write a backup of the whole store to a file on the daemon's host. A commit that lands meanwhile is in the backup whole or not at all. The file holds credentials and private keys and is written 0600. title: request data repair

Ze command Registry path: request peer notify Usage: request peer <selector> notify <code> <subcode> [hex <hex>] [text <text>] Mode: Daemon Wire method: ze-bgp:peer-notify Backends: any backend Task support: optional: the MCP call is synchronous, which is the default Subcommands: none: this command takes no subcommand Answer shape: not declared Address fields: none Column order: none Pipes, always: json, ndjson, table, text, yaml, raw, no-more, save Pipes, when the answer has rows: match, count, first, last, display, fill Pipes, while streaming: log Pipes, local process only: save Command pipes: none Pipe aliases: none Ze closes the session with a NOTIFICATION carrying the error code and error subcode given, any value from 0 to 255. Under Cease (6), subcode 2 or 4, the words after the subcode are the RFC 9003 Shutdown Communication; under every other pair they are the Data field. Both are sent as UTF-8. With no words the Data field is empty. A text that does not fit is refused and the session stays up: more than 128 octets under Cease 2 or 4 (RFC 9003 Section 3), more than 4075 octets otherwise, or text that is not UTF-8. With the word hex after the subcode, the next word is the Data field itself in hexadecimal, sent octet for octet with no encoding, and refused over 4075 octets. teardown is the Cease-only form; notify is the form for testing another implementation, and the hex form is the one the ExaBGP bridge sends for teardown with a code. title: request plugin restart
text: request plugin restart Restart a plugin, stopping it first if it runs. Ze command Registry path: request plugin restart Usage: request plugin restart <name> Mode: Daemon Wire method: ze-plugin:system-plugin-restart Backends: any backend Task support: optional: the MCP call is synchronous, which is the default Subcommands: none: this command takes no subcommand Answer shape: not declared Address fields: none Column order: none Pipes, always: json, ndjson, table, text, yaml, raw, no-more, save Pipes, when the answer has rows: match, count, first, last, display, fill Pipes, while streaming: log Pipes, local process only: save Command pipes: none Pipe aliases: none Starts a configured plugin again. A stopped one starts: one its failure policy left stopped, one the respawn limit disabled (the order lifts the limit), one whose restart or startup handshake failed. A running one is stopped first, which cuts the commands it was serving, and started again with the running configuration; its failure policy is not applied. ze doctor names this command as the fix of doctor-plugin-stopped and of the rows a new process clears. A name no configuration or auto-load started is refused, and so is a restart a plugin asks for itself (its own request would never end), a restart while a config transaction is in flight, and a restart of a plugin whose removal by a reload is still pending. A restart whose old process has not finished its cleanup fails and leaves the plugin down until that cleanup ends.
