A service whose IPv6 sockets are IPv6-only (L2TP, web) accepts :: beside an IPv4 address on the same port. Listen TCP port; 0 means OS-assigned The port range is 0 to 65535. Port 0 makes the operating system pick a free port at bind time, so no client can know the port before the listener starts. ze doctor tries to bind each configured endpoint and reports the one the host refuses. Chaos fault injection settings Ze wraps the clock, the dialer and the listener factory with a fault injector while seed is not 0. The block exists to test Ze against slow timers and failed connections. A production config leaves the block out. Fault probability per operation (0.0-1.0) 0.1 injects a fault into one operation in ten. Ze uses 0.1 for a value that is not a number, and for a value outside 0.0 to 1.0. The leaf does nothing while seed is 0. PRNG seed (0 = disabled) Ze builds the fault injector onl

title: exabgp
text: exabgp bridge add-path enumeration family address-family process <name> encoder enumeration feed <peer> event string on-exit enumeration respawn boolean run string route-refresh boolean Top-level container for ExaBGP-compatibility configuration. The bridge itself lives in the bridge container under this root, which keeps the root free for other ExaBGP compatibility settings. The plugin is registered as exabgp-bridge, so plugin { internal exabgp-bridge } starts it. The bridge refuses to start until bridge run names a script. In-process ExaBGP bridge settings. Present this container to configure the internal exabgp-bridge plugin. ADD-PATH mode for the families the bridge negotiates. RFC 7911 defines ADD-PATH. none disables it. receive accepts more than one path from the peer. send advertises more than one path to the peer. both does each of the two. Address families the bridge negotiates for the script. One example is ipv4/unicast. If this leaf-list is empty, the bridge negotiates ipv4/unicast. One ExaBGP-format script the bridge runs as a subprocess. One block per script. An ExaBGP configuration declares the same set as 'process <name> { run ... }', and the migration writes one block here for each of them. Ze starts every block, sends every event to every script, and reads commands from every script. The bridge does nothing until one block names a run command. Format the script's events are written in. json writes one JSON object per event. text writes ExaBGP's one-event-per-line format, such as 'neighbor 127.0.0.1 receive update announced 10.0.0.0/24 next-hop 10.0.0.1 origin igp'. ExaBGP spells this leaf the same way and declares it per process, so one bridge can feed a text script and a JSON script at once. The default is text, as ExaBGP's. The leaf is read with the script's API version, as ExaBGP 6.0 reads it: a script that writes 'peer ...' reads 6.0.0 JSON whatever this says, a script that writes 'announce ...' or 'neighbor ...' reads 5.x text or 5.x JSON (envelope 4.0.1), and a script that has written neither yet reads 5.x text when this is text and 6.0.0 JSON when it is json. One peer that feeds this script, and the events it feeds. An ExaBGP neighbor names the processes it feeds in 'api { processes [ ... ] }' and the message kinds it feeds them in the same block, so the relation is per peer AND per script. The migration writes one block here for each neighbor that named this script. Ze also sends a command that names no neighbor to these peers alone. A process with NO feed block is fed by every peer with every event, which is what one script and one neighbor means. Events this peer feeds this script. ExaBGP's own event names: 'receive-update', 'send-update', 'receive-open', 'send-keepalive', 'receive-notification', 'send-refresh', 'receive-operational' and their siblings, plus 'neighbor-changes', 'negotiated', 'fsm' and 'signal', and the forms a direction's messages are written in: 'receive-packets', 'receive-consolidate', 'receive-parsed' and their 'send-' siblings, as ExaBGP's 'packets', 'consolidate' and 'parsed'. An EMPTY list feeds no event from this peer, which is what an ExaBGP api block that names a process and no message kind does. Keep or withdraw the script's routes when it exits. What becomes of the routes this script announced when it exits. keep leaves them; withdraw withdraws every route the script was the last to announce, before a restarted script writes its first line. Left unset, a script that writes the ExaBGP 4 API ('announce ...', 'neighbor ...') keeps its routes, as ExaBGP 4.x and 5.x did, and any other has them withdrawn, as ExaBGP 6.0 does. Each exit is logged with the choice and its reason. ExaBGP spells this leaf the same way. Start the script again when it exits. true starts the script again the moment it exits. false leaves it stopped, which is what a script that does its work once and exits needs. A script that exits more than five times in 64 seconds stays stopped whatever this leaf holds, and Ze logs that it did. ExaBGP spells this leaf the same way and applies the same limit. Command line of the script. Two examples are './plugin.py' and 'python3 /opt/plugin.py'. Ze splits the line into words as a POSIX shell does, with no expansion: blanks separate words, and single or double quotes group them, so a quoted argument holding a space reaches the script as one argument. The first word is the executable, and the rest are its arguments. A block with no run command, or with an unclosed quote, is refused. Advertise the BGP route-refresh capability. RFC 2918 defines the route-refresh capability. When this leaf is true, Ze advertises the capability on every session the bridge feeds.

title: fib
text: fib kernel flush-on-stop boolean sweep-delay uint16 p4 device-id uint64 flush-on-stop boolean target string vpp batch-interval-ms uint16 batch-size uint16 enabled boolean table-id uint32 Forwarding Information Base configuration. The FIB is where Ze writes the best routes the system RIB chose. Each container under it is one backend: kernel programs the OS with netlink, and vpp programs VPP with the GoVPP binary API. A backend runs only while its plugin is loaded. Admin distance is not here, because it belongs to the rib container. OS kernel route programming via netlink (Linux). Ze writes each best route from the system RIB into the OS with netlink, and it stamps rtm_protocol 250 on every route it writes. That number separates a ze route from a route another daemon owns, so `ip route show proto 250` lists them. The plugin also watches the kernel, and it writes its route again where something else overwrote one of them. Remove every ze-installed route when the plugin stops. When true, the plugin removes every route it installed as it stops. The default false keeps those routes in the kernel after shutdown, which supports graceful restart. Time to wait after startup before Ze sweeps stale routes. The delay lets BGP reconverge and refresh the matching routes before Ze removes the stale ones. The default is 30 seconds. P4 switch route programming via gRPC/P4Runtime. fib-p4 subscribes to the best-change event of the system RIB and holds every route it would program into a P4 switch with P4Runtime. The gRPC client is not written yet. The plugin writes a log line for each route it adds, replaces and deletes, and it programs no switch. The command `show fib p4` prints the prefix and the next hop of each entry the plugin holds. No leaf in this container reaches a switch today. P4Runtime device ID. P4Runtime addresses one forwarding pipeline on a target by its device id, and the switch assigns that number. The default 1 matches a target that carries one pipeline. The type is a 64-bit unsigned number. The plugin opens no P4Runtime session yet, so the value reaches no switch. Remove all forwarding entries when the plugin stops. When true, the plugin deletes every forwarding entry it installed as it stops. The default false leaves those entries in the switch after shutdown, which supports graceful restart. The plugin does not read this leaf yet: the stop path keeps the entries whatever you write, and the backend programs no switch. The kernel backend carries the same leaf at fib/kernel/flush-on-stop. P4Runtime gRPC target address (host:port). Example: 127.0.0.1:9559 The value names the P4Runtime gRPC server on the switch as host:port, and 9559 is the port P4Runtime listens on by convention. There is no default, so the leaf stays unset until you write it. The plugin opens no connection to this address yet, because the gRPC client is not written. VPP FIB programming via GoVPP binary API. Ze writes each best route from the system RIB into the VPP FIB with the GoVPP call IPRouteAddDel. The plugin needs a live VPP connector. With none it falls back to a backend that programs nothing and writes a warning. Ze asks the system RIB to replay the whole table each time VPP connects, so a VPP restart reprograms every route. Maximum time in milliseconds before dispatching a partial batch. The leaf declares how long a partial batch would wait before dispatch, in milliseconds, and the plugin implements no batching. A config that writes this leaf fails to parse, with an error naming batch-interval-ms as not yet implemented, so the default 10 never applies. The leaf batch-size is deferred for the same reason. Maximum number of routes per batch dispatch. The leaf declares how many routes one batch dispatch would carry, and the plugin implements no batching. A config that writes this leaf fails to parse, with an error naming batch-size as not yet implemented, so the default 256 never applies. The system RIB already delivers one batch per address family, and the VPP call IPRouteAddDel programs one route per call. The plugin programs each route as it arrives. Enable VPP FIB programming. Routes from system RIB are programmed directly into VPP's FIB. The plugin programs the VPP FIB for as long as it runs, and it does not read this leaf. The config parser accepts the name and stores no value. Programming starts when the plugin loads and stops when it unloads, so the default false disables nothing. Unload the fib-vpp plugin to stop programming the VPP FIB. VRF table ID for route programming. 0 is the default VRF. The value names the VPP VRF that Ze programs, and the default 0 is the default VRF. Ze gives it to the IP backend and to the MPLS and SRv6 backends at the moment it builds them. A new value reaches VPP when the plugin builds a backend again, which happens when VPP connects.

title: firewall
text: firewall backend string domain-group <name> domain-names string ttl-floor uint32 flush-on-shutdown boolean global-options all-ping enumeration broadcast-ping enumeration ipv6-receive-redirects enumeration ipv6-src-route enumeration log-martians enumeration receive-redirects enumeration send-redirects enumeration source-validation enumeration syn-cookies enumeration irr interface <name> source-as-set string table <name> chain <name> hook chain-hook policy chain-policy priority int32 term <name> from connection-mark mark-value connection-state connection-state destination-address ip-prefix destination-as-set string destination-asn asn destination-domain-group string destination-local empty destination-port port-spec dscp dscp-value icmp-type string icmpv6-type string input-interface string mark mark-value output-interface string protocol protocol-name source-address ip-prefix source-as-set string source-asn asn source-domain-group string source-port port-spec then accept connection-mark-set value mark-value counter name string dnat to nat-spec drop dscp-set dscp-value exclude flow-offload flowtable string goto leafref jump leafref limit-rate burst uint32 rate rate-spec log level uint32 prefix string mark-set value mark-value masquerade persistent empty port-range string random full empty notrack redirect to port reject code uint8 with reject-type return snat to nat-spec tcp-mss-clamp-to-pmtu empty tcp-mss-set uint16 type chain-type family table-family flowtable <name> device string hook chain-hook priority int32 set <name> element <value> timeout uint32 flags-constant flags-dynamic flags-interval flags-timeout type set-type Ze-managed nftables firewall tables. Ze-managed nftables firewall tables. Table names are bare in config, and the component adds the ze_ prefix. Firewall backend implementation, nft by default. Firewall backend implementation. The default is nft, which is nftables through libnftnl. A future backend can declare itself through firewall.RegisterBackend. The ze:backend YANG extension on feature nodes declares per-feature backend support, so the commit-time gate rejects a config that uses an unsupported primitive. Address group whose members are what its DNS names resolve to. Ze resolves each name in the group and puts the addresses into an nftables set a rule can match with source-domain-group or destination-domain-group. Each name is resolved again when its own answer expires, and the set is reprogrammed only when the addresses changed. A commit naming a group Ze has never resolved is refused: run 'update firewall domain-group <name>' first. A permit rule keyed on a DNS name trusts whoever controls that name. DNS names whose addresses are the members of this group. Ze asks for the A and the AAAA record of each name and puts every address it gets into the group. Each name and each family keeps its own schedule, so a name with a short TTL does not pull the others with it. Ze accepts at most 64 addresses from one name and one family, and logs a warning when it drops the rest. Shortest interval Ze waits before it resolves a name again. A name answering with a very short TTL would otherwise drive a query and a set rewrite every few seconds. Ze waits this long at least, whatever the answer says. A TTL of 0 means 'do not cache' and Ze also waits the floor for it, rather than treating it as already expired. Remove ze-owned nftables tables when the ze process stops in an orderly way. Remove ze-owned nftables tables from the kernel when the ze process stops in an orderly way (SIGTERM). The default is true, so a stopped daemon leaves no rules behind. Set the leaf to false to use ze as a one-shot provisioner: program the rules, let the process exit, and leave them running in the kernel, like nft -f. The leaf keys off how the process exits, and it is unrelated to BGP graceful restart. A crash never runs the shutdown path, so tables always persist across a crash whatever this leaf holds. The leaf governs every ze table producer (firewall, control-plane-protection, policy-routes, ddos-local), which share one backend. Network security defaults mapped to kernel sysctls. Network security defaults mapped to kernel sysctls. The container provides VyOS-compatible keyword toggles for common settings. At apply time each keyword translates to a sysctl key and value pair emitted to the sysctl plugin. An explicit sysctl setting always overrides these. Control ICMP echo (ping) responses. The keyword writes net.ipv4.icmp_echo_ignore_all. The sysctl is inverted, so enable writes 0 and disable writes 1. A router set to disable answers no ICMP echo request. A monitoring system that pings it sees no reply. Control broadcast ICMP echo responses. Control broadcast ICMP echo responses. The sysctl is inverted, so enable sets icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts to 0. Control acceptance of IPv6 ICMP redirect messages. The keyword writes net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects. The value enable writes 1, and disable writes 0. The leaf governs IPv6 alone. The IPv4 sysctl stays under receive-redirects. Control acceptance of IPv6 packets with source routing headers. The keyword writes net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_source_route. The value enable writes 1, and disable writes 0. A source-routed packet carries a routing header that names hops it MUST pass. An accepted one lets the sender pick the path through this router. Log packets with impossible source addresses. The keyword writes net.ipv4.conf.all.log_martians. The value enable writes 1, and disable writes 0. A martian packet carries a source address that no route can reach. The kernel writes one line for each such packet, and a flood of them fills the log. Control acceptance of IPv4 ICMP redirect messages. The keyword writes net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects. The value enable writes 1, and disable writes 0. An accepted ICMP redirect installs a host route in the kernel. A neighbor on the same segment can then change where this router sends the traffic. Control sending of IPv4 ICMP redirect messages. The keyword writes net.ipv4.conf.all.send_redirects. The value enable writes 1, and disable writes 0. A router sends an ICMP redirect when it forwards a packet back out the interface the packet arrived on. Reverse path filtering mode for source address validation. The keyword writes net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter. The value disable writes 0, strict writes 1, and loose writes 2. Strict drops a packet when the best route back to its source does not use the interface it arrived on. Loose drops it only when no route back to the source exists. TCP SYN cookie protection against SYN flood attacks. The keyword writes net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies. The value enable writes 1, and disable writes 0. A kernel with cookies on answers a SYN that overflows the accept queue. It keeps no state for that half-open connection until the third packet returns the cookie. Per-interface IRR source validation. The irr plugin fetches, schedules and stores every IRR list the firewall enforces, from the server and at the interval system irr names; the BGP IRR filter enforces the same stored copy, so one query serves both. A commit that names a reference with nothing stored is refused with the update irr command that fetches it. Per-interface AS-SET binding for ingress source validation. Ze drops a packet that arrives on this interface when its source address is not in the IRR-resolved prefixes of the AS-SET. AS-SET whose IRR-resolved prefixes are the allowed source addresses. The prefixes the IRR resolves for this AS-SET form the allowed source-address set of the interface. The match needs a stored prefix list. A config commit is refused when nothing is stored. Named firewall table The kernel table is ze_<name>. Ze changes and deletes only a table that carries the ze_ prefix, so a table another tool wrote stays untouched. The chains, the named sets and the flowtables of one table reference each other by name, and no reference crosses a table. Named chain within table A chain that carries a type or a hook is a base chain, and the kernel attaches it to that hook. A chain with neither is a regular chain, and only a jump or a goto from another chain of the same table reaches it. Netfilter hook point (base chains only) A base chain MUST carry a hook, and verify refuses one that does not. The hook decides where in the kernel path the chain sees the packet. The values input, output, forward, prerouting and postrouting serve every family. The value ingress serves a netdev or inet table, and egress serves a netdev table. Default policy (base chains only) The policy decides a packet that reaches the end of the chain with no verdict from a term. A base chain MUST carry accept or drop, and verify refuses a base chain that carries neither. A regular chain takes no policy, and the packet returns to the chain that jumped to it. Chain priority (base chains only) The chain with the lower number runs first at the same hook. Verify accepts -400 to 400 and refuses a number outside that range, which catches a typo such as 500 for 50. The well-known nftables values all fit: raw -300, mangle -150, filter 0, security 50, nat prerouting -100 and nat postrouting 100. An absent leaf means 0. Named rule (from/then structure) The list is ordered-by user, and the backend writes one kernel rule for each term in that order. A term MUST carry at least one action, and verify refuses one that carries none. Match criteria Every match in this container MUST hold at the same time for the term to act, because they lower into one kernel rule. A from block that declares no match matches every packet the chain sees. Connection mark value with an optional mask. The mark lives on the conntrack entry, so every packet of one flow reads the same value in both directions. The mark leaf beside it reads the per-packet mark instead, which starts at 0 for each packet. The match is conntrack-driven, and it needs a backend that integrates with the kernel nf_conntrack module. Connection tracking state(s) the rule matches. Connection tracking state(s). The match is conntrack-driven, and it requires a backend that integrates with the kernel nf_conntrack module. Destination IP prefix or @set-name The value takes the same two forms the source-address leaf takes. A network prefix must use its network address; a value with host bits set is refused with the corrected destination-address statement. Host routes use /32 or /128. Ze reads the IPv4 destination at network-header offset 16 and the IPv6 destination at offset 24. An inet table therefore carries an nfproto guard in front of the match, so an IPv4 rule never reads IPv6 bytes. Match the destination address against the IRR-resolved prefixes of this AS-SET. The stored-list rule is the one source-as-set states. The match needs a prefix list the irr plugin stored, so run 'update irr as-set <name>' first. A config commit is refused when nothing is stored. Match the destination address against the IRR-resolved prefixes of this ASN. The stored-list rule is the one source-asn states. The match needs a prefix list the irr plugin stored, so run 'update irr asn <N>' first. A config commit is refused when nothing is stored. Match the destination address against the addresses of this domain group. The cache rule is the one source-domain-group states. The match needs the group's names to have resolved at least once, so a commit is refused when they have not: run 'update firewall domain-group <name>' first. Match a destination address this router holds The term matches a packet whose destination address is one this router holds on any of its interfaces, as the kernel's local routing table answers when the packet is seen, so an address added after the commit matches too. A packet routed through the router to another host does not match. A destination translation that carries this match captures only traffic addressed to the router, never transit traffic to the same port. Ze reads the leaf as a presence flag, so it takes no val

title: flow-export
text: flow-export collector <name> address ip-address agent-address ip-address max-datagram-size uint16 observation-domain uint32 polling-interval uint16 port uint16 protocol enumeration source-address ip-address sub-agent-id uint32 template-refresh uint32 conntrack active-timeout uint16 enabled boolean recent-flow-ring uint32 enrichment bgp boolean sampling interface <name> group uint32 rate uint32 trunc-size uint16 Flow export (sFlow, NetFlow v9, IPFIX) configuration Flow export configuration. Ze exports interface counters to every collector. It exports per-flow records as well when the conntrack container or the sampling container is enabled. Each collector names its own protocol, so one device can feed an sFlow collector and an IPFIX collector at the same time. A flow export collector endpoint A flow export collector endpoint. Ze opens one UDP sender for each entry and encodes for the protocol that entry names. address and protocol are both mandatory, so a commit that leaves either one out is rejected. max-datagram-size bounds each UDP payload, including padding. Collector IP address Collector IP address, and the leaf is mandatory. The address and port together are where Ze sends every datagram of this collector. A commit that gives a value Ze cannot parse as an address is rejected. sFlow agent address (device's own stable IP, e.g. loopback) sFlow agent address, which is the device's own stable IP address. Ze writes it into the sFlow v5 datagram header, so a collector identifies the exporter by one address whichever interface the datagram left. It is mandatory on an sflow collector, 0.0.0.0 and :: are refused, and all sflow collectors must name the same address, because Ze is one sFlow agent. Two spellings of one address, such as 2001:db8::1 and 2001:DB8:0::1, are the same address. A netflow9 or ipfix collector does not read the leaf. Largest UDP payload sent to this collector, in octets Largest UDP payload Ze sends to this collector, in octets. Encoders include padding within this bound. RFC 7011 Section 10.3.3 recommends packets of at most 512 octets when the path MTU is unknown. The default 464 reserves 48 octets for IPv6 and UDP headers. Set a larger value only for a known path MTU, after subtracting all IP, UDP and tunnel headers. The ceiling 1400 is the encoding buffer size. IPFIX/NetFlow v9 observation domain ID IPFIX and NetFlow v9 observation domain ID, default 0. Ze writes it into the message header of every counter message and every flow message of those two protocols. A collector uses it to keep the record streams of one exporter apart. An sflow collector does not read the leaf. Counter polling interval in seconds Counter polling interval in seconds, 1 to 3600, default 20. The interval is a maximum: Ze sends the interface counters to this collector at least once in each interval. Counter snapshots arrive once a second, so Ze polls from one second before the interval ends. The counter snapshot is shared between collectors, so a short interval on one collector does not make another one faster. Collector UDP port Collector UDP port. The default 6343 is the port sFlow collectors listen on, so a NetFlow v9 or an IPFIX collector usually needs its own port written here. The port is per collector, so two entries can send to one address on two ports. Export protocol Export protocol, and the leaf is mandatory. The value selects the encoder Ze builds for this collector. It also decides which of the other leaves are read. sub-agent-id and agent-address are read by sflow alone, and observation-domain by netflow9 and ipfix alone. Source IP address for outbound flow export datagrams Source IP address for outbound flow export datagrams. Ze binds the UDP socket of this collector to the address. Left out, the kernel selects a source from its route to the collector. The value does not reach the sFlow datagram header, which carries agent-address instead. sFlow sub-agent identifier sFlow sub-agent identifier, default 0. Ze writes it into the sFlow v5 datagram header. It separates several sFlow agents that share one agent-address, so a collector can keep their sequence numbers apart. Every sflow collector exports every interface, and sFlow v5 binds each data source to one sub-agent, so all sflow collectors must name the same value: the config is refused otherwise. A netflow9 or ipfix collector does not read the leaf. Template refresh interval in seconds (NetFlow v9, IPFIX) Template refresh interval in seconds, 1 to 86400, default 600. NetFlow v9 and IPFIX resend the record template on this interval, so a collector that restarts can decode the records again. The counter template and the flow template each keep their own timer. The sFlow encoder has no template and does nothing with the value. Per-flow record export from conntrack (NetFlow v9, IPFIX) Per-flow record export from conntrack. Ze dumps the kernel conntrack table on a timer and turns each live entry into a flow record for the NetFlow v9 and IPFIX collectors. The same records fill the recent-flow ring that 'show flow recent' and the DDoS characterization read. Seconds between conntrack table dumps Seconds between conntrack table dumps, 1 to 3600, default 60. Each dump turns the live conntrack entries into flow records. Ze also drops its own tracking state for a flow it has not seen for twice this time. A short timeout therefore shortens that memory too. Export per-flow records from the conntrack table Export per-flow records from the conntrack table. Left false, Ze starts no conntrack worker and allocates no recent-flow ring. 'show flow recent' then has nothing to read, and the DDoS characterization loses its flow input and falls back to its coarse target. Capacity of the recent-flow ring, in flow records. `show flow recent` reads the ring, and the ring feeds the on-box DDoS characterization. A larger value keeps more history and uses more memory. Ze allocates the ring only when conntrack export is enabled. Flow record enrichment from the BGP RIB Flow record enrichment from the BGP RIB. Ze keeps a prefix-to-AS radix tree that BGP best-path changes feed. A flow record reads its next hop and its AS numbers from that tree. The tree is swapped whole, so a record never reads a half-built tree. Enrich flow records with BGP next-hop (and AS where available) Enrich flow records with the BGP next hop, and with the AS numbers where the RIB carries them. Ze subscribes to the RIB best-path changes and rebuilds the lookup tree at most once per rebuild interval. A full-table replay event carries no AS_PATH, so those entries hold no AS until the next incremental change corrects them. Packet sampling (tc sample + psample) exported as sFlow flow samples Packet sampling exported as sFlow flow samples. Ze installs a tc sample action on each listed interface and reads the sampled headers from the kernel psample netlink family. The path is Linux only. A setup failure is logged and leaves that interface unsampled, and the rest of the exporter keeps running. Per-interface packet sampling configuration Per-interface packet sampling configuration. Ze installs the tc action for each entry on its own, so a failure on one entry does not stop another. Ze maps each sample the kernel delivers back to its entry by kernel interface index. psample group ID psample group ID, default 1. Ze writes it into the tc sample action, which tags each sample the kernel emits. Ze does not read it back. The reader joins the psample packets multicast group and maps each sample to its interface by index. This value therefore does not select which samples Ze reads. Sampling rate (1-in-N packets) Sampling rate, as one packet in N. The leaf has no default, so an entry that leaves it out fails the commit with 'rate 0 out of range 1-1000000'. Ze passes the value to the tc sample action, and the kernel does the sampling. Bytes of each sampled packet header to capture Bytes of each sampled packet header to capture, 64 to 1500, default 128. The tc sample action truncates the frame to this length before the kernel passes it up. A larger value carries more of the packet into the sFlow flow sample, and it costs more bandwidth toward the collector.

text: isis filter export filters string final enumeration import filters string final enumeration hostname string interfaces interface <name> address-family <af> circuit-type enumeration enabled boolean hello-interval uint16 hold-multiplier uint8 level enumeration level-1 auth-key-chain leafref hello-interval uint16 hold-multiplier uint8 metric uint32 priority uint8 level-2 auth-key-chain leafref hello-interval uint16 hold-multiplier uint8 metric uint32 priority uint8 metric uint32 passive boolean priority uint8 key-chains <name> key <key-id> accept-lifetime end string start string algorithm enumeration secret string send-lifetime end string start string level enumeration level-1 auth-key-chain leafref level-2 auth-key-chain leafref lsp-lifetime uint16 lsp-refresh-interval uint16 metric-style enumeration net string overload boolean system-id string IS-IS routing instance configuration. The presence of this container starts the IS-IS component. At least one `net` leaf MUST be set for the engine to run. A commit with no net is accepted, and the engine then stays idle, opens no circuit and originates no LSP. Route filter chains into the Loc-RIB and out of redistribution. A name references a filter instance defined under the top-level policy root. The import chain judges routes as they enter the Loc-RIB, and the export chain judges redistributed routes before the IGP advertises them; the IGP's own database (an IS-IS LSDB, an OSPF LSDB) is never filtered. Export policy over redistributed routes Runs on every route the redistribute import rules hand this protocol, before it enters the IGP database. A rejected route is not advertised; the sets of an accepting chain (the metric, and on ospf the metric type and tag) shape what is. Ordered filter instance references Run these filter instances in order. Each one passes the route on or rejects it; a filter type with no route evaluator is refused. Decision after every filter passes Every present export policy must set final accept or final reject, even with no filters. A filter's accept only passes the route on, so final decides. Import policy into the Loc-RIB A rejected route stays in the Loc-RIB as a hidden path that is never selected, so relaxing the chain re-admits it without the protocol sending it again. The source's chain runs first, then the rib chain. Ordered filter instance references Run these filter instances in order. Each one passes the route on or rejects it; a filter type with no Loc-RIB route evaluator is refused. Decision after every filter passes Every present import policy must set final accept or final reject, even with no filters. Dynamic hostname this IS-IS instance advertises (RFC 5301 section 3). Dynamic hostname to advertise (RFC 5301 section 3). Printable 7-bit ASCII only, from space (0x20) to tilde (0x7e). Each dot-separated label is 1 to 63 octets and the whole name is at most 255 octets, including the separators (RFC 2181 section 11). One trailing dot is permitted. A non-ASCII name is refused, not converted. IS-IS-enabled interfaces. Only an interface with an entry here runs IS-IS. Ze opens no circuit on an interface that this list omits, so no adjacency forms on it and its connected prefixes reach no LSP. Per-interface IS-IS configuration. Ze opens one circuit for each entry that is enabled and not passive. A link that comes up after start opens its circuit at that moment, and a link that goes down closes it. The connected prefixes of an enabled entry become TLV 135 and TLV 236 reachability in the node's own LSP. Enable address families on this interface. An ipv6-unicast entry enables the interface's IPv6 addresses and prefixes. On any enabled interface it also adds IPv6 to the node-wide Protocols Supported set in every Hello and LSP. IPv4 is always supported. Both families use one SPF tree. Circuit type. broadcast, the default, runs the DIS election and sources a pseudo-node LSP when this IS wins. It advertises the LAN as one TLV 22 entry that points at the pseudo-node. It also sources a periodic CSNP while this IS is DIS. point-to-point runs no election and no pseudo-node. It sends a point-to-point hello with TLV 240 and one initial CSNP when the adjacency reaches Up. IS-IS enabled on this interface. The default is true, so an entry runs IS-IS without this leaf. A false value keeps the entry in the configuration and opens no circuit. It also stops the connected prefixes of the interface from reaching the node's own LSP, which a passive interface still advertises. Hello interval. Ze sends an IIH on this circuit at this period. The IIH carries a holding time of this value multiplied by `hold-multiplier`, clamped into 1 to 65535 seconds. A neighbor drops the adjacency when no IIH arrives inside the holding time it was told. A shorter interval detects a dead neighbor faster and costs more packets on the link. `level-1/hello-interval` and `level-2/hello-interval` replace it at one level. Hold time = hello-interval * hold-multiplier. Ze advertises `hello-interval` multiplied by this value as the holding time in each IIH, clamped into 1 to 65535 seconds. The default of 3 lets two hellos be lost before a neighbor drops the adjacency. The clamp means that no configuration can advertise a holding time of 0, which would time the adjacency out at once. `level-1/hold-multiplier` and `level-2/hold-multiplier` replace it at one level. Per-interface level override. This narrows the instance `level` for one circuit. l1 forms only a Level-1 adjacency on the circuit, l2 only a Level-2 adjacency, and l1-l2 forms both. The circuit floods LSPs and advertises its reachability only at the levels it forms. A level the instance `level` does not hold stays off whatever this leaf says. Level-1 per-interface overrides. The leaves here replace the circuit-wide value for Level-1 only. One circuit can then carry a different cost, a different DIS preference, a different Hello period or a different holding time at each level. A leaf that is not set keeps the circuit-wide value. A circuit that does not form Level-1 ignores the whole container. L1 per-interface (IIH) key-chain reference. The value names a `key-chains` entry. Ze then signs and verifies the Level-1 IIH on this circuit with that chain. RFC 5304 section 2 states that 'IS-IS Hello PDUs SHALL use the Link Level Authentication String'. This leaf covers the hello only. The LSP, CSNP and PSNP take the chain that `isis/level-1/auth-key-chain` names. L1 hello-interval override. Ze sends the Level-1 IIH at this period, in place of the circuit-wide `hello-interval`. A broadcast circuit runs one Hello timer for each level it forms, because the Level-1 and the Level-2 LAN IIH are separate PDUs sent to separate multicast groups. A point-to-point circuit sends one IIH that serves both levels, so it runs one Hello timer, and that timer takes this pair whenever the circuit forms Level-1. An unset leaf keeps the circuit-wide value. L1 hold-multiplier override. Ze multiplies the Level-1 hello interval by this value and advertises the product as the holding time in each Level-1 IIH, clamped into 1 to 65535 seconds. It replaces the circuit-wide `hold-multiplier` for Level-1. An unset leaf keeps the circuit-wide value. L1 metric override. Ze advertises this cost for the circuit in the Level-1 LSP, in place of `metric`. An unset leaf keeps the circuit-wide metric. The value also becomes the metric of the connected prefixes the circuit contributes at Level-1. Under the narrow and transition `metric-style` a value above 63 is refused. L1 DIS priority override. Ze uses this priority in the Level-1 DIS election, in place of `priority`. An unset leaf keeps the circuit-wide priority, and so does the value 0: Ze reads an override only when it is more than 0. To ask for the lowest preference, set the circuit-wide `priority` to 0. Level-2 per-interface overrides. The leaves here replace the circuit-wide value for Level-2 only. One circuit can then carry a different cost, a different DIS preference, a different Hello period or a different holding time at each level. A leaf that is not set keeps the circuit-wide value. A circuit that does not form Level-2 ignores the whole container. L2 per-interface (IIH) key-chain reference. The value names a `key-chains` entry. Ze then signs and verifies the Level-2 IIH on this circuit with that chain. RFC 5304 section 2 states that 'IS-IS Hello PDUs SHALL use the Link Level Authentication String'. This leaf covers the hello only. The LSP, CSNP and PSNP take the chain that `isis/level-2/auth-key-chain` names. L2 hello-interval override. Ze sends the Level-2 IIH at this period, in place of the circuit-wide `hello-interval`. A broadcast circuit runs one Hello timer for each level it forms, because the Level-1 and the Level-2 LAN IIH are separate PDUs sent to separate multicast groups. A point-to-point circuit sends one IIH that serves both levels, so it runs one Hello timer, and that timer takes this pair only on a circuit that forms Level-2 alone. An unset leaf keeps the circuit-wide value. L2 hold-multiplier override. Ze multiplies the Level-2 hello interval by this value and advertises the product as the holding time in each Level-2 IIH, clamped into 1 to 65535 seconds. It replaces the circuit-wide `hold-multiplier` for Level-2. An unset leaf keeps the circuit-wide value. L2 metric override. Ze advertises this cost for the circuit in the Level-2 LSP, in place of `metric`. An unset leaf keeps the circuit-wide metric. The value also becomes the metric of the connected prefixes the circuit contributes at Level-2. Under the narrow and transition `metric-style` a value above 63 is refused. L2 DIS priority override. Ze uses this priority in the Level-2 DIS election, in place of `priority`. An unset leaf keeps the circuit-wide priority, and so does the value 0: Ze reads an override only when it is more than 0. To ask for the lowest preference, set the circuit-wide `priority` to 0. Circuit metric (RFC 5305 wide, 1 to 63 when narrow). The circuit advertises this cost in TLV 22, and its connected prefixes advertise it in TLV 135 and TLV 236. RFC 5305 section 3 states that 'The metric octets are encoded as a 24-bit unsigned integer', which is the 1 to 16777215 range here. Under the narrow and transition `metric-style` the cost also goes into TLV 2 and TLV 128, whose metric is 6 bits, so a value above 63 is refused there. SPF adds the value once for each hop, so a lower value makes the circuit preferred. `level-1/metric` and `level-2/metric` replace it at one level. Advertise the interface but form no adjacencies. Ze opens no circuit for a passive interface, so it sends no hello and forms no adjacency. The connected prefixes of the interface still become TLV 135 and TLV 236 entries in the node's own LSP, at the metric `metric` sets. Use it on a loopback and on a customer LAN, where the prefix MUST be reachable and no IS-IS neighbor exists. DIS election priority (broadcast circuits). The value rides in each LAN hello and decides the DIS election on a broadcast circuit. The highest priority wins, and the highest SNPA MAC address breaks a tie. A priority of 0 is valid and only lowers the preference, so it does not stop this IS from winning an election it is alone in. The leaf changes nothing on a point-to-point circuit. Named authentication key chains for hitless key rotation. A chain holds the keys that sign and verify IS-IS PDUs. Ze authenticates nothing until an `auth-key-chain` leaf names the chain. Commit refuses an `auth-key-chain` leaf that names no entry of this list, naming the chains that exist, because a circuit whose chain does not resolve sends and accepts every PDU unsigned. A key whose algorithm token Ze does not know, or whose secret does not decode, is dropped from the chain and signs nothing. Keys in this chain. title: kernel
text: kernel Kernel route redistribution. Presence enables the plugin. The container carries no leaf, so writing it is the whole configuration. The plugin watches the kernel routing table and emits each route on the redistribute event bus. A route whose netlink protocol is RTPROT_KERNEL or RTPROT_REDIRECT is dropped, so a connected subnet route and an ICMP redirect route never reach BGP. The plugin registers the kernel route source, and a redistribute statement names that source.

L2TPv2 tunnel subsystem settings (RFC 2661). Presence of this block with any content implies the subsystem is enabled. Use 'enabled false' to disable it explicitly, or 'enabled true' as a filler when no other settings are needed. Allow PPP LCP to finish with no Auth-Protocol, false by default. Allow PPP LCP authentication negotiation to proceed without an Auth-Protocol. The default is false, so a peer that rejects all configured authentication methods is disconnected, instead of being accepted as no-auth. PPP authentication for L2TP subscriber sessions. The container holds the backend that answers a credential. The l2tp-auth-local plugin fills the local container under it, and the l2tp-auth-radius plugin fills the radius container. The timing of the PPP authentication phase sits under l2tp authentication instead. Authenticate a subscriber against users declared in this config. Ze rejects every session while no user is declared here, and it logs that no user is configured. A session is matched against the list by its PPP username, and an unknown username is rejected. Local authentication answers PAP and CHAP-MD5, and it rejects MS-CHAPv2. One subscriber account, keyed by its PPP username. Ze looks the PPP username up in this list and rejects a username no entry carries. An empty list rejects every session. The match is exact, so user and user@example.net are two accounts. Shared secret for PAP cleartext and CHAP-MD5/MS-CHAPv2 challenge-response. PAP compares the SHA-256 of the received password with the SHA-256 of this value, in constant time. CHAP-MD5 computes MD5 over the identifier, this value and the challenge, which RFC 1994 Section 4.1 defines. CHAP needs the secret in clear, so this leaf holds no hash. Authenticate and account subscriber sessions against a RADIUS server. Authentication and accounting are separate exchanges to the same server. A session is authorized by an Access-Accept, and the Accounting-Request packets that follow report its traffic. Accounting interim-update interval in seconds. RFC 2869 Section 2.1 states that a locally configured value on the NAS MUST override the value found in an Access-Accept. A leaf that is set pins the cadence of every session, and the Acct-Interim-Interval attribute (type 85) of an Access-Accept then changes nothing. This leaf has no default. An unset leaf is the absent case, and it lets each Access-Accept set the cadence of that session. A session runs at 300 seconds when neither side states an interval. Which optional RADIUS attributes Ze puts in the packets it sends. Ze sends every attribute it can build, which is what a billing system usually wants, so this container is empty in most deployments. It names the attributes one deployment does not want on the wire. Nothing here reaches Acct-Status-Type, Acct-Session-Id or the NAS identity: RFC 2866 Section 5.13 counts the first two as 'Exactly one instance of this attribute MUST be present', and its Note 1 requires either NAS-IP-Address or NAS-Identifier, so an Accounting-Request without them is not a conformant record and Ze offers no way to write one. Attributes Ze does not send, each with the record types it is held back from. Name an attribute to hold it back from every record type that would carry it. Add packet-type under it to hold it back from some record types and keep it in the others. Each attribute accepts only the record types Ze can put it in, so a line naming a record type that never carries the attribute is refused when the configuration is committed rather than ignored at run time. Do not send Acct-Delay-Time (attribute 41). RFC 2866 Section 5.2 reports how many seconds the client has been trying to send this record, and Ze rewrites the value on each retransmission. A record that carries no Acct-Delay-Time is replayed byte for byte instead, under the same Identifier, which is what an Access-Request does. accel-ppp ships this attribute off by default. Record types to hold the attribute back from. Name none for all of them. Ze puts Acct-Delay-Time in the three accounting records and in no other packet, so those three are what this leaf accepts. An empty leaf holds the attribute back from all three. Do not send Acct-Terminate-Cause (attribute 49). RFC 2866 Section 5.10 states that the attribute 'can only be present in Accounting-Request records where the Acct-Status-Type is set to Stop', so the Stop record is the only one this reaches. A pipeline that keys on its own teardown signal does not need it. FreeRADIUS defaults it to NAS-Reboot in its accounting queries. Record types to hold the attribute back from. Name none for all of them. RFC 2866 Section 5.10 admits Acct-Terminate-Cause in a Stop record alone, so accounting-stop is the one value this leaf accepts. An empty leaf holds the attribute back from the Stop record, which is the same thing said with fewer words. Do not send Calling-Station-Id (attribute 31). RFC 2865 Section 5.31 carries the number the call came from, which is the L2TP Calling Number of the session, or the subscriber MAC address on the PPPoE relay path. Some operators do not store it. Check the server first: FreeRADIUS matches its IP pool queries on this attribute with no fallback value, so a pool it serves keeps leases that never expire once the attribute stops arriving. Record types to hold the attribute back from. Name none for all of them. Ze puts Calling-Station-Id in the three accounting records and in no other packet, so those three are what this leaf accepts. An empty leaf holds the attribute back from all three. Do not send Event-Timestamp (attribute 55). RFC 2869 Section 5.3 records the second at which the event happened on the NAS. A server that stamps its own receive time does not need it. FreeRADIUS falls back to the server clock in its default accounting queries, so a record without the attribute is still stored with a time. Record types to hold the attribute back from. Name none for all of them. Ze puts Event-Timestamp in the three accounting records and in no other packet, so those three are what this leaf accepts. An empty leaf holds the attribute back from all three. Do not send Framed-IP-Address (attribute 8). RFC 2865 Section 5.8 reports the IPv4 address the session negotiated, and RFC 2866 Section 4.1 requires that a record which carries the attribute carries the real address. An operator whose addressing is reported by another system can hold it back. A session with no IPv4 address sends no attribute either way, which is a different case and is not configurable. Record types to hold the attribute back from. Name none for all of them. Ze puts Framed-IP-Address in the three accounting records and in no other packet, so those three are what this leaf accepts. An empty leaf holds the attribute back from all three. Do not send NAS-Port-Id (attribute 87). RFC 2869 Section 5.17 names the access port in text, and the nas-port-id-format leaf is the template Ze resolves for it. Clearing that leaf also sends no attribute, on every packet at once. This container is the finer instrument: it holds the attribute back from the record types you name while the template stays configured for the rest. Record types to hold the attribute back from. Name none for all of them. Ze puts NAS-Port-Id in the Access-Request and in the three accounting records, so all four are what this leaf accepts. An empty leaf holds the attribute back from all four. UDP port of the RADIUS CoA and Disconnect listener, usually 3799. The listener implements RFC 5176. This leaf has no default on purpose. An unset leaf keeps the listener off, so an existing deployment does not start to accept CoA on upgrade. Ze accepts a request only from a configured RADIUS server address. Discard a CoA-Request or a Disconnect-Request that carries no Message-Authenticator. RFC 5176 Section 3.4 makes the Message-Authenticator attribute optional, so the default is false. Ze then processes a request without the attribute once its Request Authenticator verifies against the shared secret. Set this leaf to true when every Dynamic Authorization Client sends the attribute. The attribute is an HMAC-MD5 keyed with the shared secret, and it is the mitigation for the Blast-RADIUS class of attack (CVE-2024-3596), which forges a RADIUS UDP packet with a chosen-prefix MD5 collision against the authenticator. A client that sends no attribute gets no answer while this leaf is true. NAS-Identifier sent in RADIUS requests. Ze sends this text as the NAS-Identifier attribute in each Access-Request and each Accounting-Request. RFC 2865 Section 4.1 requires either NAS-IP-Address or NAS-Identifier in an Access-Request. With this leaf empty and source-address empty, Ze sends the hostname, and the plugin name where the host carries none. Template for the NAS-Port-Id attribute sent in RADIUS requests. Ze sends the NAS-Port-Id attribute (RFC 2869 Section 5.17) in an Access-Request packet and in an Accounting-Request packet. The placeholders are {nas-id}, {tunnel-id} and {session-id}. Ze copies every other character. All three values are known before the session has an interface. One session therefore sends one text in its Access-Request and in all its accounting records. A billing system can join them on it. The 253-octet limit is the largest value a RADIUS attribute can carry (RFC 2865 Section 5). The commit refuses an unknown placeholder, it refuses a {nas-id} when nas-identifier is unset, and it refuses a template whose widest resolution passes 253 octets because the nas-identifier it expands is long. An unset leaf sends no attribute. Number of retransmit attempts per server. The default is 3 and the range is 1 to 10. Ze sends the request that many times to one server, then moves to the next entry of the list. An Access-Request is replayed byte for byte. An Accounting-Request gets a new identifier and a new Acct-Delay-Time on each attempt, which RFC 2866 Section 4.1 requires. One RADIUS server Ze sends requests to, tried in the order written. title: ldp
text: ldp hello-hold-time uint16 hello-interval uint16 hop-count-max uint8 interfaces string keepalive-time uint16 lsr-id string transport-address string Label Distribution Protocol configuration The engine stays idle until lsr-id carries an address, and it says so in the log. Ze then sends Hello messages to 224.0.0.2 port 646 and opens a TCP session on port 646 to each neighbor it discovers. Hello adjacency hold time The default is 15 seconds, which is 3 hello intervals. Ze advertises this value in each Hello, and a neighbor drops the adjacency when no Hello arrives inside it. Keep it more than hello-interval, because a hold time under one interval drops the adjacency between two Hellos. Hello message interval The default is 5 seconds and the range is 1 to 65535. Ze sends one Hello for each interface at this period. A shorter interval finds a neighbor faster and puts more packets on the link. Maximum hop count a Label Mapping can carry. The default is 254 and the range is 1 to 255. RFC 5036 section 3.4.4.1 makes an LSR check the Hop Count TLV of a received message against 'its configured maximum allowable value'. A Label Mapping whose hop count exceeds this value is answered with a Loop Detected Notification and its label is not used. A change here applies to the sessions that open after it. Interfaces on which LDP discovery is enabled Ze runs one discovery listener for each interface of this list. An empty list runs one listener that the system assigns to an interface itself. A reload starts discovery on an interface added to the list and stops it on one removed, and it leaves the other interfaces alone. The connected prefixes of these interfaces are the FECs this LSR is egress for. Session keepalive interval. The default is 60 seconds and the range is 1 to 65535. RFC 5036 section 3.5.3 carries the KeepAlive Time in the Common Session Parameters of the Initialization message. The receiving LSR MUST calculate the KeepAlive Timer from 'the smaller of its proposed KeepAlive Time and the KeepAlive Time received in the PDU'. The lower of the two proposals wins. Ze proposes this value to each neighbor it opens a session to. Ze sends a KeepAlive every third of the negotiated value and closes the session when no PDU arrives inside three times it. The exchange happens one time, at the start of the session, so a session that is up keeps the value it negotiated. A change here applies to the sessions that open after it. LSR identifier (IPv4 address format) Ze refuses a value that is not an IP address, and stays idle while the leaf is empty. The first 4 bytes of every LDP PDU header carry this identifier. Ze also originates a label binding for the address itself, so a neighbor can reach this LSR by its identifier. Transport address for TCP sessions Ze advertises this address in the transport address TLV of each Hello, which is the address a neighbor connects to. Ze also binds it as the source address of the TCP connection it opens. With the leaf empty, the Hello carries no transport address TLV and the kernel picks the source address.

The container holds the extended-timestamp switch, the peer filter, the direction, and the three dump streams. No leaf chooses the ADD-PATH subtypes of RFC 8050: each record follows the ADD-PATH state negotiated for the family it holds. All BGP messages and state changes, written as BGP4MP records. The stream carries every BGP message: OPEN, UPDATE, NOTIFICATION, KEEPALIVE and ROUTE_REFRESH. It carries the FSM state transitions too. Ze writes them as BGP4MP records. Output file path, with strftime patterns for rotation. The strftime codes in the path decide when Ze opens a new file. The supported codes are %Y (year), %m (month), %d (day), %H (hour), %M (minute), %S (second), %s (unix timestamp) and %N (table name). File rotation interval in seconds. Zero disables rotation. The value 0 keeps one file open until the daemon stops. A value of more than 0 makes Ze close the file once it has been open that many seconds. Ze then opens the next one, and the strftime codes in file give the new name. A file of - writes to standard output, which never rotates. Which direction of BGP messages to record. The default is both, and both records each direction. received keeps the messages the peer sent to Ze, and sent keeps the messages Ze sent to the peer. The filter reaches the BGP messages alone, so a state change record is written whatever the value. Use BGP4MP_ET (type 17) with microsecond resolution instead of BGP4MP (type 16). The default is false, so each record header carries type 16, BGP4MP. RFC 6396 Section 5.3 names type 17 as BGP4MP_ET, and that header carries 4 more bytes for the microsecond field. The switch reaches all three streams at once. If set, only record messages from/to these peer addresses. Empty list means record all peers. Ze compares each entry with the peer address of the message, so a message of another peer reaches no file. The filter reaches the BGP messages alone: Ze writes a state change record for every peer, whatever this list holds. Periodic RIB snapshots, written as TABLE_DUMP_V2 records. Each dump writes one PEER_INDEX_TABLE record, and then the RIB entries for every address family. Ze writes them as TABLE_DUMP_V2 records, one route in each. A route of a family whose peer negotiated ADD-PATH is written under the ADD-PATH subtype of RFC 8050 with its Path Identifier; any other route under the base subtype of RFC 6396. Output file path with strftime patterns. The strftime codes in the path name the file Ze opens, exactly as they do in a dump stream. Ze writes this stream only when the path is set and interval is more than 0. A path of - writes to standard output. MRT geo-location extension (RFC 6397). Optional RFC 6397 GEO_PEER_TABLE (TABLE_DUMP_V2 subtype 7) companion record carrying WGS84 coordinates for the collector and its peers, with RFC 6397 Section 6 GEOPRIV privacy controls. Collector geo-location coordinates and privacy policy. Collector WGS84 coordinates and privacy rules (RFC 6397 Sections 4.1 and 6). Collector WGS84 latitude or NaN. WGS84 decimal degrees in [-90, 90], or NaN for private location. Collector WGS84 longitude or NaN. WGS84 decimal degrees in [-180, 180], or NaN for private location. Acknowledge non-technical measures enforcing restrictive privacy rules. Confirm non-technical measures (e.g., contractual agreements) enforce more restrictive privacy rules. Optional GEOPRIV note-well constraint. GEOPRIV note-well privacy constraint (RFC 6397 Section 6 default: empty). Location retention horizon in years (default 100). GEOPRIV retention horizon in years (RFC 6397 Section 6 default: 100). Whether location retransmission is allowed (default true). GEOPRIV retransmission-allowed rule (RFC 6397 Section 6 default: true). Optional GEOPRIV ruleset-reference URI. GEOPRIV ruleset-reference URI (RFC 6397 Section 6 default: empty). Enable RFC 6397 GEO_PEER_TABLE export. Emit a GEO_PEER_TABLE record alongside PEER_INDEX_TABLE in TABLE_DUMP_V2 dumps. Peer geo-location coordinates and privacy policy. Per-peer WGS84 coordinates and privacy rules (RFC 6397 Sections 4.1 and 6). Peer WGS84 latitude or NaN. WGS84 decimal degrees in [-90, 90], or NaN for private location. Peer WGS84 longitude or NaN. WGS84 decimal degrees in [-180, 180], or NaN for private location. Acknowledge non-technical measures enforcing restrictive privacy rules. Confirm non-technical measures (e.g., contractual agreements) enforce more restrictive privacy rules. Optional GEOPRIV note-well constraint. GEOPRIV note-well privacy constraint (RFC 6397 Section 6 default: empty). Location retention horizon in years (default 100). GEOPRIV retention horizon in years (RFC 6397 Section 6 default: 100). Whether location retransmission is allowed (default true). GEOPRIV retransmission-allowed rule (RFC 6397 Section 6 default: true). Optional GEOPRIV ruleset-reference URI. GEOPRIV ruleset-reference URI (RFC 6397 Section 6 default: empty). RIB dump interval in seconds. Minimum 60. The default is 3600 seconds and the range is 60 to 86400. Each dump writes one PEER_INDEX_TABLE record and then the RIB entries of every address family, which RFC 6396 Section 4.3.1 requires in that order. BGP UPDATE message stream (BGP4MP records). The stream carries the UPDATE messages alone. The all stream beside it carries every message type. Output file path, with strftime patterns for rotation. The strftime codes in the path decide when Ze opens a new file. The supported codes are %Y (year), %m (month), %d (day), %H (hour), %M (minute), %S (second), %s (unix timestamp) and %N (table name). File rotation interval in seconds. Zero disables rotation. The value 0 keeps one file open until the daemon stops. A value of more than 0 makes Ze close the file once it has been open that many seconds. Ze then opens the next one, and the strftime codes in file give the new name. A file of - writes to standard output, which never rotates.

The presence of this container starts the OSPFv2 engine, which RFC 2328 defines. The address-family container adds the OSPFv3 families of RFC 5340, and each one runs as a separate engine instance. More OSPF address families. The IPv6 family is OSPFv3 (RFC 5340). It runs as a second engine instance over the ospfv3 transport, which uses ff02::5 and ff02::6. It shares the FSM, the flooding and the SPF machinery with the IPv4 family. The IPv4-multicast address family over OSPFv3. RFC 5838 §2.1 gives the Instance ID range as 96 to 127. Ze computes reachability in the unicast shape. Ze does not implement the MOSPF tree computation. OSPFv3 areas for this address family. RFC 5838 section 1 maps each address family to a separate Instance ID and a separate OSPFv3 instance. Ze starts one engine instance for each configured family. An area declared here belongs to that instance alone. Per-area OSPFv3 configuration. The list is keyed by area-id. All routers in an area MUST agree on the configuration of that area. RFC 2328 Appendix C.2 states that a disagreement stops an adjacency from forming between two routers. Area type. RFC 5340 Appendix C.2 excludes every AS-external-LSA from a stub area and from an NSSA. A router inside a stub area reaches an external destination through the default inter-area route alone. The backbone MUST NOT be a stub area or an NSSA, and a virtual link MUST NOT cross either one. Virtual link across this transit area to a backbone area-border router. RFC 5340 section 4.2 defines the virtual link. The link belongs to the backbone area. Its cost is the SPF path cost across the transit area, and it is never configured. The transit area MUST NOT be the backbone, a stub area, or an NSSA. Router-dead interval on the virtual link. Ze declares the far endpoint dead after this long with no Hello. RFC 2328 Section 10.5 drops a received Hello whose RouterDeadInterval does not match, so the two endpoints MUST hold the same value. Hello interval on the virtual link. RFC 2328 Section 10.5 drops a received Hello whose HelloInterval does not match the value configured on the receiving interface. The two endpoints of the virtual link MUST hold the same value. LSA retransmit interval on the virtual link. RFC 2328 Appendix C.4 requires RxmtInterval on a virtual link. Set it well over the round-trip delay between the two routers. That delay is hard to estimate across a transit area, so a value that is too large is the safer error. Estimated LSA transmission delay (RFC 5340 / RFC 2328 InfTransDelay must be > 0). RFC 2328 Appendix C.3 defines InfTransDelay. Ze adds this value to the age of every LSA in a Link State Update before it sends the packet. OSPFv3 Instance ID of this address family. RFC 5838 §2.1 gives the IPv4-multicast range as 96 to 127. OSPFv3-enabled interfaces for this address family. RFC 5838 section 2.4 requires a router that takes part in an address family to discard a Hello whose AF-bit is clear. The base IPv6-unicast family is the one exception. An interface listed here takes part in this family only. Per-interface OSPFv3 configuration. The list is keyed by the interface name. The same interface CAN appear in the list of another address family, with its own cost and its own adjacencies. Declared area this interface belongs to. Ze enrolls the interface only when the areas container declares this area-id. An interface belongs to one area, which RFC 2328 Appendix C.3 names Area ID. Single-hop BFD failure detection for this OSPFv3 interface. RFC 5880 and RFC 5881 define single-hop BFD. When this container enables it, a Full adjacency opens an IPv6 single-hop BFD session over the link-local pair. A failure that BFD detects declares the neighbor down much faster than the router-dead interval does. Enable single-hop BFD failure detection on this interface. A BFD session that goes Down or AdminDown declares the OSPFv3 neighbor down at once. Without BFD, Ze waits for the router-dead interval, which is 40 seconds by default. Required minimum BFD receive interval (RFC 5880 Required Min RX Interval). The far system sends no faster than this value. RFC 5880 section 6.8.4 takes the agreed interval as the greater of this value and the Desired Min TX Interval of the far system. Desired minimum BFD transmit interval (RFC 5880 Desired Min TX Interval). RFC 5880 section 6.8.4 takes the agreed transmit interval as the greater of this value and the Required Min RX Interval of the far system. BFD detection multiplier (RFC 5880 Detect Mult). RFC 5880 section 6.8.4 states that Detect Mult is the number of packets that have to be missed in a row to declare the session down. The detection time is this value multiplied by the agreed transmit interval. Interface output cost. RFC 2328 Appendix C.3 requires an interface output cost of more than 0, and Ze advertises the value as the cost of this link. An absent leaf takes cost 1, whatever the speed of the link is.
