text: pki ca <name> certificate string crl string certificate <name> certificate string intermediate string ocsp-response string private key string PKI certificate and key store. PKI certificate and key store. Presence of this block enables certificate-based authentication for IPsec VPN, TLS, and other subsystems. Trusted CA certificate. Trusted CA certificate. The certificate leaf takes a PEM document, headers and line breaks included, which is what 'ze show pki local-ca pem' prints and what a .crt file holds. Base64-encoded DER with no PEM headers is also read. X.509 CA certificate, as a PEM document or as base64-encoded DER. The trust anchor itself, with no private key. Paste the PEM as it is printed, headers and line breaks included, which is what 'ze show pki local-ca pem' gives you and what a .crt file holds. Base64-encoded DER with no headers is also read, for a config written before PEM was accepted. Certificate revocation lists this CA issued, each a PEM document or base64-encoded DER. Certificate revocation lists this CA issued, each an 'X509 CRL' PEM document or base64-encoded DER. EAP-TLS on TLS 1.3 checks the revocation status of every certificate on a peer's chain except the trust anchor. RFC 9190 Section 5.4 makes that check mandatory. An EAP-TLS peer that validates against this CA and finds no current list here is refused. IKE certificate authentication also checks every certificate on a peer's chain, except the trust anchor, against the lists of each ca entry whose certificate is on that chain, once any such entry holds a list: a revoked certificate, or one whose issuer has no current list, is refused. An intermediate CA a peer's chain passes through is added as a ca entry with its own lists. Publish a fresh list before the nextUpdate of the one here passes: an expired list answers nothing about the present and refuses the same peers. A list that carries a critical extension Ze cannot process (a delta CRL indicator, an issuing distribution point, a critical entry extension) answers nothing either, per RFC 5280 Section 5.2. A list that revokes nothing is a valid answer and is what a CA publishes while it has withdrawn no certificate. Device certificate with optional private key and intermediate certificates. One entry holds the certificate this device presents, the intermediate certificates that lead toward its trust anchor, and the private key that signs with it. The certificate leaf is mandatory and the private container is not, so an entry can hold a certificate Ze sends and cannot sign with. A TLS listener that asks for the key of such an entry is refused, and is never served another certificate in its place. Ze validates every entry when it loads the config. An expired certificate refuses the commit and stops the daemon from starting. A certificate that builds no chain to a ca entry in this block does the same. X.509 device certificate, as a PEM document or as base64-encoded DER. The certificate this node presents. Paste the PEM as it is printed, headers and line breaks included, which is what a .crt file holds. Base64-encoded DER with no headers is also read, for a config written before PEM was accepted. The matching key goes in private key. Intermediate CA certificates, from the issuer toward the trust anchor. Intermediate CA certificates, each a PEM document or base64-encoded DER. Give them in order, from the one that issued this certificate toward the trust anchor. Ze stores them beside the device certificate for chain building, and sends them after it in the IKE_AUTH chain. RFC 7296 Section 3.6 requires an implementation be capable of being configured to send up to four X.509 certificates. This device certificate plus three intermediates is that maximum. A single value is still valid. OCSP response about this certificate, stapled to a peer that asks for it. An OCSP response the certificate's issuer signed about this certificate, as base64-encoded DER or as an 'OCSP RESPONSE' PEM document. Ze sends it in the certificate message when a peer asks for a Certificate Status Request, which RFC 9190 Section 5.4 makes mandatory for an EAP-TLS server on TLS 1.3. Fetch it from the responder your CA publishes, with 'openssl ocsp -respout'. Ze refuses a response about another certificate. A response carries a nextUpdate: a peer that checks the status refuses this certificate once that time passes, so replace the value before it does. An entry with no response answers a Certificate Status Request with no status, which RFC 6066 Section 8 permits, and the peer then checks revocation against the crl of the ca that issued this certificate. Private key associated with this certificate. The container holds one leaf, key, and the container is optional. An entry with no private key holds a certificate Ze sends and verifies against, and cannot sign with. Ze checks when it loads the config that the key matches the public key of the certificate beside it. Ze refuses the config when it does not, so a mismatched pair never reaches a handshake. The key leaf is marked sensitive. The config file stores it as $9$, Ze decodes it on load, and a display path prints a placeholder in its place. Private key, as a PEM document or as base64-encoded DER. Private key, as a PEM document or as base64-encoded DER. The config file stores it as $9$, and Ze decodes it on load. The supported encodings are PKCS8, SEC1 (ECDSA), and PKCS1 (RSA).

title: plugin
text: plugin external <name> encoder enumeration respawn boolean run string timeout string use string hub client <name> ca string host string port uint16 secret string source-address ip-address server <name> certificate string client <name> secret string ip ip-address port listener-port secret string internal <name> use string Plugin configuration Declares the plugins this daemon runs, and the hub transport they connect back over. A built-in plugin that claims a configured address family starts with no block here, because the engine loads it for that family. Declare an internal block to run a built-in plugin under a name you choose. Declare an external block to run a program of your own. Declare a hub block to set the TLS listener and its secrets. The name of an internal or external block is the name a peer's 'attach process' binding refers to. External plugin process Runs a plugin as a separate process. The engine starts the run command with '/bin/sh -c'. The child connects back to the hub listener over TLS. It reads the address, the certificate authority root and its token from its environment. A block that sets use instead of run runs a built-in plugin in this process, with no fork. The block name is the name a peer's 'attach process' binding refers to, and the name the hub binds the connect-back token to. Event encoding format Chooses how the engine encodes the events it sends this plugin: 'json' for JSON objects, 'text' for the line format ExaBGP plugins read. 'text' also makes the engine forward every received BGP UPDATE to the plugin. A peer's 'attach process' binding can set an encoding of its own, and that value wins over this one. With no value here and none on the binding, the engine uses 'text'. Respawn on exit States what you expect ze to do when this plugin's process exits. The plugin itself declares whether it may be started again, and this leaf is a request inside that declaration. With no leaf here the plugin's own declaration decides. With 'false' the plugin is left stopped even when it would have been started again. With 'true' against a plugin that declares it must not be restarted, ze refuses to start, and the error names the plugin and the policy it declared: ze honors neither side in silence. The spelling comes from ExaBGP, whose process block carries the same leaf. A restart is bounded at 5 in 60 seconds and 20 in the life of the daemon, after which the plugin is disabled and 'show health' reports doctor-plugin-stopped. Command to execute plugin as external process (with args) The command line that starts the plugin. The engine runs it with '/bin/sh -c', so arguments, quoting and a PATH lookup work as they do in a shell. The directory of the running ze binary is added to PATH as a fallback, so 'ze plugin <name>' finds the binary in a development tree. The child reads ZE_PLUGIN_HUB_HOST, ZE_PLUGIN_HUB_PORT, ZE_PLUGIN_HUB_TOKEN, ZE_PLUGIN_CA_PEM and ZE_PLUGIN_NAME from its environment, and connects back over TLS. A value of the form 'ze.<plugin>' names a built-in plugin, which the engine then runs in this process rather than as a fork. run and use are mutually exclusive, and a block that sets both is refused. Startup timeout (e.g., 10s, 1m) Bounds a stall in the plugin startup handshake, and does not bound the handshake itself. The handshake runs in stages across every plugin that starts together. The timer expires only when no plugin of that group completes a stage for this long. Write a duration with a unit, such as 10s or 1m: a value with no unit is refused, and so is a negative value. With no value the engine uses the ze.plugin.stage.timeout environment variable, which defaults to 5s. Raise it for a plugin that needs longer to reach its first stage. Name of a built-in plugin to run in-process (mutually exclusive with run) Names a built-in plugin to run in this process instead of a command. The block then behaves like an internal block: no fork, no TLS connect-back, and an in-memory pipe between the engine and the plugin. run and use are mutually exclusive, and a block that sets both is refused. The use leaf of an internal block is checked against the registered plugin names, and this one is not. An unknown name here fails at startup with 'unknown internal plugin'. Plugin transport and auth configuration Sets the TLS listener that plugin processes connect back to, and the outbound connection this daemon makes to a remote hub for its config. With no server block the daemon opens one on 127.0.0.1, with a kernel-chosen port and a random secret. Each plugin process reads that address and a per-plugin token from its environment. Declare a server block when a process the daemon did not start must connect, such as the plugin CLI or a remote managed client. Declare a client block when this daemon takes its config from a remote hub. Outbound hub connections (managed client mode) Each block is an outbound connection to the hub that holds this daemon's config. The daemon dials the first block only, and never dials a second block. The client validates the hub certificate, sends its name and secret, then fetches its config and commits it. A heartbeat every 30 seconds holds the connection open. It reconnects with a delay that grows from 1 second to 60 seconds, and it stops when this instance is no longer marked as managed. The daemon dials nothing here unless it runs as a managed instance with blob-backed config storage. Name of the pki ca entry holding the hub certificate authority root. Name of a pki ca entry holding the certificate authority root of the hub this client connects to. The client validates the hub certificate chain against that root and refuses any other chain, so it sends no token to a hub it did not authenticate. Export the root from the hub and paste it into a pki ca block on this client. A leaf the hub reissues still validates, because the root is the anchor and not the certificate. Remote hub address The address of the remote hub, as an IP address or a hostname. It joins the port leaf into the dial address, and it also sets the TLS server name the client verifies. The value MUST therefore appear in the hub certificate. A certificate that names a different host is refused, and the client sends its secret to no such hub. Remote hub port The TCP port of the remote hub. It MUST equal the port of the hub server block that carries this client's entry. There is no default: a block with no port dials port 0, and no hub listens there. Auth token (min 32 chars) The token this daemon sends to the hub at authentication. It holds at least 32 characters and the config is refused below that length. It MUST equal the secret of the matching client entry in the hub's server block, so rotate both sides in one change. The CLI masks the value on display, and the committed config file holds it in the clear. Source IP address for outbound hub connections. Binds the outbound hub connection to this local IP address. Set it when the route to the hub leaves an interface whose address the hub does not expect. One example is a hub that accepts one management address only. The address MUST exist on this host, because the connection fails when the kernel cannot bind it. With no value the kernel picks the source address of the outgoing route. 'ze doctor' probes the hub through the same source address, so its verdict matches what the daemon does. Named hub server instances (TLS listeners) Each block is one TLS listener. The plugin acceptor binds the first block in configuration order and no other, so a second block exists for the managed clients it names. Every block that carries client entries also starts the managed config server, which needs blob-backed config storage. Give such a block a port of its own. A block whose address the plugin acceptor already binds fails to listen, and 'ze doctor' reports that collision. Set ip and port to the listen address, and secret to the token a connection presents. Name of the pki certificate the managed-client listener on this block serves. Name of a pki certificate the managed-client listener on this block serves. An empty name serves a certificate this daemon's own certificate authority issues, and reissues as it ages. Export that authority root with 'show pki local-ca pem' and name it in each client's pki ca block, so a client validates the chain rather than one certificate. Accepted remote managed clients Each entry names a managed client this hub accepts, and the token that client presents. One entry turns the block into a managed config listener. That listener answers a config fetch. It pushes a change notice when the client's stored config is written. The config it serves is the stored file 'client-<name>.conf', so the entry name is what routes a config to a client. Every server block that carries client entries serves one certificate, and a config that names two different ones is refused. Per-client auth token (min 32 chars) The token this named client presents at authentication. It holds at least 32 characters, and the config is refused below that length with the client name in the error. An entry with no secret is refused as well. Write the same value in the secret leaf of the client block on the remote daemon. This per-client token is checked before the block secret. The CLI masks the value on display, and the committed config file holds it in the clear. Listen IP address The listener binds this address. 0.0.0.0 binds every IPv4 address of the host, and :: binds every IPv6 address. On most services :: is dual-stack: it also accepts IPv4 clients, so :: alone serves both families. Config validation refuses two listeners that share a protocol and a port when their addresses overlap. A wildcard address overlaps every address of its own family, and a dual-stack :: also overlaps every IPv4 address, so list :: alone rather than :: beside 0.0.0.0. A service whose IPv6 sockets are IPv6-only (L2TP, web) accepts :: beside an IPv4 address on the same port. Listen TCP port; 0 means OS-assigned The port range is 0 to 65535. Port 0 makes the operating system pick a free port at bind time, so no client can know the port before the listener starts. ze doctor tries to bind each configured endpoint and reports the one the host refuses. Auth token for plugin connections (min 32 chars) The token this listener accepts from a connection whose name matches no plugin this daemon started and no client entry in this block. A plugin the daemon starts receives a random per-name token in its environment instead, so no operator copies this value into a plugin. It holds at least 32 characters and the config is refused below that length. With no server block the daemon generates a random secret at each start, which no process outside it can know. The CLI masks the value on display, and the committed config file holds it in the clear. Built-in plugin running in-process Runs a plugin that ships inside the ze binary as a goroutine of this process. There is no fork, no TLS connect-back and no shell command: the engine and the plugin exchange messages over an in-memory pipe. Each block needs a use leaf naming the built-in plugin, and a block that also sets run is refused. Declare a block here to bind a built-in plugin to a peer with 'attach process', or to run one under a name of your own. A plugin that claims a configured address family loads without a block. Name of a built-in plugin to run in-process Names the built-in plugin this block runs. The value MUST be a plugin registered in this binary. A value that is not registered is refused, and the error prints the registered names. Command completion offers that same list. The leaf is required, and a block with no use is refused with 'internal plugin requires use'.

title: policy
text: policy as-path-length <name> max uint16 min uint16 as-path-list <name> entry <regex> action enumeration asn-set <name> asn uint32 community-match <name> entry <community> action enumeration type enumeration family-filter <name> action enumeration family address-family loop-detection <name> allow-own-as uint8 cluster-id ipv4-address match <name> action enumeration as-path string as-path-length string community string family string interface string level uint8 metric maximum uint32 minimum uint32 next-hop string prefix-list string protocol string reject-asn string route-type enumeration rpki-validation-state enumeration tag uint32 modify <name> decrement aigp uint32 local-preference uint32 med uint32 del med empty increment aigp uint32 local-preference uint32 med uint32 match community string extended-community string large-community string level uint8 protocol string route-type enumeration tag uint32 set as-path-prepend uint8 community-add string community-remove string distance uint8 extended-community-add string extended-community-remove string large-community-add string large-community-remove string local-preference uint32 med uint32 metric uint32 metric-type enumeration next-hop ip-address origin enumeration tag uint32 prefix-list <name> entry <prefix> action enumeration ge uint8 le uint8 reject-asn <name> anywhere asn-filter direct asn-filter indirect asn-filter nth <index> asn asn-filter origin asn-filter regex string transit asn-filter remove-private-as <name> replace-with enumeration route <name> interface string rule <name> from destination-address string destination-port string protocol protocol-name source-address string source-port string tcp-flags string order uint32 then accept empty drop empty next-hop string table uint32 tcp-mss uint16 Route policy filters and policy routing. Each filter type is a list that its plugin adds through an augment and marks ze:filter. An entry of such a list is a named filter instance, and an import or export chain references it by name. One name belongs to one filter type only. Policy routing adds its route list here too; a route entry is never a filter. Named AS-path length filter instance. Ze rejects a route whose AS-path length falls outside the configured min..max range. Both min and max are optional, and an omitted bound is open. Maximum allowed AS-path length (inclusive). Routes with longer paths are rejected. An absent leaf leaves the upper bound open, so a filter that states neither bound accepts every route. Ze counts every ASN of the path, so a member of an AS_SET counts as one hop. Minimum required AS-path length (inclusive). Routes with shorter paths are rejected. An absent leaf leaves the lower bound open. A route that carries no AS_PATH counts 0 hops. min 1 therefore rejects a route Ze originated, and a route an iBGP peer sent with an empty path. Named AS-path regex filter instance. Each list holds an ordered set of regex entries. Ze evaluates the entries in order, and the first match wins. No match is an implicit deny, so Ze rejects the route. One regex entry of the ordered list. Ze matches each entry against the space-separated AS-path string, in the configured order. The first entry that matches wins. Action applied when this entry's regex matches. The first entry whose pattern matches decides the UPDATE, and no later entry is read. A route whose path matches no entry is rejected, so a list needs no closing reject entry. A named set of AS numbers A plain set of AS numbers, with no position and no action. It is data another feature reads: role transit-asns names one to add the providers this router does not peer with to the RFC 7454 Section 9 upstream check. A filter chain cannot name an asn-set entry. AS numbers of the set The AS numbers of the set, in plain decimal. 0 is reserved (RFC 7607) and refused. Named community match filter instance. Each list holds an ordered set of match entries. Ze reads the entries in order, and the first match wins. No match is an implicit deny, so the route is rejected. Ordered match entry, checked against the route's community attributes. Ze reads the entries in order, and the first match wins. An entry checks whether the named community value is present in the route's community attributes. Action applied when this community is found in the route. The first entry whose community the route carries decides the UPDATE, and no later entry is read. A route that carries none of the listed communities is rejected, so a list needs no closing reject entry. Which community attribute type to check. Ze reads the one attribute the leaf names. An entry of type standard therefore does not see a value that sits in the LARGE COMMUNITIES attribute. Write one entry for each attribute the route can carry the value in. Named address-family filter instance. One instance matches one family, because family holds one value and is mandatory. A chain that must catch two families names two instances. Action to apply when the family matches. remove strips the MP_REACH NLRI and the MP_UNREACH NLRI of the matched family from the UPDATE, on import and on export. If that removal empties the UPDATE, Ze drops the whole UPDATE for that peer. tear-down sends a BGP NOTIFICATION that carries the Cease code and the Connection Rejected subcode, then closes the session. tear-down acts on import only. Address family to match, for example ipv4/flowspec. Ze treats an UPDATE with no MP_REACH attribute and no MP_UNREACH attribute as ipv4/unicast. Named loop detection filter instance. The instance configures AS loop detection and cluster-list loop detection, for each peer that references it. Own-AS occurrences permitted in AS_PATH before ze rejects the route. The default is 0, which rejects the route on the first occurrence (RFC 4271 Section 9). Override Router ID for CLUSTER_LIST loop detection. When this leaf is unset, ze uses the BGP Router ID (RFC 4456 Section 7). Named route match filter instance. With action accept, a route that meets every condition the instance names passes on to the next filter and any other route is rejected; with action reject, a route that meets them is rejected and any other passes on. An instance is checked against only the conditions it names, so one naming prefix-list and tag attaches to static, OSPF and the rib chain, and is refused on IS-IS, whose routes carry no tag. Accept or reject the routes this instance matches What happens to a route that meets every condition the instance names. The other routes get the opposite. Match routes whose AS path the named as-path-list accepts The UPDATE passes this condition when the named as-path-list accepts its AS path, read as the space-separated decimal string. The as-path-list is a policy as-path-list instance: the editor completes the configured ones, and a commit naming any other is refused. Only a BGP chain judges it. Match routes whose AS path length the named as-path-length allows The UPDATE passes this condition when its AS path hop count lies within the named as-path-length instance's min and max. The editor completes the configured as-path-length instances, and a commit naming any other is refused. Only a BGP chain judges it. Match routes the named community-match list accepts The route passes this condition when the named community-match list accepts it: the list's first entry whose community the route carries decides, and a route no entry matches fails. The list is a policy community-match instance: the editor completes the configured ones, and a commit naming any other is refused. A BGP chain judges it; a Loc-RIB chain refuses it, as its routes carry no community. Match routes of this address family An address family name such as ipv4/unicast or ipv6/unicast. Match routes through this interface The outgoing interface the route names. Match IS-IS routes of this level The IS-IS level the route was selected at. Only IS-IS routes carry a level. Match routes whose metric is in this range The route's metric as its source states it: the SPF metric or cost of an IGP route, a static route's configured metric. Either bound may be left out; a minimum above the maximum is refused. Highest metric that matches The highest metric that matches, inclusive. Left out, the range ends at 4294967295. Lowest metric that matches The lowest metric that matches, inclusive. Left out, the range starts at 0. Match routes whose next hop is in this prefix An address prefix the route's next hop lies in, such as 192.0.2.0/24 or 2001:db8::1/128. A route with no next hop (connected) does not match. Match routes the named prefix-list accepts The route passes this condition when the named prefix-list accepts its prefix. The prefix-list is a policy prefix-list instance: the editor completes the configured ones, and a commit naming any other is refused. Match routes from this source A route source registered by this build (static, connected, ospf, isis, bgp, ...), or ebgp or ibgp for the class of a BGP best. An unknown name is refused at load. Match routes the named reject-asn list does not reject The route passes this condition when the named reject-asn list rejects it on neither arm: no listed ASN at a listed position of its AS path, and no pattern matching the whole path. The sender is known on import only. A match naming it discharges the transit-leak filter a declared RFC 9234 role requires. The list is a policy reject-asn instance: the editor completes the configured ones, and a commit naming any other is refused. A BGP chain judges it; a Loc-RIB chain refuses it. Match OSPF routes of this path type The OSPF path type of RFC 2328 Section 11, with the NSSA types of RFC 3101. Only OSPF routes carry a route type. Match routes by RPKI origin validation state (valid, not-found, invalid) Match routes whose RPKI Route Origin Validation state (RFC 6811 Section 2, RFC 8893 Section 3) is one of the listed states. Available identically in BGP ingress, redistribution, and BGP egress policy; on egress, the state is determined from the effective origin AS as the route will be announced to the peer after egress configuration and policy. Match routes carrying this tag OSPF carries the external route tag and static carries its tag leaf. IS-IS carries no administrative tag in Ze, so a filter reading tag is refused on an IS-IS chain. Named route attribute modifier instance. Ze modifies only the declared leaves, and keeps every undeclared attribute unchanged. One modifier can change several attributes. Attributes to decrement on a matching route. Ze subtracts the stated value from the current value of the attribute. The result floors at 0, so it never underflows. decrement is mutually exclusive with set for the same attribute. Decrement AIGP metric by this value. Ze runs the operation only on a route that already carries an AIGP TLV. A route with none is left alone, because RFC 7311 Section 3.4.1 forbids Ze to add the attribute. Decrement LOCAL_PREF by this value. A route that carries no LOCAL_PREF counts as 100 before the subtraction. A decrement larger than the current value writes 0 rather than wrapping. Decrement MED by this value. A route that carries no MULTI_EXIT_DISC counts as 0, so the result is 0 and Ze writes a metric the route did not have. Use del med to remove the attribute instead. Attributes Ze deletes from a matching route. Ze applies only the leaves that are present in this container, and keeps every other attribute unchanged. Remove the MULTI_EXIT_DISC attribute (RFC 4271 type 4) from the route. RFC 4271 Section 5.1.4 requires a mechanism, based on local configuration, that removes MULTI_EXIT_DISC from a route. The same section requires the removal to happen before the route reaches Decision Process phase 1 and phase 2. The del med operation is that mechanism, so it applies on an IMPORT chain only, and the route enters the decision process with no metric. Ze refuses del med on an export chain and writes a log line, because Section 9.1.2.2 states that a comparison on MULTI

title: pppoe
text: pppoe ac-name string allow-no-auth boolean auth-method enumeration authentication-allow enumeration cookie-timeout uint16 enabled boolean interface <name> max-sessions uint16 max-sessions-per-mac uint16 service-name string lcp max-configure uint8 max-failure uint8 max-terminate uint8 restart-timer uint16 max-sessions uint16 max-sessions-per-mac uint16 padi-rate-limit uint16 service-name string PPPoE access concentrator settings (RFC 2516). This block with any content in it enables the subsystem. Use 'enabled false' to disable it explicitly. Use 'enabled true' as a filler when no other settings are needed. Access Concentrator Name advertised in PADO (RFC 2516 Section 5.2). The default is ze. Ze writes the value into the AC-Name tag, 0x0102, of each discovery reply it builds. A client that hears several concentrators reads this name to pick one. Accept a subscriber whose LCP negotiation ends with no Auth-Protocol option. The default is false. A client that rejects the configured method is then disconnected, and it is never admitted unauthenticated. PPP Auth-Protocol method the access concentrator advertises in LCP. The access concentrator advertises the method in its LCP Configure-Request (RFC 1661 Section 6.2), for every subscriber that completes PPPoE discovery. The auth handler verifies the credential (l2tp-auth-local or l2tp-auth-radius). The default requires CHAP-MD5 (RFC 1994). Set it to none only together with allow-no-auth true. Ordered set of permitted subscriber PPP authentication methods. Allowed PPP authentication methods. The list must contain auth-method and cannot be used with auth-method none. Absent or empty derives chap-md5 only for chap-md5, ms-chap-v2 only for ms-chap-v2, CHAP-MD5 then PAP for pap, and no methods for none. CHAP variants precede PAP; the configured CHAP method is first, then written CHAP order. Changes apply only to new sessions. AC-Cookie validity duration in seconds. Cookies older than this are rejected in PADR validation. The default is 5 seconds and the range is 1 to 300. The cookie is 20 bytes: 16 bytes of a truncated HMAC-SHA256 over the two MAC addresses, and 4 bytes of Unix timestamp. Each interface holds its own random key, so a cookie of one interface never verifies on another. Enable the PPPoE subsystem. The default is true when the pppoe block is present. Set it to false to disable the subsystem. Access interfaces on which PPPoE discovery listens. Each interface has an independent session ID space. Access interfaces use the session provider registered for the selected interface backend. Configuration is refused when this build has no such provider. VPP access interfaces also require VPP and its Linux Control Plane enabled. Per-interface session limit. Defaults to the global max-sessions when unset. Ze takes the global max-sessions when this leaf is absent or 0. The session identifiers come from a bitmap over the 16-bit space, and identifier 0 is reserved. A PADR that arrives at the limit gets no session, and Ze reports that the maximum is reached. Per-interface override for max-sessions-per-mac. Defaults to the global value when unset. Ze takes the global max-sessions-per-mac when this leaf is absent or 0. A PADR from a MAC already at the cap gets a PADS carrying an error tag and session ID 0x0000 instead of a new session. Per-interface Service-Name filter. Overrides the global service-name list when set. Ze answers a PADI whose Service-Name tag holds a value of this list, and it answers a PADI whose tag is empty. A PADI naming any other service gets no PADO. An empty list here takes the global list, and an empty global list accepts every Service-Name. LCP retransmission timer and limits for new sessions. LCP retransmission settings for new sessions. Established sessions retain their admitted values. Unanswered Configure-Request transmission limit, 1 to 255, default 10. Maximum Configure-Request transmissions without a valid Configure-Ack, Configure-Nak or Configure-Reject. Changes apply to new sessions only. Configure-Nak limit before rejecting unacceptable options, 1 to 255, default 5. Configure-Naks sent without a Configure-Ack before unacceptable options are rejected and desired options are no longer appended. Changes apply to new sessions only. Unanswered Terminate-Request transmission limit, 1 to 255, default 2. Maximum Terminate-Request transmissions without a Terminate-Ack, including the first request. Changes apply to new sessions only. LCP Restart timer in milliseconds, 100 to 60000, default 3000. Wait after each Configure-Request or Terminate-Request, and after zeroing the Restart counter. A shorter interval increases per-session wakeups. Changes apply to new sessions only. Maximum concurrent PPPoE sessions per interface. The 16-bit session ID range limits the count to 1 through 65535. Maximum concurrent sessions one subscriber MAC address may hold. The default is 8 and the range is 1 to 65535. RFC 2516 places no limit on concurrent sessions from one peer MAC, so this bounds replay rather than a legitimate multi-session client: a PADR from a MAC already at the cap gets a PADS carrying an error tag and session ID 0x0000 instead of a new session. The per-interface max-sessions-per-mac overrides this value. Maximum PADI packets accepted per second on one interface. The default is 100 and the range is 1 to 10000. Ze counts the PADI packets of one interface inside a one-second window and discards every packet over the count. Ze also discards a second PADI from one source MAC address inside the same second. The range starts at 1, so no configuration turns the limiter off. Accepted Service-Name values (RFC 2516 Section 5.1). An empty list accepts any Service-Name. The per-interface service-name list overrides this global list.

title: redistribute
text: redistribute destination <protocol> import <source> filters string final enumeration Route redistribution between protocols. Each destination protocol has its own container that holds the import rules. To add a destination protocol, add a key here. Destination protocol for redistributed routes. Each entry names a protocol that declared itself a destination, for example bgp or ospf. Import routes from a source into this destination. With no filters and no final, Ze imports every route of the source. Ordered filter instance references Run these filter instances, defined under the top-level policy root, in order. Each one passes the route on, with what it sets, or rejects it. A filter of a type with no route evaluator, or one reading a field a redistributed route does not carry, is refused. Select a family or a tag with a match filter: match V4 { family [ ipv4/unicast ]; }. Decision after every filter passes The decision after every filter passes. An import with filters must set it. An import with neither filters nor final imports every route from the source.

title: rib
text: rib distance connected uint8 ebgp uint8 ibgp uint8 isis uint8 ospf uint8 static uint8 fib-withhold string filter import filters string final enumeration System RIB configuration. The system RIB takes the best route each protocol offers and selects one system best for each prefix. The FIB plugins program that winner into the kernel with netlink, into VPP, or into a P4 switch. The kernel FIB carries no administrative distance field, so the ranking happens here and only the winner reaches netlink. The distance container below is the one declaration of every protocol's administrative distance. The fib-withhold leaf-list beside it names the protocols whose winners are not programmed. Routes reach the system RIB from the protocols, never from this block. Administrative distance per protocol. Administrative distance ranks one protocol against another for the same prefix, and the lower value wins. It is NOT an IGP metric and NOT the IGP distance to a next hop: those measure a path, this ranks the protocol that offered it. RFC 4271 mandates no values; these follow the Cisco and Juniper convention. This container is the only place any protocol's distance is declared, and every protocol takes its value from here whether or not you write the block. Directly connected networks. A connected route is the prefix an interface address covers. The default 0 is the best distance a route can hold, so a connected route wins the prefix against every protocol that carries a higher value. This is the only distance leaf whose range starts at 0. The other five start at 1. Raise it above another protocol's distance to let that protocol win the same prefix. The value applies whether or not you write the rib block, because sysrib resolves every protocol from these schema defaults when it starts. External BGP routes. An eBGP route comes from a peer in another autonomous system. The default 20 ranks eBGP above every IGP declared here and below a static route. The range is 1 to 255. The Loc-RIB looks this value up for each eBGP path when it ranks it, so it decides selection before sysrib sees the route, and a change re-ranks the routes already installed. Internal BGP routes. An iBGP route comes from a peer in the same autonomous system. The default 200 is the highest of the six declared here, so an iBGP route loses the prefix to any other protocol that holds it. The range is 1 to 255. The Loc-RIB ranks each iBGP path at this value when it ranks it. The eBGP distance is a separate leaf, so the two BGP classes rank apart. IS-IS routes. The default 115 ranks IS-IS below OSPF and above iBGP. The range is 1 to 255. The Loc-RIB ranks each IS-IS path at this value when it ranks it, and a change re-ranks the routes already installed. One value covers level 1 and level 2: Ze declares no separate distance for each level. OSPF routes. The default 110 ranks OSPF below eBGP and above IS-IS. The range is 1 to 255. The Loc-RIB ranks each OSPF path at this value when it ranks it, and a change re-ranks the routes already installed. One value covers every OSPF route: Ze declares no separate distance for an external LSA. Static routes. A static route is one the operator wrote under the static configuration. The default 10 ranks a static route above every dynamic protocol declared here and below a connected route. The range is 1 to 255. The Loc-RIB ranks each static route at this value unless the route carries its own distance leaf, which wins over it. Raise it to more than 20 to let an eBGP route win the same prefix. Protocols whose selected routes are not programmed into the FIB. An empty list programs all. This list names the protocols Ze does not program. Selection is unchanged: the system RIB ranks the candidates for each prefix on administrative distance and picks one winner. A winner from a protocol named here stays in the RIB, `show rib` reports it, redistribution can offer it to another protocol, and the protocol's own event stream still carries it. Ze declines the write to the kernel, to VPP or to a P4 switch. It holds the prefix off `system-rib/best-change`, the stream every FIB writer reads, so the list applies to every FIB. Ze also releases the next-hop tracking for the prefix, so `show nexthop-table` stops listing it under its next-hop. An empty list withholds nothing, which is the behavior of a router that says nothing here. Withholding is one of the reasons a selected route is not programmed: a route the operating system installs, and a route whose SRv6 SID reaches nothing, are not written either. The values are the protocol names this build registered: the editor completes them, and a name nothing registered is refused at commit. Route filter chains into the Loc-RIB. A name references a filter instance defined under the top-level policy root. The chain judges routes as they enter the Loc-RIB. Import policy into the Loc-RIB A rejected route stays in the Loc-RIB as a hidden path that is never selected, so relaxing the chain re-admits it without the protocol sending it again. The source's chain runs first, then the rib chain. Ordered filter instance references Run these filter instances in order. Each one passes the route on or rejects it; a filter type with no Loc-RIB route evaluator is refused. Decision after every filter passes Every present import policy must set final accept or final reject, even with no filters.

title: routing-table
text: routing-table table <name> id uint32 Named routing table definitions. Each entry maps a name to a kernel routing table ID. Ze builds one registry from these entries, and a static route or a policy route resolves its table name against that registry. The name default is built-in and resolves to table 0, so no entry can carry that name. A named routing table. One entry maps one name to one kernel table identifier. Ze refuses an entry named default, and refuses an entry with no id. Two entries CAN carry the same identifier, because the registry keys on the name. Kernel routing table ID; not 0, 253-255 or a range Ze reserves The leaf is mandatory. The range refuses 0 and 253 to 255, because 253 is the kernel default table, 254 is the main table and 255 is the local table. Ze also refuses an identifier inside a range Ze reserves for its own tables (internal/core/iprule, ZeTableRanges: VRF tables, policy routing auto tables, IPsec source-guard tables), and an identifier this build cannot program through netlink without truncation.

title: rsvp-te
text: rsvp-te bypass <name> explicit-route <index> address string type enumeration merge-point string node-protection boolean interface <name> address string max-bandwidth string max-reservable-bandwidth string refresh-multiplier uint8 refresh-period uint16 reservation-policy default-action enumeration rule <index> action enumeration endpoint-prefix string sender-prefix string router-id string tunnel <name> bandwidth string destination string explicit-route <index> address string type enumeration fast-reroute backup enumeration bandwidth-protection boolean hop-limit uint8 node-protection boolean hold-priority uint8 setup-priority uint8 tunnel-id uint16 RSVP-TE traffic engineering configuration RSVP-TE traffic engineering configuration. Signaling is IPv4 only. Without a router-id the engine stays idle, and no tunnel and no bypass signals. RSVP-TE does not consume a traffic-engineering database or run CSPF, so paths are configured explicitly. Facility-backup bypass LSP from this PLR to a merge point (RFC 4090 Section 3.2). Facility-backup bypass LSP (RFC 4090 Section 3.2): an LSP from this PLR to a merge point, explicitly routed to avoid the protected resource. A protected transit LSP is redirected onto this bypass on a local failure. The redirected LSP is one whose next hop (link protection) or next-next hop (node protection) is this bypass's merge point. RSVP-TE does not consume a traffic-engineering database or run CSPF to compute a backup path. Bypass path hops (must avoid the protected resource) Bypass path hops. The route has to avoid the link or the node this bypass protects, because a backup that crosses the protected resource fails with it. RSVP-TE does not run CSPF, so the operator supplies the hops. The hops are ordered by the numeric index key. Hop address (IPv4 prefix) Hop address, given as an IPv4 prefix such as 10.0.0.8/30. A commit that gives a bare address with no prefix length is rejected. The address and the prefix length both go into the ERO IPv4 prefix subobject of the bypass PATH. Hop type (strict or loose) Hop type. strict is the default and asks that the previous hop reaches this one directly. loose sets the L bit of the ERO subobject and permits other hops between them. Ze reads any value other than loose as strict. Merge point address (IPv4) where this bypass rejoins the protected LSPs. Merge point address (IPv4). The address is the protected LSPs' next hop (link protection) or next-next hop (node protection), where this bypass rejoins them. This bypass merges at a next-next hop, so it gives node protection This bypass merges at a next-next hop, so it gives node protection. A protected LSP that asked for node protection is armed onto a bypass only when this leaf is true. Left false, the bypass protects the link alone, and a node-protection request finds no bypass at this PLR. Per-interface RSVP-TE configuration Per-interface RSVP-TE configuration. Bandwidth admission control accounts each reservation against one entry of this list. An interface that no entry names carries no limit, so every reservation that resolves onto it is admitted. Local link prefix in IPv4 CIDR form, for example 10.0.0.4/30. Local link prefix (IPv4 CIDR, for example 10.0.0.4/30). When more than one interface is configured, admission control maps an LSP to this interface. The map applies when the neighbor address falls within the prefix. Maximum link bandwidth (bps) Maximum link bandwidth. The value is reported by 'show rsvp-te interface' and it is not an admission limit. Only max-reservable-bandwidth bounds what admission control accepts. Maximum reservable bandwidth (bps) Maximum reservable bandwidth. Admission control denies a reservation when the accounted total plus the new request is more than this value. A shared-explicit session counts its largest LSP once rather than the sum, so a make-before-break reroute is not double-counted. Left unset, the limit is 0 and every tunnel that requests bandwidth on this interface is denied. Number of missed refreshes before state cleanup Number of missed refreshes before state cleanup, 1 to 255, default 3. State expires when the last refresh is older than refresh-period multiplied by this number, which is 90 seconds at the defaults. Expiry releases the reserved bandwidth, the MPLS forwarding entry and the label, then sends an lsp-down event. PATH/RESV refresh interval (RFC 2205 soft-state) PATH and RESV refresh interval, 1 to 65535 seconds, default 30. The same 65535-second ceiling caps the period a neighbor advertises in TIME_VALUES. A neighbor therefore cannot hold state alive for years. A reload reaches the running LSPs at the next refresh tick. Local reservation authorization by sender and tunnel endpoint Local network-address authorization for RSVP reservations. Rules match the IPv4 sender in SENDER_TEMPLATE or FILTER_SPEC and the tunnel endpoint in SESSION. Authorization and bandwidth admission must both permit a reservation. This policy does not provide cryptographic user authentication or interpret POLICY_DATA objects. Action when no reservation rule matches Action when no rule matches. The default is permit, so configurations without a reservation policy keep their existing authorization behavior. Reservation authorization rule Rules are evaluated by ascending numeric index. The first matching rule decides. Both configured prefixes must match. An omitted prefix matches every address; a rule with neither prefix matches every reservation. Authorization action for a matching reservation Required authorization decision for a matching reservation. A permit still requires bandwidth admission. Tunnel endpoint IPv4 prefix IPv4 prefix for the SESSION tunnel endpoint. A /32 matches one host and /0 matches every IPv4 endpoint. Host bits are masked before matching. Omit this leaf to match any tunnel endpoint. Sender IPv4 prefix IPv4 prefix for the sender address. A /32 matches one host and /0 matches every IPv4 sender. Host bits are masked before matching. Omit this leaf to match any sender. Router identifier (IPv4 address format) Router identifier, in IPv4 address format. A commit that gives an IPv6 address is rejected. The address is the PATH sender address, the address the transport socket binds, and the seed of the session key each tunnel and bypass derives. A change after startup is logged and refused, and the running router-id stays in use until the daemon restarts. RSVP-TE LSP tunnel definition RSVP-TE LSP tunnel definition. Each entry signals a PATH from the local router-id toward destination. A commit that changes only the explicit route starts a make-before-break reroute (RFC 3209 Section 6.1) and leaves the live tunnel in place. Requested bandwidth (bps) Requested bandwidth. The value fills the SENDER_TSPEC token rate, token bucket and peak rate. Admission control charges it against the interface entry the LSP neighbor resolves onto, and it denies the LSP when the charge is more than max-reservable-bandwidth. Tunnel endpoint (IPv4 address) Tunnel endpoint, an IPv4 address. The address is the SESSION tunnel endpoint the PATH carries. A node whose own router-id equals this address acts as the egress and answers with a RESV. Every other node on the path acts as a transit node. Explicit route hops Explicit route hops. The list becomes the ERO object the PATH carries (RFC 3209 Section 4.3). RSVP-TE does not run CSPF, so the operator supplies the hops. A tunnel with no hop here is signaled with no ERO object. A commit that changes the list starts a make-before-break reroute. Hop address (IPv4 prefix) Hop address, given as an IPv4 prefix such as 10.0.0.4/30. A commit that gives a bare address with no prefix length is rejected. The address and the prefix length both go into the ERO IPv4 prefix subobject. Hop type (strict or loose) Hop type. strict is the default and asks that the previous hop reaches this one directly. loose sets the L bit of the ERO subobject and permits other hops between them. Ze reads any value other than loose as strict. Fast Reroute (RFC 4090) local protection for this LSP Fast Reroute (RFC 4090) local protection for this LSP. The container has presence. Absent, the head-end PATH carries no SESSION_ATTRIBUTE and no FAST_REROUTE object, and no transit PLR arms a backup. Present, it also puts setup-priority, hold-priority and the tunnel name on the wire. Backup method: facility (one bypass protects many LSPs) or one-to-one (a detour per LSP) Backup method. facility is the default and asks each PLR for one bypass LSP that protects many LSPs (RFC 4090 Section 3.2). one-to-one asks for one detour per LSP (Section 3.1). As a PLR, Ze arms only a facility bypass from its own bypass list. Ze signals a one-to-one request and builds no detour for it. Request a backup that guarantees the reserved bandwidth Request a backup that guarantees the reserved bandwidth. Ze sets the bandwidth-protection flag in SESSION_ATTRIBUTE (RFC 4090 Section 4.3) and records it in the RESV route object. Ze's own bypass selection does not compare the bypass bandwidth, so the flag is a request to the PLR downstream. Maximum number of hops the backup path can take Maximum number of hops the backup path can take, 0 to 255, default 16. The value goes into the FAST_REROUTE object (RFC 4090 Section 4.1) for the PLR that computes the backup. A Ze facility bypass is routed by its own explicit-route list, so this limit does not shorten it. Request NNHOP (node) protection rather than NHOP (link) protection Request NNHOP (node) protection rather than NHOP (link) protection. Ze sets the node-protection flag in SESSION_ATTRIBUTE (RFC 4090 Section 4.3). As a PLR, Ze then arms only a bypass whose merge point is the next-next hop of the explicit route. That bypass also has to set its own node-protection leaf. With no such bypass, the LSP gets no protection. Hold priority (0 = highest) Hold priority, where 0 is the highest and 7 is the default. It states how hard this LSP holds its reservation against a setup of higher priority. Ze signals it beside setup-priority, and only for a tunnel that declares fast-reroute. Setup priority (0 = highest) Setup priority, where 0 is the highest and 7 is the default. Ze signals the value in the SESSION_ATTRIBUTE and FAST_REROUTE objects, and it adds both objects only for a tunnel that declares fast-reroute. Ze preempts no LSP of its own, so the priority acts on the routers downstream. Tunnel identifier Tunnel identifier, the part of the SESSION that separates this LSP from another to the same endpoint. Ze reserves 61440 to 65535 for the bypass LSPs it derives from a bypass name, and a commit that puts a tunnel in that range is rejected.

title: service
text: service as112 address-family enumeration allow-from ip-prefix asn asn community string doh enabled boolean listen-port port path string enabled boolean facility string hostname string ipv4-anycast-listener <name> ip ip-address port listener-port ipv6-anycast-listener <name> ip ip-address port listener-port location string tls cert-file string certificate string enabled boolean key-file string listen-port port watchdog boolean dhcp-server enabled boolean listen-interface string pxe boot-script-url string bootfile-bios string bootfile-uefi string enabled boolean tftp-server string shared-network <name> subnet <prefix> default-router string dns-server string dns-source mode enumeration received-interface node-name source dns-source-class domain-name string lease-time uint32 range <name> start string stop string server-identifier string static-mapping <name> ip-address string mac-address string dns-resolver allow-from ip-prefix cache max-negative-ttl uint32 max-ttl uint32 size uint32 enabled boolean forward dns-source mode enumeration received-interface node-name source dns-source-class server <ip> port port limit outstanding uint32 per-client-rate uint32 listener <name> ip ip-address port listener-port mode enumeration timeout uint8 geodns client-ip-source enumeration default-ttl uint32 doh enabled boolean listen-port port path string enabled boolean host-set <name> host <name> address ip-address srv port uint16 priority uint16 target string weight uint16 ttl uint32 type enumeration listener <name> ip ip-address port listener-port nameserver ipv4-address soa contact string expire uint32 minimum uint32 mname string refresh uint32 retry uint32 serial uint32 serial-mode enumeration source <prefix> host-set leafref tls cert-file string certificate string enabled boolean key-file string listen-port port zone string image-server boot-directory string enabled boolean image-directory string listen-interface string listen-port uint16 rescue-auth string ssh-password-hash string ssh-username string tftp-server enabled boolean listen-interface string max-transfers uint16 max-windowsize uint16 root-directory string timeout uint8 Service settings. The container holds the settings of each service Ze runs, and the as112 container under it configures the AS112 node. AS112 anycast DNS node. The container holds the enable switch, the address family, the node identification strings, the access list, the BGP settings and the secure listeners. Restrict the service to one address family. RFC 7534 Section 3.4 and RFC 7535 Section 3.1 give the single-stack option. The anycast addresses themselves are fixed constants, and an operator never types one. Client-source access list of the queries the node answers. An empty list, which is the default, answers every source and matches the standard AS112 public-sink behavior. With one prefix or more, the node answers a query only when its source IP is inside one of those prefixes. It drops every other query and sends no response. A loopback source and an on-box source are always permitted, whatever this list holds, so the 'request as112 healthcheck' probe is never blocked. A set list makes the node non-public. That is correct for a local-use mirror, and wrong for an AS112 contributor the whole internet reaches. Origin AS the AS112 covering prefixes carry when redistributed into BGP. The redistribute statement is `redistribute { destination bgp { import as112 } }`. The default is the well-known AS112 number 112 (RFC 7534 Section 3.2), because the redistribute source models an AS112 virtual router. Set an operator ASN, or an RFC 6996 private-use ASN, to originate under a coordinated AS or a local-use AS instead. Ze ignores this leaf unless 'import as112' is configured under redistribute. BGP communities attached to the redistributed AS112 covering prefixes. The leaf takes an AA:NN standard community (RFC 1997) and a well-known name such as no-export or nopeer (RFC 3765). Those are the values RFC 7534 Section 3.4 recommends to restrict AS112 route propagation. The type is 'string' rather than the AA:NN-only ze-types community pattern, so a well-known name is accepted. The canonical community parser validates every value at config time. Ze ignores this leaf unless 'import as112' is configured under redistribute. DNS-over-HTTPS listener (RFC 8484). The listener reuses the certificate material of the tls container. It binds the fixed anycast addresses and the loopback address on 'listen-port', at 'path'. Enable the DNS-over-HTTPS listener (RFC 8484). The default is false. Ze binds DoH on every IP the cleartext listeners use, on listen-port, at path. The listener drives the same handler as cleartext DNS, so allow-from answers a DoH client exactly as it answers a UDP client. A query the handler refuses gets HTTP 403. TCP port for the DoH HTTPS listener (RFC 8484). The default is 443, and the range is 1 to 65535. Ze refuses a port of 0. A GET carries the query base64url-encoded in the dns parameter, and a POST carries it in an application/dns-message body of 65535 bytes at most. HTTP request path the DoH endpoint answers on. RFC 8484 defines the URI Template. The default path is /dns-query. Enable the AS112 anycast DNS node. The AS112 node does not start while this leaf is false, and false is the default. Facility name in the HOSTNAME.AS112.NET/ARPA TXT answers. The facility name is the name of the site, for example 'Example Datacenter'. It is surfaced beside the location. Node identification string in the HOSTNAME.AS112.NET/ARPA TXT answers. RFC 7534 Section 3.5 defines those answers. The string tells an operator which anycast instance answered a query. An empty value omits the TXT string. Presence-only anchor for port 53 on the fixed IPv4 anycast addresses. as112 always occupies port 53 on its fixed IPv4 anycast addresses while it is enabled. The Go-level default, RegisterListenerDefault, fills in the representative address, because no operator-facing command populates this list. Listen IP address The listener binds this address. 0.0.0.0 binds every IPv4 address of the host, and :: binds every IPv6 address. On most services :: is dual-stack: it also accepts IPv4 clients, so :: alone serves both families. Config validation refuses two listeners that share a protocol and a port when their addresses overlap. A wildcard address overlaps every address of its own family, and a dual-stack :: also overlaps every IPv4 address, so list :: alone rather than :: beside 0.0.0.0. A service whose IPv6 sockets are IPv6-only (L2TP, web) accepts :: beside an IPv4 address on the same port. Listen TCP port; 0 means OS-assigned The port range is 0 to 65535. Port 0 makes the operating system pick a free port at bind time, so no client can know the port before the listener starts. ze doctor tries to bind each configured endpoint and reports the one the host refuses. Presence-only anchor for port 53 on the fixed IPv6 anycast addresses. as112 always occupies port 53 on its fixed IPv6 anycast addresses while it is enabled. Listen IP address The listener binds this address. 0.0.0.0 binds every IPv4 address of the host, and :: binds every IPv6 address. On most services :: is dual-stack: it also accepts IPv4 clients, so :: alone serves both families. Config validation refuses two listeners that share a protocol and a port when their addresses overlap. A wildcard address overlaps every address of its own family, and a dual-stack :: also overlaps every IPv4 address, so list :: alone rather than :: beside 0.0.0.0. A service whose IPv6 sockets are IPv6-only (L2TP, web) accepts :: beside an IPv4 address on the same port. Listen TCP port; 0 means OS-assigned The port range is 0 to 65535. Port 0 makes the operating system pick a free port at bind time, so no client can know the port before the listener starts. ze doctor tries to bind each configured endpoint and reports the one the host refuses. City and country in the HOSTNAME.AS112.NET/ARPA TXT answers. The location is surfaced beside the facility, for example 'London, UK'. DNS-over-TLS listener, and the certificate material it shares with DoH. RFC 7858 defines DNS-over-TLS (DoT). When it is enabled, the DoT listener binds the fixed anycast addresses and the loopback address on 'listen-port'. When cert-file and key-file are both unset, Ze uses an ephemeral self-signed certificate, which a strict client cannot validate. Supply an operator PEM file for a node the public trusts. Path to the PEM server certificate presented on DoT and DoH. When this leaf and key-file are both unset, Ze uses an ephemeral self-signed certificate. Name of the PKI store certificate served on DoT and DoH. The listeners send the leaf certificate and every intermediate certificate the store entry holds. This leaf excludes cert-file and key-file. Setting both is a configuration error. The PKI store lives in the hub process, so a geodns plugin or an as112 plugin started as an external process cannot resolve the name. The secure listeners then do not start, and Ze logs the error. Cleartext DNS still runs. Enable the DNS-over-TLS listener (RFC 7858). The default is false. Ze binds DoT on every IP the cleartext listeners use, on listen-port. DoT is TCP only, because RFC 7858 Section 3.1 defines no UDP counterpart. When the TLS material fails to load, Ze starts no secure listener and the cleartext listeners keep running. Path to the PEM private key matching cert-file. Must be set together with cert-file. Ze reads cert-file and key-file on each apply, so a rotated pair reaches the listener without a restart. One of the two alone stops the secure listeners with an error, and the cleartext listeners keep running. The certificate leaf names a PKI store entry instead, and Ze refuses a config that writes both sources. TCP port for the DoT listener. The RFC 7858 well-known 'domain-s' port is 853. A commit with the value 53 is refused, because RFC 7858 Section 3.1 forbids DNS over TLS on the cleartext DNS port, which AS112 already serves. Announce the covering prefixes only while the node serves DNS. RFC 7534 Section 3.3 states that a node does not advertise the service prefix while the name server is not running. With true, which is the default, Ze announces the covering prefixes only while the as112 node serves. Ze withdraws them when serving is lost, when the service is disabled, and when the node shuts down. With false, Ze announces as soon as the node is enabled and imported, with no serving-state gate. Ze ignores this leaf unless 'import as112' is configured under redistribute. DHCP server settings DHCP server settings. Ze speaks DHCPv4 only (RFC 2131 and RFC 2132), so every address leaf under this container is IPv4. The server binds one listener for each name in listen-interface. A listener answers a client no relay forwarded only from the shared networks that hold a subnet its interface is addressed in, and a relayed client from the shared network that holds the relay's address (giaddr). Enable DHCP server Enable the DHCP server. Left false, the plugin still parses and validates the config, and it binds no socket and builds no handler. A commit that sets it true rebuilds one handler for each subnet and binds the listeners again. Interfaces to serve DHCP on Interfaces to serve DHCP on. Ze binds one UDP listener for each name in the list. A name that fails to bind is logged as an error and skipped. When no name binds, the server logs that it is not serving and answers nothing. PXE boot server settings (RFC 4578) PXE boot server settings (RFC 4578). Ze adds these options only when the client vendor class in option 60 starts with PXEClient:. An ordinary DHCP client sees none of them. With pxe enabled, a commit also requires tftp-server, bootfile-bios and bootfile-uefi. HTTP URL for iPXE boot script (sent as option 67 to iPXE clients) HTTP URL for the iPXE boot script. Ze sends it as option 67 only to a client whose user class in option 77 starts with iPXE. That reply carries option 60

title: static
text: static filter import filters string final enumeration table <name> route <prefix> action discard blackhole forward next hop <address> bfd-profile string interface string weight uint16 interface <name> weight uint16 unreachable reject description string distance uint8 metric uint32 tag uint32 Static route configuration. Ze programs each route into the kernel through netlink, or into the VPP dataplane, and marks it with the static protocol number. A route the backend cannot program is skipped and logged, and the rest of the section still applies. Every route in the default table, forward, blackhole and reject alike, reaches the redistribute bus, where BGP can announce it. Route filter chains into the Loc-RIB. A name references a filter instance defined under the top-level policy root. The chain judges routes as they enter the Loc-RIB. Import policy into the Loc-RIB A rejected route stays in the Loc-RIB as a hidden path that is never selected, so relaxing the chain re-admits it without the protocol sending it again. The source's chain runs first, then the rib chain. Ordered filter instance references Run these filter instances in order. Each one passes the route on or rejects it; a filter type with no Loc-RIB route evaluator is refused. Decision after every filter passes Every present import policy must set final accept or final reject, even with no filters. A named routing table that holds static routes. A named routing table grouping. The table name is resolved to a kernel table ID through the routing-table registry. Use 'default' for the main routing table. A static route entry. The prefix is the key, so one table holds one entry for each prefix. Ze compares every leaf of the entry at a reload, the description included, and reprograms the route when one of them changed. What to do with matching packets. One case is required. Ze stops the load for a route that names none of next, blackhole and reject, and it names the prefix in the error. Every case reaches the redistribute bus. Drop the packet and tell the sender nothing. The case holds the blackhole container, and the presence of that container selects the action. Ze installs the route with the kernel blackhole type, so the kernel drops the packet and answers nothing. Drop the packet and send no ICMP message to the sender. The sender sees a timeout rather than a refusal, so a traceroute stops at this hop with no reply. Use reject when the sender SHOULD learn the destination is unreachable. Send the packet on toward a next hop. The case holds the next container, which carries gateway next hops and interface next hops. Two or more next hops of either kind become one ECMP route. A redistribute consumer sees this route only while one of its next hops is active. Forward action. Contains gateway and interface next-hops that may be combined for ECMP. Ze reads the hop list and the interface list, and joins the two into one set of next hops. A route whose next container holds neither one stops the config load. One next hop becomes a plain route, and two or more become a multipath route. Forward via gateway. Multiple entries produce ECMP with traffic distributed by weight. The gateway address is the key, so one route holds one entry for each gateway. Ze shares the traffic between the entries in proportion to their weights. An entry can name its own BFD profile, and a next hop whose BFD session goes down leaves the group. BFD profile name for this next-hop, from the bfd/profile list. BFD profile name (from bfd/profile list). When the BFD session to this next-hop goes down, Ze removes the next-hop from the ECMP group. Ze then reprograms the route with the remaining active next-hops. Commit, ze config validate and a SIGHUP reload refuse a name no bfd profile defines, naming the profiles that exist; the editor completes those names. The leaf names a list of another module that a build without BFD leaves out, so it is a ze:reference, not a leafref. The session is single-hop, so a commit is also refused when the profile sets passive (RFC 5881 Section 3). Outgoing interface. Required when the next-hop is a link-local IPv6 address. Ze resolves the name to a kernel interface index and sets it on the route. A link-local IPv6 gateway needs it, because the same address can exist on every link. A name that resolves to no interface skips this one route, which show static routes then reports with its reason. ECMP weight of this next-hop, 1 by default. ECMP weight. A higher value receives proportionally more traffic. The default of 1 gives equal distribution. Forward through the interface only, with no gateway address. Forward through the interface only, with no gateway address. This form serves point-to-point links, such as PPPoE and GRE tunnels, where the next-hop is implicit. Multiple entries can coexist with gateway next-hops for mixed ECMP. ECMP weight. Higher values receive proportionally more traffic. The range is 1 to 65535, and Ze reads 0 as 1. The weight counts only against the other next hops of the same route. A route with one next hop ignores it. Drop the packet and answer the sender. The case holds the reject container, and the presence of that container selects the action. Ze installs the route with the kernel unreachable type, so the kernel answers with ICMP destination unreachable. Drop the packet and send an ICMP unreachable to the sender. The sender learns at once rather than waiting for a timeout, which is what separates this from blackhole. The reply itself costs a packet per dropped packet. Operator note for this route. The note reaches show static routes and nothing else. It is not sent to the kernel, and no filter reads it. Ze compares the note at a reload, so a change to the note alone reprograms the route. The length is 0 to 255 characters. Administrative distance for this route alone (overrides rib distance static). Ze ranks this route at the value against every other protocol's route for the same prefix, in place of the distance rib distance static declares. The value applies to this route alone. Lower wins, and 0 is the best rank. Without the leaf the route ranks at the declared static distance, and a reload that changes the declaration re-ranks it. Route metric. Used as kernel route priority (lower is preferred) and carried in redistribute. Ze writes the value into the netlink route priority. The kernel prefers the lower priority when two routes cover the same prefix. 0 leaves the attribute out, so the kernel applies its own default. The redistribute event carries the same value. Opaque tag Ze attaches to this route for policy and redistribution. Ze prints the value in the tag field of show static route and in the config diff. A redistribute import rule can select routes by tag: write the same value in a tag leaf under redistribute destination <proto> import static. When Ze redistributes the route into OSPF, it writes the value into the External Route Tag of the AS-external LSA, and the tag on the route wins over the tag configured for the source. Ze writes the value into no kernel route, because Linux has no route tag attribute. A change to tag alone re-applies the route, because the config diff compares the field.

title: storage
text: storage smart check-interval uint32 enabled boolean self-test long day enumeration interval string time string short interval string time string temperature critical uint8 difference uint8 informational uint8 Storage device management The container holds the smart block alone. Ze reads it at config load and at each reload, and starts or stops the health manager to match. SMART disk health monitoring and self-test scheduling Ze polls each ATA and NVMe device it finds, and turns SMART on for a device that has it off. A reading past a threshold raises a warning or an error on the report bus, and a reading back under the threshold clears it. show storage smart prints the last reading of each device. Health poll interval in seconds 1800 seconds, which is 30 minutes, is the default, and the range is 60 to 86400 seconds. Ze polls once when the manager starts, and then at each interval. Every temperature test and every self-test decision happens on that poll, so this interval bounds how late an alert can arrive. Enable SMART monitoring on all detected ATA/NVMe devices false is the default, and nothing else under this container is read while the leaf holds false. Ze reads the leaf as false unless it holds exactly true. A change to false at a reload stops the poll loop, and clears every warning and error this component raised. Periodic SMART self-test scheduling Ze decides at each health poll whether a test is due, so check-interval bounds how close to the wanted time a test can start. Ze starts no test on a device that is already running one, and tries again at the next poll. Extended self-test schedule Ze starts the extended test at a poll where three conditions hold. The weekday matches the day leaf, the time of day has passed, and the interval since the last test has passed. The extended test takes a weekday of its own, and the short test does not. Preferred day of week for extended self-tests The seven weekday names are the accepted values, and sunday is the default. Ze reads the weekday from the local time of the appliance. The extended test starts on that day alone, whatever the interval leaf holds. Interval between extended self-tests, for example 7d The last letter names the unit: h for hours, d for days, m for minutes and s for seconds. A bare number is read as seconds. 7d is the default. A shorter interval still waits for the day leaf, so the test runs once in that week. Preferred time of day for extended self-tests (HH:MM) Ze starts the test at the first poll at or after this time on the named day. The clock is the local time of the appliance. 03:00 is the default. Ze skips the extended test while a short test is still running, and tries again at the next poll. Short self-test schedule Ze starts the short test at a poll where two conditions hold. The interval since the last test has passed, and the time of day has passed. The short test needs no weekday, and the extended test does. Interval between short self-tests, for example 24h The last letter names the unit: h for hours, d for days, m for minutes and s for seconds. A bare number is read as seconds. 24h is the default, and Ze keeps the default and logs a warning for a value it cannot read. Preferred time of day for short self-tests (HH:MM) Ze starts the test at the first poll of the day at or after this time, and only when the interval has also passed. The clock is the local time of the appliance. 02:00 is the default. Temperature alert thresholds in degrees Celsius Ze reads the temperature at each poll and compares it against the three leaves. A device that reports 0 degrees is read as having no reading, and Ze then raises nothing for it. Temperature above which a critical error is raised A reading at or above this value raises the temp-critical error, and clears the temp-high warning. 55 degrees is the default. Ze does not check that critical is more than informational, so a critical value at or under informational hides the informational warning completely. Temperature change threshold for rate-of-change alerts Ze compares the reading against the reading of the previous poll. A rise of this many degrees or more raises the temp-rising warning, and a smaller rise clears it. The first poll of a device raises nothing, because no previous reading exists. The range is 1 to 50 degrees, and 4 is the default. Temperature above which an informational warning is raised A reading at or above this value raises the temp-high warning, and a lower reading clears it. 45 degrees is the default. Ze tests the critical value first, so this warning never appears while the reading is also at or above critical.

title: sysctl
text: sysctl profile <name> setting <name> value string setting <name> value string Kernel tunable management. A setting entry applies to the host, and a profile entry applies to the interface units that name the profile. Ze validates a key it knows against the type and the range of that key. Ze accepts a key it does not know, and the kernel then refuses a value it cannot take. A named collection of kernel tunables that Ze applies together to interface units. A user-defined profile overrides a built-in profile that has the same name. Kernel tunables in this profile. The list holds 50 entries at most. Ze applies these settings to each interface unit that names the profile, and it replaces <iface> in each key with the name of that unit. One profile therefore serves every interface. Value to set for this key. The leaf is mandatory, so Ze refuses a profile setting with no value. Every interface unit that names this profile gets the same value, because only the key carries the <iface> placeholder. A kernel tunable that Ze sets persistently. The name uses kernel-native naming, for example net.ipv4.conf.all.forwarding. Value to set for this key. The leaf is mandatory, so Ze refuses a setting with no value. Ze writes the text into the /proc/sys file of the key. A key Ze knows is checked first: a bool key takes 0 or 1, and a range key takes an integer inside its own bounds.
