uint32 maintenance-window end string start string restart immediate empty time string spread uint32 url string System-level settings The container holds the system-wide settings. This module attaches the local user accounts under authentication, and the command authorization profiles under authorization. Named config archive destinations. Each entry names one destination, and Ze writes a copy of the config to every entry its trigger fires for. Filename format with token substitution. The tokens are {name} for the config basename, {host}, {domain}, {date} as YYYYMMDD, {time} as HHMMSS, and {archive} for the block name. Ze appends .conf. Archive destination URL (file://, http://, https://). A file:// URL writes to the local filesystem. An http:// or https:// URL uploads the config with an HTTP request. Any other scheme is refused when the config is validated. Time-based only: skip if config unchanged since last archive. With true, Ze skips a daily or hourly archive when the config did not change since the last one. The leaf changes nothing for the commit trigger and the manual trigger. HTTP upload timeout, in Go duration format, for example 30s. Ze gives up on an upload that passes this timeout. The format is the Go duration format, such as 30s or 2m, and the value must be above zero. An absent timeout is 30s. When to archive. The triggers are commit, manual, daily and hourly. System authentication settings System authentication settings. The user list under it holds the local accounts, which the local AAA backend reads. That backend runs after TACACS+ in the chain, so it answers when the remote server is unreachable. A configuration with no user rejects every local login. RADIUS servers for operator login over SSH, web and MCP (RFC 2865). This block is separate from the L2TP subscriber RADIUS path, which lives under the l2tp root. Credential the Access-Request carries for an operator login. RFC 2865 Section 4.1 and RFC 3579 Section 3.3 Note 1 permit one credential and never two, so ze sends exactly one. Select chap only when the RADIUS server holds the operator password in cleartext. RFC 2865 Section 2.2 states that 'CHAP requires that the user's password be available in cleartext to the server so that it can encrypt the CHAP challenge and compare that to the CHAP response. If the password is not available in cleartext to the RADIUS server then the server MUST send an Access-Reject to the client.' A server that stores password hashes cannot verify CHAP and rejects every login. With pap the password is recoverable from a captured request by anyone who holds the shared secret, because Section 5.2 hides it with a reversible XOR. The two eap values run a full RADIUS/EAP conversation: ze answers EAP itself, as the peer, with the password the operator typed, and the server drives it through Access-Challenge packets. eap-md5 carries the same cleartext-password requirement as chap. eap-mschapv2 needs the server to hold the NT hash instead, which is what an Active Directory backed server holds. Ze authorization profiles used when the Access-Accept carries no profile-attribute. This leaf is optional. Leave it unset when the RADIUS server always names a profile through profile-attribute. When the server does not name one, and no default is set here, the login names no profile and is denied. Ze never authorizes a user it cannot attach a profile to. Access-Accept reply attribute that names the user's ze authorization profiles. Filter-Id is the only value. RFC 2865 Section 5.25 says of Class that 'the client MUST NOT interpret the attribute locally', so ze cannot read a profile name out of Class. Transmit attempts per server before failover The value counts the transmissions Ze sends to one server, and not the retransmissions after the first. With the default 3, Ze sends the Access-Request and retransmits it twice before it moves to the next server. The range is 0 to 10, and a configured 0 reaches the client as 3, because the client reads 0 as unset. The budget that bounds one login can then cancel the exchange partway through those transmissions. The login falls through to the local accounts, which is the answer a slow server gets too. Read timeout for the wait between the transmissions. RADIUS servers, tried in configured order Ze sends the Access-Request to the first server, and it moves to the next one when that server does not answer. The order is the config order, because the list is ordered-by user. Each server gets a new Identifier, a new Request Authenticator, and the User-Password hidden again under the key of that server. RFC 2865 Section 4.1 requires the new Request Authenticator: 'The Request Authenticator value MUST be changed each time a new Identifier is used.' Where every server fails, the AAA chain moves on to the local accounts, so an unreachable server never locks the operator out. A row that carries no key builds no RADIUS backend at all, rather than a shorter server list. RADIUS shared secret (RFC 2865). RFC 2865 Section 3 states that the secret MUST NOT be empty (length 0). An empty secret lets an attacker forge packets. UDP authentication port (default 1812) 1812 is the port officially assigned to RADIUS. RFC 2865 Section 3 states that 'Exactly one RADIUS packet is encapsulated in the UDP Data field, where the UDP Destination Port field indicates 1812 (decimal).' The range is 1 to 65535. Ze joins this port to the server address and resolves the pair as udp4. This block sends Access-Requests only, so it addresses the authentication port, and no accounting port is configured here. Discard answers without Message-Authenticator (default true) When true, Ze silently discards an Access-Accept, Access-Reject, Access-Challenge or Protocol-Error from this server that carries no Message-Authenticator. This closes BlastRADIUS (CVE-2024-3596), where an attacker forges an Access-Accept from an Access-Reject. draft-ietf-radext-deprecating-radius Section 4.1 asks for this per-server flag. Set it false only for a server that predates 2024 and cannot sign its answers. Ze signs every Access-Request whatever this leaf says. Source IP for outbound RADIUS requests Ze binds the outbound udp4 socket to this address, so every Access-Request leaves with it as the source. An IPv4 address here is also sent as NAS-IP-Address (RFC 2865 Section 4.1). Where the leaf is absent, the kernel picks the address of the outgoing interface and no NAS-IP-Address is sent. NAS-Identifier carries the hostname of this device either way, so the request meets Section 4.1 with the leaf unset. An address this host does not hold refuses the bind, and Ze logs the failure. The RADIUS backend then contributes nothing, and login falls through to the local accounts. Per-server request timeout in seconds The value bounds the wait for one answer from one server. Each wait after a miss doubles the one before it. The default 3 therefore waits 3 seconds, then 6, then 12, across the three transmissions the default retries allows. The range is 1 to 60 seconds. The time one login spends on RADIUS is capped at 2 minutes, whatever timeout and retries hold. The login then falls through to the local accounts. TACACS+ server configuration (RFC 8907) The TACACS+ backend joins the AAA chain at priority 100, in front of the local backend at priority 200. Ze builds the backend only where the server list holds one entry or more. Authorization or accounting selected without a server is a configuration error. Authentication runs as soon as one server exists. Authorization and accounting are selected independently. RFC 8907 Section 10.5 requires a network providing privacy, integrity and separation from other traffic. TACACS+ obfuscation and source-address selection do not provide those protections. Enable accounting for every entered command Set it true to account for every entered command, irrespective of its authorization method. A server is required. One worker sends START and STOP records from a bounded 64-record queue. A full queue delays command admission rather than losing a record; shutdown drains accepted records within the configured server timeout bounds. Transport failures are logged and do not deny command execution. Enable per-command TACACS+ authorization The default false authorizes each command from the local profiles alone and sends the server nothing. Set it true and Ze sends an AUTHOR REQUEST for each command, with service=shell, cmd=<verb> and one cmd-arg for each argument (RFC 8907 Section 6). PASS_ADD and PASS_REPL permit execution only when the effective arguments describe the original command and every mandatory policy can be enforced. FAIL refuses the command. Ze sends privilege level 1 on these requests. TACACS+ servers, tried in configured order Ze tries the servers in the order you write them and moves to the next one when a connection or an exchange fails. The order is the config order, because the list is ordered-by user. Where every server fails, the AAA chain moves on to the local backend, so the local accounts still answer. Shared secret this server obfuscates its packets with The key is the shared secret RFC 8907 Section 4.5 builds the MD5 pseudo-pad from, and both ends must hold the same value. A client with no secret has no conformant packet to send. Section 10.5.2 requires a shared secret and forbids a client to set TAC_PLUS_UNENCRYPTED_FLAG. Omitting the key refuses the config: a commit, a load and a boot all stop on the missing mandatory field. The leaf is sensitive, so display paths mask it. Keys of 32 characters or longer are supported. Use at least 16 characters; doct

title: telemetry
text: telemetry prometheus basic-auth enabled boolean password string plaintext-password string realm string username string collector <name> enabled boolean interval uint16 enabled boolean interval uint16 netdata collector <name> enabled boolean interval uint16 enabled boolean interval uint16 prefix string path string prefix string server <name> ip ip-address port listener-port Telemetry export configuration. The container holds the Prometheus export settings and the Netdata- compatible collector settings. Prometheus metrics HTTP export. The container holds the enable switch, the listen endpoints, the metrics path, the HTTP Basic Authentication settings and the collector settings. HTTP Basic Authentication for the Prometheus service. The container holds the enable switch, the realm, the username and the two password leaves. Require HTTP Basic Authentication on the metrics and health endpoints. Ze asks for no credentials while this leaf is false, and false is the default. Hashed Basic Auth password (bcrypt or SHA-crypt); write plaintext to plaintext-password Ze compares the password of each request with this hash, and it compares the username in constant time. The hash is bcrypt, or a SHA-crypt hash ($6$ or $5$) kept from another system. A value that is neither stops the metrics server with an error, and the config check warns about it at commit. With basic-auth enabled, a username and this password are both required. Write-only password. On commit, the config system hashes this value into password and removes this leaf. The value is never written to the config file, and a display path renders the secret placeholder for it. HTTP Basic Authentication realm. A client shows the realm to the user when it asks for the credentials. The default is 'ze prometheus'. HTTP Basic Authentication username. The username pairs with the password leaf beside it. Deprecated: use netdata/collector. Per-Netdata-collector overrides (enable/disable, interval). Write netdata/collector instead. Ze reads this list only when the netdata container carries no collector list, and it then logs the deprecated path it read. A netdata collector list replaces this one whole, and the two are never merged. Enable or disable this collector. With false, Ze runs every other collector and stops this one. The default is true. Override sampling interval for this collector (seconds). Inherits global interval if not set. The range is 1 to 60 seconds. An absent leaf gives the collector the interval of the netdata container. The leaf lives under a deprecated list, so write netdata/collector/interval instead. Enable the Prometheus metrics endpoint. Ze serves no metrics endpoint while this leaf is false, and false is the default. Deprecated: use netdata/interval. Netdata-compatible OS collector sampling interval in seconds. Write netdata/interval instead. Ze reads this leaf only when the netdata container carries no interval leaf, and it then logs the deprecated path it read. The range is 1 to 60 seconds and the default is 1. Netdata-compatible OS collector metrics. These settings do not affect Ze-native metrics. The default of enabled is true, so an absent container still runs the collectors. The three settings under it replace the deprecated prefix, interval and collector leaves beside this container. Ze reads a deprecated leaf only when the matching leaf here is absent, and it logs the path it read. Per-Netdata-collector overrides of the enable state and the interval. Each entry names one collector, and it overrides the settings of that collector alone. Enable or disable this Netdata-compatible OS collector. With false, Ze runs every other collector and stops this one. The default is true. Override the sampling interval of this collector, in seconds. When this leaf is not set, the collector uses the global Netdata interval. Enable the Netdata-compatible OS collectors. With false, Ze exports the Ze-native metrics alone. The default is true. Netdata-compatible OS collector sampling interval in seconds. Each Netdata-compatible OS collector samples the operating system once in this interval. The range is 1 to 60 seconds, and the default is 1. Metric name prefix for Netdata-compatible OS collector metrics only. Ze puts the prefix in front of each Netdata-compatible OS collector metric name. It does not change a Ze-native metric name. The default is netdata. HTTP path of the metrics endpoint. A scraper reads the metrics at this path on each listen endpoint. The default path is /metrics. Deprecated: use netdata/prefix. The leaf sets the metric name prefix for Netdata-compatible OS collector metrics only. Prometheus listen endpoints. Each entry names one listen endpoint. The default endpoint is 127.0.0.1 on port 9273. Listen IP address The listener binds this address. 0.0.0.0 binds every IPv4 address of the host, and :: binds every IPv6 address. On most services :: is dual-stack: it also accepts IPv4 clients, so :: alone serves both families. Config validation refuses two listeners that share a protocol and a port when their addresses overlap. A wildcard address overlaps every address of its own family, and a dual-stack :: also overlaps every IPv4 address, so list :: alone rather than :: beside 0.0.0.0. A service whose IPv6 sockets are IPv6-only (L2TP, web) accepts :: beside an IPv4 address on the same port. Listen TCP port; 0 means OS-assigned The port range is 0 to 65535. Port 0 makes the operating system pick a free port at bind time, so no client can know the port before the listener starts. ze doctor tries to bind each configured endpoint and reports the one the host refuses.

title: traffic
text: traffic control backend string interface <name> qdisc class <name> ceil rate-bps match <type> value string priority uint8 rate rate-bps default-class leafref rate rate-bps type qdisc-type usage enabled boolean interfaces interface <name> enabled boolean max-entries uint32 stale-timeout uint32 track-ip boolean interval uint32 max-entries uint32 stale-timeout uint32 track-ip boolean Traffic subsystem: QoS control and byte-usage accounting. Two subtrees sit under it, and they are independent. control programs the queueing disciplines of each interface, which decides which packet leaves first. usage counts bytes with an eBPF program, and it changes no packet. Each subtree comes from its own plugin, so removing one plugin removes that subtree alone. Traffic control configuration of each interface. One entry exists for each interface Ze programs. The backend leaf names the program that applies the entries. Traffic control backend that programs the queueing disciplines. The default backend is tc, the queueing disciplines of Linux iproute2. Another backend declares itself through traffic.RegisterBackend. The ze:backend YANG extension on a feature node declares which backend supports that feature. The commit-time gate reads that extension and rejects a config that names a qdisc or a filter type the backend does not support. Traffic control of one named interface. The list key is the interface name. The root queueing discipline of the interface. Ze attaches this qdisc at the root of the interface, and every class hangs beneath it. An interface entry with no qdisc block attaches none. One traffic class of the queueing discipline. The list key is the class name. A class carries a rate, a ceil, a priority, and the filters that select its traffic. Largest rate this class can reach. An absent leaf takes the value of the rate leaf. A filter that classifies a packet into this class. The list key is the match type, so one class carries at most one match of each type. Value the filter matches. A mark filter takes a hex value. A dscp filter takes a DSCP name. A protocol filter takes a protocol name. Scheduling priority of this class. The value 0 is the highest priority. Rate this class is guaranteed. The value is a number and a unit, for example 10mbit or 100kbps. Name of the class that takes the unclassified traffic. The value is the name of a class in the class list of this qdisc. The leafref refuses a name no class of this qdisc carries. Rate of the classless TBF root. Root TBF rate. Required by backend tc for tbf, which has no configurable classes. The backend refuses a rate it cannot represent without truncation. VPP uses class policers instead and refuses this leaf. Type of the queueing discipline. The commit-time gate rejects a type the configured backend does not support. Per-interface eBPF TCX byte accounting (port/protocol always; per-IP via track-ip). Ze attaches two eBPF programs to each accounted interface with TCX, one on ingress and one on egress. They count bytes into per-interface LRU hash maps, keyed by L4 port and protocol. Where track-ip is true they also key by IPv4 address. One poll loop reads the maps and publishes the counts as metric series. The programs count only: they drop no packet and they change none. Enable traffic-usage accounting. The default false attaches nothing and starts no poll loop. Set it true and the config also needs one enabled interface or more under interfaces. Without one, the commit is refused and the error names the missing interface list. An accounting that would report nothing never reaches the kernel. Interfaces to account on. Ze accounts on the interfaces listed here and on no other. An interface with no entry is not accounted, and an entry whose enabled leaf is false is dropped before the attach. With usage enabled and this list empty, the commit is refused. Per-interface traffic-usage accounting. The entry names one interface and can override three leaves of the usage container: track-ip, stale-timeout and max-entries. What the entry does not set, it takes from the leaf of the same name under usage. An entry with a name and no body is accounted with every global value. A change to track-ip or to max-entries makes Ze detach the eBPF programs and attach them again, because both decide the shape of the maps. Account traffic on this interface. The default true accounts on the interface, so an entry with no body needs nothing more. Set it false and Ze drops the entry before it attaches anything. The accounting on that interface stops, and the rest of the list is not touched. To stop the whole feature, use the enabled leaf under usage. Override the global max-entries (per-map LRU capacity) for this interface (inherits when unset). The leaf overrides the max-entries leaf under usage for this interface alone, and an unset leaf takes the global value. The value is the capacity of each LRU map of the interface, so it also sets the memory the interface costs. An effective value of 0 is refused at commit. A change makes Ze attach the eBPF programs again, because a map takes its capacity at creation. Override the global stale-timeout for this interface, in milliseconds. 0 disables the cleanup for this interface. When the leaf is unset, this interface inherits the global stale-timeout. Override the global track-ip for this interface (inherits the global value when unset). The leaf overrides the track-ip leaf under usage for this interface alone, and an unset leaf takes the global value. True adds two more LRU maps to this interface, one for ingress and one for egress, keyed by IPv4 address. A change makes Ze attach the eBPF programs again, because the map set changes. Map poll interval in milliseconds (100ms..1h). One poll loop reads every map of every accounted interface at this period, so the value sets how fresh a metric series is. The default 1000 reads once a second. A value outside 100 milliseconds to 1 hour is refused at commit. The eBPF programs count at line rate whatever this value is, so a longer interval loses no bytes. Per-map LRU capacity; least-recently-used entries are evicted beyond this, keeping top talkers. The value is the capacity of each LRU map, and an interface takes it unless its own max-entries leaf overrides it. Ze creates two maps for each accounted interface, and two more where track-ip is true, so the value sets the memory the accounting costs. Beyond the capacity the kernel evicts the least recently used entry, which keeps the top talkers and loses the quiet ones. Remove a metric series unseen within this many milliseconds; 0 disables cleanup. Ze removes a metric series it has not seen within this time, which stops the series of a talker that left from staying forever. The value 0 disables the cleanup, so every series stays until the plugin stops. An interface can override the value with its own stale-timeout leaf. An interface value that is not 0 and less than 1 second is refused at commit. Account bytes per IPv4 address as well as per interface. The address is the source address on ingress and the destination address on egress. The default is false, which limits the number of metric series.

Ze declares one subsystem under it today, which is ipsec. That subsystem holds the ESP groups, the IKE groups and the site-to-site peers. IPsec VPN configuration. Ze speaks IKEv2 (RFC 7296) and installs each negotiated Child SA into the Linux XFRM stack. A peer references one ESP group and one IKE group, and those two carry the algorithms and the timers of the tunnel. Whether applications may override the SPD per socket: deny or allow. Whether a user or application may override this Security Policy Database. RFC 4301 Section 4.4.1: 'However, the system administrator MUST be able to specify whether or not a user or application can override (default) system policies.' On Linux an application overrides the SPD by setting a per-socket policy (IP_XFRM_POLICY, IPV6_XFRM_POLICY and the IPSEC_POLICY spellings), which outranks every SPD entry, the discard catch-all included. deny attaches a setsockopt guard to the cgroup2 root that refuses those four options with EPERM to every process in Ze's network namespace except Ze's own IPsec dataplane, so it needs ze to hold CAP_BPF and CAP_NET_ADMIN, a cgroup2 mount and Linux 6.10 or later; a guard that cannot attach fails the commit. allow attaches nothing, and Linux lets any process holding CAP_NET_ADMIN set one. A process holding CAP_NET_ADMIN can still write the SPD itself, which no setsockopt guard sees: ze doctor names every such process. Number of half-open IKE SAs tolerated before a COOKIE challenge. Number of half-open IKE SAs tolerated before an inbound IKE_SA_INIT must answer a COOKIE challenge. RFC 7296 Section 2.6 makes the challenge the answer to state and CPU exhaustion from forged source addresses. The default of 0 challenges every inbound initiation, which costs one extra round trip and stops a single spoofed datagram taking a peer's only half-open handshake slot. Raise it to tolerate that many half-open handshakes before challenging. ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload) group. The group carries the ESP proposals a peer offers for its Child SAs and the lifetime those SAs run under. A group MUST hold at least one proposal, and commit refuses an empty one. One group holds at most 255 proposals. SA lifetime in seconds. 0 disables expiry. The Child SA rekey trigger sits ahead of the lifetime by the larger of a random 10 percent and one retransmit budget. That lead is capped at half the lifetime. RFC 7296 Section 2.8 states the rule. 'When the lifetime of a Security Association expires, the Security Association MUST NOT be used.' Ze therefore tears the SA down at that point, even when a rekey is still in flight. The value 0 starts no rekey and no expiry. Perfect Forward Secrecy for Child SA rekeying. With enable, Ze puts a KEi payload in the CREATE_CHILD_SA request, and the replacement Child SA is keyed from a fresh Diffie-Hellman secret. With disable, Ze sends no KEi, and the replacement is keyed from SK_d alone, so one leaked SK_d reads every replacement Child SA. RFC 7296 Section 2.17 gives both KEYMAT forms. An ESP proposal carries no Diffie-Hellman group of its own, so Ze offers the group the IKE SA already negotiated. The default is enable, and Ze refuses a response that disagrees with what its request carried. ESP proposal, where a lower number is a higher priority. ESP proposal. Lower number = higher priority. One group offers at most 255 proposals, because RFC 7296 Section 3.3.1 numbers them in one octet. Encryption algorithm. chacha20poly1305 selects a fixed 256-bit AEAD key; omit hash. 3des selects a fixed 192-bit DES-EDE key including parity and requires hash. These ciphers are ESP-only. null selects integrity-only ESP, which RFC 4303 Section 1 requires to be negotiable. RFC 4303 Section 3.2 forbids ESP with neither confidentiality nor integrity, so a null proposal without a hash is refused at commit. Integrity algorithm. Integrity algorithm. It is required beside a non-AEAD cipher, and refused beside an AEAD cipher. RFC 7296 Section 3.3 gives an AEAD cipher its own integrity, so an ESP proposal offers the integrity transform NONE. An ESP proposal carries no PRF transform, so this leaf never names one. sha1 selects legacy HMAC-SHA-1-96 with a 160-bit key. It is supported for ESP integrity only, not for IKE. IKE (Internet Key Exchange) group. The group carries the IKE proposals, the IKE SA lifetime and the Dead Peer Detection timers. A group MUST hold at least one proposal, and commit refuses an empty one. One group holds at most 255 proposals. Action when peer closes the IKE SA. The default is none. The parser stores the value and no other code reads it, so none, start and restart leave the daemon with the same behavior. A session whose IKE SA the peer deletes tears its Child SA down and reconnects on a growing backoff. The session loop does this after every failure. Dead Peer Detection (DPD) settings (RFC 3706). The timers run whether or not this container is present. A peer with no DPD block probes every 30 seconds and waits 120 seconds for the answer. The probe is an empty INFORMATIONAL request, which is the liveness check of RFC 7296 Sections 1.4 and 2.4. Action when DPD detects a dead peer. The default is hold. One log line reads the value when the peer is declared dead, and no other code reads it. The three values restart, hold and clear leave the same behavior. Ze deletes the Child SA, ends the session, and reconnects on a growing backoff. DPD probe interval in seconds. Ze sends the next probe this long after the last one, and it sends none while a probe is outstanding. The default is 30 seconds. DPD timeout in seconds before declaring peer dead. The value bounds the whole liveness budget, so it covers the first probe and every repeat of it. RFC 7296 Section 2.4 allows the verdict only when 'repeated attempts to contact it have gone unanswered for a timeout period'. Ze repeats the probe on a growing backoff inside the budget and tears the SA down when the budget runs out. The default is 120 seconds. IKE protocol version. The default is ikev2 and the engine writes major version 2 into every header it sends. The parser stores the value and no other code reads it, so a group that names ikev1 commits and still runs IKEv2. IKE SA lifetime in seconds, where 0 starts no rekey. Ze rekeys the IKE SA before the lifetime runs out, on the trigger the ESP group lifetime describes. It also rekeys the SA as the message id space nears its ceiling. RFC 7296 Section 2.2 requires that. 'In the unlikely event that Message IDs grow too large to fit in 32 bits, the IKE SA MUST be closed or rekeyed.' The value 0 starts no rekey, so the SA runs until the peer or the operator ends it. IKE proposal, where a lower number is a higher priority. IKE proposal. Lower number = higher priority. One group offers at most 255 proposals, because RFC 7296 Section 3.3.1 numbers them in one octet. Diffie-Hellman group number (RFC 7296 Section 3.3.2). The number is Transform Type 4 of RFC 7296 Section 3.3.2. That section lists the values current at publication, up to 18, and sends the reader to the IANA registry for later ones. Ze takes 1 to 31 and refuses a group this build carries no transform for. The refusal lists the numbers the build does carry, which stops the reserved Transform ID 0 reaching the wire. Encryption algorithm. chacha20poly1305 and 3des are ESP-only in this build and are refused here. RFC 7296 Section 5 forbids ENCR_NULL for the IKE SA, so null is refused here too. The refusal lists the algorithms the build does implement for the IKE SA. PRF and integrity algorithm. It is required beside every cipher, and an AEAD cipher is no exception. RFC 7296 Section 3.3.3 makes the PRF a mandatory transform for an IKE proposal, and this leaf names it. An ESP proposal reads the same leaf as integrity alone, and refuses it beside an AEAD cipher. sha1 is ESP-only integrity in this build and has no IKE PRF, so it is refused here. The refusal lists the algorithms the build implements for IKE. WAN interface for IPsec traffic. Commit accepts a name no interface on the host carries yet, so a WAN created after Ze (a PPPoE unit) can be named; the doctor check ipsec-interface reports a name the host does not hold. The first IPv4 address of the interface fills the local-address of every peer that names none, and Ze follows it: when an address appears (a PPPoE or DHCP WAN that came up after Ze), those peers start; when it changes, they restart from the new address; when it leaves, they stop and remove their Child SAs, and wait. The IKE socket on port 500 binds there. The NAT-T socket on port 4500 also binds there unless live XFRM migration is available, when it listens on the wildcard and selects each SA's source address explicitly. A peer with its own local-address keeps its own socket and is never restarted by an interface address event. A reload whose interface holds no IPv4 address is refused, and the same case at startup runs, writes a warning, and the doctor check ipsec-interface-address names the waiting peers. Operator-authored Security Policy Database entry. An entry of the Security Policy Database that Ze installs directly, rather than one a Child SA negotiation produces. RFC 4301 Section 4.4.1 gives the database three dispositions: 'PROTECT, BYPASS, or DISCARD'. A peer under site-to-site produces the PROTECT entries, because those name a transform and a peer to negotiate it with. The other two name neither, so they are written here: BYPASS lets traffic cross the IPsec boundary in the clear, and DISCARD stops it at the boundary. Section 7.4 makes the discard disposition an obligation: 'All implementations MUST support DISCARDing of fragments using the normal SPD packet classification mechanisms.' This list is the management interface that Section 4.4.1 requires for it. Ze installs every entry when the configuration is applied and removes it when the entry leaves the configuration. An entry needs no peer, no key and no negotiation, so it is in force whether o

title: vpp
text: vpp api-socket string cpu main-core uint8 poll-sleep string worker-cores string workers uint8 dpdk interface <pci-address> name string rx-queues uint8 tx-queues uint8 enabled boolean external boolean lcp auto-subint boolean enabled boolean netns string sync boolean memory buffers uint32 hugepage-size enumeration main-heap string plugins af-packet boolean dpdk boolean wireguard boolean startup-cli-file string stats poll-interval uint16 segment-size string socket-path string VPP data plane configuration. Ze reads this subtree at startup and writes /etc/vpp/startup.conf from it, then starts /usr/bin/vpp. A change committed later logs "config reload requires daemon restart to take effect" and does not reach VPP until the daemon restarts. The enabled leaf is false by default, so every other leaf here changes nothing until you set it to true. GoVPP binary API Unix socket path. Ze writes this path into the socksvr section of startup.conf and then connects to it through GoVPP. The path MUST be absolute, MUST NOT contain "..", and MUST be 108 characters or less, which is the Unix socket path limit. Under external true Ze writes no startup.conf, so this leaf is the only setting Ze needs to reach a VPP process another supervisor started. Ze retries the connection 10 times, one second apart, inside a 30-second budget. VPP CPU pinning configuration. These leaves write the cpu section of startup.conf, and the main-core leaf pins the VPP main thread. The workers leaf asks for a count, and Ze takes those cores from the set the kernel isolated, which it reads from /sys/devices/system/cpu/isolated. The worker-cores leaf names the cores instead, and it MUST NOT be set beside workers. The poll-sleep leaf sits here for the operator, and Ze emits it in the unix section, because that is where VPP reads poll-sleep-usec. Omit every leaf to let VPP place its own threads, and Ze checks a placement leaf you set at commit. Ze refuses a core the host does not hold, a worker core that is also main-core, and a worker count the host cannot satisfy. CPU core for VPP main thread. Omit for automatic assignment. Ze writes this core number into the cpu section of startup.conf as main-core. The core is excluded from the worker set, so the main thread and a worker never share a CPU. Omit the leaf and VPP picks the main core itself, and Ze still counts the worker list from core 1. A core the host does not hold online is refused at commit. Fixed sleep between VPP main-loop polls, in whole milliseconds. Fixed sleep between VPP main-loop polls, expressed in whole milliseconds, which is the only accepted unit, for example 10ms. Ze emits it as unix { poll-sleep-usec N } in startup.conf, where 1ms is 1000 microseconds. Omit the leaf for VPP's default, where the workers busy-poll at 100% CPU with no sleep, and the latency is lowest. Set a non-zero value up to 100ms on a shared or dev host, to trade latency for idle CPU. An explicit 0ms is emitted and equals the default. Explicit CPU core list for the VPP worker threads. Ze writes these cores into the corelist-workers line of the cpu section in startup.conf, and writes no line when neither leaf is set. The syntax is the one the kernel uses for isolcpus: single cores, ranges, or both, as in 2-4 or 2,4,6. Set this leaf when the isolated set holds cores to keep for something else, and omit it to derive the cores from workers. It MUST NOT be set beside workers, because the two are separate answers to the same question, and Ze refuses a config that carries both. A core the host does not hold online, a core that is also main-core, and a core listed twice are each refused at commit. Cores outside the kernel's isolated set are accepted, and the vpp-cpu-isolation doctor check reports them. Number of VPP worker threads. Omit for automatic (one per available core). Ze turns this count into the corelist-workers line of the cpu section in startup.conf, and the worker-cores leaf names those cores instead. Ze takes the cores from the set the kernel isolated at boot, lowest first, with main-core excluded. Isolated 2-4 with main-core 2 and workers 2 therefore emits corelist-workers 3-4. When the kernel isolated no core, the list is contiguous and starts one core after main-core, so 4 workers with main-core 1 emits corelist-workers 2-5. The vpp-cpu-isolation doctor check then reports that the workers share their CPUs with Linux. A count the host cannot satisfy is refused at commit, and a value of 0 emits no line, which is what an absent leaf does. DPDK NIC configuration. Every NIC listed here is unbound from its kernel driver and bound to vfio-pci before VPP starts, so Linux loses the interface. Ze saves the original driver name and rebinds it when the daemon stops. Under external true Ze binds nothing, because the external supervisor owns that step. An empty list emits no dpdk section in startup.conf. DPDK-managed network interface. The list key is the PCI address, so this list holds one entry for each NIC. Ze loads the vfio, vfio_pci and vfio_iommu_type1 kernel modules, then binds each listed address to vfio-pci. A bind failure on one NIC unbinds every NIC Ze bound in the same pass, and VPP does not start. Short interface name (e.g. xe0, e1). Used in ze CLI and config. Ze writes this name into the dev entry of the dpdk section in startup.conf, so VPP calls the interface by it. The name is 1 to 15 characters of letters, digits, underscore, hyphen and dot, and a hyphen or a dot MUST NOT come first. Omit the leaf and Ze writes no name line, so VPP picks the interface name itself. Number of receive queues. Omit for VPP default. Ze writes this count into the dev entry of the dpdk section as num-rx-queues. An explicit 0 is written out, so it is not the same as an absent leaf. Omit the leaf and the line is absent, which leaves VPP on its own default. Ze does not compare the count against the queues the NIC holds. Number of transmit queues. Omit for VPP default. Ze writes this count into the dev entry of the dpdk section as num-tx-queues. An explicit 0 is written out, so it is not the same as an absent leaf. Omit the leaf and the line is absent, which leaves VPP on its own default. Ze does not compare the count against the queues the NIC holds. Enable VPP integration, so Ze manages the VPP lifecycle. Enable VPP integration. When this leaf is true, Ze manages the VPP lifecycle. Ze generates startup.conf, binds the DPDK NICs, starts the VPP process, and connects through GoVPP. Let an external supervisor own the VPP process, false by default. When this leaf is true, Ze does not exec or supervise the VPP process, generate startup.conf, or bind DPDK NICs. The external supervisor owns all of that. Ze only connects through GoVPP to api-socket. Use this leaf for systemd-managed VPP, for a container sidecar deployment, or for the `le test vpp` stub harness. The default is false, where Ze owns the VPP lifecycle. Linux Control Plane plugin settings. Linux Control Plane plugin. The plugin creates TAP mirrors in Linux for VPP interfaces. A routing daemon such as ze BGP can then use Linux TCP on a VPP-managed NIC. Auto-create sub-TAPs for dot1q/QinQ sub-interfaces. When this leaf is true, Ze writes lcp-auto-subint into the linux-cp section of startup.conf. A dot1q or QinQ sub-interface created in VPP then gets its own Linux sub-TAP. When it is false, Ze omits the line, so a sub-interface has no mirror in Linux and only its parent interface does. The default is true, and lcp enabled MUST also be true before Ze writes the line. Enable LCP plugin in VPP. When this leaf is true, Ze enables linux_cp_plugin.so and linux_nl_plugin.so in startup.conf, and writes the linux-cp and linux-nl sections. When it is false, no other lcp leaf reaches startup.conf and the netns leaf is not validated. The default is true. LCP gives each VPP interface a TAP mirror in Linux, so a routing daemon binds an ordinary Linux socket. Network namespace for LCP TAP interfaces. Routing daemons run in this namespace. Ze writes this name into the linux-cp section of startup.conf as default netns. VPP then creates the TAP mirrors under /var/run/netns/NAME. An EMPTY value is valid, and Ze then omits the line. It is the one value that leaves the TAPs in the namespace Ze runs in. An absent leaf is not the same as an empty one, because Ze seeds the default "dataplane" when the leaf is absent. With any name, Ze binds BGP in its own namespace and cannot bind on an LCP TAP address, which the doctor check vpp-lcp-netns reports. A name with a path separator, a space or an unprintable character is refused at commit. VPP truncates a name at a space, so the namespace it then opens under /var/run/netns/ does not exist. Sync VPP state changes (link, MTU, IP) to Linux TAP mirrors. When this leaf is true, Ze writes lcp-sync into the linux-cp section of startup.conf. A link, MTU or address change made in VPP then reaches the Linux TAP mirror. When it is false, Ze omits the line and the two sides drift apart. The default is true, and lcp enabled MUST also be true before Ze writes the line. VPP memory and buffer configuration. These leaves select VPP memory sizing and the buffers and statistics page mode. In a hugepage mode the ze doctor check adds the main heap, buffer memory and stats segment together and warns when the reservation is insufficient. Explicit default selects native base pages and does not require a hugepage reservation. An omitted hugepage-size still selects 2M. Number of packet buffers per NUMA node. 128000 is proven for full DFZ at 10G. Ze writes this count into the buffers section of startup.conf as buffers-per-numa, beside a fixed default data-size of 2048 bytes. The packet data alone costs the count multiplied by 2048 bytes on each NUMA node, so the default 128000 needs 250 MiB plus buffer metadata and alignment. A value of 0 is refused at commit with "vpp: memory buffers must be > 0". Hugepage size for VPP buffers. For 1G Ze writes page-size 1G into both buffers and statseg. For 2M it writes default-hugepage, which uses the kernel default hugepage size. Explicit default writes page-size default and uses native base pages, whose size is a kernel fact, without a hugepage reservation. The default remains 2M and no failed hugepage request falls back to base pages. The doctor check warns about an unsupported 1G CPU and reports missing or insufficient reservations for hugepage modes. VPP main heap size (e.g. 512M, 1G, 1536M). Production with full DFZ: 1536M. Ze writes this size into the memory section of startup.conf as main-heap-size. The value MUST be digits followed by M or G, so 1536M is accepted and 1.5G is refused at commit. The ze doctor check counts this size toward the reservation only when a hugepage mode is selected. Optional VPP plugins to load. Explicit VPP plugin enablement. startup.conf disables plugins by default. DPDK remains enabled by default and can be disabled only when no DPDK interfaces are configured. AF_PACKET is opt-in. uRPF always loads because configured IPv4 reverse-path checks depend on it. Linux Control Plane plugins load when lcp is enabled, and selected features register their own requirements. Load the AF_PACKET native plugin for a configured host-interface path. Load af_packet_plugin.so so an explicitly configured AF_PACKET native access path can use host interfaces. Omission leaves it disabled. This selection does not create an interface, change the interface backend or provide the required Linux Control Plane pair. Load the DPDK native plugin, enabled by default. Load dpdk_plugin.so. The default preserves existing startup output. Explicit false is for a configured non-DPDK access path and is refused while any DPDK interface is configured. A missing installed plugin never changes this selection automatically. Load wireguard_plugin.so for the vpp interface backend. Load wireguard_plugin.so so the vpp interface backend can program WireGuard tunnels. The tunnels are configured as interface wireguard under back

title: Configuration Syntax Changes
text: Configuration Syntax Changes Ze has not shipped a stable release, so there is no deprecation lifecycle for its config syntax. The infrastructure that converts a config written in an older format of Ze's own syntax is kept: ze config migrate and the start-time schema evolution run every conversion a package registers, and the load parsers refuse a registered relocated block or retired leaf naming that fix (syntax, "Schema Evolution and Migration"). The conversion of one format change is written only once Ze has a stable release, so none is registered today. When the syntax changes, the configurations in the repository are converted in the same change. A config file records the schema stamp of the release that wrote it, and recovery after a downgrade chooses the newest rollback file that the running binary can parse. Compatibility rules Case What Ze does Current config ze config validate <file> checks it directly. Older pre-release Ze syntax The parse fails, naming the line and the unknown keyword. Edit the file to the current syntax. ExaBGP syntax ze exabgp migrate converts the shapes it supports and warns about the extensions it does not translate. Newer schema stamp after downgrade Startup tries rollback files newest-first and writes back the first one this binary can parse. Unsupported ExaBGP extensions ze exabgp migrate translates the capability keywords Ze has a session setting for, and WARNS about every other keyword the block holds. The warning goes to stderr, names the peer and names each keyword in one line. The migrated session negotiates less than the ExaBGP config asked for, so read the warnings before you deploy the output. The set is derived, not listed: migrateCapability declares the keywords it translates (route-refresh, extended-message, link-local-nexthop, asn4, graceful-restart, software-version, add-path), and anything else in the block reaches the warning. A keyword ExaBGP adds later is therefore reported without an edit here. Syntax Result capability { multi-session; } Warns: peer <name>: the capability block asks for "multi-session", which `ze exabgp migrate` does not translate, so the migrated config does not ask for it capability { aigp enable; } Same warning, naming aigp. Ze's AIGP codec is always on and has no per-peer switch, so there is no setting to translate the keyword into Several in one peer One warning names them all, in the order the block declares them operational { ... } under an ExaBGP neighbor ze exabgp migrate stops at the parser: line N: unknown field in neighbor: operational capability { multi-session; } in Ze syntax ze config migrate stops at the parser: line N: unknown field in capability: multi-session operational { ... } under a peer, in Ze syntax ze config migrate stops at the parser: line N: unknown field in peer: operational The capability block is the only place a warning replaces a refusal. An operational { ... } block, in either syntax, is a parse error: the grammar has no such field, so there is nothing to leave out. Two of the keywords are worth knowing by name, because each comes from an IETF draft that expired without becoming an RFC. Extension Draft Expired Codepoint multi-session draft-ietf-idr-bgp-multisession-07 2013-03-16 Section 4 assigns capability code 68 operational draft-ietf-idr-operational-message-00 2012-09-01 Section 9 requests a capability code and a BGP message type from IANA. Neither was allocated operational therefore has no assigned value to put on the wire. ExaBGP fills both with private values of its own, capability 0xB9 and message type 0x06. Ze does not copy a private codepoint. Commands # Check whether a file matches the current binary ze config validate config.conf # Convert an ExaBGP config to Ze syntax ze exabgp migrate exabgp.conf # Rewrite a current Ze config in the set or hierarchical form ze config migrate format hierarchical config.conf # List the format conversions this binary carries ze config migrate --list See Configuration Migration for command details.

title: Ze Features
text: Ze Features Ze is an open-source configuration and protocol engine written in Go. The network operating system built on it runs on any Linux or as a gokrazy appliance. Status values: Supported means every completion criterion its kind requires holds, including a current recorded green run of each real-path test and of each counted interop scenario; Experimental means implemented and reachable through its real entry point, without the evidence Supported requires; Stub-backed means implemented, with the evidence for its external dependency coming only from a stub harness; (partial) after a level means the named scope gaps are not implemented or not proven; Future means planned but not shipped; Rejected means unsupported by design. Protocols Feature Status Description AIGP (RFC 7311) Experimental (partial) Accumulated IGP Metric path attribute: wire encoding and decoding, receive validation, structured JSON exposure with RFC 4271 attribute flags, per-session enablement (internal sessions on, external sessions off unless configured), configured origination, next-hop-self accumulation, and best-path selection after LOCAL_PREF and before AS_PATH (RFC 7311 Section 4.1). AIGP is an attribute, not a capability, so capability { aigp } is refused. Next-hop-self source-cost propagation is not yet established end to end, and automatic origination is not enabled. Scope gaps: next-hop-self source-cost propagation end to end; automatic origination. AS112 Anycast DNS Experimental (partial) Authoritative sink for misdirected RFC 1918 / link-local reverse-DNS queries (RFC 7534) and the EMPTY.AS112.ARPA DNAME-redirection zone (RFC 7535). Four fixed anycast host addresses (never operator-typed), registered against the iface address-ownership registry and bound via IP_FREEBIND. Optional allow-from client-source access list (loopback always permitted). BGP integration composes existing healthcheck/watchdog/update-block mechanisms: the anycast route announces only once a probe against a real anycast service address confirms the DNS service is healthy, with an operator-chosen community and optional AS112-origin AS_PATH override. show as112, as112 health [target <ip>], ze_as112_* metrics. The four covering prefixes can also be BGP-originated directly through the redistribute path (redistribute { destination bgp { import as112 } }) with a configurable origin ASN (asn, default 112) and community, health-gated by the watchdog serving-state check (RFC 7534 Section 3.3). Compile-out-able with the ze_as112 build tag: default-on in ZE_FEATURES, dropped from ze-stripped / bare ze_core builds, with its config block rejected as unknown. Scope gaps: RFC 7858 and RFC 8484 MUST gaps for DoT and DoH; RFC 7535 is not proven; no DNS interop. Authoritative DNS Answer Policy Experimental One harness serves as112 and geodns, so both answer a malformed or out-of-scope query the same way. A name outside every served zone gets REFUSED with the AA bit CLEAR, because RFC 1035 Section 4.1.1 gives AA one meaning and a responder that keeps it set on a Refused reply asserts an authority it does not have. A name inside a served zone that the zone does not own gets NXDOMAIN. A name that exists with no record of the requested type gets NOERROR with an empty Answer. Both negative answers carry the zone SOA in the Authority section, which RFC 2308 Section 3 requires so a resolver can cache them. A non-query opcode gets NOTIMP. A UDP reply is bounded to 512 octets (RFC 1035 Sections 2.3.4 and 4.2.1) or to the larger buffer the requestor advertised in an OPT record (RFC 6891 Section 6.2.3), with TC set; an advertisement below 512 does not lower the bound. TCP, DoT and DoH are unbounded. BFD Liveness Detection Experimental (partial) RFC 5880 Bidirectional Forwarding Detection plugin: pinned single-hop (UDP 3784) and multi-hop (UDP 4784) sessions, profile-driven timer bundles, GTSM enforcement (IP_TTL=255 outbound / IP_RECVTTL ingress gate), multi-hop min-TTL floor, RFC 5880 §6.8.7 TX jitter (0-25%, clamped to [10%, 25%) when detect-multiplier=1), SO_BINDTODEVICE for single-hop interface and multi-VRF binding, BGP peer opt-in with RFC 9384 Cease subcode 10 teardown, BFD strict mode (draft-ietf-idr-bgp-bfd-strict-mode: capability 74 negotiated in OPEN, the BFD session opened before the BGP FSM starts, the BGP session held in OpenSent until BFD is Up, the BfdHoldTimer for a negotiated hold time of zero, and FSM events 30 to 35), show bfd sessions/session/profile commands, ze_bfd_* Prometheus metrics, RFC 5880 §6.7 Keyed SHA1/MD5 (meticulous variants included) authentication with file-backed sequence-number persistence, and RFC 5880 §6.4 Echo mode config/wire advertisement (transport half tracked as spec-bfd-6b-echo-transport). Compile-out-able with the ze_bfd build tag (default-on in ZE_FEATURES): a stripped build drops the engine, session, transport, auth, and command surface and rejects a bfd {} block, while the nil-able client seam (bfd/api, with the bfd/packet State/Diag types) stays always-on so BGP, OSPF, and static route monitors run without BFD by their existing warn-and-degrade path. Scope gaps: RFC 5880 and RFC 5881 obligations the ledger marks Partial; Echo mode transport half (spec-bfd-6b-echo-transport). BGP Protocol Experimental (partial) For ordinary BGP transit, attach the same bgp-rib process to the source and destination peers. Ze advertises the selected learned route to each destination whose export policy accepts it. On a new session or a route refresh, Ze sends the current exportable selection. Ordinary transit configuration bgp peer <address> timer delay-open <seconds> holds the local OPEN until the remote OPEN arrives or the configured 1–240 second timer expires. Zero disables the wait. Strict BFD keeps the handshake bounded while waiting for BFD Up. An incoming connection validates its role without changing an incumbent's learned relationship; selection publishes its retained OPEN pair before peer-up. bgp aggregate <prefix> makes bgp-rib synthesize one IPv4 or IPv6 aggregate route while selected routes more specific than the prefix exist, following RFC 4271 Section 9.2.2.2, install it in the Loc-RIB and announce it. Routes whose MULTI_EXIT_DISC differs are not aggregated: the aggregate is suppressed and a warning names the prefix. ORIGIN is the worst of the contributors (INCOMPLETE, then EGP, then IGP). When the contributors' NEXT_HOPs differ, next-hop names the local address to use, and the aggregate is suppressed when that address is not local; without it Ze picks a local session or interface address of the family. The AS_PATH is the contributors' common leading AS_SEQUENCE and never holds an AS_SET, and ATOMIC_AGGREGATE is set when a contributor carries it or when AS numbers were left out. The contributors' AGGREGATOR attributes are discarded, and Ze attaches its own (local AS and router ID) unless aggregator false. brief-origin-as <asn> truncates the AS_PATH after the right-most instance of that AS, the consistent brief aggregation of RFC 9774 Section 5.2. Unit tests cover the synthesis; no functional test or interop scenario configures aggregation yet. 23 address families, 14 capabilities, 15 path attributes. bgp update-delay max-delay <seconds> holds the first advertisement of a speaker that has just started until every configured peer has sent its End-of-RIB marker, until an optional establish-wait expires, or until max-delay expires, so a neighbor receives one settled route set instead of an initial set followed by corrections. show bgp update-delay reports whether the speaker is holding and what it waits for. With max-delay set, bgp-rib also defers best-path selection per address family, as RFC 4724 Section 4.1 requires of a restarting speaker: a family is selected once every configured peer has negotiated and each one that advertised Graceful Restart without the Restart State bit has sent its End-of-RIB for that family, or once max-delay expires. title: Glossary
text: Glossary Terms used in Ze documentation and operator output. BGP and routing Adj-RIB-In Routes accepted from a peer and retained before or alongside local best-path selection. Ze does not keep every import-rejected route unless a component explicitly records it. Adj-RIB-Out Routes selected and prepared for advertisement to one peer. AFI/SAFI Address Family Identifier and Subsequent Address Family Identifier. Together they identify a BGP family such as IPv4 unicast, EVPN, or FlowSpec. AS path The sequence of autonomous systems a BGP route has traversed. Ze uses it for loop detection, policy, best-path selection, and topology display. BART Balanced Routing Table, the gaissmai/bart library under Ze's prefix-keyed route store. It is Knuth's Allotment Routing Table (ART) laid out as a stride-8 multibit trie. It is unrelated to the Adaptive Radix Tree (Leis et al., 2013), which shares the ART acronym. BGP Role An RFC 9234 relationship such as provider, customer, peer, route server, or route-server client. Roles help detect route leaks and control OTC processing. End-of-RIB A BGP marker indicating that the initial or refreshed update stream for a family is complete. FIB Forwarding Information Base. The routes programmed into a dataplane such as the Linux kernel, VPP, or P4. Loc-RIB The local set of selected routes after protocol and policy processing. NLRI Network Layer Reachability Information. The family-specific route payload carried by BGP. RIB Routing Information Base. A route store used for candidate, accepted, selected, or advertised routing state, depending on context. RPKI Resource Public Key Infrastructure. Ze uses validated ROA data received over RTR to determine whether a route origin is Valid, Invalid, or NotFound. RTR RPKI-to-Router protocol used between a validating cache and a router. Resilience and policy ADD-PATH A BGP capability that allows more than one path for the same prefix to cross a session. Send and receive modes are negotiated per family. Graceful Restart RFC 4724 behaviour that retains stale forwarding state while a BGP speaker restarts and refreshes its routes. Long-Lived Graceful Restart RFC 9494 extension that retains and deprioritises stale routes beyond the ordinary Graceful Restart window. Import filter An ordered policy chain applied to a route received from a peer before it enters eligible local routing state. Export filter An ordered policy chain applied for one destination peer before advertisement. OTC Only-to-Customer, the RFC 9234 path attribute used with BGP Roles to detect and prevent route leaks. Route reflection RFC 4456 distribution of iBGP routes through reflectors and clients, avoiding a full iBGP mesh. Route server A BGP speaker that distributes eligible routes between participants while preserving the participant next hop and applying per-member policy. Ze configuration and operation Active configuration The configuration revision currently applied to the running system. Candidate configuration A proposed configuration revision being edited and validated before commit. Commit The transaction that verifies, applies, and activates a candidate configuration. In route injection, a named commit window groups route operations atomically. Component A Ze subsystem that owns runtime behaviour, configuration, commands, health, metrics, or plugins. Doctor Offline readiness checks run with ze doctor. Findings have structured diagnostic codes that can be inspected with ze show diagnostic. Handler A callback registered by a component or plugin for configuration, commands, events, codecs, validation, or lifecycle stages. Plugin A registered Ze extension. Plugins may run in process or as external programs and can own configuration, commands, events, filters, families, services, or dataplane integration. Plugin hub The authenticated transport and dispatch layer used by external plugins and managed components. It is separate from Fleet Management even when configuration shares a surrounding plugin block. ZeFS Ze's blob artifact format (.zefs): a seed, a backup, or an import source carrying the same keys as the live database/ store. It is never the live store. Operator surfaces CLI The interactive or one-shot command interface reached over Ze's SSH server. gNMI The OpenConfig gRPC Network Management Interface used for YANG-oriented Capabilities, Get, Set, and Subscribe operations. Looking Glass The public read-only BGP peer, route, search, and AS-path view. It runs separately from the authenticated web workbench. MCP Model Context Protocol. Ze exposes registered commands and structured resources to authorised AI clients through its MCP server. Web workbench The authenticated browser interface for configuration, commands, operational tables, and live state. Testing Functional transcript A .ci scenario that drives real processes, commands, files, HTTP requests, peers, and expected outputs. Interop test A scenario that runs Ze against another real implementation such as FRR, BIRD, GoBGP, strongSwan, xl2tpd, or accel-ppp. Property An invariant checked across a scenario, such as convergence, route isolation, or state consistency. Shrink Reduction of a recorded chaos event sequence to the smallest sequence that still reproduces a failure.

title: RFC Implementation Status
text: RFC Implementation Status This page is Ze's public RFC proof ledger. It lists the RFCs Ze implements, in part or in full, and for each one how much of what the RFC requires is proven. It reports proof only: whether an operator can use a capability is a property of the feature that carries it (features/<id>.md, its Scope), not of the RFC. Every row below is declared by the RFC's own summary, in the ## Meta table of rfc/short/<stem>.md. A row belongs here only when current docs, source code, tests, or learned closure notes tie the RFC to a Ze feature, and a summary that ties to none writes | Support | - | instead. The per-requirement detail behind each row is published at /quality/rfc-compliance/<stem>/, one page for every summary under rfc/short/, naming each requirement, the tests bound to it, the audit verdict a reader recorded, and every gap and untested MUST under its own requirement id. The 24 of 243 summaries (9.9%) with no row on this page are published there too, and the index at /quality/rfc-compliance/ links all of them. Area is the one cell an author writes, a classification. Every other cell is derived, and no author can change it: Proof is N of M MUST proven: of the M MUST-level requirements the summary gates, the N whose tests a recorded break still verifies (rfc/discrimination/<stem>/<requirement-id>.json), counting a requirement a layer under Ze performs once its recorded break proves the state Ze installs for that layer (OS verified). A tag with no verifying record, and a record that escapes the break (no-break, kernel-producer), prove nothing here. An RFC whose requirement list has not been walked against the RFC's own text (no valid rfc/extraction/<stem>.json) reads not walked and publishes no number, because its list bounds nothing. A walked RFC gating no MUST-level requirement reads no MUST rows. Evidence counts the rows Ze's tests prove by the strongest kind of test behind each (interop, then functional, editor, unit), and the OS verified rows as os, so the counts sum to N. Unmet lists the requirement ids the summary annotates {gap}, {partial} or {linux-limit}, and those an audit judged not met, at every level. A brief table (Internet-Drafts and other standards) carries Area, Proof and Unmet and leaves Evidence out, so an unmet requirement of a draft is still named by its id. How strong the proof behind a row is. Every requirement's evidence is listed in that RFC's own file under rfc/requirements/, with a kind/tier cell per test link. kind is the layer the test exercises (unit, functional, editor, interop); tier is whether anything executes it. verify means it runs in ./le verify current on every push. interop/nightly runs only in the scheduled, advisory evidence-nightly workflow -- so a requirement whose evidence is entirely nightly-tier is marked **nightly-only** on its row there, and counted in its own column of the coverage rollup in ai/RFC-REQUIREMENTS.md. A tag in a suite no pipeline runs is refused outright rather than published with a caveat. ./le rfc check refuses an enrolled RFC that carries an unmet requirement and renders no row here, and a row that disappears while its summary remains. title: Security Policy
text: Security Policy Supported Versions The project is not yet released. Security fixes will be provided for the latest released version. We intend to provide a smooth upgrade path, allowing users to update to the latest version if/when required. Scope Ze is a Network OS handling BGP sessions, SSH access, and configuration management. The following areas are particularly security-sensitive: BGP message parsing and wire protocol handling SSH/CLI authentication and authorization Plugin process isolation and IPC boundaries Configuration injection or unauthorized modification Web UI and MCP server access control Regular bugs (crashes, incorrect route selection, CLI rendering) should be filed as normal issues unless they can be triggered by an unauthenticated remote peer or escalated into unauthorized access. Reporting a Vulnerability To report vulnerabilities, contact Thomas Mangin by email: ze@mangin.com What to expect: Acknowledgment within 7 days. An initial assessment and next steps within 14 days. Coordinated disclosure once a fix is available. We will credit reporters unless they prefer anonymity. Please include: affected version or commit, steps to reproduce, and potential impact.

title: Style guide.
text: Design system Style guide. The palette, components, and content rules this site follows -- so new pages stay consistent without re-deriving them from scratch. Support a memorable headline with concrete information. A generic slogan does not explain the product's value. 3. ### Explain advantages through their consequences Connect each technical capability to what the reader can accomplish. Explain the practical value of shared configuration, external plugins and ExaBGP migration with examples and their limitations. A protocol list establishes breadth, but cannot carry the whole argument. 4. ### Show the product doing useful work Use authentic interfaces, readable configuration examples, demonstrations and explanatory diagrams. Each visual makes a clear point and has enough space to show it. A terminal thumbnail that cannot be read provides little evidence. Choose useful preview frames, explain them with captions and provide access to the full recording. 5. ### Create hierarchy without emptying the page Let readers understand the proposition at a glance, scan the reasons to explore, then examine the details. Use scale, grouping, alignment, contrast and spacing to distinguish these levels. A long page is useful when each section gives readers a reason to continue. 6. ### Use visual richness deliberately Color, gradients, shadows, layered surfaces and illustration can give the site character and depth. Use them consistently to establish emphasis and relationships. Give demonstrations, evidence, feature comparisons and articles compositions suited to their content instead of putting everything into identical cards. Use white space to aid comprehension, rather than merely enlarge the page. 7. ### Give every section a reader purpose and a useful next step Each section helps readers understand Ze, assess its fit, inspect evidence or choose how to try it. Keep documentation, migration, appliance, developer and community paths discoverable. Label links with the destination or the action they offer. 8. ### Make credibility visible and specific Retain meaningful statistics, interoperability evidence, source links and updates. Explain what the numbers measure and distinguish capabilities from test evidence and production maturity. Keep the pre-release status clear. Place evidence with the claim it supports, rather than using counters as decoration. 9. ### Use a coherent, accessible system Share typography, spacing, color roles, elevation, controls and interaction states. Adapt layouts to homepages, references, documentation and articles while preserving Ze's identity. Check keyboard access, contrast, zoom, mobile layouts and redu
