title: Immutable appliance A/B lifecycle and safe rollback
displayTitle: Immutable appliance A/B lifecycle and safe rollback
text: Immutable appliance A/B lifecycle and safe rollback Build a self-contained read-only Ze appliance image on gokrazy, deploy OS updates to the inactive A/B root slot with --testboot before committing permanently, protect live configuration changes with timed commit confirmed rollback windows, and back up both the live ZeFS store and encrypted bastion state. Role and topology Operator workstation (./ze-host) Ze gokrazy appliance (10.12.104.10) ├── appliance.json + encrypted DR export ├── Root slot A (active, read-only) ├── HTTPS OTA push (--testboot / permanent) ──► ├── Root slot B (inactive, next image) └── SSH config-push + commit confirmed ──► └── /perm (persistent ZeFS store & certs) Appliance manifest (appliance.json) Define credentials, management listeners, TLS identity, target device address, and image geometry in one manifest (based on docs/guide/appliance.md): { "credentials": { "username": "exa", "admin-enabled": true }, "ssh": { "host": "0.0.0.0", "port": "2222" }, "web": { "enabled": true, "host": "0.0.0.0", "port": "8080" }, "tls": { "cert-name": "router.local", "validity-years": 10 }, "identity": { "hostname": "ze-prod" }, "device": { "address": "10.12.104.10", "update-port": 443 }, "image": { "arch": "amd64", "size-bytes": 2147483648, "kernel-profile": "hardware-kms" } } Automatic config archiving on commit Retain local commit history and ship snapshots to /perm or an HTTPS archive endpoint automatically on every commit (based on docs/guide/config-archive.md): system { host router1; domain dc1.example.com; commit-revisions 20; archive local-backup { location file:///perm/backups/ze; trigger commit; } archive offsite { location https://archive.example.com/configs; trigger daily; on-change true; timeout 10s; filename "{host}-{date}-{time}"; } } (For writable Linux/systemd hosts rather than read-only gokrazy appliances, Ze also supports system { update-check { url ...; maintenance-window { ... }; } } with update system firmware check|download|apply|restart|rollback; see the self-update guide.) Build, A/B testboot, and promote workflow Build the host driver and appliance disk/ISO image from your workstation: ./le build host-driver ./ze-host appliance init ze-prod ./ze-host appliance build ze-prod ./ze-host appliance iso ze-prod Take a live ZeFS backup on the appliance before upgrading: request data backup path /perm/ze/pre-upgrade.zefs Push the new image to the inactive root slot as a one-shot testboot (a subsequent reboot falls back to the previous root slot automatically): ./ze-host appliance push --testboot ze-prod Verify health and running version over SSH before making the new slot permanent: show version --extended show system platform show doctor show config running Promote the tested slot permanently (or push across a fleet with --all --parallel 4): ./ze-host appliance push ze-prod Safe live config changes (commit confirmed) In the SSH or web configuration editor, bare commit is refused. Use commit confirmed <seconds> (1 to 3600 seconds) so a bad change that locks out management reverts automatically when the timer expires: commit verify commit confirmed 120 # Verify connectivity and routing, then confirm permanently: commit accept # Or revert immediately: commit abort To restore a previous store snapshot on the running appliance: request data restore path /perm/ze/pre-upgrade.zefs config # Or replace the full store (clean shutdown + restart): request data restore path /perm/ze/pre-upgrade.zefs full For workstation disaster recovery of the appliance credentials and manifest, export an Argon2id + XChaCha20-Poly1305 encrypted bundle: ./ze-host appliance export ze-prod # Restore on another workstation: ./ze-host appliance import ze-prod.ze.enc Lab evidence Real gokrazy A/B OTA in QEMU (image build, HTTPS push, reboot, version check, /perm persistence): ./le test qemu appliance-ota (internal/le/test/qemu/install_ota.go) SSH config-push + reboot persistence in QEMU: ./le test qemu appliance-config (internal/le/test/qemu/install_config_push.go) Appliance functional tests: ./le test functional appliance (test/appliance/) Commit-confirmed timeout, accept, abort, disconnect, and restart tests: ./le test bgp plugin --pattern session-editor-commit-confirmed (test/plugin/session-editor-commit-confirmed-*.ci) Live and offline backup/restore tests: test/plugin/data-backup.ci, test/plugin/data-backup-live.ci, test/plugin/data-backup-refused-live.ci Current limits Shared boot partition and persistent /perm: Gokrazy maintains two root slots, while the boot partition is shared and /perm persists across root-slot rollbacks. Rolling back a --testboot image does not revert config edits saved in /perm. Operator verification required on --testboot and config-push: Neither --testboot nor ./ze-host appliance config-push runs automatic routing health checks; operators verify SSH and routing state before promoting. No external shell plugins on gokrazy: Read-only gokrazy images have no /bin/sh or PATH, so only built-in internal plugins run on the appliance. Separate backups for workstation vs. live store: ./ze-host appliance export backs up the bastion manifest and keys, not disk images or the appliance's live ZeFS database (keep request data backup separately). update system firmware is Linux/systemd only: Self-update is not supported on read-only gokrazy filesystems; use ./ze-host appliance push. Related guides Appliance guide Appliance install lab Config editor guide Config archive guide Self-update guide

title: AS-Path Topology
text: AS-Path Topology Use the built-in Looking Glass to turn the AS paths for a prefix into a topology view. The graph is an operational aid for comparing what different peers advertise, not a complete map of the Internet. RFC completion: the Looking glass coverage page shows which requirements have passed the recorded test checks for this use case. What the graph shows For one prefix, Ze collects eligible paths visible through the Looking Glass and builds a directed AS graph. Nodes are AS numbers and edges are observed AS-path adjacencies. Multiple peers may contribute the same edge or different paths to the same origin. The graph helps answer: Which origins are visible for this prefix? Which transit sequence did each peer advertise? Are several peers showing the same upstream path? Did a route leak or unexpected prepend change the shape? Does the selected best path match the available alternatives? Deploy a complete lab The graph reads routes through the command dispatcher, so load bgp-rib and enable the read-only Looking Glass. Save this configuration as as-path-lab.conf: plugin { internal rib { use bgp-rib; } } environment { looking-glass { enabled true; server main { ip 127.0.0.1; port 8443; } } } bgp { router-id 192.0.2.10; session { asn { local 64500; } } filter { import { final accept; } export { final reject; } } peer transit-a { connection { local { ip 192.0.2.10; } remote { ip 192.0.2.1; } } session { asn { remote 64496; } family { ipv4/unicast { prefix { maximum 1000000; } } } } } peer transit-b { connection { local { ip 198.51.100.10; } remote { ip 198.51.100.1; } } session { asn { remote 64497; } family { ipv4/unicast { prefix { maximum 1000000; } } } } } } Validate and start it, then announce 203.0.113.0/24 from both lab peers with different AS paths: ze config validate as-path-lab.conf ze start as-path-lab.conf ze cli -c "show bgp rib best prefix 203.0.113.0/24" curl -fsS "http://127.0.0.1:8443/api/looking-glass/routes/search?prefix=203.0.113.0%2F24" curl -fsS "http://127.0.0.1:8443/lg/graph?prefix=203.0.113.0%2F24" -o as-path.svg Open http://127.0.0.1:8443/lg/search?prefix=203.0.113.0%2F24 for the route details and inline graph. The graph endpoint returns SVG without a client-side graph engine or external topology service. Interpret the result Read paths from the observing peer toward the origin. Repeated AS numbers may be intentional prepending. Private ASNs, confederation segments, and path sanitization can change what the graph can display. Compare the graph with route detail. A graph shows adjacency and path alternatives, while route detail carries local preference, MED, communities, validation state, next hop, and the reason one path won. Operator uses Investigate a path change Capture the graph before and after a best-path change. Compare which peer introduced or removed an edge, then inspect that route's attributes and recent BGP events. Explain multi-homing Use the graph to show how two transits reach the same origin. This is often clearer than comparing raw AS-path strings one at a time. Check a suspected leak Look for an unexpected customer or peer appearing between a known transit and origin. Confirm with the raw route, RPKI state, and the announcing peer before treating the drawing as proof. Validate route-server visibility At an IXP, compare paths received from members and confirm the route server has not rewritten the member next hop or AS path. Limits The graph contains only routes visible to this Ze instance. Import-rejected routes are absent unless another retained source exposes them. AS-path adjacency does not prove a commercial relationship. Aggregation and path hiding can remove intermediate detail. A public graph can expose routing information the operator considers sensitive. Apply the same exposure policy and rate limits as the rest of the public Looking Glass.

title: AS112 anycast DNS inside a network
displayTitle: AS112 anycast DNS inside a network
text: AS112 anycast DNS inside a network Run Ze as the AS112 sink for RFC 1918 and link-local reverse DNS, then learn the four AS112 covering prefixes from Ze over BGP. RFC completion: the DNS coverage page shows which requirements have passed the recorded test checks for this use case. This example runs AS112 inside a local network. If you intend to advertise an AS112 node to public Internet peers, coordinate it first as RFC 7534 expects, and keep the import and export filters below. The software cannot do that human coordination for you. Topology Item Value in this example Ze node as112-ze Ze BGP transport, IPv4 172.30.0.2 Core router BGP transport, IPv4 172.30.0.1 Ze BGP transport, IPv6 2001:db8:112::2 Core router BGP transport, IPv6 2001:db8:112::1 Ze BGP ASN 65001 Core router ASN 65000 AS112 origin ASN carried by the routes 112 IPv4 covering prefixes to accept 192.175.48.0/24, 192.31.196.0/24 IPv6 covering prefixes to accept 2620:4f:8000::/48, 2001:4:112::/48 DNS service addresses hosted by Ze 192.175.48.1, 192.31.196.1, 2620:4f:8000::1, 2001:4:112::1 The prefixes you route are the covering /24 and /48 prefixes. The host addresses are the DNS service addresses Ze binds on lo; do not import or advertise /32 or /128 host routes for AS112. Ze config import as112 is the trigger. Without it, Ze can answer AS112 DNS locally, but BGP will not receive the AS112 covering prefixes. service { as112 { enabled true hostname "as112-ldn1.example.net" facility "Example London" location "London, GB" asn 112 community [ no-export ] watchdog true } } bgp { router-id 172.30.0.2 session { asn { local 65001 } } filter { import { final accept; } export { final accept; } } peer core-v4 { connection { remote { ip 172.30.0.1 } local { ip 172.30.0.2 } } session { asn { remote 65000 } family { ipv4/unicast { prefix { maximum 1000 } } } } } peer core-v6 { connection { remote { ip 2001:db8:112::1 } local { ip 2001:db8:112::2 } } session { asn { remote 65000 } family { ipv6/unicast { prefix { maximum 1000 } } } } } } redistribute { destination bgp { import as112 } } What this does: Ze answers AS112 DNS authoritatively on the four fixed service addresses. Ze registers those service addresses on lo; you do not configure them by hand. Ze originates the two IPv4 /24 and two IPv6 /48 covering prefixes into BGP. watchdog true keeps the BGP routes withdrawn until the DNS listener is serving. The top-level session sets Ze's local ASN once; each peer declares only the remote ASN. community [ no-export ] marks the routes so the network can keep them local. Use nopeer instead, or in addition, for a bilateral AS112 peering policy. FRR core router This FRR config accepts only the AS112 covering prefixes from Ze and exports nothing back to the Ze node. frr defaults traditional hostname core-frr log file /tmp/frr.log informational ! ip prefix-list AS112-V4 seq 10 permit 192.175.48.0/24 ip prefix-list AS112-V4 seq 20 permit 192.31.196.0/24 ipv6 prefix-list AS112-V6 seq 10 permit 2620:4f:8000::/48 ipv6 prefix-list AS112-V6 seq 20 permit 2001:4:112::/48 ! route-map AS112-V4-IN permit 10 match ip address prefix-list AS112-V4 ! route-map AS112-V4-IN deny 100 ! route-map AS112-V6-IN permit 10 match ipv6 address prefix-list AS112-V6 ! route-map AS112-V6-IN deny 100 ! route-map DROP-ALL deny 10 ! router bgp 65000 bgp router-id 172.30.0.1 no bgp ebgp-requires-policy neighbor 172.30.0.2 remote-as 65001 neighbor 2001:db8:112::2 remote-as 65001 ! address-family ipv4 unicast neighbor 172.30.0.2 activate neighbor 172.30.0.2 route-map AS112-V4-IN in neighbor 172.30.0.2 route-map DROP-ALL out exit-address-family ! address-family ipv6 unicast neighbor 2001:db8:112::2 activate neighbor 2001:db8:112::2 route-map AS112-V6-IN in neighbor 2001:db8:112::2 route-map DROP-ALL out exit-address-family ! Useful checks: show bgp ipv4 unicast 192.175.48.0/24 show bgp ipv4 unicast 192.31.196.0/24 show bgp ipv6 unicast 2620:4f:8000::/48 show bgp ipv6 unicast 2001:4:112::/48 BIRD core router This BIRD 2 config uses one IPv4 BGP session and one IPv6 BGP session, both receive-only. log stderr all; router id 172.30.0.1; protocol device { } filter as112_v4_in { if net = 192.175.48.0/24 then accept; if net = 192.31.196.0/24 then accept; reject; } filter as112_v6_in { if net = 2620:4f:8000::/48 then accept; if net = 2001:4:112::/48 then accept; reject; } protocol bgp ze_as112_v4 { local 172.30.0.1 as 65000; neighbor 172.30.0.2 as 65001; ipv4 { import filter as112_v4_in; export none; }; } protocol bgp ze_as112_v6 { local 2001:db8:112::1 as 65000; neighbor 2001:db8:112::2 as 65001; ipv6 { import filter as112_v6_in; export none; }; } Useful checks: birdc show protocols birdc show route for 192.175.48.0/24 all birdc show route for 2620:4f:8000::/48 all VyOS core router This VyOS config receives the AS112 covering prefixes from Ze and applies exact prefix filters on import. set protocols bgp system-as '65000' set protocols bgp parameters router-id '172.30.0.1' set policy prefix-list AS112-V4 rule 10 action 'permit' set policy prefix-list AS112-V4 rule 10 prefix '192.175.48.0/24' set policy prefix-list AS112-V4 rule 20 action 'permit' set policy prefix-list AS112-V4 rule 20 prefix '192.31.196.0/24' set policy prefix-list6 AS112-V6 rule 10 action 'permit' set policy prefix-list6 AS112-V6 rule 10 prefix '2620:4f:8000::/48' set policy prefix-list6 AS112-V6 rule 20 action 'permit' set policy prefix-list6 AS112-V6 rule 20 prefix '2001:4:112::/48' set policy route-map AS112-V4-IN rule 10 action 'permit' set policy route-map AS112-V4-IN rule 10 match ip address prefix-list 'AS112-V4' set policy route-map AS112-V4-IN rule 100 action 'deny' set policy route-map AS112-V6-IN rule 10 action 'permit' set policy route-map AS112-V6-IN rule 10 match ipv6 address prefix-list 'AS112-V6' set policy route-map AS112-V6-IN rule 100 action 'deny' set protocols bgp neighbor 172.30.0.2 remote-as '65001' set protocols bgp neighbor 172.30.0.2 address-family ipv4-unicast route-map import 'AS112-V4-IN' set protocols bgp neighbor 2001:db8:112::2 remote-as '65001' set protocols bgp neighbor 2001:db8:112::2 address-family ipv6-unicast route-map import 'AS112-V6-IN' Useful checks: run show bgp ipv4 unicast 192.175.48.0/24 run show bgp ipv6 unicast 2620:4f:8000::/48 Junos core router This Junos config uses exact route filters and imports only the four AS112 covering prefixes. policy-options { policy-statement AS112-V4-IN { term exact-as112 { from { route-filter 192.175.48.0/24 exact; route-filter 192.31.196.0/24 exact; } then accept; } then reject; } policy-statement AS112-V6-IN { term exact-as112 { from { route-filter 2620:4f:8000::/48 exact; route-filter 2001:4:112::/48 exact; } then accept; } then reject; } policy-statement REJECT-ALL { then reject; } } protocols { bgp { group ZE-AS112-V4 { type external; local-address 172.30.0.1; peer-as 65001; family inet { unicast; } import AS112-V4-IN; export REJECT-ALL; neighbor 172.30.0.2; } group ZE-AS112-V6 { type external; local-address 2001:db8:112::1; peer-as 65001; family inet6 { unicast; } import AS112-V6-IN; export REJECT-ALL; neighbor 2001:db8:112::2; } } } Useful checks: show route receive-protocol bgp 172.30.0.2 192.175.48.0/24 extensive show route receive-protocol bgp 2001:db8:112::2 2620:4f:8000::/48 extensive Cisco IOS XR core router This IOS XR config receives the four AS112 covering prefixes from Ze and sends no routes back. prefix-set AS112-V4 192.175.48.0/24, 192.31.196.0/24 end-set prefix-set AS112-V6 2620:4f:8000::/48, 2001:4:112::/48 end-set route-policy AS112-V4-IN if destination in AS112-V4 then pass else drop endif end-policy route-policy AS112-V6-IN if destination in AS112-V6 then pass else drop endif end-policy route-policy DROP-ALL drop end-policy router bgp 65000 bgp router-id 172.30.0.1 neighbor 172.30.0.2 remote-as 65001 address-family ipv4 unicast route-policy AS112-V4-IN in route-policy DROP-ALL out ! ! neighbor 2001:db8:112::2 remote-as 65001 address-family ipv6 unicast route-policy AS112-V6-IN in

title: BGP performance testing with Ze
text: BGP performance testing with Ze A route-server performance test is simple in outline: create a route source, connect it to a device under test, watch a monitor peer, and publish how many routes arrived and how long convergence took. RFC completion: the BGP core coverage page shows which requirements have passed the recorded test checks for this use case. AMS-IX used ExaBGP as a lightweight BGP route source. bgperf formalized the same idea with tester, target, and monitor containers. Ze can run that setup with le perf: Ze supplies the sender and receiver, the target is any BGP speaker you want to test, and the output is a repeatable report instead of a stopwatch and screenshots. This page shows Ze in the tester role. The device under test can be FRR, BIRD, GoBGP, OpenBGPD, a route-server appliance, or Ze itself. What a good test answers A performance test has to answer these questions and publish the evidence for each. Question Evidence to publish Can the DUT establish the sessions? Sender and receiver BGP sessions reach Established Can the DUT ingest the route set? Expected route count arrives at the receiver Did it lose routes? routes-lost is zero How long did convergence take? convergence-ms, throughput, and latency percentiles from le perf Does the result repeat? Several iterations, warmups discarded, standard deviation reported Can someone reproduce it? DUT config, route count, family, batch size, hardware, runtime, and raw JSON A useful run checks the complete route path: generated routes enter the device under test, pass through its policy and routing table, leave the device, and arrive at a BGP receiver. A route count alone shows that the routers exchanged routes. Repeated runs with zero loss and published inputs let others assess the performance result. Topology The test is three nodes: a sender and a receiver that Ze runs, with the device under test between them. le perf sender ---> DUT under test ---> le perf receiver AS 65001 AS 65000 AS 65002 Node AS Played by Job Sender 65001 le perf Generate the route set and inject it into the DUT Device under test 65000 FRR, BIRD, GoBGP, OpenBGPD, Ze, or another BGP speaker Receive the routes, apply policy, and re-advertise them Receiver 65002 le perf Record when each prefix arrives le perf matches the prefixes the sender injected against the ones the receiver saw, so it can report convergence, throughput, latency percentiles, withdrawal time, and lost routes. In bgperf terms, the sender is the tester, the DUT is the target, and the receiver is the monitor. Fastest working test Use the native Docker runner from the main Ze checkout when you want the whole setup built for you. ./le perf run dut frr ./le perf compare test/perf/results/*.json Run a smaller wiring test first when you are adding a new DUT target. ./le perf send \ --dut-addr 172.31.0.2 \ --dut-asn 65000 \ --dut-name frr \ --routes 10 \ --repeat 1 \ --warmup-runs 0 If 10 routes do not converge, fix the BGP sessions or DUT policy before running a scale test. A 100k route run This is the Ze equivalent of using ExaBGP as the injector in the original route-server tests. ./le perf send \ --dut-addr 172.31.0.2 \ --dut-asn 65000 \ --dut-name frr \ --sender-addr 172.31.0.10 \ --sender-asn 65001 \ --receiver-addr 172.31.0.11 \ --receiver-asn 65002 \ --routes 100000 \ --repeat 10 \ --warmup-runs 2 \ --iter-delay 3s \ --output results/frr-100k.json The sender and receiver addresses must be valid local addresses in the lab where le perf runs. The Docker runner handles that wiring. In a manual lab, bind those addresses on the host or run le perf in the right network namespace. Then render the report. ./le perf compare results/frr-100k.json Use --family ipv6/unicast for IPv6. Use --force-mp to encode IPv4 NLRI through MP_REACH_NLRI and test the DUT multiprotocol path. Use --batch-size 1 when you want one prefix per UPDATE instead of packed UPDATEs. FRR as the DUT This FRR config accepts the Ze sender and exports the received routes to the Ze receiver. frr defaults traditional hostname dut-frr log stdout informational ! route-map ACCEPT permit 10 ! router bgp 65000 bgp router-id 172.31.0.2 no bgp ebgp-requires-policy neighbor 172.31.0.10 remote-as 65001 neighbor 172.31.0.11 remote-as 65002 ! address-family ipv4 unicast neighbor 172.31.0.10 activate neighbor 172.31.0.10 route-map ACCEPT in neighbor 172.31.0.11 activate neighbor 172.31.0.11 route-map ACCEPT out exit-address-family ! Useful checks while debugging: show bgp ipv4 unicast summary show bgp ipv4 unicast 10.0.0.0/24 PfxRcd on the sender neighbor should reach the generated route count. The receiver side should receive the same count. BIRD as the DUT This BIRD 2 config imports routes from the Ze sender and exports them to the Ze receiver. log stderr all; router id 172.31.0.2; protocol device { } protocol bgp ze_sender { local 172.31.0.2 as 65000; neighbor 172.31.0.10 as 65001; ipv4 { import all; export none; }; } protocol bgp ze_receiver { local 172.31.0.2 as 65000; neighbor 172.31.0.11 as 65002; ipv4 { import none; export all; }; } Useful checks: birdc show protocols birdc show route count What Ze reports le perf reports the fields that are easy to lose when the test is driven by an external injector. Field Why it matters convergence-ms Time from the sender writing the first UPDATE to the receiver collecting the expected routes throughput-rps Sustained route propagation rate over the convergence window latency-p50-ms, latency-p90-ms, latency-p99-ms, latency-max-ms Per-route propagation distribution withdrawal-ms Time for the receiver to become idle after withdrawal routes-lost Route loss, which invalidates a throughput claim until fixed repeat, warmup-runs, repeat-kept How much measurement stability the run has seed, family, force-mp, batch-size Inputs needed to reproduce the route stream Use JSON for anything you intend to publish. ./le perf send --dut-addr 172.31.0.2 --dut-asn 65000 --routes 100000 --output result.json What to publish with the number Publish the method with the result. Field Why it matters DUT name, version, commit, and config Policy and defaults change results Hardware or VM resources CPU, memory, and virtualization dominate control-plane tests Runtime Bare metal, Docker, Colima, QEMU, and VM networking are different tests Route source Synthetic routes, MRT replay, and production captures stress different code paths Number of peers and routes per peer One peer sending many routes and many peers sending fewer routes find different bugs Route count and family IPv4 inline NLRI, IPv4 MP_REACH, and IPv6 MP_REACH exercise different paths Batch size Packed UPDATEs and one prefix per UPDATE are different workloads Repeats and warmups One run is a smoke test Lost routes Loss must be explained before throughput matters Raw JSON The number can be checked later How close Ze is to the full route-server test Ze already covers the core of the test: sender, DUT, receiver, route count, convergence, loss, and repeatable output. The current le perf setup is one sender session and one receiver session. That is enough to test route propagation and DUT table pressure, but not hundreds of independent BGP client sessions in one run. For a full AMS-IX or bgperf-style route-server scale test, Ze would need a multi-peer mode: Test not yet supported Feature to add 500 small route-server clients N sender sessions, each with its own local address, ASN, and route slice MRT replay as route source Route input from MRT, with count and skip controls External generator with Ze monitor Receiver-only mode that records first route, last route, loss, and receive window Per-client reporting JSON grouped by sender peer and route family That would let Ze reproduce the full route-server topology while keeping Ze's timing and JSON reporting. Prior art AMS-IX published route-server performance slides at RIPE64 with 500 IPv4 peers, 128,000 prefixes, BIRD table-mode comparisons, an MTU test with 1012 IPv6 peers, and a note t

title: Chaos-Tested BGP Peering
text: Chaos-Tested BGP Peering Use le chaos run before deployment to check that a peer configuration converges, survives selected faults, and produces a reproducible failure record when it does not. RFC completion: the BGP session operations coverage page shows which requirements have passed the recorded test checks for this use case. Start from a validated peer Build the intended peer or group with the BGP peering guide. Validate the configuration and run ordinary interop or lab checks first. Once those pass, chaos testing can check how the deployment recovers from faults. Run one complete reproducible scenario Use a fixed seed and keep the generated configuration beside the event log. This sequence first makes the configuration inspectable, validates it, then runs the same four-peer topology: mkdir -p evidence/seed-42 ./le chaos run --config-only --seed 42 --peers 4 --config-out evidence/seed-42/ze.conf ze config validate evidence/seed-42/ze.conf ./le chaos run --event-log evidence/seed-42/run.ndjson --seed 42 --peers 4 --duration 60s For a deterministic in-process run that also varies route activity: ./le chaos run --in-process --event-log evidence/seed-42/in-process.ndjson --seed 42 --duration 60s --chaos-rate 0.1 --route-rate 0.05 Replay the captured run before accepting the result: ./le chaos run --replay evidence/seed-42/run.ndjson If replay preserves a failure, reduce it to the smallest event sequence: ./le chaos run --shrink evidence/seed-42/run.ndjson Keep ze.conf, the event logs, the seed, the Ze version, and the final command output as one evidence bundle. See the chaos testing guide for pipeline, FRR, BIRD, and dashboard modes. State the properties A useful scenario has explicit properties rather than a general expectation that the daemon remains running. Typical properties include: all intended sessions eventually establish; every announced route reaches every eligible destination; withdrawals remove the route everywhere; a restarted session converges before its deadline; no route crosses a policy or family boundary; the final RIB agrees with the final peer state; warning and error output contains no unexplained event. Choose deadlines from the intended timers and route volume. A deadline copied from a small lab is not evidence for a full table. Inject meaningful faults Select faults that exercise the deployment's real risks: connection failure and reconnect; partial reads or writes; session reset during an update stream; route churn during restart; slow consumers and backpressure; malformed messages on an untrusted peer; plugin delay or failure where policy depends on a plugin. Run one type of fault at a time before combining them. This makes failures easier to trace and helps the tool reduce a failing run to the events that caused it. Replay and shrink When a scenario fails: ./le chaos run --replay run.ndjson ./le chaos run --shrink run.ndjson Replay checks whether the failure repeats with the same input. Shrink removes unrelated events until the smallest useful reproduction remains. Keep the seed, event log, configuration, binary version, and final report together. Checks before deployment Before accepting the peer configuration: The ordinary session and route checks pass. Every declared chaos property passes for repeated fixed seeds. A deliberately broken configuration or handler makes the relevant property fail. Replay reproduces a captured failure. The final route and peer state is clean after recovery. The test records the Ze version and scenario inputs. A scenario must fail when the behavior it is meant to protect is deliberately broken. Otherwise, a passing result cannot establish that the behavior works.

title: ExaBGP Migration
text: ExaBGP Migration Ze provides tools for converting ExaBGP configurations and running existing ExaBGP plugins with Ze as the BGP engine. RFC completion: the BGP core coverage page shows which requirements have passed the recorded test checks for this use case. Config Migration Convert an ExaBGP configuration file to Ze-native format: ze exabgp migrate exabgp.conf > ze.conf ze config validate ze.conf # Validate the result What Gets Converted ExaBGP Ze neighbor <ip> { ... } peer <ip> { ... } local-as, peer-as session { asn { local ... } } / session { asn { remote ... } } router-id session { router-id ... } (same keyword, moved under session) family { ... } family { ... } capability { ... } capability { ... } static { route ... } Static route config or update commands Template inheritance Group-based inheritance Limitations Complex ExaBGP features (watchdog groups, split configurations) may need manual adjustment Process scripts need the compatibility bridge (see below) Migration is one-time; the output is Ze-native config Plugin Compatibility Bridge Run existing ExaBGP process scripts with Ze using the compatibility bridge: plugin { external my-exabgp-plugin { run "ze exabgp plugin /path/to/my-plugin.py"; encoder json; } } bgp { router-id 10.0.0.2; session { asn { local 65000; } } filter { import { final accept; } export { final accept; } } peer upstream1 { connection { remote { ip 10.0.0.1; } local { ip 10.0.0.2; } } session { asn { remote 65001; } family { ipv4/unicast { prefix { maximum 10000; } } } } attach process my-exabgp-plugin { receive [ update state ]; } } } How It Works The bridge translates bidirectionally: Direction From To Events (to plugin) Ze JSON events ExaBGP JSON format Commands (from plugin) ExaBGP text commands Ze command format When Ze's process manager launches the bridge, the bridge detects ZE_PLUGIN_HUB_TOKEN and connects back via TLS using the SDK. The SDK handles the 5-stage startup protocol and MuxConn multiplexing automatically. In standalone mode (no env var), the bridge uses stdin/stdout with inline MuxConn framing. After each route command, the bridge sends peer <addr> flush and waits until the forward pool drains. The engine processes the route before continuing. Bridge Flags Flag Description --family <family> Address families to support (repeatable) --route-refresh Enable route refresh capability --add-path <mode> ADD-PATH mode: receive, send, or both Example with flags: run "ze exabgp plugin --family ipv4/unicast --family ipv6/unicast /path/to/plugin.py" Automatic Prefix Defaults The migration tool adds prefix { maximum 10000; } to every converted address family. Ze requires per-family prefix limits (RFC 4486), and ExaBGP configs do not have them. The default of 10,000 is a conservative starting point; adjust per-peer based on expected route counts (full table peers typically need 1,000,000+). Migration Workflow Convert config: ze exabgp migrate old.conf > new.conf Review prefix limits: Check prefix { maximum ... } values match expected route counts Validate: ze config validate new.conf Bridge plugins: Update run directives to use ze exabgp plugin Test: Run Ze with the new config and verify sessions establish Port plugins: Gradually rewrite plugins to use the Ze SDK directly Worked migration Consider an ExaBGP process that receives updates from two transit sessions and writes route commands to stdout: process inject-routes { run python3 /opt/scripts/inject.py; encoder json; } neighbor 10.0.0.1 { description "transit-a"; router-id 10.0.0.2; local-address 10.0.0.2; local-as 65000; peer-as 65001; api { processes [ inject-routes ]; receive { parsed; update; } } } neighbor 10.0.1.1 { description "transit-b"; router-id 10.0.0.2; local-address 10.0.1.2; local-as 65000; peer-as 65002; api { processes [ inject-routes ]; receive { parsed; update; } } } Convert the complete configuration, retain the original as a read-only reference, and validate the generated Ze file: cp exabgp.conf exabgp.conf.before-ze ze exabgp migrate exabgp.conf > ze.conf ze config validate ze.conf Review the generated file before starting. In particular: Give each peer a stable, meaningful name. Confirm every local and remote address and ASN. Adjust the generated per-family prefix maximum. The migration default is a starting point, not a full-table recommendation. Confirm which peers bind the converted process. Review static announcements and next-hop handling. Remove capabilities that the remote peer should not negotiate. Run the existing script through the bridge: plugin { external inject-routes { run "ze exabgp plugin python3 /opt/scripts/inject.py"; encoder json; } } Bind that process only to the peers whose events it should receive. The bridge keeps the ExaBGP JSON and text-command contract at the script boundary while Ze uses its native event and command model internally. Start Ze and verify each boundary rather than treating an Established session as sufficient proof: ze start ze.conf ze cli -c "show bgp" ze cli -c "show bgp peer transit-a detail" ze cli -c "show bgp rib status" ze cli -c "show warnings" ze cli -c "show errors" Trigger one representative announcement and withdrawal through the existing script. Confirm the route appears in the expected peer's outbound RIB, reaches the adjacent router, and disappears after withdrawal. Cutover checklist The converted configuration validates. Every intended address family and capability is negotiated. Received and advertised prefix counts match the old deployment. Existing process scripts receive the events they depend on. Announcements, withdrawals, and watchdog actions behave as before. Warnings, errors, and operational reports contain no unexpected entries. The old ExaBGP configuration and binary remain available for rollback during the first maintenance window. Port scripts to the native SDK one at a time after the bridge deployment is stable. This avoids combining a routing-engine migration with an application rewrite. When to Port Plugins The compatibility bridge adds translation overhead. Consider porting to native Ze plugins when: You need access to Ze-specific features (RPKI events, cache commands, commit workflow) Performance matters (native plugins skip the translation layer) You want to use the Go SDK for direct in-process execution

title: Fleet configuration management
text: Fleet configuration management Manage a fleet of Ze routers from a central Ze hub over authenticated TLS connections: enroll devices against the hub's CA, push live configuration edits with zero daemon restart, prevent accidental out-of-band drift while managed, and resolve emergency local edits through audited adopt or revert workflows. Role and topology Central Ze Hub (10.0.0.1:1791, TLS) stores client-edge-01.conf, client-edge-02.conf / \ TLS + per-client secret TLS + per-client secret / \ edge-01 (managed) edge-02 (managed) local edits frozen local edits frozen boots from cache if hub down boots from cache if hub down Hub configuration The hub exposes a dedicated server listener for managed clients on a separate port from its local plugin listener. Every secret must be at least 32 characters (based on docs/guide/fleet-config.md): plugin { hub { server local { ip 127.0.0.1; port 1790; secret "local-plugin-secret-of-32-characters"; } server central { ip 0.0.0.0; port 1791; secret "remote-plugin-secret-of-32-character"; client edge-01 { secret "edge-01-secret-of-at-least-32-chars"; } client edge-02 { secret "edge-02-secret-of-at-least-32-chars"; } } } } Managed client configuration (stored on the hub) Save each device's full configuration on the hub as client-<name>.conf (for example client-edge-01.conf). Keep the client edge-01 block inside the pushed config so the device stays bound to the hub after applying updates: plugin { hub { server local { ip 127.0.0.1; port 1790; secret "local-secret-of-at-least-32-characters"; } client edge-01 { host 10.0.0.1; port 1791; secret "edge-01-secret-of-at-least-32-chars"; } } } bgp { ... } Enrollment and live rollout workflow Export the hub's local CA certificate and import the client configuration on the running hub: ze show pki local-ca pem > hub-root.pem ze data import client-edge-01.conf Provision and start the managed device (or pass --hub-trust-first-use for initial lab setup): ze init --managed --hub-ca hub-root.pem ze start Edit and push live configuration changes from the hub without restarting the remote daemon: ze config edit client-edge-01.conf # or re-import an updated file: ze data import client-edge-01.conf Committing on the hub sends config-changed over TLS to edge-01, which validates and applies the new running configuration immediately. If the hub is unreachable at boot, the managed device boots from its last cached configuration. Emergency local edits and divergence resolution While a device is managed, local commits, imports, restores, and rollbacks are frozen and refused. During an incident where the hub cannot be reached, an operator can unfreeze the device locally, make an emergency change, and reconnect later: # On edge-01: leave managed mode to unfreeze local edits, then rejoin when ready ze request fleet disable # ... emergency local edit ... ze request fleet enable When edge-01 reconnects with a different active hash, the hub holds automatic pushes and records the divergence for explicit resolution: # On the hub: inspect the masked diff and device/hub versions ze show fleet divergence list ze show fleet divergence name edge-01 # Either adopt the device's emergency edit into the hub's authoritative copy: ze update fleet divergence name edge-01 adopt version <device-version> # Or revert the device back to the hub's authoritative copy: ze request fleet divergence name edge-01 revert version <device-version> hub-version <hub-version> Both adopt and revert are hash-pinned against concurrent edits and recorded in show audit. Verification commands ze show fleet status ze show fleet divergence list ze show fleet divergence name edge-01 ze config history client-edge-01.conf ze doctor Lab evidence Managed fleet functional suite (test/managed/, 32 .ci tests): ./le test functional managed Key scenarios include client-first-boot.ci, client-cached-boot-hub-down.ci, fleet-config-change-live.ci, fleet-freeze-refuses-commit.ci, fleet-divergence-adopt.ci, fleet-divergence-revert.ci, fleet-status.ci, and data-restore-client-live.ci. Current limits Full per-device files (no templates or canary waves): Each managed client has its own complete client-<name>.conf; Ze does not render config templates or run staged canary rollouts across groups. 1 MiB divergence upload cap: Configurations larger than 1 MiB are not uploaded automatically on divergence and must be reconciled manually via ze data cat and ze data import. Running hub required for adopt/revert: Divergence resolution commands require a running hub so audit records are always written. Keep the client block in pushed configs: Pushing a configuration that omits plugin { hub { client <name> { ... } } } disconnects the device from future hub updates. Related guides Fleet management Fleet configuration guide Audit log guide

title: FlowSpec Injection
text: FlowSpec Injection Use Ze to inject or relay BGP FlowSpec rules when an automation system must distribute traffic filters to routers. Keep the route source, policy, and withdrawal path explicit because a stale FlowSpec rule can affect live traffic. RFC completion: the DDoS detection and mitigation by sending FlowSpec upstream coverage page shows which requirements have passed the recorded test checks for this use case. Choose the router's role The router can take either of these roles: A FlowSpec route reflector receives rules from an authorized controller and reflects them to clients. A protected router receives FlowSpec and translates accepted rules into local firewall actions. The existing FlowSpec route-reflector and protected-router guides cover those complete roles. This page explains how an automation system sends and withdraws rules. Complete injection lab The destination peer must negotiate the FlowSpec family. Save this minimal sender configuration as flowspec-sender.conf; configure the remote router as AS 64501 at 192.0.2.20. plugin { internal rib { use bgp-rib; } } bgp { router-id 192.0.2.10; session { asn { local 64500; } } filter { import { final reject; } export { final accept; } } peer flowspec-client { connection { local { ip 192.0.2.10; } remote { ip 192.0.2.20; } } session { asn { remote 64501; } family { ipv4/flow { prefix { maximum 1000; } } } } } } Validate and start the sender, then confirm family negotiation: ze config validate flowspec-sender.conf ze start flowspec-sender.conf ze cli -c "show bgp peer flowspec-client capabilities" In a lab, inject a discard rule for TCP destination port 443: ze cli -c "send bgp flowspec-client update text extended-community [rate-limit:0] nhop self mp ipv4/flow add destination-ipv4 203.0.113.0/24 protocol tcp destination-port =443" The command uses the same registered dispatcher through CLI, REST, gRPC, and MCP. Confirm the remote router installed the rule, then withdraw the exact NLRI: ze cli -c "send bgp flowspec-client update text mp ipv4/flow del destination-ipv4 203.0.113.0/24 protocol tcp destination-port =443" Send related rules together When several rules form one mitigation, stage and inspect them before release: ze cli -c "request commit start mitigation-42" ze cli -c "send bgp flowspec-client update text extended-community [rate-limit:0] nhop self mp ipv4/flow add destination-ipv4 203.0.113.0/24 protocol tcp destination-port =443" ze cli -c "send bgp flowspec-client update text extended-community [rate-limit:9600] nhop self mp ipv4/flow add destination-ipv4 203.0.113.0/24 protocol udp destination-port =53" ze cli -c "request commit show mitigation-42" ze cli -c "request commit end mitigation-42" Use request commit rollback mitigation-42 instead of end if validation or review fails. This prevents clients from observing a partial mitigation policy. Authorization and policy Treat route injection as a privileged operation: restrict it with Ze authorization profiles; bind the controller to only the intended peers and families; validate component ranges, actions, and traffic rates; reject rules outside the protected address space; record the actor and request in the audit trail; arrange for another service or an operator to withdraw temporary rules when they expire. A controller must be able to withdraw every rule it installs. Do not rely on process exit as cleanup. Verification After injection: ze cli -c "show bgp peer flowspec-client capabilities" ze cli -c "show bgp rib status" ze cli -c "show warnings" ze cli -c "show errors" Then verify the destination appropriate to the deployment: On a reflector, confirm the rule is present in the client's received FlowSpec RIB. On a protected router, confirm the translated firewall rule and counters. In both cases, withdraw the rule and confirm the destination state disappears. Test rule replacement as well as add and withdraw. A mitigation controller often changes rate or match criteria while an incident is active. Failure cases The peer did not negotiate the FlowSpec family. Import policy rejected the rule. The controller targeted the wrong peer selector. A multi-rule update was released before all rules were staged. The protected router cannot translate one component or action. The controller restarted without recovering its installed-rule inventory. The BGP withdrawal succeeded but local firewall cleanup failed. Monitor both BGP state and the enforcement backend. One without the other is incomplete evidence.

title: Home and SMB FTTP CPE
text: Home and SMB FTTP CPE Use Ze as a single-box Linux CPE on a PPPoE fiber circuit: terminate PPPoE on the WAN interface, request an IPv6 prefix via DHCPv6-PD, advertise delegated /64 subnets on the LAN via Router Advertisements, serve DHCPv4 leases, forward LAN DNS queries to upstream resolvers learned over PPPoE, and enforce TCP MSS clamping and source NAT with nftables. Role and topology ISP / BNG (accel-ppp) │ PPPoE + IPv6CP + DHCPv6-PD (/56 or /60) ▼ eth1 -> pppoe0 (MTU 1492) Ze CPE (Linux, netlink backend) │ lan0 / br0 (192.168.50.1/24 + delegated /64) ▼ LAN hosts (DHCPv4 + IPv6 SLAAC + local caching DNS) Ze configuration WAN PPPoE client with IPv6CP, DHCPv6-PD, and LAN delegated-prefix Router Advertisements (based on test/interop-topology/scenarios/pppoe-dhcpv6-pd-ze-client/ze-cpe.conf): interface { ethernet eth1 { } ethernet lan0 { unit 0 { ipv6 { forwarding true; delegated-prefix pppoe0 { subnet-id 1; } router-advertisement { enabled true; maximum-interval 4; minimum-interval 3; router-lifetime 1800; } } } } pppoe-client pppoe0 { source-interface eth1; mtu 1492; service-name internet; authentication { username alice; password s3cr3t; } ipv6 { enabled true; accept-ra 2; autoconf true; forwarding true; dhcpv6 { enabled true; pd { length 56; } } } } } Default IPv4 route, nftables TCP MSS clamping (avoiding PMTUD blackholes across the 1492-byte PPPoE MTU), IPv4 NAT masquerade, LAN DHCPv4 server, and LAN caching DNS resolver forwarding to PPPoE-learned upstream resolvers with a static fallback (based on test/interop-topology/cpe/ze-cpe.conf and test/pppoe/dns-resolver-forward-ppp-lease.ci): static { table default { route 0.0.0.0/0 { distance 10; next { interface pppoe0 { } } } } } firewall { backend nft; table wan-mss { family ip; chain mss { type filter; hook postrouting; priority -300; policy accept; term pppoe0-mss { from { output-interface pppoe0; protocol tcp; } then { tcp-mss-set 1400; } } } } table nat-source { family ip; chain postrouting { type nat; hook postrouting; priority 100; policy accept; term rule-100-a { from { output-interface pppoe0; source-address 192.168.50.0/24; } then { masquerade; } } } } } service { dhcp-server { enabled true; listen-interface br0; shared-network LAN { subnet 192.168.50.0/24 { range 0 { start 192.168.50.100; stop 192.168.50.199; } lease-time 86400; default-router 192.168.50.1; dns-source { source self; } static-mapping res-a { mac-address 02:00:5e:50:00:30; ip-address 192.168.50.30; } } } } dns-resolver { enabled true; listener lan { ip 192.168.50.1; port 53; } allow-from [ 192.168.50.0/24 127.0.0.0/8 ]; forward { server 192.0.2.53 { port 53; } dns-source { source [ received configured ]; received-interface [ pppoe0 ]; mode first-usable; } } } } Access concentrator configuration (accel-ppp) Tested against accel-ppp 1.14.0 (test/interop-topology/scenarios/pppoe-dhcpv6-pd-ze-client/accel-ppp.conf): [modules] log_file cli pppoe auth_pap chap-secrets ippool ipv6pool ipv6_nd ipv6_dhcp [pppoe] interface=eth1 ac-name=ze-pd-ac service-name=internet verbose=1 [ppp] mtu=1492 mru=1492 ipv4=require ipv6=allow ipv6-intf-id=0:0:0:1 ipv6-accept-peer-intf-id=1 lcp-echo-interval=30 lcp-echo-failure=3 mppe=deny [ip-pool] gw-ip-address=10.198.0.1 10.198.0.2-10 [ipv6-pool] 2001:db8:198::/48,64 delegate=2001:db8:2000::/40,60 [ipv6-nd] AdvAutonomousFlag=1 [ipv6-dhcp] pref-lifetime=60 valid-lifetime=120 route-via-gw=1 Verification commands show interface pppoe-client show interface delegated-prefix show system dns show dns resolver show route ze doctor show interface pppoe-client reports session state, negotiated addresses, learned WAN DNS servers, and delegated IPv6 prefixes with remaining lifetimes. show interface delegated-prefix reports each LAN unit's delegated /64, interface address, and prefix lifetimes. show system dns shows learned WAN DNS records alongside the upstream server selected by dns-resolver and the local address advertised by dhcp-server. Lab evidence PPPoE + DHCPv6-PD + RA against accel-ppp: ./le test integration interop-topology scenario pppoe-dhcpv6-pd-ze-client (test/interop-topology/scenarios/pppoe-dhcpv6-pd-ze-client/) Full CPE over PPPoE -> LAC -> L2TP -> LNS with DHCP, NAT, and MSS: ./le test integration interop-topology scenario access-up, access-reconnect, and lan-services (test/interop-topology/cpe/ze-cpe.conf) PPPoE client interop against accel-ppp: ZE_PPPOE_INTEROP_SCENARIO=01-pppoe-chap-ipv4 ./le test deployment docker-pppoe-accel (and ./le test qemu pppoe-accel) WAN DNS lease forwarding and DHCP self-DNS: test/pppoe/dns-resolver-forward-ppp-lease.ci, test/dhcp/dhcp-server-dns-source-self.ci, test/plugin/show-interface-pppoe-client.ci, and test/plugin/show-system-dns.ci Current limits WAN client is PPPoE only: Ze has interface { pppoe-client } for CPE WANs. Ze's L2TP implementation is an RFC 2661 BNG LNS/LAC rather than a CPE L2TP client. DHCPv4 server only: service { dhcp-server } serves IPv4 leases; LAN IPv6 hosts autoconfigure via SLAAC and Router Advertisements. There is no show dhcp lease table command yet. Linux netlink backend required: pppoe-client and router-advertisement require Linux with backend netlink, and Router Advertisements require ipv6 { forwarding true; }. Forwarding DNS resolver: service { dns-resolver } operates in forwarding mode over plain UDP/TCP only (no full root recursion, DNSSEC validation, DoT/DoH, or wildcard 0.0.0.0/:: listeners). Related guides PPPoE guide DNS resolver guide Interfaces PPPoE interop lab

title: Campus and IGP edge (OSPF, IS-IS, BFD, and VRRP)
displayTitle: Campus and IGP edge (OSPF, IS-IS, BFD, and VRRP)
text: Campus and IGP edge (OSPF, IS-IS, BFD, and VRRP) Deploy Ze as a campus or distribution router without BGP: pair OSPFv2 (with single-hop BFD fast failure detection) or dual-stack IS-IS with VRRPv3 first-hop redundancy and uplink interface tracking. Role and topology Upstream core (FRR: OSPF+BFD or dual-stack IS-IS) │ eth1 (point-to-point) ▼ Ze Router A (VRRP prio 200) ─── eth0 (VIP 172.30.0.100/24) ─── keepalived / Ze Router B (prio 100) │ Access VLAN hosts Ze configuration: OSPFv2 with BFD Both the top-level bfd { enabled true; } container and the per-interface bfd block under ospf are required so the BFD plugin starts and registers sessions (based on test/interop/scenarios/ospf-bfd-frr/ze.conf): bfd { enabled true; } ospf { router-id 172.30.0.2; areas { area 0.0.0.0 { area-type normal; } } interfaces { interface eth1 { area 0.0.0.0; network-type point-to-point; hello-interval 10; dead-interval 40; cost 10; bfd { enabled true; min-tx 300; min-rx 300; multiplier 3; } } interface lo { area 0.0.0.0; passive true; } } } Note the unit difference: inline ospf ... bfd { min-tx; min-rx; } timers are in milliseconds, while named profiles under bfd { profile <name> { desired-min-tx-us; required-min-rx-us; } } are in microseconds. Ze configuration: dual-stack IS-IS alternative For IS-IS networks carrying IPv4 and IPv6 together on point-to-point links (based on test/interop/scenarios/isis-dualstack-frr/ze.conf): isis { net 49.0001.0000.0000.0000.0002.00; level l1-l2; hostname ze-ds; interfaces { interface eth1 { metric 10; level l1-l2; circuit-type point-to-point; address-family ipv4-unicast {} address-family ipv6-unicast {} } interface lo { passive true; address-family ipv4-unicast {} address-family ipv6-unicast {} } } } Ze configuration: VRRPv3 with uplink tracking VRRPv3 runs on the access-facing interface and decrements priority by 150 if uplink eth1 goes down, triggering deterministic failover to the standby router (based on test/interop/scenarios/vrrp-mastership-keepalived/ze.conf and docs/guide/vrrp.md): interface { backend netlink; ethernet eth0 { unit 0 { ipv4 { address [ 172.30.0.2/24 ]; vrrp { group vip { vrid 10; virtual-address [ 172.30.0.100 ]; priority 200; preempt true; checksum rfc5798-compatible; advertise-interval-milliseconds 1000; track { interface eth1 { priority-decrement 150; } } } } } } } } Adjacent peer configurations FRR OSPFv2 + BFD (test/interop/scenarios/ospf-bfd-frr/frr.conf): interface eth1 ip ospf network point-to-point ip ospf area 0.0.0.0 ip ospf bfd ! interface lo ip ospf area 0.0.0.0 ! router ospf ospf router-id 172.30.0.3 passive-interface lo ! bfd profile ospf-fast transmit-interval 300 receive-interval 300 detect-multiplier 3 ! ! FRR dual-stack IS-IS (test/interop/scenarios/isis-dualstack-frr/frr.conf): interface eth1 ip router isis ZE ipv6 router isis ZE isis circuit-type level-1-2 isis network point-to-point ! interface lo ip router isis ZE ipv6 router isis ZE isis passive ! router isis ZE net 49.0001.0000.0000.0000.0003.00 is-type level-1-2 metric-style wide ! keepalived 2.4.3 VRRPv3 standby (test/interop/scenarios/vrrp-mastership-keepalived/keepalived.conf): global_defs { vrrp_garp_master_refresh 0 } vrrp_instance VI_1 { state BACKUP interface eth0 virtual_router_id 10 priority 100 advert_int 1 version 3 virtual_ipaddress { 172.30.0.100/24 } } Verification commands show ospf neighbor detail show ospf route show isis neighbor show isis route show bfd sessions show vrrp show vrrp statistics Lab evidence OSPF + BFD against FRR: INTEROP_SCENARIO=ospf-bfd-frr ./le test integration interop (also ospfv3-bfd-frr, ospf-multiarea-frr, ospf-lfa-frr, ospf-gr-frr) Dual-stack IS-IS against FRR: INTEROP_SCENARIO=isis-dualstack-frr ./le test integration interop (also isis-p2p-frr, isis-lan-dis-frr, isis-auth-frr) BFD against FRR and BIRD: INTEROP_SCENARIO=bfd-frr ./le test integration interop and bfd-simple-password-bird VRRPv3 against keepalived: INTEROP_SCENARIO=vrrp-mastership-keepalived ./le test integration interop and QEMU lab ./le test qemu vrrp-keepalived Current limits BFD is not wired to IS-IS yet: Ze wires BFD session notifications to BGP, OSPF, and static routes; IS-IS does not yet consume BFD events. Experimental status: OSPF and VRRP are currently marked Experimental. VRRP interoperability details: VRRP requires Linux backend netlink (not VPP), CAP_NET_RAW, CAP_NET_ADMIN, and net.ipv4.ip_forward=1. Against keepalived on IPv4 VRRPv3, set checksum rfc5798-compatible in Ze and version 3 in keepalived. accept-mode defaults to false (RFC 9568), so non-owner Active routers drop pings to the VIP unless accept-mode true is configured. track monitors interface operational state only (route and script tracking are not implemented). Related guides OSPF guide IS-IS guide BFD guide VRRP guide

title: Route Server at an IXP
text: Route Server at an IXP Use Ze as an RFC 7947 route server when each member should maintain one eBGP session and receive eligible routes from the other members without next-hop rewriting. RFC completion: the IXP route server coverage page shows which requirements have passed the recorded test checks for this use case. Topology Ze route server AS 65000 192.0.2.254 | +----------------+----------------+ | | | Member A Member B Member C AS 65001 AS 65002 AS 65003 192.0.2.1 192.0.2.2 192.0.2.3 Each member peers only with the route server. The route server distributes accepted paths to other members while preserving the member's next hop. Components A practical deployment uses: bgp-rs for route-server forwarding; bgp-adj-rib-in for retained inbound routes and eligible-route replay; bgp-rib where local RIB operations or route visibility require it; BGP Role for route-server and route-server-client relationships; RPKI and IRR policy where the IXP requires them; the Looking Glass for member-facing visibility. Use the generated plugin catalog to confirm current dependencies and configuration roots. Build peer groups with the BGP peering guide and policy chains with the BGP policy guide. Complete lab configuration Save the following as route-server.conf. It declares three members, origin validation, retained inbound routes, route-server forwarding, BGP Role, and a loopback-only Looking Glass: plugin { internal rib { use bgp-rib; } internal rs { use bgp-rs; } internal adj-rib-in { use bgp-adj-rib-in; } internal rpki { use bgp-rpki; } internal role { use bgp-role; } internal transit-filter { use bgp-filter-path-asn; } } environment { looking-glass { enabled true; server main { ip 127.0.0.1; port 8443; } } } policy { reject-asn NO-TRANSIT { indirect [ 174 701 3356 ]; } match reject-asn-NO-TRANSIT { reject-asn NO-TRANSIT; } } bgp { router-id 192.0.2.254; session { asn { local 65000; } } rpki { cache-server 192.0.2.100 { port 323; trusted-network true; } action { invalid reject; not-found accept; } } group members { session { rs-client true; family { ipv4/unicast { prefix { maximum 10000; } } } } role { import rs; strict false; } attach process rpki { receive [ update-received state ]; } filter { import { filters [ reject-asn-NO-TRANSIT ]; final accept; } export { filters [ reject-asn-NO-TRANSIT ]; final accept; } } attach process adj-rib-in { receive [ update-received state ]; send [ update ]; } attach process rib { receive [ update state refresh ]; } attach process rs { receive [ update-received state open-received refresh ]; send [ update ]; } peer member-a { connection { local { ip 192.0.2.254; } remote { ip 192.0.2.1; } } session { asn { remote 65001; } } } peer member-b { connection { local { ip 192.0.2.254; } remote { ip 192.0.2.2; } } session { asn { remote 65002; } } } peer member-c { connection { local { ip 192.0.2.254; } remote { ip 192.0.2.3; } } session { asn { remote 65003; } } } } } Replace the RTR cache address, prefix maximum, and transit-AS list with the values approved for the IXP. The example permits plaintext RTR only on a trusted network; use TLS for a cache outside that boundary. Invalid routes remain visible in Adj-RIB-In but cannot be selected or exported. Validate the exact file before starting it: ze config validate route-server.conf ze start route-server.conf The route-server plugin distributes eligible routes without prepending the server's ASN. Configure ADD-PATH only after both directions and every member implementation have been tested. Session policy For every member: Set an explicit local and remote address and ASN. Enable only the required address families. Set per-family prefix limits from the member's declared policy. Configure the RFC 9234 route-server relationship. Apply import validation before a route reaches the forwarding path. Apply member export controls per destination. Preserve the original next hop. ADD-PATH is useful when members should receive multiple eligible paths and make their own best-path decision. It must be negotiated in the required direction on both ends. Treat missing ADD-PATH as an operational condition to detect, not as proof that the route server is forwarding every path. Minimum import checks An IXP policy normally rejects: prefixes outside the member's registered policy; RPKI Invalid announcements where the IXP policy drops them; default routes and over-specific prefixes; malformed or prohibited AS paths; control communities owned by the IXP when a member is not authorized to set them. The exact policy is an IXP decision. Keep policy objects named and reviewable rather than embedding unrelated actions in one chain. Verification After applying the configuration: ze cli -c "show bgp" ze cli -c "show bgp peer member-a capabilities" ze cli -c "show bgp rib status" ze cli -c "show bgp rib peer member-a" ze cli -c "show warnings" ze cli -c "show errors" Test the complete path with a test route: Announce a prefix from Member A. Confirm it is accepted from Member A. Confirm policy permits it toward Members B and C. Confirm both members receive Member A's next hop, not the route server's address. Withdraw it and confirm it disappears everywhere. Reconnect one member and confirm replay affects only that member. Member visibility Expose the read-only Looking Glass behind the deployment's normal TLS and rate-limiting boundary. Members should be able to inspect peer state, route lookup, and AS-path topology without receiving authenticated operator access. See the Looking Glass guide for the browser and Birdwatcher-compatible interfaces. Operational risks A prefix limit that is too low tears down a valid member when their route count grows. A limit that is too high weakens protection against a leak. Missing ADD-PATH can reduce the paths sent to a member. RPKI or IRR cache failure behavior must match the IXP's written policy. A slow member can create backpressure during churn. Route-server role compatibility must be checked before enabling strict enforcement. Monitor peer state, route counts, policy failures, forwarding-pool utilization, and replay duration during every maintenance window.

title: Site-to-site IPsec and WireGuard VPN
text: Site-to-site IPsec and WireGuard VPN Connect branch offices or cloud sites to a Linux router using Ze's native IKEv2 IPsec stack (programmed directly into Linux XFRM VTI interfaces) or kernel WireGuard interfaces, paired with static or dynamic routing through the tunnel interface. Role and topology Site A (Ze, 10.78.1.0/24) Site B (strongSwan or Ze, 10.78.2.0/24) 172.30.0.1 ═══ IKEv2/ESP (XFRM vpn-xfrm) ═══ 172.30.0.2 198.51.100.1 ═══ WireGuard (wg0) ═══ 198.51.100.2 Ze configuration: route-based IPsec IKEv2 Route-based IPsec binds an IKEv2 peer to an xfrm interface (if-id 42) and routes remote subnets into that interface (based on demos/terminal/topics/ipsec/ and test/interop-ipsec/scenarios/psk-site-to-site/ze.conf): interface { xfrm vpn-xfrm { if-id 42; mtu 1400; } } static { table default { route 10.78.2.0/24 { next { interface vpn-xfrm {} } } } } vpn { ipsec { interface eth0; ike-group IKE-PSK { key-exchange ikev2; lifetime 28800; proposal 1 { encryption aes256gcm; hash sha256; dh-group 14; } dead-peer-detection { interval 30; timeout 120; } } esp-group ESP-PSK { lifetime 3600; pfs enable; proposal 1 { encryption aes256gcm; } } site-to-site { peer responder { ike-group IKE-PSK; esp-group ESP-PSK; connection-type initiate; mode tunnel; local-address 172.30.0.1; remote-address 172.30.0.2; vti { bind vpn-xfrm; } traffic-selector 1 { local { prefix 10.78.1.0/24; } remote { prefix 10.78.2.0/24; } } authentication { mode pre-shared-secret; local-id "172.30.0.1"; remote-id "172.30.0.2"; pre-shared-secret "interop-test-psk"; } } } } } X.509 certificate authentication uses pki { ca ...; certificate ...; } with authentication { mode x509; ca-certificate ...; certificate ...; } (see test/interop-topology/cpe/ze-cpe.conf). Ze configuration: WireGuard site-to-site For lightweight peer-to-peer tunnels, declare a wireguard interface and point a static route at wg0 (generate keys with request wireguard keypair; based on test/reload/tx-iface-wireguard-apply.ci): interface { wireguard wg0 { listen-port 51820; fwmark 0; private-key "$9$..."; peer site2 { public-key "<base64-32-byte-pubkey>"; preshared-key "$9$..."; endpoint { ip 198.51.100.2; port 51820; } allowed-ips [ 10.0.0.2/32 192.168.10.0/24 ]; persistent-keepalive 25; } unit 0 { ipv4 { address [ 10.0.0.1/24 ]; } } } } static { table default { route 192.168.10.0/24 { next { interface wg0 {} } } } } Adjacent peer configuration (strongSwan 6.1.0) Responder configuration tested in test/interop-ipsec/scenarios/psk-site-to-site/swanctl.conf: connections { ze { local_addrs = 172.30.0.2 remote_addrs = 172.30.0.1 local { auth = psk; id = 172.30.0.2 } remote { auth = psk } proposals = aes256gcm16-sha256-modp2048 children { ze-child { local_ts = 0.0.0.0/0 remote_ts = 0.0.0.0/0 esp_proposals = aes256gcm16 mode = tunnel } } } } secrets { ike-ze { secret = "interop-test-psk" } } Verification commands show vpn ipsec status show vpn ipsec sa show vpn ipsec peer name responder show vpn ipsec dataplane sa show vpn ipsec dataplane policy show vpn ipsec dataplane drift show interface type wireguard show static show vpn ipsec dataplane drift compares the IKE engine's installed state against kernel XFRM SAs and policies and exits non-zero if they diverge. Lab evidence strongSwan 6.1.0 interop (PSK, IPv6-in-IPv4 VTI, Child rekey, MOBIKE, BGP over IPsec, EAP-TLS 1.3): IPSEC_INTEROP_SCENARIO=psk-site-to-site ./le test integration interop-ipsec and IPSEC_INTEROP_SCENARIO=vti-ipv6-inner-ipv4-outer ./le test integration interop-ipsec (test/interop-ipsec/scenarios/) Linux kernel XFRM cipher proof (AES-GCM, AES-CBC/SHA256, ChaCha20-Poly1305): ./le test qemu vpn-kernel X.509 management tunnel and WireGuard road-warrior topologies: ./le test integration interop-topology scenario mgmt-tunnel and road-warrior Functional reload and dataplane checks: test/ipsec/ipsec-sa-installed.ci, test/ipsec/ipsec-child-rekey-xfrm.ci, test/reload/tx-iface-wireguard-apply.ci Current limits Experimental status: Ze's native IPsec engine is currently marked Experimental / Pre-Alpha. Linux netlink only for XFRM: interface { xfrm } requires Linux with backend netlink. Establishing an IKE and Child SA does not install routes automatically; add a static route or run a routing protocol over the XFRM interface. MOBIKE kernel requirement: MOBIKE address migration requires Linux 7.2's XFRM_MSG_MIGRATE_STATE API (CONFIG_XFRM_MIGRATE). WireGuard constraints: endpoint.ip accepts a numeric IP address only (no DNS resolution). $9$ values in configuration files are reversible obfuscation rather than encryption. VPP WireGuard device creation is not wired, and interface-only static next-hops (next { interface wg0 {} }) do not support BFD. Related guides IPsec VPN guide Interfaces IPsec interop lab

title: Transit Edge with RPKI
text: Transit Edge with RPKI This example uses Ze at an Internet edge with two transit sessions, origin validation, explicit import policy, and local preference to select the preferred transit and its backup. RFC completion: the RPKI coverage page shows which requirements have passed the recorded test checks for this use case. Topology Transit A AS 64496 | | Ze edge AS 64500 | | Transit B AS 64497 The two sessions may carry full tables or a constrained lab table. Size prefix limits and host resources for the intended route volume. Complete edge configuration Save this two-transit example as transit-edge.conf. Transit A receives local preference 200 and Transit B receives 100, so Transit A wins when both paths are otherwise eligible. RPKI Invalid routes remain in Adj-RIB-In but cannot be selected or exported. plugin { internal rib { use bgp-rib; } internal adj-rib-in { use bgp-adj-rib-in; } internal rpki { use bgp-rpki; } internal role { use bgp-role; } internal modify { use bgp-filter-modify; } internal transit-filter { use bgp-filter-path-asn; } } policy { reject-asn NO-TRANSIT { indirect [ 174 701 3356 ]; } match reject-asn-NO-TRANSIT { reject-asn NO-TRANSIT; } modify TRANSIT-A-PREF { set { local-preference 200; } } modify TRANSIT-B-PREF { set { local-preference 100; } } } bgp { router-id 192.0.2.10; session { asn { local 64500; } } rpki { cache-server 203.0.113.53 { port 323; trusted-network true; } action { invalid reject; not-found accept; } } group transit { session { family { ipv4/unicast { prefix { maximum 1000000; } } } } role { import customer; strict false; } attach process rpki { receive [ update-received state ]; } filter { export { filters [ reject-asn-NO-TRANSIT ]; final accept; } } attach process adj-rib-in { receive [ update-received state ]; send [ update ]; } attach process rib { receive [ update state refresh ]; } peer transit-a { connection { local { ip 192.0.2.10; } remote { ip 192.0.2.1; } } session { asn { remote 64496; } } filter { import { filters [ modify:TRANSIT-A-PREF ]; final accept; } } } peer transit-b { connection { local { ip 198.51.100.10; } remote { ip 198.51.100.1; } } session { asn { remote 64497; } } filter { import { filters [ modify:TRANSIT-B-PREF ]; final accept; } } } } } Replace the documentation addresses, RTR cache, ASNs, limits, and transit-AS list. The example permits plaintext RTR on a trusted network; use TLS for a cache outside that boundary. Keep strict false until both providers advertise a compatible BGP Role, then test and enable strict enforcement deliberately. ze config validate transit-edge.conf ze start transit-edge.conf For a full table, confirm memory and convergence evidence on the performance page before treating a configuration maximum as a capacity claim. Add origin validation Configure one or more RTR cache servers and apply RPKI validation in the import chain. The deployment policy must state what happens to Valid, Invalid, and NotFound routes. A common starting policy is: accept Valid; reject Invalid; accept or mark NotFound while monitoring its proportion. The correct choice depends on the network's policy and rollback plan. See RPKI origin validation for cache configuration, validation flow, policy actions, and operator commands. Import policy RPKI is one input to policy, not a replacement for prefix and AS-path controls. A transit edge normally combines: AS loop prevention; RPKI origin validation; bogon and default-route rejection where appropriate; maximum prefix protection; local preference or another explicit primary/backup policy; community handling for operator and upstream control. Use BGP policy to keep these filters ordered and independently testable. Failure behavior After a cache disconnects, Ze retains its last complete payload set until the original RTR expiration deadline. Expiry removes that set and revalidates retained routes against the remaining cache data. Pending validations have a separate fail-open timeout. Test both transitions with the deployment's Invalid and NotFound actions; a disconnected cache alone does not make its unexpired VRPs disappear. A transit failure and an RPKI cache failure are different events. Monitor them separately so a routing incident does not hide a validation outage. Verification ze cli -c "show bgp" ze cli -c "show bgp peer transit-a capabilities" ze cli -c "show bgp rpki status" ze cli -c "show bgp rpki cache" ze cli -c "show bgp rpki summary" ze cli -c "show bgp rib best" ze cli -c "show warnings" Test at least four routes: A Valid route from the preferred transit. An Invalid route that must be rejected. A NotFound route with the deployment's chosen action. The same valid prefix from both transits, proving the expected best path and failover. Then disconnect the preferred transit. Confirm the alternate path becomes selected in the RIB. If the deployment also configures a forwarding backend, check its FIB and packet delivery separately. Restore the session and verify the intended preference returns without stale paths. What to watch RTR session state and serial updates Valid, Invalid, and NotFound route counts Prefix-limit utilization per peer and family Best-path changes and installed next hops Policy timeout or fail-open warnings Session resets during large validation updates Memory and convergence time for the actual table size Do not treat an Established BGP session as proof that validation and failover work. Exercise the route state transitions directly.

title: Zeledon.
text: Mascot Zeledon. Ze's mascot, and the voice behind the update reports. Zeledon, the Ze bird mascot Zeledon. Who is Zeledon? Zeledon is Ze's mascot, and also the name for the voice that narrates the project. The update reports in this site's changelog and the posts in Ze's Discord ze-news channel are written as Zeledon. They describe changes available in Ze, in plain language, without hype. Zeledon never says "I built this". It says "Ze can now do this", so the project speaks for itself, and whoever is behind the keyboard that week stays out of the sentence. Update reports see Zeledon's voice in the archive Discord: ze-news where updates post first How Zeledon writes. Confident and factual, never hype. Clear and factual Updates explain what changed and what that lets an operator do. Specific behavior gives network engineers something they can evaluate for themselves. Third person, always Zeledon reports on the project in the third person: "Ze can now..." or "This week's changes include...". Only what shipped Updates describe changes already included in Ze. Plans and designs are not presented as available features. No internal process language Updates explain what a change means for someone using Ze. Development and review details appear only when they help explain the resulting behavior. # from the Week of 2026-06-25 update The installer's old busybox shell initrd is gone, replaced by a single pure-Go PID-1 binary that boots the same way over PXE or off USB/ISO media. What this isn't Not: "We're thrilled to announce a game-changing new installer, the culmination of months of work!" Zeledon reports the capability, not the effort behind it.
